field-theory.assignments-survive.lay: Choosing the spacetime volume element as the complex unit could in principle disturb the series' derivation of the particle content. It does not: the content, the charges and their consistency do not depend on the unit, and the only freedom is to conjugate all the particles together. Mixed choices are inconsistent, except for the neutral right-handed neutrino.

field-theory.boost-modes.formal: On a plane's mode operators the real-rapidity rotor acts by scaling, preserves the CAR, and is not a $*$-map; uniformly over many planes it has no bounded extension to the CAR algebra. The imaginary-rapidity rotor is unitary and acts by phases. So on the modes the series' geometric boost is the imaginary-time (KMS-strip) map, and the unitary real-time flow is the rotor at imaginary rapidity.
field-theory.boost-modes.technical: On a tower plane's mode operators the real-rapidity rotor acts by scaling $v$ and $v^*$ by inverse factors: it preserves the CAR but is not a $*$-map, and uniformly over many planes it has no bounded extension to the CAR algebra. The rotor at imaginary rapidity is unitary and acts by phases. So on the modes the series' geometric boost is the imaginary-time (KMS-strip) map, and the unitary real-time flow is the rotor at imaginary rapidity.
field-theory.boost-modes.lay: In the series a boost between observers is a rotation in a plane of the algebra. Acting on the tower's quantum modes, such a boost stretches and squeezes them rather than rotating them, so it is not a quantum symmetry in the usual sense. Its imaginary-angle counterpart is one, and the two are related as real and imaginary time are in thermal field theory.

field-theory.composite-gauge-bosons-what.formal: The GA current transforms as a vector, $J(Sf, Sg) = SJ(f,g)\tilde S$, for every element $S$ of definite parity; so a nonzero vector condensate breaks Lorentz invariance, and a massless composite photon as a Goldstone mode of one (Bjorken) conflicts with the exact Lorentz invariance of the series' exterior. Massless composites charged under a covariant current of the fermions are excluded by Weinberg and Witten. Massive composite vectors and gauge bosons of an emergent gauge symmetry are not addressed. The elementary route was taken because the author chose it, not because it is forced.
field-theory.composite-gauge-bosons-what.technical: The geometric-algebra current transforms as a vector, $J(Sf, Sg) = SJ(f,g)\tilde S$ for every element $S$ of definite parity, so a nonzero vector condensate breaks Lorentz invariance, and a massless composite photon as a Goldstone mode of one (Bjorken's) conflicts with the exact Lorentz invariance of the series' exterior. Massless composites charged under a covariant current of the fermions are excluded by the Weinberg-Witten theorem. Massive composite vectors and gauge bosons of an emergent gauge symmetry are not addressed, so the elementary route is the author's choice, not forced.
field-theory.composite-gauge-bosons-what.lay: One could try to build the photon out of pairs of fermions. Two standard versions are ruled out: a photon arising from a vector condensate would break the exact relativity symmetry of the series' spacetime, and a known theorem forbids massless charged composites of this kind. Other composite routes are left open, so making the photon elementary was a choice, not a necessity.

field-theory.composite-scalars-mean-fiel.technical:
At mean-field level. The two-mode block $H = K(n_a + n_c) + \mu w_aw_c + \mu^*v_cv_a$ with $\mu \in \mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$ is self-adjoint, with $\operatorname{ad}_H^2 = K^2 + |\mu|^2$ on all four mode operators and block spectrum $\{K - E, K, K, K + E\}$, $E = \sqrt{K^2 + |\mu|^2}$; with $\mu = mB$, $B = B_N(f(k), f(-k))$ the mass pairing of Proposition \claimref{field-theory.mass} on unit-normalised plane-wave modes ($|B| = 1$), the dispersion is $E^2 = K^2 + m^2$. The tower element $H_4 = \sum_b K(n_a + n_c) - GP^*P$, $P = \sum_b w_aw_c$, is self-adjoint, conserves the axial number and has exact pair states of energy $2Kn - Gn(n_b - n + 1)$; pairs enter the ground state exactly when $G > 2K/n_b$, the threshold of the mean-field energy.

In the block ground state $\langle w_aw_c\rangle = -\mu^*/(2E)$, so the gap equation holds: the fermion mass is $G$ times the pair condensate. The axial phase is an inner unitary of the tower, $UH(\mu)U^* = H(\mu e^{-2\theta I_4})$, so the mean-field energy has an exactly flat phase direction.
field-theory.composite-scalars-mean-fiel.lay: A pair of fermion modes in the tower can bind into a scalar condensate that gives the fermions mass, the mechanism of Nambu and Jona-Lasinio. At mean-field level these exact computations reproduce its ingredients: the massive energy relation, the coupling above which pairs condense, the gap equation, and a direction in which the condensate's phase can turn at no cost.

field-theory.conserved-numbers-mass-bloc.formal: On the mass block of Proposition \claimref{field-theory.composite-scalars-mean-field-level}(1) the quasi-particle annihilators $\gamma_a = \alpha w_a + \beta v_c$, $\gamma_c = \alpha'w_c + \beta'v_a$ satisfy $[H, \gamma] = -E\gamma$, and $H = E(N_a + N_c) + (K - E)$ exactly, with $N = \gamma^*\gamma/\{\gamma, \gamma^*\}$. A single rung number does not commute with $H$ when $\mu \neq 0$, and the massive vacuum has $\langle n_a\rangle = (E - K)/(2E)$. The charge $Q = n_a - n_c$ lies in the rung algebra, commutes with $H$, equals $N_a - N_c$ and vanishes on the massive vacuum; one massive quantum is the rung state $v_aP_0$ itself.

__notes__.note.field-theory.setting-gravitys-sourc: The series registers that gravity entangles two masses, each held in a superposition of two places, by the standard phase $\Phi = (Gm_Am_B/\hbar)\int(1/r_{11} + 1/r_{22} - 1/r_{12} - 1/r_{21})\,dt$, under the element reading, in which the geometry's coefficients lie in a commuting algebra of the matter's number operators. The masses are the field theory's fermions; gravity is not quantised here.
__notes__.note.field-theory.what-does-registration: Nothing. The registered phase and its wording stand: ``the commuting algebra of the rungs' number operators'' is right when read as the conserved ones, which the block charge supplies inside the rung algebra. A first version of the run proposed changing the wording to quasi-particle numbers; review showed the charge serves equally, and the proposal was withdrawn.
__notes__.note.field-theory.setting-open: (1) Pair creation, antiparticle modes and Compton scattering in the coupled system. (2) Gauge invariance beyond current conservation, and Lorentz covariance of the Coulomb-gauge construction beyond tree level. (3) Loops and renormalisation. (4) Non-abelian gauge fields, which bring the axial anomaly into play. (5) The composite scalar beyond mean field: the Goldstone pole, a covariant regularisation, the sigma mode, and whether the contact term of Proposition \claimref{field-theory.contact-interactions-tower} has an attractive scalar channel. (6) The map from the palatial ladder module's conformal-energy basis to the plane-wave Fock space, which would turn the analogy of Proposition \claimref{field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes}(1) into a construction. (7) The terminology conflict recorded in the first run: T03 calls the tower second quantisation and T09 calls the palatial storey second quantisation; on the attachment found here the palatial storey supplies the one-particle space and the tower's CAR over it is second quantisation, which is T03's usage. (8) Whether the Higgs is composite, which the tower supports at mean-field level, or elementary: a modelling decision. (9) The relative sign of the twistor's complex unit and the field's, which now carries T12's orientation, and a check of the conventions of T12's Fact on twistor charge and helicity against T09 and T07. (10) For the gravity prediction: retardation and the radiative sector, non-rigid bodies, and the shared spinor factor of two masses in one tower.
__notes__.note.field-theory.setting-what-series-ow: Three things. (i) Where the field theory's one-particle structure comes from: the palatial storey, not the tower (Proposition \claimref{field-theory.twistor-attachment}); the tower supplies the CAR and nothing about spacetime (Proposition \claimref{field-theory.ground-does-not-attach-modes}). (ii) Why the canonical commutation relations must be adjoined: the tower's own bosons are $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ quasi-spins (Proposition \claimref{field-theory.how-close-tower-comes-ccr}), the field-theory form of T09's statistics no-go. (iii) What one complex unit fixes: with the unit $I_4$, positive frequency is positive helicity for every massless field, so the opposite helicities and chiralities enter conjugated in one stroke (Propositions \claimref{field-theory.second-quantisation}(4), \claimref{field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes}(3)). The dictionary of Proposition \claimref{field-theory.boost-modes}, the boost on the modes as the KMS-strip map, is transport-convenient: its mathematics is that of any hyperbolic plane, its use the series'.
__notes__.note.field-theory.abstract: The tower of the series has the canonical anticommutation relations as its limit; this note asks whether that limit reaches a quantum field theory. It does, in one way. The palatial storey supplies a positive-energy one-particle space, the Penrose transform supplies the mode functions, and the tower's anticommutation relations are the second quantisation over that space. In real geometric algebra the construction needs one operator imaginary unit, and the pseudoscalar $I_4$ serves: it is Lorentz-invariant, and with it positive frequency is positive helicity for every massless field. A massive fermion is then two right-handed fields joined by the epsilon pairing; tower contact interactions give the textbook scattering laws; a tower pairing interaction condenses into a fermion mass; gauge bosons are adjoined as a bosonic Fock space; and the coupled system gives one-photon exchange exactly, for distinguishable and identical fermions. Pointed at the series' gravity prediction, the field theory is consistent with its matter premises and leaves the registered phase unchanged. Pointed at the Standard-Model paper, the assignments survive, and the paper's undetermined orientation is relocated into the relative sign of the twistor's complex unit and the field's. Almost every result is standard physics in the series' algebra; the series' own content is where the one-particle structure comes from, why the commutation relations must be adjoined, and what one complex unit fixes. Exact-arithmetic checks accompany every claim.
__notes__.note.field-theory.setting-introduction:
The relation of T16, $\{e_a, e_b\} = 2g_{ab}$, has two readings: a metric one in an orthogonal basis and the canonical anticommutation relations (CAR) in a Witt basis. The tower of T03 iterates the ascent and has the CAR algebra as its limit. That limit is many-fermion quantum mechanics. Whether it reaches a quantum field theory, with fields on spacetime that are local, covariant and of positive energy, is a different question, and the claim that general relativity and quantum theory are two faces of one object covers field theory only if the answer is yes.

This note collects the answer, built in eight exact-arithmetic runs on 15 and 16 October 2026, each with a preregistration, an independent adversarial review and its corrections. The answer is yes, in one way. The note is a consolidation: each result is stated at its level and cited to the run and check that establish it, and the runs' findings files carry the detail.

The plan. the section “Setting and imports” fixes the setting and the imports. the section “Attaching the modes to spacetime” attaches the modes to spacetime. the section “The imaginary units in real geometric algebra” identifies the imaginary units in real geometric algebra. the section “Second quantisation in one algebra” second-quantises multivector-valued fields in one algebra with the unit $I_4$. the section “Mass and contact interactions” treats mass and contact interactions, the section “Bosons” the bosons, and the section “The photon's Fock space and the coupled system” the photon's Fock space and the coupled system. the section “Gravity's source: the registered prediction” and the section “The Standard-Model paper's chirality” point the result at two of the series' own claims: the registered gravity prediction and the Standard-Model paper's chirality. the section “The ledger” states what is the series' own, what is imported, and what is open.
__notes__.note.field-theory.setting-prior-art: Second quantisation, Coulomb-gauge quantum electrodynamics and old-fashioned perturbation theory are textbook (Sakurai; Weinberg, \emph{The Quantum Theory of Fields}, vol.~I). The spacetime algebra, its plane waves, its chirality and its photon polarisations are Hestenes' and Doran and Lasenby's; the geometric-algebra treatment of twistors with the conformal pseudoscalar as imaginary unit is Arcaute, Lasenby and Doran's. Two-component spinor technique is Dreiner, Haber and Martin's. The Nambu-Jona-Lasinio mechanism, Weinberg and Witten's theorem, Bjorken's composite photon and Anderson's quasi-spin are standard and credited where used. What the note claims for the series is the placement of these structures in the series' own algebra and storeys, and the consequences of using a single complex unit for all of them.
__notes__.note.field-theory.setting-setting-import: The ground is $\Cl(1,3)$ with signature $(+,-,-,-)$ and pseudoscalar $I_4 = \gamma_0\gamma_1\gamma_2\gamma_3$, $I_4^2 = -1$. Tower planes $(e_j, f_j)$ with $e_j^2 = 1$, $f_j^2 = -1$ are adjoined after the ground; $v_j = (e_j + f_j)/2$ creates and $w_j = (e_j - f_j)/2$ annihilates. T03's adjoint $*$ is the antiautomorphism with $x^* = x$ on generators of square $+1$ and $x^* = -x$ on generators of square $-1$; so $I_4^* = -I_4$ and $w_j^* = v_j$. Hestenes' unit $\IS = \gamma_2\gamma_1$ acts on the right. The chirality projectors on even elements are $\chi_\pm(\phi) = (\phi \mp I_4\phi\IS)/2$, so that $I_4\phi = \phi\IS$ on $\chi_+$.
__notes__.note.field-theory.choice-unit: The author adopted the unit $I_4$ for the series' field theory on 16 October 2026. The reasons are Lorentz invariance and centrality; the cost is that every field is read in one chirality. Proposition \claimref{field-theory.mass} shows the cost is the standard two-component one.
__notes__.note.field-theory.what-does-t12: T12's orientation bit, which the dark-matter paper shows the descent cannot derive, is not removed by the unit $I_4$; it moves into the relative sign of the conformal spinors' unit ($\pm I_6$, the twistor's unit) and the field's. If the series fixes that sign, and if the label copy's parity is identified with the conformal spinors' (the twistor's; the theorem T12 calls the same missing theorem as Hypothesis (S)), the orientation is fixed, through T12's Fact on the charge and helicity read on the conformal spinor space (twistor charge and helicity), whose conventions were not checked here. Its physical content would be at most the sign of CP violation.
__notes__.note.field-theory.setting-what-standard: Everything else: two-component mass, Fermi contact scattering, the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio condensate, Coulomb-gauge exchange and the quasi-spin are textbook results reproduced in the series' algebra. None of the runs produced a transport-essential result. The gravity run left the registered prediction unchanged and found its matter premises consistent with the field theory; the Standard-Model run found T12's assignments independent of the unit and relocated, but did not remove, its orientation bit.
__notes__.note.field-theory.setting-decisions-take: The author chose the unit $I_4$ (16 October), composite bosons first and elementary bosons on their failure, then the elementary photon, and then to point the field theory at the gravity prediction and at T12.

__notes__.note.synthesis.grading-of-the-bit-ladder:
The ladder has four chosen primitives, each a postulate of the foundation, and every other step except the last (argued) is a theorem. The grades are those of the source: \emph{chosen} (assumed), \emph{proved} (a theorem in the store or filed with this note), \emph{argued} (an inference from evidence, not a proof).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[0.] \emph{The bit (chosen: premise (F1)).} One distinction, states $0$ and $1$, combined by comparison, $1 + 1 = 0$: the group $\Z_{2}$, and with the product $1 \cdot 1 = 1$ the field $\mathbb{F}_{2}$. It has no sign: $1 = -1$.
\item[1.] \emph{Independence (chosen, part of (F1); counting proved).} $n$ independent distinctions give the configurations $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ under symmetric difference, $2^{n}$ of them, $\binom{n}{k}$ of grade $k$: the index sets of the blades, with no order and no sign.
\item[2.] \emph{Minimal non-commutativity (chosen: premise (F2)).} A group $G$ generated by the directions and one bit $c \ne 1$, a central extension of $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ by that bit, with $e_{i}e_{j} = c\,e_{j}e_{i}$ for $i \ne j$. Proved from it: $c^{2} = 1$ (for $n \ge 2$), every square and commutator lies in $\{1, c\}$, the squares form a quadratic form $q$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ whose polar form is the commutator, the centre, and for even $n$ an extraspecial group; $q$ fixes the type of the algebra (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form}; the group statements in the integer-algebra result filed alongside). The sign $-1$, the signature and a plane of square $-1$ appear here, before any addition.
\item[3.] \emph{Superposition over the integers (chosen: premise (F3)).} The algebra is $\Z[G]/(c + 1)$. Proved: it is free of rank $2^{n}$ with basis the blades, $v^{2} = Q(v)$ for integer vectors (the contraction rule as a theorem), and it has the universal property of the Clifford algebra of the $\pm 1$ form over every commutative ring: $\Cl_{\Z}(p,q)$. Over $\Z$ the orthogonal presentation $\Z[G]/(c + 1)$ and the null (Witt) presentation generate different orders, and only the latter contains matrix units (the note on the two presentations over the integers, on \claimref{std-algebra.cl11-matrix}); the Witt pairs need $\tfrac12$, so the qubit reading, $\Cl(k,k) \cong \Mat_{2^{k}}$ (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.fock-representation}, stated over $\R$), sits at step 4 for the orthogonal presentation.
\item[4.] \emph{Division (proved, no new primitive).} Inverting the vectors that are not null, $v^{-1} = v/Q(v)$ (Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.inverse-of-vector}), forces the coefficients from $\Z$ to $\Q$ and to nothing smaller; null vectors and zero divisors survive except in $\Cl_{\Q}(0,0)$, $\Cl_{\Q}(0,1)$, $\Cl_{\Q}(0,2)$ (the rational counterpart of Theorem \claimref{transport.exceptional-division-algebras}).
\item[5.] \emph{Completion (chosen: premise (F4)).} The coefficients are extended to a complete ordered field. Proved: such a field is Euclidean, every real quadratic space has an anticommuting basis of squares $1, -1, 0$ with invariant counts (Sylvester's law, derived in geometric algebra, \claimref{synthesis.completion-recovers-the-real-clifford-algebras}(iii), which replaced the imported Fact), and every real Clifford algebra of the store is a rational one of a $\pm 1$ form extended by scalars, or a subalgebra of one. The signs need only a Euclidean field; over $\Q$ square classes remain. Completeness proper is used by limits (the exponential of a bivector and $\pi$; the nilpotent exponential of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.nilpotent-steps-derivative-exponential-and-boost} is a finite sum and needs none) and by roots of odd-degree polynomials (for which a real closed field suffices).
\item[6.] \emph{The number systems inside (proved, after (F4)).} $\R$, $\Cl(0,1) \cong \C$, $\Cl(0,2) \cong \HH$ are the only finite-dimensional associative real division algebras (Frobenius, derived in geometric algebra); split-complex and dual numbers and the matrix algebras sit inside, with the classification by $p - q \bmod 8$ (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.periodicity}); every finite-dimensional associative real algebra embeds in a corner of some $\Cl(k,k)$.
\item[7.] \emph{Bosons (proved in the store, conditional where stated).} Collective pair modes of the infinite tower obey canonical commutation relations in the limit (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.central-limit-of-tower-fluctuation-states-with-the-kernel-unit}); they need step 5 and a state on the tower, and are not a further primitive.
\item[8.] \emph{The algebra of physics (argued).} That nature uses exactly this structure is the argued reading of the companion note, not a theorem.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Where the stored algebra sits.} The store's standard algebra is stated over $\R$ and so sits at step 5; much of its content is already algebraic and holds over $\Q$ or $\Z$ (the blade products, inverses of vectors, the matrix units of $\Cl(1,1)$ over $\Z$), but its statements do not yet say so, and no stored entity assumes the four premises.
__notes__.note.synthesis.scope-of-the-quantum-fiel:
The quantum field theory of the series is perturbative and lives on a classical gravitational field. This note concerns the matter and gauge sector only; the gravitational gauge fields are classical throughout (conventions, section ``Gravity and the graviton''). What is stored: free Dirac and photon fields with the unit $I_{4}$ (\claimref{field-theory.second-quantisation}, \claimref{field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes}); tree-level exchange (\claimref{field-theory.coupled-system-tree-level}); one-loop electrodynamics with regulator fields under the Krein-form premise (\claimref{synthesis.one-loop-qed-in-the-spacetime-algebra}, \claimref{synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-inner-product-for-gauge-fields}); the one-loop vacuum polarisation by extension of distributions with no regulator (\claimref{synthesis.one-loop-vacuum-polarisation-extends-without-a-regulator-and-ward-preserving-extensions-differ-only-by-the-renormalisation-constants}), and on the Euclidean section a pair of extensions of the one-loop self-energy and vertex obeying the Ward-Takahashi identity (\claimref{synthesis.one-loop-self-energy-and-vertex-extend-with-the-ward-identity-holding-at-a-common-cut-off-length}); the two-loop vacuum polarisation in dimensional regularisation (\claimref{synthesis.two-loop-qed-in-the-spacetime-algebra-continued-in-dimension-gives-the-second-beta-coefficient}); one S-matrix element (\claimref{synthesis.electron-positron-to-muon-pairs-in-the-spacetime-algebra-lsz-tree-cross-section-and-one-loop-unitarity}); the chiral anomaly and its cancellation per generation (\claimref{synthesis.triangle-anomaly-in-the-spacetime-algebra-is-the-pseudoscalar-part-of-the-field-square-and-cancels-per-generation}); and the imported framework of causal perturbation theory with local covariance on gravitational fields (\claimref{synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extension-theorem-and-ward-preserving-time-ordered-products}, \claimref{synthesis.imported-local-covariance-with-scaling-of-time-ordered-products}). Each is a coefficient of a formal power series in the couplings, with its scheme stated on it.

Nothing stored defines an interacting theory beyond that series. The series claims neither that a continuum interacting theory of its matter and gauge sector exists, nor that the physical theory is a cut-off theory in which covariance is emergent. The question should not be reopened without one of the following, none of which the store holds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] \emph{A limit of a regulated theory.} The floors of the tower keep the charge and no boost (\claimref{synthesis.floor-regulator-keeps-the-charge-and-the-central-term-below-the-cut-off}). That excludes them as a covariant regulator. It does not exclude them as a cut-off whose limit is shown to be covariant. The limit and the proof of its covariance are missing.
\item[(2)] \emph{A continuum limit of the rotor lattice.} The store defines the weak factor on a lattice of rotors without gauge fixing and computes its strong-coupling expansion (\claimref{synthesis.weak-factor-rotor-lattice-strong-coupling-area-law}, \claimref{synthesis.non-abelian-gauge-fixing-has-gribov-copies-and-the-weak-rotor-lattice-with-doublets-has-a-perimeter-law}, \claimref{synthesis.a-finite-subgroup-of-colour-shares-its-strong-coupling-expansion-through-link-degree-three}). Missing: the weak-coupling limit; dynamical fermions with the series' chiral content (the stored lattice results have a frozen doublet only); the abelian factor and the scalar quartics, of which the store shows the quartics reaching strong coupling within a few TeV on one branch (\claimref{synthesis.rung-field-quartics-run-to-strong-coupling-within-a-few-tev-on-the-transmutation-branch}); the recovery of Lorentz and displacement-gauge covariance in the limit; and reflection positivity stated in the series' algebra.
\item[(3)] \emph{A positive state space beyond perturbation theory.} The Krein-form premise and the stored BRST construction are perturbative; only the gauge-invariant lattice avoids them, and it is at finite spacing.
\item[(4)] \emph{Control of the infrared.} Charged states, the adiabatic limit of causal perturbation theory, the on-shell normalisation of the electron field, and confinement in the continuum, which does not follow from the stored strong-coupling area law.
\item[(5)] \emph{Elementary or composite gauge bosons.} The tower gives anticommutation relations only (\claimref{field-theory.no-canonical-commutation-relations-tower}), and the photon is attached as an elementary Fock field; a theory built on the tower has to say which the gauge bosons are.
\end{enumerate}
Under these limits the stored loop results are to be read as the perturbative content of whatever theory exists. \emph{Prior art, as far as checked.} Interacting theories obeying the standard axioms have been constructed in two and three spacetime dimensions (the polynomial scalar theories in two, the quartic scalar theory in three), and the four-dimensional problem is unresolved (A. Jaffe, Constructive Quantum Field Theory, survey). The scaling limit of the lattice-regulated quartic scalar field in four dimensions is Gaussian (Aizenman and Duminil-Copin, arXiv:1912.07973). Both were checked on the web on 10 November 2026 at the level stated in the note of this entity; no other literature is relied on here.
__notes__.note.synthesis.n-plus-orientation-datum: Premise (N$_{+}$) (\claimref{synthesis.n-plus-null-ground-state}) assumes the orientation of the field's unit $I_{4}$ relative to the time orientation, which decides between the null vacuum and the filled positive-energy sea. Three facts now locate that datum. First, with the unit $I_{4}$ every massless mode's helicity is locked to its frequency sign, every map commuting with the Lorentz rotors is $I_{4}$-linear, and among the discrete maps of the massless field the frequency sign flips exactly under reversal of spatial orientation; Hestenes' charge conjugation flips the chirality of massless even spinors and not the frequency sign, and a CP map flips the frequency sign and not the chirality (\claimref{synthesis.massless-frequency-sign-relative-to-i4-is-not-the-chirality}). So the datum is odd under P and under CP, it is not that chirality, and no CP-invariant interaction fixes it. Second, on the Witt flags of $\R^{2,4}$ adapted to the conformal energy, the energy sign of a flag's vacuum and the stored flag bit flip together on each pair of conjugate flags (\claimref{synthesis.z-adapted-witt-flags-energy-sign-follows-the-flag-bit}), so read as the energy sign of the flag's vacuum the datum is the descent's flag bit (\claimref{dark-matter.premise-flag-as-datum}) up to the descent's kinematic sign on the four-space orthogonal to $Z$. Third, on every field the Hadamard deposit premise reaches, the datum is carried by that premise, through results that rest on no postulate (\claimref{synthesis.hadamard-scaling-limit-premise}). What is not shown is that the generators' modes inherit the descent's flag; on the eternal hole and eternal de Sitter, which no descent reaches, the datum stays assumed.

field-theory.elementary-photon-ga.technical:
With the unit $I_4$ and complex coefficients on the left, the polarisation $\epsilon_h = t_1 - hI_4t_2$ satisfies $B_q\cdot\epsilon_h = hI_4\epsilon_h$ for the rotation bivector $B_q$ about $q$, on and off the coordinate axes; the geometric product of complex vectors is sesquilinear, $\proj(J\epsilon) = J\cdot\bar\epsilon$, because $I_4$ anticommutes with vectors; and the helicity sum $\tfrac12\sum_h\proj(J_A\epsilon_h)\proj(J_B\epsilon_{-h})$ is the transverse product $J_A^\perp\cdot J_B^\perp$.

Coulomb-gauge exchange, two time orderings and the instantaneous Coulomb term, equals the covariant $-e^2J_A\cdot J_B/t$, given current conservation, and massive vector exchange reduces to the contact term with $G = e^2/M^2$.

field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes.technical:
On polynomials with $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$ coefficients, $a_m = \partial/\partial z_m$ and $a_m^* = z_m$ satisfy the CCR exactly, and $a_m^*$ is the adjoint of $a_m$ for $\ip{z^n}{z^{n'}} = n!\,\delta$: the polynomial representation of the palatial algebra, with variables indexed by photon modes, the relation to the palatial algebra itself being an analogy, not a construction. For null $k$ the bivectors $f$ with $kf = 0$ form a real two-dimensional $I_4$-stable space, one $I_4$-complex mode per momentum.

The positive-frequency mode $f\exp(-I_4k\cdot x)$ has helicity $+1$, and every massless even spinor of either chirality has the left-$I_4$ rotation phase of helicity $+\tfrac12$; so with the unit $I_4$ positive frequency is positive helicity for every massless even field, and the field operator is the Riemann-Silberstein form $F = \sum N\,2X\,[\exp(-I_4k\cdot x)\,a_+ + \exp(+I_4k\cdot x)\,a_-^*]$, which annihilates helicity $+1$ and creates helicity $-1$.
field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes.lay: The photon's quantum states are built on polynomials, the standard representation of boson operators, with the spacetime volume element as imaginary unit. Each photon momentum then carries one complex mode, and with this choice of unit positive frequency coincides with positive helicity for every massless field, so the field operator destroys one helicity and creates the other.

field-theory.ground-does-not-attach-mode.formal: Over the conformal ground every even ground element commutes with every mode operator of every higher plane. In particular the conformal bivectors, the chart translations and the Lorentz rotors act trivially on the modes, so a field $\psi(x) = \sum_j u_j(x)a_j$ on which the ground's translations act covariantly has constant mode functions. The obstruction is finite-dimensionality: a noncompact group has no nontrivial unitary representation on a finite floor.

field-theory.how-close-tower-comes-ccr.formal: For $n$ tower pairs, $B = \sum_jw_{c_j}w_{d_j}$ gives $[B, B^*] = n - (N_c + N_d)$; with $K_3 = (N_c + N_d - n)/2$ the triple $(B^*, B, K_3)$ is an $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ quasi-spin, the ladder has $n + 1$ states, and $[b, b^*] = 1 - 2k/n$ on $k$-pair states for $b = B/\sqrt{n}$. The CCR is the Inonu-Wigner contraction $n \to \infty$; the operator limit holds only on states of bounded boson number.

field-theory.imported-standard-field-the.formal:
The Jost-point form of the spin-statistics theorem (Streater and Wightman, ch.~4), whose complex Lorentz path reads in geometric algebra as the rotation of one chirality through $2\pi$, $(1-\Pi) + \Pi\exp(\theta\gamma_1\gamma_2)$ with $\Pi = (1 - E)/2$, ending at conjugation by $E$, the total inversion $x \mapsto -x$ on the conformal model; the Penrose transform, whose kernels the spacetime algebra writes as $x\psi_0\gamma_0/Q(x)^2$ (spin $\tfrac12$), $xBx/Q(x)^3$ (Maxwell) and $1/Q(x)$ (scalar), and its $H^1$ isomorphism with cohomology on regions of the projective spinor space $\PCS$ (projective twistor space); the Weinberg-Witten theorem (massless particles of spin greater than one half carry no charge under a conserved Lorentz-covariant current); the random-phase Goldstone pole of the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model; the Coulomb-gauge Hamiltonian of quantum electrodynamics; the Adler-Bell-Jackiw anomaly.

\emph{Note (spin and statistics, 2026-11-01).} For the attached free fields (scalar, spinor, photon) the statistics follow from locality with a positive norm, given the massless two-point function (\claimref{synthesis.locality-of-the-attached-free-fields-fixes-their-statistics}); the Jost-point form imported here is kept for interacting fields. The KMS condition at rapidity period $2\pi$ of the thermal premises (\claimref{synthesis.n-plus-null-ground-state}, and (R$_{\mathrm{loc}}$) of \claimref{synthesis.c-loc-local-horizon-premise}) holds for CAR and CCR modes alike and does not fix statistics (\claimref{synthesis.modular-period-on-values-is-the-dual-plane-turn}); modular covariance of the wedge algebras, which would fix them through an imported theorem, is not a premise of the store.

\emph{Note (the Jost import, 2 November 2026).} The Jost-point form is needed only beyond perturbation theory: in causal perturbation theory the interacting fields keep the spin-statistics connection of the free fields to every order, on every field with an even number of ghost factors (\claimref{synthesis.interacting-fields-of-causal-perturbation-theory-keep-the-spin-statistics-connection-at-even-ghost-number}). Beyond perturbation theory a premise remains. Kuckert's modular P$_{1}$CT symmetry (the modular conjugation of each wedge algebra acts on the local algebras as the wedge's reflection), with covariance under the covering group, the spectrum condition and compact internal symmetries, is a weaker alternative premise from which the connection follows (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-kuckert-modular-pct-spin-statistics-and-borchers-theorem}; its spacetime-algebra form, \claimref{synthesis.wedge-reflections-compose-to-the-two-pi-rotor-so-geometric-modular-conjugations-give-interacting-spin-statistics}); it is recorded here as a note only, not adopted, and nothing in the store supplies it. The imports listed above are unchanged.
field-theory.imported-standard-field-the.technical:
Six standard results that the field-theory note imports: the Jost-point form of the spin-statistics theorem; the Penrose transform and its $H^1$ isomorphism; the Weinberg-Witten theorem, that massless particles of spin greater than one half carry no charge under a conserved Lorentz-covariant current; the random-phase Goldstone pole of the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model; the Coulomb-gauge Hamiltonian of quantum electrodynamics; and the Adler-Bell-Jackiw anomaly. (Note, 7 November 2026: the Adler-Bell-Jackiw anomaly is imported with its sources and its equation in Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-adler-bell-jackiw-axial-anomaly}, which is its home in the store; it is named here as the note names it.) (Note, 2026-11-01: for the attached free fields the spin-statistics connection follows from locality with a positive norm, \claimref{synthesis.locality-of-the-attached-free-fields-fixes-their-statistics}; the Jost-point import is kept for interacting fields, and the thermal period alone does not fix statistics, \claimref{synthesis.modular-period-on-values-is-the-dual-plane-turn}.) (Note, 2 November 2026: the Jost-point import is needed only beyond perturbation theory, since causal perturbation theory carries the free fields' spin-statistics connection to interacting fields order by order, \claimref{synthesis.interacting-fields-of-causal-perturbation-theory-keep-the-spin-statistics-connection-at-even-ghost-number}; Kuckert's modular P$_{1}$CT symmetry with the spectrum condition would be a weaker premise there, noted and not adopted, \claimref{synthesis.wedge-reflections-compose-to-the-two-pi-rotor-so-geometric-modular-conjugations-give-interacting-spin-statistics}.)

In geometric algebra Jost's complex Lorentz path is the rotation of one chirality through $2\pi$, ending at conjugation by the ascent bivector $E$, and the Penrose transform's kernels are $x\psi_0\gamma_0/Q(x)^2$ for spin $\tfrac12$, $xBx/Q(x)^3$ for Maxwell and $1/Q(x)$ for the scalar, with the cohomology taken on regions of the projective spinor space $\PCS$.

field-theory.imported-statistics-no-go-p.formal: The palatial algebra $[Z^\alpha, \bar Z_\beta] = \hbar\,\delta^\alpha_\beta$ has no nonzero finite-dimensional representation and no embedding into any finite-dimensional algebra. It is realised on polynomials by $\bar Z_\beta = -\hbar\,\partial/\partial Z^\beta$. \emph{Provenance:} T09, Prop.~prop:statistics and Lemma lem:weyl. For the bounded CAR algebra the corresponding statement is the Wielandt-Wintner theorem: no bounded operators satisfy $[a, a^*] = 1$.
field-theory.imported-statistics-no-go-p.technical: The palatial algebra $[Z^\alpha, \bar Z_\beta] = \hbar\,\delta^\alpha_\beta$ has no nonzero finite-dimensional representation and no embedding into any finite-dimensional algebra, and it is realised on polynomials by $\bar Z_\beta = -\hbar\,\partial/\partial Z^\beta$. For the bounded CAR algebra the corresponding statement is the Wielandt-Wintner theorem: no bounded operators satisfy $[a, a^*] = 1$.
field-theory.imported-statistics-no-go-p.lay: The canonical commutation relations of bosons cannot be realised by finite matrices, nor inside any finite-dimensional algebra such as a floor of the tower; they need infinitely many states, as in the standard representation on polynomials. Even in the infinite tower they cannot be realised by bounded operators.

field-theory.mass.formal: For the four even right factors $N \in \{\gamma_0\gamma_1, \gamma_0\gamma_2, \gamma_1\gamma_3, \gamma_2\gamma_3\}$ that anticommute with $\IS$, $B_N(\psi, \phi) = \proj(\tilde\psi\phi N)$ is a nonzero, antisymmetric, nondegenerate, Lorentz-invariant, $I_4$-bilinear pairing on $\chi_+$ (in two-component form, a labelled reading, the epsilon pairing $\lambda^{\mathsf T}\epsilon\lambda$), of charge two under the common phase. A massive Dirac plane wave splits as $\chi + \psi_-$ with $\eta = \psi_-N \in \chi_+$; $\chi$ and $\eta$ have opposite $I_4$-charges, the Dirac equation is the coupled pair, and the mass density is $2B(\chi, \eta)$. The common $I_4$ phase is axial and the mass breaks it. Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-one-datum-massive-law} stands: $I_4$ is the field algebra's unit, not the massive law's complex structure.
field-theory.mass.technical:

So the common $I_4$ phase is axial and the mass breaks it, and the one-datum fact stands: $I_4$ is the field algebra's unit, not the massive law's complex structure.

field-theory.operator-newtonian-coupling.formal: With $H_N = -G\sum_{i<j}M_iM_jN_iN_j/r_{ij}$ built from commuting conserved numbers (rung numbers of massless modes, quasi-particle numbers or block charges of massive ones), the branch states are eigenstates and the relative phase $\arg(c_{11}c_{22}/(c_{12}c_{21}))$ under $\exp(-I_4Ht)$ is $+\Phi$, the registered phase with its sign. The operator source gives no interaction between a body's own branches, unlike the mean-field (Schr\"odinger-Newton) source, which entangles nothing. For rigid composite bodies the phase is that of the total mass plus a correction of relative order $(a/R)^2$.

field-theory.orientation-relocated.technical:
Left multiplication by $e_+$ maps the even half $T$ of the conformal spinor module onto the odd half $T'$, commutes with $I_4$ and the Lorentz rotors and swaps the $E$-doublets, so the unit $I_4$ and Lorentz symmetry alone cannot tell the halves apart. The unit commuting with Clifford multiplication is right multiplication by $I_6$, $J$; with it the halves are inequivalent, and on the momentum doublet $\ker n_0$, the $E = +1$ doublet of both halves, $J = +I_4$ in $T$ and $J = -I_4$ in $T'$.

Since the commutant fixes $J$ only up to sign, with the field's unit $I_4$ the question of which half's momentum spinors are complex-linear is the relative sign of $J$ and $I_4$.
field-theory.orientation-relocated.lay: The Standard-Model paper's matter keeps one binary choice, an orientation that tells particles from antiparticles. Fixing the field's imaginary unit does not remove it: the two halves of the conformal spinor space look the same to that unit and to relativity. The choice reappears as the relative sign between the field's unit and the conformal spinors' own unit.

field-theory.second-quantisation.formal:
With Definition \claimref{obj.field-theory.single-algebra-field}:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\Lambda(k) = k\gamma_0/(2k_0)$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\ker k$.
\item The field's anticommutator has no tower part and equals $\ip{\phi_1}{\sum_j 2\alpha_j\cos(k_j\cdot\xi)\Lambda(k_j)\chi\,\phi_2}$; in the continuum it is $\chi(\nabla D)\gamma_0$ with $D$ the Pauli-Jordan function, so the field is local.
\item The span$\{1, I_4\}$ part of $\Psi^*M\Psi$ is the second-quantised $d\Gamma(M)$ on particle modes; antiparticle terms need normal ordering.
\item With the unit $I_4$ a field carrying both chiralities gives the right-handed part complex-linearly and the left-handed part conjugated. With Hestenes' $i = \IS$ the same field quantises as a whole Dirac field, at the cost of a frame-dependent unit. The split is forced by the choice of the unit $I_4$, not by the algebra.
\end{enumerate}
field-theory.second-quantisation.technical:
With the single-algebra field, $\Lambda(k) = k\gamma_0/(2k_0)$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\ker k$, and the field's anticommutator has no tower part and equals $\ip{\phi_1}{\sum_j 2\alpha_j\cos(k_j\cdot\xi)\Lambda(k_j)\chi\,\phi_2}$; in the continuum it is $\chi(\nabla D)\gamma_0$ with $D$ the Pauli-Jordan function, so the field is local. The $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$ part of $\Psi^*M\Psi$ is the second-quantised $d\Gamma(M)$ on particle modes, with antiparticle terms needing normal ordering.

With the unit $I_4$ a field carrying both chiralities gives the right-handed part complex-linearly and the left-handed part conjugated; with Hestenes' $i = \IS$ the same field quantises as a whole Dirac field, at the cost of a frame-dependent unit. The split is forced by the choice of the unit $I_4$, not by the algebra.
field-theory.second-quantisation.lay: Fields whose values are elements of the spacetime algebra and whose modes are tower planes can be quantised inside one algebra, with the volume element as imaginary unit. The resulting field is local, and its observables are the standard second-quantised ones. The price of this unit is that a field's two chiralities enter differently, one directly and one conjugated; Hestenes' unit avoids that at the cost of choosing a frame.

field-theory.twistor-attachment.formal:
The attachment available to the series is the one through the conformal spinor space $\CS$ (the twistor attachment): the palatial storey supplies a positive-energy one-particle space with a conformal-group action, the Penrose transform supplies the mode functions, and the tower's CAR is the second quantisation over that space. In the oscillator model the helicity-$s$ module has energies $|s| + 1 + n$ with multiplicity $(n+1)(n + 2|s| + 1)$; the conformal energy is the palatial quadratic of the reversion form $h$ on $\CS$ (the twistor form); the sixteen generators of $\mathfrak{u}(2,2)$, the algebra preserving $h$, preserve each positive-energy, fixed-helicity module. On this attachment the tower's floors are energy cut-offs, not regions of spacetime. Spin-statistics constrains it: a CAR lift is local exactly when $2s$ is odd, and the series' fermion assignments pass.

\emph{Note (spin and statistics, 2026-11-01).} For the attached free fields (scalar, spinor, photon) the clause on CAR lifts follows from locality with a positive norm, given the massless two-point function (\claimref{synthesis.locality-of-the-attached-free-fields-fixes-their-statistics}); the Jost-point form of Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-standard-field-theory} is kept for interacting fields. The positive norm is needed: with an indefinite (Krein) form a CAR scalar is local, the case of the Faddeev-Popov ghosts. The KMS condition at rapidity period $2\pi$ of the thermal premises (\claimref{synthesis.n-plus-null-ground-state}, and (R$_{\mathrm{loc}}$) of \claimref{synthesis.c-loc-local-horizon-premise}) holds for CAR and CCR modes alike and does not fix statistics (\claimref{synthesis.modular-period-on-values-is-the-dual-plane-turn}); modular covariance, which would fix them through an imported theorem, is not a premise of the store.
field-theory.twistor-attachment.technical:
The series' modes attach to spacetime through the conformal spinor space: the palatial storey gives a positive-energy one-particle space with a conformal-group action, the Penrose transform gives the mode functions, and the tower's CAR second-quantises over that space. In the oscillator model the helicity-$s$ module has energies $|s| + 1 + n$ with multiplicity $(n+1)(n + 2|s| + 1)$, the conformal energy is the palatial quadratic of the reversion form $h$, and the sixteen generators of $\mathfrak{u}(2,2)$ preserve each positive-energy, fixed-helicity module.

The tower's floors are then energy cut-offs, not regions of spacetime, and spin-statistics constrains the attachment: a CAR lift is local exactly when $2s$ is odd, which the series' fermion assignments satisfy. (Note, 2026-11-01: for the attached free fields this follows from locality with a positive norm, \claimref{synthesis.locality-of-the-attached-free-fields-fixes-their-statistics}; the Jost-point import is kept for interacting fields, and the thermal period alone does not fix statistics, \claimref{synthesis.modular-period-on-values-is-the-dual-plane-turn}.)
field-theory.twistor-attachment.lay: Since spacetime symmetries do not act on the tower's modes directly, the link must come from elsewhere. It comes from the series' conformal spinor storey, which provides positive-energy particle states with the right symmetry, while the Penrose transform turns them into waves in spacetime. On this reading the tower's levels are energy cut-offs rather than places, and the usual link between spin and statistics holds for the series' fermions.

field-theory.where-each-lives.technical:
The centre of $\Cl^+(1,3)$ is $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_4\}$ and that of $\Cl^+(2,4)$ is $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_6\}$, with $I_6 = I_4E$ for the ascended plane's bivector $E = e_+e_-$, $E^2 = 1$, $[I_4, E] = 0$. The conformal spinor space $\CS = \Cl^+(2,4)P$ has commutant $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_6\}$, so its complex unit is $\pm I_6$, acting by right multiplication; at a point it splits into the Lorentz-invariant $E = \pm 1$ eigenspaces $L_0 \oplus L_\infty$, on which $I_6 = +I_4$ and $-I_4$: the two chiral doublets.

For massless fields the complex structure is the pseudoscalar, $\pm I_4$ by helicity sector for Maxwell, and on the chiral subspaces of the Weyl field $I_4$ agrees with Hestenes' right $\IS$ up to the chirality sign; a mass term anticommutes with $I_4$.
field-theory.where-each-lives.lay: Every square root of minus one the field theory needs is an element of the real geometric algebra. The conformal spinors' unit is the conformal volume element, which on the spinors at a point becomes the spacetime volume element with a sign set by chirality. For massless fields the unit is the spacetime volume element, which agrees with Hestenes' choice up to that sign, while a mass term does not commute with it.

synthesis.a-finite-subgroup-of-colour-sh.formal:
Let $V$ be the span of $e_{3}, \dots, e_{8}$ in $\Cl(9,0)$, $J = e_{34} + e_{56} + e_{78}$, and $j(v) = v\cdot J$ the complex structure ($e_{3} \mapsto e_{4}$, $e_{4} \mapsto -e_{3}$, and so on), with $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega = e_{357} - e_{368} - e_{458} - e_{467}$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega = e_{457} + e_{367} + e_{358} - e_{468}$, the real and imaginary parts of the $J$-complex volume form on the frame $e_{3}, e_{5}, e_{7}$. Let $SU(3)$ be the group of rotations of $V$ that commute with $j$ and fix $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ (for a $j$-linear rotation, fixing $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ is unit $J$-determinant), with Haar measure $dU$, and let $G$ be its subset of signed permutations of $e_{3}, \dots, e_{8}$. For a link $U$ write $\mathrm{tr}\,U = \sum_{a}e_{a}\cdot U(e_{a})$ (twice the real part of the $J$-complex trace) and $\chi(U) = \tfrac16\mathrm{tr}\,U$; the lattice weight is $\prod_{p}\exp(\beta\chi(U_{p}))$, $\beta = 6/g^{2}$, as in Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(i).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The colour group and a finite subgroup; computed.)} The bivectors of $V$ commuting with $J$ and with $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ form an eight-dimensional Lie algebra orthogonal to $J$, the $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ summand of Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}. $G$ is a group of order $96$; each element is $v \mapsto RvR^{-1}$ for a rational even versor $R$ with $RJR^{-1} = J$ and $R\,\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega\,R^{-1} = \mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$. The linear maps of $V$ commuting with $G$ are the span of $1$ and $j$, so $G$ is irreducible on the $J$-complex three-space and its central elements have the form $a + bj$; the only such element of $G$ is $1$, so its centre is trivial. The centre of $SU(3)$ is $\{1, \omega, \omega^{2}\}$, $\omega = -\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}j$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Equal averages through degree three; proved.)} For $k = 1, 2, 3$ the $G$-invariant subspace of $V^{\otimes k}$ is the $SU(3)$-invariant one: $0$; the span of the metric and the form of $J$; the span of $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega$. Hence $\int f(U)\,dU = \tfrac{1}{96}\sum_{g \in G}f(g)$ for every polynomial $f$ of degree at most three in the components of $U$, and, for finitely many independent links, for every polynomial of degree at most three in each link.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Degree four separates them; computed.)} In $V^{\otimes 4}$ the invariants have dimension $12$ for $SU(3)$ and $20$ for $G$. The derivation of $J$ vanishes on the $SU(3)$-invariants and has eigenvalues $\pm 4$ times the unit of $J$ on a two-dimensional part of the $G$-invariants, on which $\omega$ would act by $\omega^{\pm 4} \neq 1$: for the $J$-complex trace $t$, $\tfrac{1}{96}\sum_{G}t^{4} = 1$ while $\int t^{4}\,dU = 0$; and $\tfrac{1}{96}\sum_{G}(\mathrm{tr}\,U)^{4} = 20$ against $\int(\mathrm{tr}\,U)^{4}dU = 12$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Shared strong-coupling data; proved, sampled for the loops.)} For $j$-linear $X$, $Y$, $\int\mathrm{tr}(XU)\,dU = 0$ and $\int\mathrm{tr}(XU)\,\mathrm{tr}(U^{-1}Y)\,dU = \tfrac13\mathrm{tr}(XY)$, and the same over $G$. So every term of the strong-coupling expansion (the expansion of $\prod_{p}\exp(\beta\chi(U_{p}))$ in powers of $\beta$) whose integrand has degree at most three in each link has the same value for $G$ and for $SU(3)$. In particular, for every $R \times T$ rectangular fundamental loop $C$ the term of order $\beta^{RT}$ in $\langle\chi(U_{C})\rangle$ from the $RT$ plaquettes of the rectangle is $(\beta/18)^{RT}$ for both (summed over $G$ for $1 \times 1$ and $2 \times 1$); for $SU(3)$ it is the leading term, by its centre, while for $G$, which has no centre, it is not shown to be leading; and the term of a connected plaquette correlator from a tube of plaquettes joining the two, each to first order, has degree two on every link and agrees.
\item[(v)] \emph{(The plaquette; proved.)} With $z(\beta) = \int\exp(\beta\chi(U))\,dU$ (for $G$, the average over $G$), $(\ln z)'(\beta) = \kappa_{2}\beta + \tfrac12\kappa_{3}\beta^{2} + \tfrac16\kappa_{4}\beta^{3} + O(\beta^{4})$, $\kappa_{n}$ the cumulants of $\chi$: $\tfrac{\beta}{18} + \tfrac{\beta^{2}}{216} + 0\cdot\beta^{3}$ for $SU(3)$ and $\tfrac{\beta}{18} + \tfrac{\beta^{2}}{216} + \tfrac{\beta^{3}}{972}$ for $G$. On the hypercubic lattice of dimension at least three $\langle\chi(U_{p})\rangle = (\ln z)'(\beta) + O(\beta^{5})$ for both, the first closed surface being the boundary of an elementary cube (standard).
\item[(vi)] \emph{(A gapped finite weight; computed.)} $\chi(g) \le \tfrac13$ for every $g \neq 1$ in $G$, while on $SU(3)$ the rational elements $\mathrm{diag}(z, \bar z, 1)$, $z = ((n^{2} - 1) + 2nj)/(n^{2} + 1)$, have $1 - \chi = 4/(3(n^{2} + 1))$.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Reading (argued).} No term of the colour lattice's strong-coupling expansion that uses link moments of degree at most three (the term of every rectangle from its own plaquettes, the plaquette through $\beta^{2}$, and the tube terms of plaquette correlators from which the leading strong-coupling glueball decay rate is read) distinguishes $SU(3)$ from $G$, a finite group without centre whose weight is gapped at the identity, so that its plaquettes freeze at weak coupling and it has no continuum limit. For $G$ a fundamental line can end on sheets through the degree-four invariant of (iii), so its large loops need not follow the rectangle's own term. With the stored comparison with compact $U(1)$ (same form, \claimref{synthesis.weak-factor-rotor-lattice-strong-coupling-area-law}(vi); deconfined and massless at weak coupling, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(iv)), strong-coupling terms of this kind are not evidence of confinement or of a mass gap in the continuum, which needs $\beta \to \infty$ and asymptotic freedom (the sign of the stored one-loop colour coefficient). The Yang-Mills mass-gap problem is not addressed.
synthesis.a-finite-subgroup-of-colour-sh.technical: The strong-coupling expansion of a lattice gauge theory computes its coefficients from averages of products of link variables over the gauge group. In the colour block of the series' algebra, the six vectors $e_{3}, \dots, e_{8}$ with the complex structure $J = e_{34} + e_{56} + e_{78}$, the colour group is the set of rotations commuting with $J$ that fix the real part of the $J$-complex volume trivector; its Lie algebra is the eight $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ bivectors. Inside it the $J$-commuting signed permutations of the six vectors that fix that trivector form a finite group of order 96, each element the action of a rational versor; it is irreducible on the complex three-space, so by Schur's lemma its centre consists of complex scalars, and it has none but $1$. Its averages agree exactly with the colour group's Haar averages for every polynomial of degree at most three in a link, which is shown without importing any Haar integral: in degrees one to three its invariant tensors are exactly those the $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ bivectors annihilate (the metric and the form of $J$; the real and imaginary volume trivectors). So every strong-coupling term with each link to degree at most three is the same for both groups: the gluing factor $\tfrac13$, the term $(\beta/18)^{A}$ that a rectangle's own plaquettes contribute to its fundamental Wilson loop with $\beta = 6/g^{2}$ (the leading term for the colour group, by its centre; for the finite group, which has no centre, not shown to be leading), the tube terms of plaquette correlators, and the plaquette average $\beta/18 + \beta^{2}/216$. They first differ in degree four, where the finite group has twenty invariants against twelve, including the fourth power of the complex trace, which the colour group's centre forbids; the plaquette average then differs at $\beta^{3}$. The finite group's weight is gapped at the identity. As a reading (argued): the finite group freezes at weak coupling and has no continuum limit, so, with compact $U(1)$, already stored as sharing the form of the area law and known to be massless at weak coupling, strong-coupling terms of this kind decide neither confinement nor a mass gap in the continuum. Transport-absent.
synthesis.a-finite-subgroup-of-colour-sh.lay: A standard way to study the strong nuclear force is to put it on a grid and expand in powers of a small number valid when the force is very strong. This result shows, exactly, that many of the first terms of that expansion are the same for the true symmetry of the strong force and for a finite group of 96 discrete rotations that sits inside it. The finite version behaves very differently when the force is weak: it freezes and has no smooth limit. So these terms cannot tell whether the real force confines quarks or produces a mass gap, which is a famous unsolved problem that this result does not touch.

proofs.main:
\emph{Conventions.} Lattice weights, Haar measure, the absence of gauge fixing and $\beta = 2N/g^{2}$ ($= 6/g^{2}$ here) are those of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(i); the tree gauge and the Haar change of variables are those of the proof of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.weak-factor-rotor-lattice-strong-coupling-area-law}(iv), (v). The colour factor is the $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ summand of Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}, in the colour block of $\Cl(9,0)$ as in the stored field-level BRST result for the derived gauge fields. A bivector $B$ acts on $V$ by $v \mapsto \tfrac12(vB - Bv)$; the check computes with $6 \times 6$ matrices of these actions and of signed permutations, each first matched with the Clifford product.

\emph{Step 1 (the colour group; computed, with a standard reading).} A rotation $U$ of $V$ commuting with $j$ is complex linear for the complex structure $j$ and unitary for the Hermitian form whose real part is the metric, so the group of such rotations is $U(3)$. On the complexified trivectors, $U$ preserves the complex line spanned by the $J$-volume form, and acts on it by its $J$-determinant (or its conjugate, by convention); on the real plane spanned by $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega$ this is the rotation by the argument of the determinant. So $U$ fixes $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ exactly when its determinant is $1$, and the group is $SU(3)$, which is connected. The check confirms the convention on $\mathrm{diag}(j, 1, 1)$, of determinant $j$, which turns $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ into $\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega$. Its Lie algebra consists of the bivectors $B$ of $V$ with $[B, J] = 0$ and $[B, \mathrm{Re}\,\Omega] = 0$ (the derivative of $RXR^{-1}$ along $R = \exp(\epsilon B/2)$ is $\tfrac12[B, X]$); solving these linear conditions on the fifteen bivectors of $V$ gives an eight-dimensional space, closed under the commutator and orthogonal to $J$ in the trace form: $e_{45} - e_{36}$, $e_{35} + e_{46}$, $e_{47} - e_{38}$, $e_{37} + e_{48}$, $e_{56} - e_{34}$, $e_{67} - e_{58}$, $e_{57} + e_{68}$, $e_{78} - e_{34}$. This is (i), first part.

\emph{Step 2 (the finite subgroup; computed).} Let $G$ be generated by the $j$-linear signed permutations with complex matrices $\mathrm{diag}(j, -j, 1)$, $\mathrm{diag}(1, j, -j)$, the cyclic permutation of $e_{3}, e_{5}, e_{7}$ (with $e_{4}, e_{6}, e_{8}$), and the exchange of the first two complex coordinates with the sign of the third reversed. The closure has $96$ elements, the monomial complex matrices with entries in $\{\pm1, \pm j\}$ and determinant $1$. For each element the check builds, by successive reflections, a product $R$ of an even number of vectors with rational components with $RvR^{-1} = g(v)$ on all six basis vectors, and confirms $RJR^{-1} = J$, $R\,\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega\,R^{-1} = \mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ and $R\,\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega\,R^{-1} = \mathrm{Im}\,\Omega$; so $G \subset SU(3)$. The check solves for the real linear maps of $V$ commuting with the four generators: they form the two-dimensional span of $1$ and $j$. So the only $J$-linear maps commuting with $G$ are the $J$-scalars, $G$ is irreducible on the $J$-complex three-space, and by Schur's lemma every central element of $G$ is a $J$-scalar $a + bj$. Such a signed permutation acts on every complex coordinate by the same unit, so it is one of $\pm1$, $\pm j$, with determinants $1$, $-1$, $\mp j$; so the centre of $G$ is $\{1\}$. The centre of $SU(3)$ consists of the $J$-scalars with $(a + bj)^{3} = 1$, that is $a^{3} - 3ab^{2} = 1$ and $b(3a^{2} - b^{2}) = 0$: either $b = 0$ and $a = 1$, or $b^{2} = 3a^{2}$, whence $-8a^{3} = 1$, $a = -\tfrac12$, $b^{2} = \tfrac34$; so the centre is $1$, $\omega$, $\omega^{2}$, $\omega = -\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}j$, and $\omega$ has an irrational component (the check confirms that $\tfrac34$ is not the square of a rational). This is (i).

\emph{Step 3 (averages are projectors).} Let $K$ be a compact group with normalised Haar measure acting orthogonally on a real space $W$ (here $W = V^{\otimes k}$, $U \mapsto U^{\otimes k}$), and $P = \int\rho(U)\,dU$. Invariance of the measure gives $\rho(h)P = P = P\rho(h)$, so $P^{2} = P$ and the image of $P$ is the invariant subspace; inversion invariance gives $P^{\mathsf T} = \int\rho(U^{-1})\,dU = P$. So $P$ is the orthogonal projector onto the $K$-invariants, and the same holds for the uniform average over a finite group. A polynomial of degree $k$ in the components of $U$ is a linear functional of $U^{\otimes k}$, so its average is determined by $P$. For $G \subset SU(3)$, the $SU(3)$-invariants are $G$-invariant; conversely, a $G$-invariant tensor annihilated by every element of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ acting as a derivation is invariant under $\exp$ of the algebra, hence under the connected $SU(3)$. So if the $G$-invariants are all annihilated by $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, the two invariant subspaces coincide and the averages agree in that degree.

\emph{Step 4 (degrees one to three; proved with computation).} $G$ acts on the basis tensors of $V^{\otimes k}$ by signed permutations, so its invariants are spanned by the signed orbit sums of the orbits on which no element reverses a tensor's sign; the check finds $0$, $2$ and $2$ such orbits for $k = 1, 2, 3$, identifies the spans with the metric and the form of $J$ ($k = 2$) and with the tensors of $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,\Omega$ ($k = 3$), and finds that the eight derivations annihilate them. By Step 3 the averages agree in each degree $k \le 3$; the check also compares the $G$-average of $U^{\otimes k}$ entry by entry with the projector on a set of index pairs. For independent links the average of a product factorises (Fubini), and a polynomial of degree at most three in each link is a sum of products of per-link polynomials of degree at most three, so its averages agree as well. This is (ii).

\emph{Step 5 (degree four; computed).} For $k = 4$ the check finds $20$ signed orbits for $G$ and a $12$-dimensional subspace of their span annihilated by $\mathfrak{su}(3)$; so the invariant spaces differ, and $\int(\mathrm{tr}\,U)^{4}dU = \mathrm{tr}\,P = 12$ against $20$ for $G$ (also by summing over $G$). The derivation $D$ of $j$ commutes with $G$; it vanishes on the $12$ colour invariants, and on the $20$ invariants of $G$ its kernel has dimension $18$ and the kernel of $D^{2} + 16$ dimension $2$. On the complexification, $D$ is $j(p - q)$ on the tensors with $p$ factors from the $+j$ eigenspace and $q$ from the $-j$ eigenspace, and $\omega = \exp(2\pi J/3)$ acts there by $\omega^{p - q}$; so the two extra directions with $D^{2} = -16$ have $p - q = \pm4$, on which $\omega$ acts by $\omega^{\pm1} \neq 1$. Concretely, the $J$-complex trace $t = \sum_{k}(U_{2k,2k} + jU_{2k+1,2k})$ has $\tfrac{1}{96}\sum_{G}t^{4} = 1$ and $\tfrac{1}{96}\sum_{G}|t|^{4} = 3$ (computed), while for $SU(3)$ the substitution $U \mapsto \omega U$ preserves $dU$ and multiplies $t^{4}$ by $\omega^{4} = \omega$, so $\int t^{4}\,dU = 0$. This is (iii).

\emph{Step 6 (shared strong-coupling data; proved).} The gluing integrals are polynomials of degree one and two in $U$, so by Step 4 they may be computed over $G$; the check does so on the eighteen basis maps $E_{kl}$, $jE_{kl}$ of the $j$-linear maps (complete by bilinearity) and finds $0$ and $\tfrac13\mathrm{tr}(XY)$. Expanding the weight, the strong-coupling expansion of $\langle O\rangle$ for a gauge-invariant polynomial observable $O$ is a ratio of sums of integrals $\int O\prod_{p}\chi(U_{p})^{n_{p}}/n_{p}!$ over finitely many links, and each such integral with degree at most three in each link agrees by Step 4. For the rectangle, fix the tree of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.weak-factor-rotor-lattice-strong-coupling-area-law}(v) to $1$ (the Haar measure, and the average over $G$, are invariant under the change of variables): the plaquettes become $V_{x+1,y}V_{x,y}^{-1}$ and the loop the product of the right-hand column; integrating the columns one at a time with the gluing rule gives, at each of the $A = RT$ integrations, a factor $\tfrac13$ and a weight $\tfrac{\beta}{6}$, and the last trace $\tfrac16\mathrm{tr}\,1 = 1$, so the term is $(\tfrac{\beta}{6}\cdot\tfrac13)^{A} = (\beta/18)^{A}$. Every link of the rectangle occurs in two factors, degree two, so the same holds for $G$; the check sums over $G$ in the tree gauge for the $1 \times 1$ loop ($\tfrac{1}{18}$) and the $2 \times 1$ loop ($\tfrac{1}{324}$). A tube of plaquettes joining two plaquettes, each to first order, also has every link in exactly two factors. So the term from the rectangle's own plaquettes is shared. Whether it is the leading term for $G$ is not decided here: for $SU(3)$ the centre excludes every lower term, but $G$ has no centre, and by Step 5 it has the degree-four invariant $t^{4}$, which lets a fundamental line end on sheets (four fundamental indices fusing to a $G$-invariant at a link), so surfaces whose plaquette count grows with the perimeter can contribute to $G$'s loops where $SU(3)$'s vanish; for large rectangles such terms may lie below order $\beta^{A}$ (argued, not computed here). This is (iv).

\emph{Step 7 (the plaquette; proved).} With $m_{k}$ the moments of $\chi$, $m_{k} = 6^{-k}\int(\mathrm{tr}\,U)^{k}dU = 6^{-k}$ times the dimension of the invariants of $V^{\otimes k}$ (the trace of the projector, as $\mathrm{tr}(U^{\otimes k}) = (\mathrm{tr}\,U)^{k}$). For $SU(3)$: $m_{1} = 0$, $m_{2} = \tfrac{2}{36} = \tfrac1{18}$, $m_{3} = \tfrac{2}{216} = \tfrac1{108}$, $m_{4} = \tfrac{12}{1296} = \tfrac1{108}$; for $G$ the same except $m_{4} = \tfrac{20}{1296} = \tfrac{5}{324}$ (also by summing $\chi^{k}$ over $G$). The cumulants are $\kappa_{2} = m_{2}$, $\kappa_{3} = m_{3}$, $\kappa_{4} = m_{4} - 3m_{2}^{2}$, which is $0$ for $SU(3)$ and $\tfrac{1}{162}$ for $G$, and $(\ln z)' = \sum_{n}\kappa_{n+1}\beta^{n}/n!$ gives the two series; the check also expands the ratio $\int\chi e^{\beta\chi}/\int e^{\beta\chi}$ over $G$ directly. On the lattice, the character expansion $e^{\beta\chi} = z(\beta)\bigl(1 + \sum_{r \neq 1}d_{r}a_{r}(\beta)\chi_{r}\bigr)$ with $a_{r} = O(\beta)$ holds for any compact group; a product of non-trivial characters integrates to zero unless every link of its plaquettes lies in at least two of them (Schur, $\int\chi_{r}(XU)\,dU = 0$), and the smallest such set in dimension at least three is the boundary of an elementary cube, six plaquettes (standard, as in Drouffe and Zuber's account, cited from memory). So $\ln Z$ is the number of plaquettes times $\ln z$ plus terms of order $\beta^{6}$, and $\langle\chi(U_{p})\rangle = (\ln z)' + O(\beta^{5})$. This is (v).

\emph{Step 8 (the gap at the identity; computed).} The check takes the maximum of $\chi$ over the $95$ elements $g \neq 1$ of $G$: $\tfrac13$ (for instance at $\mathrm{diag}(j, -j, 1)$, real trace $2$). For $SU(3)$, $z = ((n^{2} - 1) + 2nj)/(n^{2} + 1)$ has $z\bar z = 1$, so $\mathrm{diag}(z, \bar z, 1) \in SU(3)$, with $\mathrm{tr} = 2 + 4(n^{2} - 1)/(n^{2} + 1)$ and $1 - \chi = 4/(3(n^{2} + 1))$, which tends to $0$. This is (vi).

\emph{Step 9 (reading; argued).} By (ii) and (iv) no term of the strong-coupling expansion with link degree at most three separates $SU(3)$ from $G$, including the terms $(\beta/18)^{A}$ from a rectangle's own plaquettes and the tube terms of plaquette correlators from which the leading glueball decay rate is read. $G$ has no centre, so nothing like $N$-ality protects its fundamental loop at higher orders, and its weight is gapped at the identity by (vi), so at large $\beta$ each plaquette is frozen to $1$ except with weight at most $e^{-2\beta/3}$: a finite gauge group has no continuum limit, and by the standard low-temperature (Peierls) argument for finite gauge groups in four dimensions its Wilson loops have a perimeter law at weak coupling (cited from memory, not imported). The stored comparison with compact $U(1)$ gives the same form, $(\beta/2)^{A}$ (\claimref{synthesis.weak-factor-rotor-lattice-strong-coupling-area-law}(vi)), for a theory that deconfines with a massless phase at weak coupling (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(iv)). Every finite subgroup of $SU(3)$ differs from Haar in some degree (a nonzero polynomial vanishes on any finite set), so such a double reaches only finitely many orders; but confinement and a mass gap in the continuum concern $\beta \to \infty$, reached by no finite order and needing asymptotic freedom ($b_{3} < 0$ in the stored one-loop running coefficients, under their content and premises). A survey of the store's finiteness premises and stored gaps, none of which gives the gauge field a lattice spacing or a spectral gap, is recorded in the extraction note; it is a statement about the store's contents and is not part of this proof.

\emph{Status.} (i), (iii), (vi) computed exactly; (ii), (iv), (v) proved, with the loops sampled and the closed-surface count of (v) standard; the reading argued. Standard lattice gauge theory recomputed in the colour block; transport-absent.

synthesis.attachment-transport-is-flat-o.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a torsion-free gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), $\Omega_{T}$ its tractor gauge field and $F_{T}$ the field strength of $\Omega_{T}$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.gtg-tractor-gauge-field-reproduces-tractor-connection}), and let a bivector of $\Cl(2,4)$ act on the conformal spinor space $\CS$ (Proposition \claimref{field-theory.where-each-lives}) by left multiplication, so that a $\CS$-valued field is parallel when $a\cdot\nabla\psi + \tfrac12\Omega_{T}(a)\psi = 0$ for every $a$, and a bivector field $X$ (an adjoint tractor) when $a\cdot\nabla X + \Omega_{T}(a)\times X = 0$. Write $\mathcal{W}$ for the Weyl curvature, an $I_{4}$-linear map on spacetime bivectors, and give each point the Petrov type of $\mathcal{W}$ there. Two units act here and are not identified: $I_{4}$ acts on spacetime bivectors by left multiplication (duality), for which $\mathcal{W}$ is linear, and complex dimensions of subspaces of $\CS$ are taken over the conformal spinors' unit $I_{6} = I_{4}E$ acting by right multiplication (Proposition \claimref{field-theory.where-each-lives}(1), (2)).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Ricci blindness; proved.)} $F_{T}(A\wedge B) = -\mathcal{W}(A\wedge B) + \nO\wedge C(A, B)$, with $C$ the Cotton term: the Schouten map, hence the Ricci curvature, enters only through $C$, which vanishes on every Einstein space (Ricci curvature proportional to the metric, $\Sch = \tfrac{\Lambda}{6}\id$); under Einstein's equations with matter it does not vanish in general.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Parallel conformal spinors; proved.)} A parallel $\CS$-valued field is annihilated by every $F_{T}(A\wedge B)$ at every point. The subspace of $\CS$ annihilated by the Weyl bivectors has complex dimension $4$ at type O points, $2$ at type N points, where it is the subspace annihilated by left multiplication by the repeated principal null vector $k$, and $0$ at points of type I, II, D and III; a nonzero Cotton term can only reduce it. Where $F_{T} = 0$ on a simply connected region (in four dimensions this is the case exactly where $\mathcal{W} = 0$, by the twistor-flat result (\claimref{synthesis.twistor-flat-fields-give-nordstrom-not-einstein})) the parallel conformal spinors form a space of complex dimension $4$ carrying the attachment's $\mathfrak{u}(2,2)$ action, form $h$ and grading $Z$ unchanged.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(No conformal-energy generator; proved.)} The bivectors of $\Cl(2,4)$ commuting with every $F_{T}(A\wedge B)$, which contain every parallel adjoint tractor, span $15$ dimensions at type O points, $5$ at type N points and $1$ (the multiples of $E = e_{+}e_{-}$) at points of type I, II, D and III; at every point with $\mathcal{W} \neq 0$ each of them annihilates a null vector under the commutator product, while every nonzero multiple of a rotor conjugate of the attachment's conformal-energy generator $Z = e_{0}\nu$ (the grading of the massless, conformally invariant modules; for massive fields $Z$ is not a symmetry even where $\mathcal{W} = 0$) annihilates only a negative-definite $4$-plane. So no conformal-energy generator is parallel through a point where the Weyl curvature is nonzero.
\end{enumerate}
Hence the tractor transport carries the attachment's one-particle structure across a region only where $\mathcal{W} = 0$: on a general gravitational field the attachment's tractor transport does not construct the one-particle space and supplies no state (no choice of positive frequency); a state must come from another construction, which this result does not exclude.
synthesis.attachment-transport-is-flat-o.technical:
The series attaches its modes to spacetime through the conformal spinor space: a four-dimensional complex space with an invariant form of signature $(2,2)$, the conformal algebra $\mathfrak{u}(2,2)$ acting on it, and the central rotation $Z$, whose grading gives the positive conformal energy. On a gravitational field the natural way to carry this space from point to point is the tractor gauge field, and the space survives transport only where that field's curvature annihilates it.

The curvature acting on conformal spinors is minus the Weyl curvature plus a Cotton term; the Ricci curvature, and with it the matter, drops out. Where the Weyl curvature vanishes the whole space is parallel (on such regions the Cotton term vanishes too, by the twistor-flat result (\claimref{synthesis.twistor-flat-fields-give-nordstrom-not-einstein})). Where it does not, the annihilated part has complex dimension $2$ at points of Petrov type N (the spinors killed by the repeated principal null vector) and $0$ at points of every other type, the standard integrability condition of the twistor equation reproduced in $\Cl(2,4)$. No conformal-energy generator commutes with a nonzero Weyl curvature either: everything that does annihilates a null vector, while such a generator annihilates only a negative-definite plane.

So off Weyl-flat regions the attachment's tractor transport gives no one-particle space and supplies no state, the choice of positive frequency; that choice has to come from another construction. The grading $Z$ concerns the massless, conformally invariant modules. The result is transport-convenient.
synthesis.attachment-transport-is-flat-o.lay: The series links its quantum modes to spacetime through a special four-dimensional space of spinors, which in flat space comes with a built-in notion of positive energy. In a gravitational field one has to carry that space from point to point, and gravity's tidal part, the Weyl curvature, twists it on the way. This result shows that the space survives only where that tidal part vanishes: at a point of one special radiation type half of it can survive, and at every other point none of it, and the built-in notion of positive energy is lost. So in a general gravitational field this way of attaching the modes does not fix the quantum state; the state has to be supplied in some other way.
