synthesis.clifford-conjugation-is-the-tw.formal:
Units and signature of the store. Complex scalars are $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{7}\}$, $I_{7} = I_{6}e$ the central pseudoscalar of the odd extension $\Cl(3,4) = \Cl(2,4)_{\C}$, which commutes with every generator (\claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}). Let $\CS$ be the eight-dimensional conformal spinor module of $\Cl(2,4)$ with the generators $e_{1}$ ($e_{1}^{2} = 1$, the time), $e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}$ (squares $-1$) and the ascent plane $e_{\pm}$ ($e_{\pm}^{2} = \pm 1$), the positive Hermitian structure $h$ for which every generator is unitary, $J = I_{7}e_{1}e_{+}$ and the twistor form $\Sigma(\psi, \varphi) = h(\psi, J\varphi)$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-form-at-imaginary-time}. Write $A^{\dagger}$ and $A^{\sharp}$ for the adjoints of an operator $A$ on $\CS$ for $h$ and for $\Sigma$, $\bar A$ for Clifford conjugation (the anti-automorphism with $\bar a = -a$ on vectors, extended antilinearly to complex combinations), and $\tau(A) = \tfrac18\operatorname{tr}A$. Polarisation vectors $u, w$ are vectors of the span of $e_{1}, \dots, e_{4}$, with $u\cdot w$ the store's metric, $Q(e_{1}) = 1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The twistor adjoint is Clifford conjugation; proved.)} $A^{\sharp} = JA^{\dagger}J$; for every $A$ in $\Cl(2,4)$ acting on $\CS$, $A^{\sharp} = \bar A$, so $B^{\sharp} = (-1)^{k(k+1)/2}B$ for a blade $B$ of grade $k$; and $A^{\sharp}$ is unchanged when $\Sigma$ is replaced by $\lambda\Sigma$, $\lambda$ real and nonzero.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Its trace form on vectors is minus the metric; proved.)} For real vectors $a, b$ of $\Cl(2,4)$, $\tau(a^{\sharp}b) = \langle\bar ab\rangle_{0} = -a\cdot b$, of signature $(4, 2)$; the identity $\langle\bar ab\rangle_{0} = -a\cdot b$ holds in every Clifford algebra, with no module and no twistor form. $\tau(a^{\dagger}b)$ is the Euclidean form in which the six generators are orthonormal. The two are related by $J$: $\tau(a^{\sharp}b) = \tau(a^{\dagger}JbJ)$, where $b \mapsto JbJ$ reverses $e_{1}$ and $e_{+}$ and fixes $e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}, e_{-}$. On polarisation vectors the first is the one-particle Gupta-Bleuler form $-u\cdot w$, negative on $e_{1}$ and positive on $e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}$ (the sign from the store's signature, the normalisation by the choice of $\tau$); the second is the Euclidean form of the time $e_{1}$; and $J$ acts as $u \mapsto -e_{1}ue_{1}$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Invariance; proved.)} $\tau(a^{\sharp}b)$ is invariant under every rotor of $\Cl(2,4)$; the positive form $\tau(a^{\dagger}b)$ is not invariant under the boost $\tfrac54 + \tfrac34e_{1}e_{2}$, which takes $e_{1}$ to a vector of positive norm $\tfrac{257}{32}$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Uniqueness; proved.)} The real bilinear forms on the polarisation space invariant under the six Lorentz bivectors form a one-dimensional space spanned by the metric. Hence every Lorentz-invariant Hermitian form on the complex polarisations is a real multiple of $-u\cdot w$, and none is definite.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Second quantisation; proved.)} On the polynomials in $z_{0}, \dots, z_{3}$ with the form $\langle z^{\alpha}, z^{\beta}\rangle = \alpha!\,\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ (Proposition \claimref{field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes}), the bosonic Fock form over the one-particle form $\tau(u^{\sharp}w)$ is $\langle z^{\alpha}, (-1)^{n_{0}}z^{\beta}\rangle$, and for it the adjoint of $a_{\mu} = \partial/\partial z_{\mu}$ is $-Q(\gamma_{\mu})z_{\mu}$, so $[a(u), a(w)^{\dagger}] = -u\cdot w$ on all four polarisations: the Feynman-gauge ($\alpha = 1$) realisation of the form in clause (K1) of Premise \claimref{synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-inner-product-for-gauge-fields}, with fundamental symmetry the second quantisation of $b \mapsto JbJ$. Covariant gauges with $\alpha \neq 1$ use the dipole state space with an auxiliary field, not a Fock space over a one-particle form, and are not described here.
\item[(vi)] \emph{(The ghost twist; computed.)} $J = 2n_{c} - 1$, with $n_{c}$ the number operator of the mode $c = \tfrac12(e_{1} + I_{7}e_{+})$; on a floor of two tower modes $b, d$ (Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-tower-limit}) the ghost twist $S = 1 - (b^{*} - d^{*})(b - d)$ of (K2) is $1 - 2n_{-}$, the parity of the mode $(b - d)/\sqrt2$. Both twists are parities of one mode; every fundamental symmetry of this kind on a fermion floor has that form, so this does not single out (K2).
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Reading (argued).} The one-particle form of (K1) is minus the store's metric, the trace form of Clifford conjugation in any Clifford algebra; the twistor form supplies the involution $J$ that relates it to the positive polarisation form, so the frame that the positive form singles out is the attachment's imaginary time point. Clause (K1) as a premise, that the polarisation and ghost state spaces carry the indefinite form, is not derived, and neither are (K2) to (K4). The covariant and the positive forms are both present in the attachment, as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-form-at-imaginary-time}(iv), where the covariant form is the one on the whole space and states exist only for positive structures. Standard; transport-absent.
synthesis.clifford-conjugation-is-the-tw.technical: The Krein premise of the series' gauge-field theory gives the polarisations of a gauge field the indefinite Gupta-Bleuler form, minus the Minkowski metric. This result places that form among the series' structures. The adjoint of the twistor form on the conformal spinor module of Cl(2,4) is Clifford conjugation, the anti-automorphism that negates every vector, whatever the real factor of the twistor form; its normalised trace form on vectors is minus the metric. That last identity holds in every Clifford algebra, so the one-particle Gupta-Bleuler form is simply the series' metric with its sign reversed, and the twistor form adds the involution J, which relates it to the positive structure's trace form, the Euclidean form of the time used for the stored photon, and whose second quantisation is the stored fundamental symmetry (-1)^{n_0}. Every Lorentz-invariant Hermitian form on the polarisations is a multiple of this one (computed). The Fock space over it is the Feynman-gauge realisation; other covariant gauges need a dipole state space and are not covered. The ghost twist is, like J, the parity of one fermion mode, which every such twist is. Nothing here derives that the unphysical modes must carry the indefinite form, the regulator fields, or positivity of the physical space. Standard; transport-absent.
synthesis.clifford-conjugation-is-the-tw.lay: The indefinite "length" used to quantise force fields covariantly gives the time direction negative length and the space directions positive length. This is the series' own spacetime metric with its sign reversed. The result shows that the conformal spinors of the series carry the same rule, and that the ordinary positive length used for light corresponds to choosing a time direction. It does not show that the series must use the indefinite length for its unphysical states; that remains an assumption.

proofs.main:
\emph{Conventions.} Complex scalars are $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{7}\}$, $I_{7} = I_{6}e$ central in $\Cl(3,4) = \Cl(2,4)_{\C}$ (\claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}). $\CS$, $h$, $J = I_{7}e_{1}e_{+}$ and $\Sigma = h(\cdot, J\cdot)$ are those of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-form-at-imaginary-time}; in its model the generators are realised on three fermion modes in the Jordan-Wigner basis and $h$ is the identity Gram matrix. The check uses that model in exact Gaussian rationals $\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{Q}}\{1, I_{7}\}$. Adjoints are antilinear in complex scalars.

\emph{Step 1 (the $\Sigma$-adjoint; proved).} By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-form-at-imaginary-time}(i), $J^{2} = 1$ and $J^{\dagger} = J$. For operators $A$, $\Sigma(\psi, A\varphi) = h(\psi, JAJ\,J\varphi) = h((JAJ)^{\dagger}\psi, J\varphi) = \Sigma(JA^{\dagger}J\psi, \varphi)$, so $A^{\sharp} = JA^{\dagger}J$. Replacing $\Sigma$ by $\lambda\Sigma$ with $\lambda$ real and nonzero multiplies both sides of the defining identity $\Sigma(A^{\sharp}\psi, \varphi) = \Sigma(\psi, A\varphi)$ by $\lambda$, so $A^{\sharp}$ is unchanged (the check also computes $(\lambda\Sigma)^{-1}A^{\dagger}(\lambda\Sigma)$ for $\lambda = -3, \tfrac27$). The map $A \mapsto A^{\sharp}$ is an antilinear anti-automorphism of $\operatorname{End}\CS$. By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-form-at-imaginary-time}(iii) the $\Sigma$-adjoint of every real vector is minus itself (directly: $e_{k}^{\dagger} = e_{k}^{-1} = e_{k}/Q(e_{k})$, and $J$ anticommutes with $e_{1}, e_{+}$, the generators of square $+1$, and commutes with the others, so $e_{k}^{\sharp} = -e_{k}$ for all six). Clifford conjugation is the unique anti-automorphism of $\Cl(2,4)$ that negates vectors, since the vectors generate the algebra; hence $A^{\sharp} = \bar A$ on $\Cl(2,4)$, and on a blade of grade $k$, $\bar B = (-1)^{k}\widetilde B = (-1)^{k}(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}B = (-1)^{k(k+1)/2}B$. The check compares $JB^{\dagger}J$ with $(-1)^{k(k+1)/2}B$ on all $64$ blades. This is (i).

\emph{Step 2 (trace forms on vectors; proved).} The complexified $\Cl(2,4)$ acts irreducibly on the eight-dimensional $\CS$, and $\tau(B) = 0$ for every blade $B \neq 1$: if $B$ has even grade below six it contains a generator $e$ with $eBe^{-1} = -B$; if $B$ has odd grade some generator $f$ is missing from $B$ and $fBf^{-1} = -B$; the pseudoscalar anticommutes with every generator. So $\tau(A) = \langle A\rangle_{0}$ for $A$ in the algebra. Then $\tau(a^{\sharp}b) = \langle\bar ab\rangle_{0} = -\langle ab\rangle_{0} = -a\cdot b$ for real vectors, a form of signature $(4,2)$ because $a\cdot b$ has signature $(2,4)$; and $\tau(e_{j}^{\dagger}e_{k}) = \langle e_{j}^{-1}e_{k}\rangle_{0} = \delta_{jk}$, the Euclidean form of the frame. By Step 1, $\tau(a^{\sharp}b) = \tau(Ja^{\dagger}Jb) = \tau(a^{\dagger}JbJ)$ by cyclicity, and $JbJ = (e_{1}e_{+})b(e_{1}e_{+})^{-1}$ ($I_{7}^{2} = -1$ and $(e_{1}e_{+})^{2} = -1$), which reverses $e_{1}$ and $e_{+}$ and fixes the other four generators. Restricted to $u, w$ in the span of $e_{1}, \dots, e_{4}$: $\tau(u^{\sharp}w) = -u\cdot w$, negative on $e_{1}$ and positive on $e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}$ (Gram matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-1, 1, 1, 1)$, checked), $\tau(u^{\dagger}w)$ is the Euclidean form with $e_{1}$ as time, and $JuJ = -e_{1}ue_{1}$ there. The check computes all $36$ Gram entries of both forms, the identity on three sample vectors with all six components, and the action of $J$. The identity $\langle\bar ab\rangle_{0} = -\langle ab\rangle_{0} = -a\cdot b$ uses only $\bar a = -a$, so it holds in every Clifford algebra; the check also computes it directly in $\Cl(1,3)$ and $\Cl(2,4)$ with no module and no twistor form. The sign that makes $e_{2}, e_{3}, e_{4}$ positive is the store's signature, $Q(e_{1}) = 1$; the normalisation is the choice of $\tau$ and of the sign in front of it. What the twistor form contributes is the identification of $\sharp$ with Clifford conjugation and the involution $J$ between the two forms. This is (ii).

\emph{Step 3 (invariance; proved).} For a rotor $R$ (even, $R\widetilde R = 1$), Clifford conjugation equals reversion on even elements, so $\overline{RaR^{-1}} = \overline{R^{-1}}\,\bar a\,\bar R = R\bar a\widetilde R$, and $\tau(\overline{RaR^{-1}}\,RbR^{-1}) = \langle R\bar ab\widetilde R\rangle_{0} = \langle\bar ab\rangle_{0}$. The check computes the invariance for the boost $\tfrac54 + \tfrac34e_{1}e_{2}$, the rotation $\tfrac35 + \tfrac45e_{2}e_{3}$, the translation $1 + \tfrac12e_{3}n_{\infty}$ ($n_{\infty} = e_{+} - e_{-}$) and the dilation $\tfrac54 + \tfrac34e_{+}e_{-}$, on sample vectors, by conjugating the $8 \times 8$ matrices. The boost takes $e_{1}$ to $\tfrac{17}{8}e_{1} \pm \tfrac{15}{8}e_{2}$, whose positive norm is $\tfrac{289 + 225}{64} = \tfrac{257}{32} \neq 1$ while its $\Sigma$-norm stays $-1$. That no positive structure is boost invariant is Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-form-at-imaginary-time}(iv). This is (iii).

\emph{Step 4 (uniqueness; proved).} Let $X_{ij}$ be the matrices of $u \mapsto e_{i}e_{j}u - ue_{i}e_{j}$ on the span of $e_{1}, \dots, e_{4}$, computed in $\Cl(1,3)$. A real bilinear form with matrix $M$ is invariant under the Lorentz algebra if and only if $X_{ij}^{T}M + MX_{ij} = 0$ for the six pairs. These are $96$ linear equations in the $16$ entries of $M$; their solution space, computed exactly, is one-dimensional and spanned by $\operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$. A Hermitian form $H = S + I_{7}A$ ($S$ real symmetric, $A$ real antisymmetric) on $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{7}\}^{4}$ is invariant under the real matrices $X_{ij}$ exactly when $S$ and $A$ are (the equations are real-linear and the $X_{ij}$ are real); $A$ lies in the solution space and is antisymmetric, so $A = 0$ and $H$ is a real multiple of the metric, hence of $-u\cdot w$, and not definite. This is the computed form of Schur's lemma for the real irreducible vector representation. This is (iv).

\emph{Step 5 (second quantisation; proved).} For a one-particle space with an orthogonal basis $z_{\mu}$ of norms $\kappa_{\mu} = \pm1$, the bosonic Fock form on monomials is $\langle z^{\alpha}, z^{\beta}\rangle_{K} = \delta_{\alpha\beta}\,\alpha!\prod_{\mu}\kappa_{\mu}^{\alpha_{\mu}}$. By Step 2, $\kappa = (-1, 1, 1, 1)$ for $\tau(u^{\sharp}w)$, so $\langle z^{\alpha}, z^{\beta}\rangle_{K} = (-1)^{\alpha_{0}}\alpha!\,\delta_{\alpha\beta} = \langle z^{\alpha}, (-1)^{n_{0}}z^{\beta}\rangle$ with the form $\langle z^{n}, z^{n'}\rangle = n!\,\delta$ of Proposition \claimref{field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes}. For $a_{\mu} = \partial/\partial z_{\mu}$: $\langle z^{\alpha}, a_{\mu}z^{\beta}\rangle_{K} = \beta_{\mu}\langle z^{\alpha}, z^{\beta - e_{\mu}}\rangle_{K}$, nonzero only for $\alpha = \beta - e_{\mu}$, where it is $\beta!\,\kappa^{\beta}/\kappa_{\mu} = \kappa_{\mu}\langle z_{\mu}z^{\alpha}, z^{\beta}\rangle_{K}$. So the $K$-adjoint of $a_{\mu}$ is $\kappa_{\mu}z_{\mu} = -Q(\gamma_{\mu})z_{\mu}$ and $[a(u), a(w)^{\dagger}] = -u\cdot w$ for real polarisations, the form (K1) of Premise \claimref{synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-inner-product-for-gauge-fields}; its fundamental symmetry $(-1)^{n_{0}}$ is the second quantisation of $u \mapsto JuJ$, which reverses $e_{1}$ only. The check verifies both identities on all monomials of degree at most three. The commutator $-u\cdot w$ on all four polarisations of each mode, with propagator $-\gamma_{\mu}\cdot\gamma_{\nu}/k^{2}$, is the Feynman-gauge ($\alpha = 1$) realisation. A covariant gauge with $\alpha \neq 1$ adds to the propagator a term $(1 - \alpha)k_{\mu}k_{\nu}/k^{4}$, whose two-point function has dipole support ($\delta'(k^{2})$); its state space needs the auxiliary (Nakanishi-Lautrup) field and is not a Fock space over a one-particle form at fixed momentum, so it is neither obtained nor excluded here (standard, cited from memory). This is (v).

\emph{Step 6 (the ghost twist; computed).} With $c = \tfrac12(e_{1} + I_{7}e_{+})$: $c^{2} = \tfrac14(e_{1}^{2} - e_{+}^{2}) = 0$ and $c^{\dagger}c = \tfrac14(e_{1} - I_{7}e_{+})(e_{1} + I_{7}e_{+}) = \tfrac12(1 + I_{7}e_{1}e_{+}) = \tfrac12(1 + J)$, so $n_{c} = c^{\dagger}c$ is a projection and $J = 2n_{c} - 1$: up to sign, $J$ is the parity of the mode $c$. On a floor of two tower modes $b, d$ with the CAR of Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-tower-limit}, $n_{-} = \tfrac12(b^{*} - d^{*})(b - d)$ is the number operator of $(b - d)/\sqrt2$, $n_{-}^{2} = n_{-}$, and $S = 1 - 2n_{-}$, with $S^{2} = 1$, $S^{*} = S$ and $SbS = d$. Every fundamental symmetry that is the parity of one mode has this form, so the computation records the shape of (K2) and does not select it; the operative content of (K2) is the pairing of ghost and antighost in the indefinite form. This is (vi).

\emph{Step 7 (what does not follow; argued).} (a) The forms above are the covariant ones; the positive ones $\tau(a^{\dagger}b)$ and $h$ are equally present in the attachment. That a field theory's polarisation and ghost state spaces carry the covariant form rather than a frame's positive form is the content of (K1) and (K2) as a premise, and it is not derived here; Step 4 shows only that a Lorentz-invariant polarisation form is $-u\cdot w$ up to a real factor, which is standard. (b) Clause (K3) concerns additional massive fields entering loops with negative weights; nothing here says which fields exist. (c) Clause (K4) needs a BRST charge, that is, dynamics; positivity of its cohomology is computed in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.self-adjoint-brst-charge-needs-a-krein-form-and-the-tower-supplies-the-ghosts} only for the free charge at a null momentum up to three quanta. (d) The Fock form over an indefinite one-particle form is the standard construction; Clifford conjugation and its trace form, the Gupta-Bleuler form and the twistor form are standard. What is recorded is that, inside the store, the one-particle form of the premise is the trace form of the twistor adjoint (as of Clifford conjugation in any Clifford algebra), and that the fundamental symmetry and the frame of the positive form are supplied by the same $J$.

\emph{Status.} (i) to (v) proved, with exact checks; (vi) computed; the reading argued. A restatement of the one-particle content of (K1), not a derivation of the premise. Transport-absent.

synthesis.colour-centre-flux-bounds-poly.formal:
Represent the $\su(3)$ summand of $\su(2) \oplus \su(3) \oplus \uu(1)$ (Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}) as in \claimref{synthesis.field-level-brst-differential-of-the-derived-gauge-fields-is-nilpotent}: the eight bivectors of the block $e_3, \dots, e_8$ of $\Cl(9,0)$ that commute with $J = e_{34} + e_{56} + e_{78}$ and are orthogonal to it. Let $P_k = e_{34}, e_{56}, e_{78}$, $I = e_{345678}$, $E = \prod_k\tfrac12(1 + IP_k)$, $\Omega_R = e_{357} - e_{368} - e_{458} - e_{467}$, $\Omega_I = e_{457} + e_{367} + e_{358} - e_{468}$, $j(v) = v\cdot J$. A colour rotor is a rotor $R$ of the block (an even element with $R\widetilde{R} = 1$ and $Rv\widetilde{R}$ a vector for every vector $v$ of the block, equivalently a product of an even number of unit vectors) with $RE = E$; $f_R(v) = Rv\widetilde{R}$. On a hypercubic lattice give each oriented link a colour rotor ($\widetilde{U}$ reversed), let $U_p$ be the plaquette product, $w(U) = \tfrac13(4\langle U\rangle_0 - 1)$, and take the weight $\prod_p\exp(\beta w(U_p))$ with Haar measure.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The group at rotor level.)} $E^2 = E = \widetilde{E}$, $\langle E\rangle_0 = \tfrac14$, $JE = -3IE$, and a bivector $B$ of the block has $BE = 0$ exactly when $B \in \su(3)$. Every colour rotor commutes with $J$, $f_R$ fixes $\Omega_R$ and $\Omega_I$, and $R \mapsto f_R$ is an isomorphism of the colour rotors onto $SU(3)$; for a rotation $f$ commuting with $j$ whose $j$-complex determinant is $\cos\varphi + \sin\varphi\,j$, $f(\Omega_R) = \cos\varphi\,\Omega_R + \sin\varphi\,\Omega_I$. So $\det = 1$ is $RE = E$ on rotors and $f(\Omega_R) = \Omega_R$ on vectors.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Character.)} The triplet character, written in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I\}$ with $I$ standing for $j$, is $\chi(R) = 4(\langle R\rangle_0 + \langle R\rangle_6) - 1$; so $w = \tfrac13\mathrm{Re}\Tr$, the weight is Wilson's with $\beta = 6/g^{2}$, and $1 - w(U) = \tfrac43(1 - \langle U\rangle_0)$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Lemma: the link moments used.)} $\int f_R(a)\,dR = 0$, $\int(x\cdot f_R(a))(y\cdot f_R(b))\,dR = \tfrac16\big((x\cdot y)(a\cdot b) + (x\cdot j(y))(a\cdot j(b))\big)$, $\int f_R(a)\wedge f_R(b)\wedge f_R(c)\,dR = \tfrac14\big(\langle(a\wedge b\wedge c)\widetilde{\Omega_R}\rangle_0\Omega_R + \langle(a\wedge b\wedge c)\widetilde{\Omega_I}\rangle_0\Omega_I\big)$ (the cubic moment is totally antisymmetric) and $\int R\,dR = E$; in characters $\int\chi = \int\chi^2 = \int\chi^2\bar\chi = 0$, $\int\chi\bar\chi = \int\chi^3 = 1$, $\int\chi(XR)\chi(\widetilde{R}Y)\,dR = \tfrac13\chi(XY)$, $\int\chi(XR)\chi(YR)\,dR = 0$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Centre and flux.)} The centre is $\{1, z, z^2\}$, $z = -\prod_k(\tfrac12 - \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}P_k)$, acting on vectors as $\omega = -\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}j$, with $w(z) = -\tfrac12$. A moment $\int\prod_{i \le a}\chi(X_iR)\prod_{k \le b}\chi(\widetilde{R}Y_k)\,dR$ vanishes unless $a \equiv b \pmod 3$, and every nonvanishing term of the expansion of the weight carries a $\Z_3$ two-chain of plaquette charges whose boundary is minus the observable's charge chain, and has order at least the size of its support.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Fundamental against $N$-ality zero.)} On any finite box with free boundary containing an $R \times T$ rectangle $C$ of area $A$, no term of order below $A$ contributes, and $\langle w(U_C)\rangle = (\beta/18)^{A} + O(\beta^{A+1})$, the rectangle's own plaquettes being the only term of order $A$. The centre bound does not apply to lines of zero triality: for example three coincident fundamental lines along any closed path, joined by the volume form, give $\tfrac14\langle f_{U_C}(\Omega_R)\widetilde{\Omega_R}\rangle_0 = 1$ identically.
\item[(vi)] \emph{(Polyakov lines.)} On a box with $N_t$ periodic time steps and free spatial boundary, with $P(x) = \tfrac13\chi(\prod_\tau U_0(x, \tau))$: $\langle P(x)\rangle = \langle P(x)P(y)\rangle = 0$ at every $\beta$; for $y = x + re_i$, $\langle P(x)\overline{P(y)}\rangle = \tfrac19(\beta/18)^{N_tr} + O(\beta^{N_tr+1})$; for the three neighbours $x + e_i$ of a site, $\langle P(x+e_1)P(x+e_2)P(x+e_3)\rangle = \tfrac1{27}(\beta/18)^{3N_t} + O(\beta^{3N_t+1})$, from three sheets on a junction at $x$ carried by $\int\chi^3 = 1$.
\item[(vii)] \emph{(Glueball tube.)} For a spatial plaquette $p$ and its translate $p_t$ by $t \ge 1$ time steps in a box with free boundary, the connected correlator of $w(U_p)$ and $w(U_{p_t})$ has no term of order below $4t$ and equals $\tfrac1{18}(\beta/18)^{4t} + O(\beta^{4t+1})$, from the tube of $4t$ plaquettes: the leading terms decay at the rate $4\ln(18/\beta)$ per time step.
\end{enumerate}
These are statements at a fixed finite order of the strong-coupling expansion on a finite lattice; uniformity in $t$ (a gap at small $\beta$) and the continuum limit, which needs $\beta \to \infty$, are not proved, so nothing here bears on the Yang-Mills existence and mass-gap problem.
synthesis.colour-centre-flux-bounds-poly.technical: The colour factor of the derived gauge algebra is realised by bivectors of the $e_3, \dots, e_8$ block commuting with $J$. Its group is the set of rotors fixing the pure-spinor idempotent $E = \prod_k\tfrac12(1 + IP_k)$ ($I$ the block's pseudoscalar); this one condition gives both commutation with $J$ and unit determinant, and on vectors unit determinant is that the rotation fixes the $J$-complex volume trivector. Because the rotor's spinor space is the colour triplet plus a singlet, the triplet character is $4(\langle R\rangle_0 + \langle R\rangle_6) - 1$, Wilson's action is the scalar part of the plaquette rotor as for the weak factor, and the average of the rotor is $E$. The centre is a rotor $z$ acting on vectors as a cube root of unity; changing one link by $z$ shows that every term of the strong-coupling expansion that survives carries a $\Z_3$ flux sheet ending on the observable. That bounds every term from below: a rectangular fundamental loop of area $A$ has no term below order $A$ and leading term $(\beta/18)^{A}$, while the centre bound does not apply to lines of zero triality; for example three coincident lines joined by the volume form give exactly one (the adjoint loop's perimeter behaviour is argued, not proved). With periodic time, a Polyakov line and a pair of like Polyakov lines vanish at every coupling; a line and an antiline at distance $r$ give $\tfrac19(\beta/18)^{N_tr}$ at leading order, and three lines meeting at a baryonic junction give $\tfrac1{27}(\beta/18)^{3N_t}$, through the cubic Haar moment that exists for $SU(3)$ and not for $U(3)$. The connected correlator of two plaquettes $t$ steps apart has leading term $\tfrac1{18}(\beta/18)^{4t}$ from the tube joining them, a leading decay rate $4\ln(18/\beta)$. All are finite-order strong-coupling statements on a finite lattice and do not reach the continuum limit.
synthesis.colour-centre-flux-bounds-poly.lay: The strong force's symmetry, which the series derives, can be put on a spacetime lattice in the form Wilson introduced, with each link carrying a rotation of a six-dimensional geometric algebra; here the rotations are singled out by fixing one special element of the algebra. The symmetry has a three-element centre, and that centre controls which configurations can contribute when the coupling is strong. Exactly at leading order: a quark and antiquark are bound with a cost growing with the area between them, three quarks can bind at a single junction as in a baryon, and the correlation between two plaquettes falls, at leading order, by a definite factor per time step (the strong-coupling estimate usually read as the lightest glueball's mass; that reading needs uniformity in the separation, not proved here). All of this holds only at strong coupling on a lattice of finite spacing. It says nothing about the continuum theory, and it makes no progress on the open problem of proving that quantum Yang-Mills theory exists and has a mass gap.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting.} The bivectors of the block $e_3, \dots, e_8$ span $\so(6)$; those commuting with $J$ span $\uu(3)$ (nine dimensions), and those orthogonal to $J$ for $\langle X\widetilde{Y}\rangle_0$ span the $\su(3)$ of \claimref{synthesis.field-level-brst-differential-of-the-derived-gauge-fields-is-nilpotent}(i), which proves it simple of dimension $8$, isomorphic to the colour summand of Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}. On vectors $j(v) = v\cdot J$ sends $e_3 \mapsto e_4 \mapsto -e_3$ (and likewise on $e_5, e_6$ and $e_7, e_8$) and is the complex structure; $\Omega_R$ and $\Omega_I$ are the real and imaginary parts of the complex volume form on the frame $e_3, e_5, e_7$, whose $j$-partners are $e_4, e_6, e_8$. The check multiplies even elements of the block with a blade table built from GA's blade product and compares it with the Clifford product on all $32^2$ basis pairs.

(i) The $P_k$ commute with each other and with $I$, and $(IP_k)^2 = I^2P_k^2 = 1$, so the $\tfrac12(1 + IP_k)$ are commuting idempotents and $E^2 = E$; $\widetilde{I} = -I$ and $\widetilde{P_k} = -P_k$, so $\widetilde{IP_k} = P_kI = IP_k$ and $\widetilde{E} = E$. Expanding the product, the scalar terms are $1$ and $I^3P_{34}P_{56}P_{78} = I^4 = 1$, so $\langle E\rangle_0 = \tfrac14$. $P_k(1 + IP_k) = P_k - I = -I(1 + IP_k)$ gives $P_kE = -IE$, hence $(P_j - P_k)E = 0$ and $JE = -3IE \neq 0$. \emph{Computed:} on the fifteen bivectors the kernel of $B \mapsto BE$ is eight-dimensional and spans the same space as the eight $\su(3)$ bivectors; every $\su(3)$ bivector commutes with $J$, $\Omega_R$ and $\Omega_I$, while $[J, \Omega_R] = -6\Omega_I$ and $[J, \Omega_I] = 6\Omega_R$.

\emph{Why the vector condition.} In six dimensions $R\widetilde{R} = 1$ does not make an even element a rotor: with $\cos\tfrac\varphi2 = \tfrac35$, $R = \exp(-\tfrac32\varphi I)\exp(-\tfrac\varphi2J)$ is rational and even, $R\widetilde{R} = 1$ and $RE = E$ (since $\exp(-\tfrac\varphi2J)E = \exp(\tfrac32\varphi I)E$), but $Re_3\widetilde{R}$ has parts of grades $1$ and $5$ (computed). Elements with $R\widetilde{R} = 1$ fixing $E$ form a $U(3)$ on which $R \mapsto f_R$ is not a rotation; requiring $Rv\widetilde{R}$ to be a vector for every $v$ removes them. \emph{Colour rotors commute with $J$.} If $RE = E$ then $\widetilde{R}E = E$, and $f_R(B)E = RB\widetilde{R}E = R(BE)$ for every bivector $B$. For $B = J$ this is $R(-3IE) = -3IE = JE$, so $f_R(J) - J$ lies in the kernel, $\su(3)$, which is orthogonal to $J$. Writing $f_R(J) = J + S$, $\langle f_R(J)\widetilde{f_R(J)}\rangle_0 = \langle J\widetilde{J}\rangle_0$ gives $\langle S\widetilde{S}\rangle_0 = 0$, so $S = 0$ (the form is positive definite on bivectors of $\Cl(9,0)$).

\emph{Determinant.} A rotation $f$ commuting with $j$ is complex linear and orthogonal, so unitary on $(\R^6, j) \cong \C^3$. $U(3)$ is the product of $SU(3)$ and the scalars $\exp(\varphi j) = \cos\varphi + \sin\varphi\,j$, and the scalars are the $J$-rotations with rotors $\pm\exp(-\varphi J/2)$. On trivectors $\su(3)$ acts trivially on $\Omega_R, \Omega_I$ and $J$ turns them by the brackets above, so $\exp(-\varphi J/2)$ sends $\Omega_R$ to $\cos3\varphi\,\Omega_R + \sin3\varphi\,\Omega_I$, and every $f = \exp(\varphi j)g$ with $g \in SU(3)$ (generated by $\exp\su(3)$) does the same, its determinant being $\exp(3\varphi j)$; so $f(\Omega_R) = \Omega_R$ exactly when $3\varphi \in 2\pi\Z$, that is $\det f = 1$. \emph{Computed:} the quarter turn $j$ itself ($\varphi = \tfrac\pi2$, determinant $-j$) sends $\Omega_R \mapsto -\Omega_I$ and $\Omega_I \mapsto \Omega_R$. At rotor level, a rotor of $f = \exp(\varphi j)g$ is $\pm\exp(-\varphi J/2)R_g$ with $R_g$ a product of exponentials of $\su(3)$ bivectors, so $R_gE = E$; and $\exp(-\varphi J/2)E = \exp(\tfrac32\varphi I)E$ since $JE = -3IE$. Hence $RE = E$ forces $\exp(\tfrac32\varphi I) = \pm1$, $\varphi \in \tfrac{2\pi}{3}\Z$, $\det f = 1$: a colour rotor covers an element of $SU(3)$. Conversely every element of $SU(3)$ is a product of exponentials of $\su(3)$ (it is connected), whose rotors fix $E$; and of the two rotors $\pm R$ of a rotation only one fixes $E$. So $R \mapsto f_R$ is an isomorphism of the colour rotors onto $SU(3)$.

(ii) Both sides are class functions. Every element of $SU(3)$ is conjugate in $SU(3)$ to a diagonal one (an orthonormal eigenbasis, with one vector rescaled by a phase so the conjugating matrix has determinant $1$), whose colour rotor is $T_\theta = \prod_k(\cos\tfrac{\theta_k}{2} - \sin\tfrac{\theta_k}{2}P_k)$ with $\theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3 = 0$: by $P_kE = -IE$, $T_\theta E = \exp(\tfrac12(\theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3)I)E$, which is $E$ for this choice. Expanding, $\langle T_\theta\rangle_0 = c_1c_2c_3$ and $\langle T_\theta\rangle_6 = -s_1s_2s_3I$ ($c_k, s_k$ the half-angle cosines and sines; products of two $P_k$ have grade four). With $\sum\theta_k = 0$ the product formulas give $4c_1c_2c_3 = 1 + \sum_k\cos\theta_k$ and $-4s_1s_2s_3 = \sum_k\sin\theta_k$, and $f_{T_\theta}$ rotates each plane $P_k$ by $\theta_k$, so it is the scalar $\exp(\theta_kj)$ on the $k$-th plane. So $\chi = 4(\langle R\rangle_0 + \langle R\rangle_6) - 1$ is the trace of the triplet, $\sum_k(\cos\theta_k + I\sin\theta_k)$, written with $I$ standing for $j$. For a $j$-linear $f$ the trace, so written, is $\tfrac12\tr_{\R}f - \tfrac12\tr_{\R}(j\circ f)\,I$, which gives the two vector formulas. \emph{Computed:} on all $96$ elements of the group below and on $36$ conjugates of three rational torus rotors. So $w = \tfrac13\mathrm{Re}\Tr$, the weight is Wilson's $\exp(-\beta\sum_p(1 - \tfrac1N\mathrm{Re}\Tr U_p))$ up to a constant with $N = 3$, and $\beta = 6/g^{2}$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(i), $\beta = 2N/g^{2}$); $1 - w = \tfrac43(1 - \langle U\rangle_0)$ is immediate.

(iii) This lemma supplies the moments the later clauses use. \emph{Averages are projectors.} For a compact group with normalised Haar measure and an orthogonal representation $\rho$, $P = \int\rho(R)\,dR$ satisfies $\rho(S)P = P$ (left invariance), $Pv = v$ for every invariant $v$, and $P^{T} = \int\rho(R^{-1})\,dR = P$ (inversion invariance), so $P$ is the orthogonal projector onto the invariants; the same holds for the uniform average over a finite group. \emph{The group.} $G$ is generated by the colour rotors of the quarter turns acting as $(j, -j, 1)$ and $(1, j, -j)$ on the three planes ($\tfrac12(1 - P_{34})(1 + P_{56})$ and $\tfrac12(1 - P_{56})(1 + P_{78})$), the cyclic permutation of the three complex coordinates and minus a transposition (products of $\tfrac12(e_3 - e_5)(e_4 - e_6)$, $\tfrac12(e_5 - e_7)(e_6 - e_8)$ and $P_{78}$), each with the sign that fixes $E$. \emph{Computed:} $G$ has $96$ elements, all rational, all fixing $E$, $-1 \notin G$; their vector actions are $J$-commuting signed permutation matrices (this is $\Delta(96)$). By (i) $G$ is a subgroup of the colour rotors, so every $SU(3)$-invariant tensor is $G$-invariant. \emph{Computed:} the dimension of the $G$-invariants of $f^{\otimes k}$, the average of $(\tr f)^{k}$, is $0, 2, 2$ for $k = 1, 2, 3$. In degree $2$ the tensors $\delta$ and $j$ are fixed by every colour rotor ($f$ orthogonal and commuting with $j$), in degree $3$ the totally antisymmetric tensors of $\Omega_R$ and $\Omega_I$ are (by (i)); each pair is independent. So in each degree the $SU(3)$-invariants and the $G$-invariants coincide, the two projectors are equal, and the Haar moments are the $G$-averages, which the check computes entry by entry: $0$ in degree $1$, $\tfrac16(\delta\delta + jj)$ in degree $2$ (norms $|\delta|^2 = |j|^2 = 6$), and $\tfrac1{24}(\Omega_R\Omega_R + \Omega_I\Omega_I)$ in degree $3$ (tensor norm $24$), which in wedge form is the displayed formula with $\langle\Omega_R\widetilde{\Omega_R}\rangle_0 = 4$, checked on all twenty basis trivectors. For left multiplication on the even subalgebra (orthogonal for $\langle X\widetilde{Y}\rangle_0$), $\tr L_R = 32\langle R\rangle_0$ averages to $8$ over $G$, and the right ideal $E\Cl^{+}$, fixed by every colour rotor, has dimension $8$; so the projectors agree there too and $\int R\,dR = \int L_R(1)\,dR$ is the $G$-average of the rotors, which is $E$. \emph{Characters.} For $J$-commuting $X$, $Y$ (so $jYj^{T} = Y$) the two terms of the degree-two moment give $\int\tr_{\R}(Xf)\tr_{\R}(f^{T}Y) = \tfrac16(\tr_{\R}(XY) + \tr_{\R}(jYj^{T}X)) = \tfrac13\tr_{\R}(XY)$, hence $\int w(XR)w(\widetilde{R}Y) = \tfrac1{18}w(XY)$ with $w = \tfrac16\tr_{\R}$; read on $\C^3$, the real invariants $\delta$ and $j$ are the real and imaginary parts of the one invariant of the triplet times the antitriplet, and the triplet times itself has none, so $\int\chi(XR)\chi(\widetilde{R}Y) = \tfrac13\chi(XY)$ and $\int\chi(XR)\chi(YR) = 0$; the degree-three moment gives $\int\chi^3 = 1$ (one invariant, the volume form) and $\int\chi^2\bar\chi = 0$. \emph{Computed:} the five single-link averages, and the three gluing identities for all $96^2$ pairs $(X, Y)$ in $G$; both sides are bilinear in the complex matrices of $X$ and $Y$, and the vector actions of $G$ span the eighteen-dimensional space of $J$-commuting matrices (Burnside), so the check on $G \times G$ is complete. \emph{Contrasts.} The cubic moment averages to zero over the $J$-rotations, which turn the pair $(\Omega_R, \Omega_I)$ by the angle $3\varphi$ (checked on the quarter turns), so over $U(3)$ it vanishes; for the weak factor every odd moment vanishes ($-1 \in SU(2)$). Nothing below uses moments of degree $4$.

(iv) $z$ is $-T_\theta$ for $\theta = (\tfrac{2\pi}{3}, \tfrac{2\pi}{3}, \tfrac{2\pi}{3})$, that is $T_\theta$ for $(\tfrac{2\pi}{3}, \tfrac{2\pi}{3}, -\tfrac{4\pi}{3})$, so it is a colour rotor; its vector action multiplies by the scalar $\omega = -\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}j$, so $z$ is central, $z^3 = 1$, and $w(z) = \mathrm{Re}\,\omega = -\tfrac12$. \emph{Computed} in $\Q(\sqrt3)$: $zE = E$, $z^3 = 1 \neq z^2$, $\langle z\rangle_0 = -\tfrac18$, $z$ commutes with the generators of $G$ and with all eight $\su(3)$ bivectors, and $f_z(e_k) = -\tfrac12e_k + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}e_{k+1}$ for $k = 3, 5, 7$. By left invariance under $R \mapsto zR$ the displayed moment equals $\omega^{a - b}$ times itself, so it vanishes unless $a \equiv b \pmod 3$. On the lattice, expand $\exp(\beta w) = \exp(\tfrac\beta6\chi)\exp(\tfrac\beta6\bar\chi)$, so each term is a product over plaquettes of monomials $\chi(U_p)^{a_p}\bar\chi(U_p)^{b_p}$ of order $a_p + b_p$, times the observable's monomials; give $p$ the charge $n_p = a_p - b_p \bmod 3$. The change of variables $U_\ell \mapsto zU_\ell$ on one link preserves the Haar measure and multiplies such a term by $\omega$ to the net charge through $\ell$ ($z$ central, so it passes to the front of every plaquette product containing $\ell$, with $\bar\omega$ for the reversed orientation). So a term survives only if $n = \sum_pn_pp$ is a $\Z_3$ two-chain with $\partial n$ equal to minus the observable's charge chain, and its order is at least the number of plaquettes with $n_p \neq 0$.

(v) \emph{No lower order.} The observable $w(U_C) = \tfrac16(\chi + \bar\chi)(U_C)$ has charge $\pm1$ on $C$, so $\partial n = \mp C$. The projection onto the plane of $C$ along the two other axes is a chain map; it sends plaquettes parallel to the plane to plaquettes and the others to degenerate cells, so it maps $n$ to a $\Z_3$ two-chain of the plane with boundary $\mp C$. The plane has no nonzero finite two-cycle, so this chain is $\mp$ the sum of the $A$ plaquettes inside $C$, and over each of them $n$ has a plaquette with $n_p \ne 0$: every surviving term has order at least $A$. At order $A$ exactly there is one such plaquette over each interior position, all at first order and none elsewhere; a plaquette next to $C$ must lie in the plane of $C$ to produce its edge, and two plaquettes over adjacent positions must lie at the same transverse position to cancel their common edge, so by connectedness the plaquettes are those of the rectangle. The normalisation is $1 + O(\beta^2)$, since $\int w = 0$. So the coefficient of $\beta^{A}$ is $\int w(U_C)\prod_{p \subset C}w(U_p)$, the only term of that order. \emph{Its value.} As for the weak factor: fix the tree of all horizontal links and the left vertical links to $1$, change variables row by row to the independent Haar rotors $P_p = V_{x+1,y}\widetilde{V_{x,y}}$, and integrate one $P_p$ at a time with the gluing rule of (iii) at $Y = 1$ (using $w(\widetilde{P}) = w(P)$); each step gives $\tfrac1{18}$, so the value is $(\tfrac1{18})^{A}$ and the leading coefficient is $(\beta/18)^{A}$. \emph{Computed:} $\tfrac1{18}$ and $\tfrac1{324}$ for the $1 \times 1$ and $2 \times 1$ loops by summing over $G$ in the tree gauge; independently, $18^{-1}$, $18^{-3}$, $18^{-4}$ for $1 \times 1$, $3 \times 1$, $2 \times 2$ by contracting the degree-two moment over every link of the disc (each link lies on exactly two of the faces, the loop counted as a face). Gauge invariance of closed loops and the failure for an open line are checked on a $2 \times 2$ patch with site rotors in $G$. \emph{$N$-ality zero.} Three fundamental lines along the same closed path joined by the volume form at the base point are, by complex multilinearity, $\tfrac14\langle f_{U_C}(\Omega_R)\widetilde{\Omega_R}\rangle_0$, which is $1$ for every configuration by (i): no suppression at any order, in contrast with the bound above, which needs nonzero charge.

(vi) The box has periodic time and free spatial boundary (a periodic spatial extent would let a chain wind the short way round). \emph{Exact zeros.} Multiplying every temporal link of one time slice by $z$ preserves the measure and every plaquette (a temporal plaquette contains one such link and the inverse of another, and $z$ is central), and multiplies $P(x)$ by $\omega$; so $\langle P(x)\rangle = \omega\langle P(x)\rangle = 0$ and $\langle P(x)P(y)\rangle = \omega^2\langle P(x)P(y)\rangle = 0$ at every $\beta$, while $P\bar P$ and $PPP$ are invariant. \emph{No lower order.} In each time slab the temporal plaquettes are the edges of the spatial lattice, and the charge condition at the temporal links of the slab says that their charges form a $\Z_3$ one-chain with boundary $\pm(x - y)$, or $\pm(a + b + c)$ for three lines at $a, b, c$. For $y = x + re_i$, projecting on the $i$-th axis shows that such a chain has at least $r$ edges, with equality only for the straight segment; for $a, b, c = x + e_1, x + e_2, x + e_3$, which are pairwise not adjacent, at least three edges are needed, each containing one of them, and their other ends must carry boundary $0 \bmod 3$, which forces a common end, the only common neighbour $x$ (charge $3 \equiv 0$: the baryonic junction). So the order is at least $N_tr$, respectively $3N_t$, and at that order there are no spatial plaquettes, whence the spatial links at each time force the same strip (respectively star) in every slab. \emph{Values.} In each strip integrate the spatial links one by one with $\int\chi(XS)\chi(\widetilde{S}Y) = \tfrac13\chi(XY)$, and the last with $\int\chi(XSY\widetilde{S}) = \tfrac13\chi(X)\chi(Y)$ (from the degree-two moment): a strip of $N_t$ plaquettes of width one, each carrying $\tfrac\beta6\chi$ with the orientation that pairs with the lines, becomes $(\tfrac\beta{18})^{N_t}\bar\chi(L_u)\chi(L_v)$ for its two edges $u$, $v$, with $L$ the line products, which are independent Haar rotors. Gluing the $r$ columns with $\int\chi\bar\chi = 1$ on the inner lines and pairing with $P(x)\overline{P(y)} = \tfrac19\chi(L_x)\bar\chi(L_y)$ gives $\tfrac19(\beta/18)^{N_tr}$; for the junction the three sheets give $(\tfrac\beta{18})^{3N_t}\chi(L_x)^3\prod_k\bar\chi(L_{x+e_k})$, and $\int\chi^3 = 1$ (the baryonic moment) with three factors $\int\chi\bar\chi = 1$ gives $\tfrac1{27}(\beta/18)^{3N_t}$. \emph{Computed} by sums over $G$ in a tree gauge: $\tfrac1{162}$ for $N_t = r = 1$, $\tfrac19\cdot18^{-2}$ for $N_t = 2$, $r = 1$, zero for $P(x)P(y)$ at the same order, each sheet of the junction reducing to $\chi(U_x)/54$ for every $U_x \in G$, and $\tfrac1{27}\cdot18^{-3}$ for the junction at $N_t = 1$.

(vii) Write $\exp(\beta w(U)) = c_0(1 + h(U))$ with $c_0 = \int\exp(\beta w)$, so $\int h = 0$ and $h = \beta w + O(\beta^2)$. In a box with free boundary expand $\prod_p(1 + h_p)$ over sets $S$ of plaquettes; the term of $S$, with the observables $O_0 = w(U_p)$, $O_t = w(U_{p_t})$ inserted or not, vanishes if some link lies in exactly one member of $S \cup \{p, p_t\}$ (or of $S$ with the observables absent), by integrating that link ($\int h_q(AU_\ell B)\,dU_\ell = \int h = 0$ and $\int w = 0$). Put a parameter $s_\tau$ on every $h_q$ with $q$ a temporal plaquette of slab $\tau$, $0 \le \tau < t$. The connected correlator $C = N/Z - N_0N_t/Z^2$ is a formal power series in $\beta$ with coefficients polynomial in the $s_\tau$. (a) At $s_\tau = 0$ no remaining factor contains a temporal link of slab $\tau$ and the links split into those at times $\le \tau$ and those at times $\ge \tau + 1$, so the measure factorises with $O_0$ below and $O_t$ above, and $C = 0$; so every monomial of $C$ contains every $s_\tau$. (b) In a nonvanishing term the slab-$\tau$ plaquettes of $S$ form, as edges of the spatial lattice, a graph with no vertex of degree one (their temporal links meet no observable), so if nonempty it contains a cycle, of length at least $4$ in the cubic lattice; every term of $N$, $Z$, $N_0$ and $N_t$, and hence every product in the expansion of $C$, has $s_\tau$-degree $0$ or at least $4$. With (a), every monomial of $C$ has degree at least $4$ in each $s_\tau$, and since $h = O(\beta)$ its order is at least $4t$. At order $4t$ every factor is $\beta w$ and there are exactly four per slab and none elsewhere. A term of $N_0$ or $N_t$ with slab plaquettes would leave the spatial links at the top (or bottom) of its last slab in one plaquette only, so $N_0N_t/Z^2$ contributes nothing, and $Z - 1 = O(\beta^2)$ adds order; in $N$ the four plaquettes of each slab are a unit square, and the spatial links at each time force all squares to be the boundary of $p$. So the coefficient of $\beta^{4t}$ is $\int O_0O_t\prod_{\mathrm{tube}}w$. \emph{Its value.} By (iv) only the two consistent orientations survive; for each, integrating the four temporal links of a slab with the gluing rules gives $3^{-4}\chi(S_\tau)\bar\chi(S_{\tau+1})$ for the squares $S_\tau$ at the two ends, and $\int\chi\bar\chi = 1$ joins consecutive slabs and the ends: $3^{-4t}$, so the coefficient is $2\cdot6^{-(4t+2)}\cdot3^{-4t} = \tfrac1{18}(\tfrac1{18})^{4t}$, and $-\tfrac1t\ln$ of the leading term tends to $4\ln(18/\beta)$. \emph{Computed:} $18^{-5}$ and $18^{-9}$ for $t = 1, 2$ by contracting the degree-two moment over every link of the closed tube.

\emph{What is proved and what is not.} Proved: (i)-(vii) as stated, each at the stated order on a finite lattice; the Haar moments of degree at most three without importing them; the leading terms and the absence of lower-order terms. Not proved: the remainders' uniformity in the separation (for (vii), a gap of size $4\ln(18/\beta) + O(\beta)$ at small $\beta$ in infinite volume), which is expected to follow from the convergent strong-coupling expansion of Osterwalder and Seiler (cited from memory, not imported; their area law and analyticity are Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(ii)). \emph{Argued, not proved here:} the centre bound of (iv) does not apply to loops of $N$-ality zero (the cases of (v) and (vi) are examples), and the adjoint loop is screened at large size, its leading terms growing with the perimeter. The same leading structure holds for compact $U(1)$ (the weak-factor result computes $(\beta/2)^{A}$), and four-dimensional compact $U(1)$ deconfines at weak coupling (Fact (iv)); so these strong-coupling statements are not evidence of confinement in the continuum. The continuum limit needs $\beta \to \infty$, where the expansion does not converge (the leading rate $4\ln(18/\beta)$ is not small there), and asymptotic freedom (the store's one-loop running coefficients from spacetime-algebra spin traces); the Yang-Mills existence and mass-gap problem is a statement about that limit and is not addressed. Transport-absent.

synthesis.colour-triplets-give-the-funda.formal:
Let $V$, $J$, $j$, $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$, $SU(3)$ (the rotations of $V$ commuting with $j$ and fixing $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$, the $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ factor of Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}), $\mathrm{tr}\,U = \sum_{a}e_{a}\cdot U(e_{a})$ and $\chi = \tfrac16\mathrm{tr}$ be as in the colour block of $\Cl(9,0)$ ($V = \mathrm{span}(e_{3}, \dots, e_{8})$, $J = e_{34} + e_{56} + e_{78}$), with Haar measure on each link, at infinite gauge coupling ($\beta = 0$ in the weight of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(i)). Write $x = e_{3}\cdot U(e_{3})$ and $\Pi$ for the orthogonal projector onto $\mathrm{span}(e_{3}, e_{4})$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Haar moments of an entry; computed.)} $\int x^{2}\,dU = \tfrac16$, $\int x^{4}\,dU = \tfrac1{16}$, $\int U\,x\,dU = \tfrac16\Pi$ and $\int U\,x^{3}\,dU = \tfrac1{16}\Pi$, obtained from the invariant tensors of degrees two and four (the fourth moment is not reproduced by the order-$96$ subgroup of $J$-commuting signed permutations, which gives $\tfrac16$).
\item[(ii)] \emph{(A frozen triplet; proved.)} Give each site a unit vector $\varphi_{x} \in V$ (Haar measure on the unit sphere) and the weight $\prod_{\ell}\exp(\kappa\,\varphi_{x}\cdot U_{\ell}(\varphi_{y}))$. For every closed path $C$ that uses $P$ distinct links once each, $\langle\chi(U_{C})\rangle = \tfrac13c(\kappa)^{P}$ exactly, with $c(\kappa) = \int x\,e^{\kappa x}dU/\int e^{\kappa x}dU = \tfrac{\kappa}{6} - \tfrac{\kappa^{3}}{288} + O(\kappa^{5})$, positive for $\kappa > 0$; the mean link in the unitary gauge $\varphi = e_{3}$ is $c(\kappa)\Pi$, of rank one over the $J$-complex numbers. At $\kappa = 0$ every such loop vanishes.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Wilson quarks; proved.)} Let $n_{f}$ flavours of colour-triplet quarks carry the hopping operator $H$ with factor $(1 - d_{\mu})U_{\ell}$ for a hop along $+\mu$ and $(1 + d_{\mu})U_{\ell}^{-1}$ along $-\mu$, $d_{1}, \dots, d_{4}$ the vectors of $\Cl(4,0)$, the spinor trace being four times the scalar part, and the weight $\det(1 - \kappa H)^{n_{f}}$. For every closed rectangle with sides along $d_{\mu}$, $d_{\nu}$ and perimeter $P$, the spin trace of the product of hop factors round it is $-2^{P - 1}$ in either orientation, and the leading term of $\langle\chi(U_{C})\rangle$ in $\kappa$ for every $R \times T$ rectangular fundamental loop is $\tfrac{n_{f}}{6}(2\kappa)^{P}$, $P = 2(R + T)$.
\end{enumerate}
So at $\beta = 0$ a frozen colour triplet gives every simple loop exactly a perimeter law, and Wilson quarks give every rectangle a leading hopping term of perimeter form. (Argued:) at small $\beta > 0$ the perimeter term exceeds the area-law term $(\beta/18)^{RT}$ for large loops; this compares leading terms only and is not a bound on the full expectation.
\emph{Reading (argued).} With colour triplets the fundamental Wilson loop is no criterion of confinement for colour, as \claimref{synthesis.non-abelian-gauge-fixing-has-gribov-copies-and-the-weak-rotor-lattice-with-doublets-has-a-perimeter-law}(iv) found for the weak factor with doublets. The series' colour sector carries quark triplets ($n_{g}$ generations, an input of the stored one-loop running coefficients, $3$ at the imported values), so its physical colour question is the one with quarks, while the Yang-Mills mass-gap problem concerns the pure gauge field; nothing here addresses it.
synthesis.colour-triplets-give-the-funda.technical: At infinite gauge coupling a lattice gauge theory without matter has every Wilson loop zero, and the leading strong-coupling term of the fundamental loop is an area law. In the colour block of the series' algebra, with the colour group the rotations of $e_{3}, \dots, e_{8}$ that commute with $J = e_{34} + e_{56} + e_{78}$ and fix the real $J$-volume trivector, two kinds of colour-triplet matter change this exactly. A frozen triplet, a unit vector at each site with hopping strength $\kappa$, gives every closed path of $P$ distinct links at infinite coupling the expectation $c(\kappa)^{P}/3$, exactly a perimeter law, with $c = \kappa/6 - \kappa^{3}/288 + \dots$; unlike the weak doublet, whose mean link is a multiple of the identity, the triplet's mean link is a multiple of the projector onto one complex colour direction, because a triplet leaves an $SU(2)$ of colour unbroken. The colour averages are derived as invariant tensors of the colour block, the fourth moment included. Dynamical quarks, as Wilson fermions with hop factors $1 \mp d_{\mu}$ in the spacetime algebra of four Euclidean directions, give every rectangular fundamental loop at infinite coupling the leading term $(n_{f}/6)(2\kappa)^{P}$ in the hopping parameter, of perimeter form at leading hopping order: along each side the hop factors are idempotent up to a factor two, and the four corners give the same spin trace for every rectangle. So with colour triplets the fundamental loop is no confinement criterion at infinite coupling, as with the doublets in the weak factor. As a reading (argued): since the series has quarks, its physical colour question is the one with quarks, not the pure Yang-Mills mass-gap problem, which is not addressed. Transport-absent.
synthesis.colour-triplets-give-the-funda.lay: On a lattice, the usual sign of quark confinement is that a loop of colour field lines costs energy in proportion to the area it encloses. This result shows, exactly and in the series' own algebra, that once particles carrying colour are present, the cost at infinite coupling grows only with the loop's length: exactly for colour charges fixed in place, and at the leading order of the expansion in the quarks' hopping for moving quarks; the field line can break by creating a quark pair. Since the series contains quarks, this test of confinement, on this reading, does not apply to it directly. The famous open problem about a mass gap concerns the force field without quarks and is not touched here.

proofs.main:
\emph{Conventions.} The colour factor is the $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ summand of Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}, realised in the colour block as the bivectors of $V$ commuting with $J$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ (the check solves for them: eight). Lattice weights and Haar measure are those of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(i), at $\beta = 0$. The frozen-matter argument follows Step 4 of the proof of \claimref{synthesis.non-abelian-gauge-fixing-has-gribov-copies-and-the-weak-rotor-lattice-with-doublets-has-a-perimeter-law}, with the doublet replaced by a triplet.

\emph{Step 1 (moments; computed).} For a compact group the average of $U^{\otimes k}$ is the orthogonal projector onto the invariant tensors of $V^{\otimes k}$ (invariance of the measure gives $P^{2} = P$ with image the invariants, inversion invariance gives $P^{\mathsf T} = P$). The finite group $G$ of $J$-commuting signed permutations of $e_{3}, \dots, e_{8}$ that fix $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ (order $96$) lies in $SU(3)$, so the $SU(3)$-invariants are the $G$-invariants annihilated by the eight $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ derivations ($SU(3)$ is connected). The check computes them in degree two (two: the metric and the form of $J$) and degree four (twelve, inside the twenty $G$-invariants), and reads off $\int x^{2} = \tfrac16$, $\int x^{4} = \tfrac1{16}$, $\int U_{ab}x = \tfrac16\Pi_{ab}$, $\int U_{ab}x^{3} = \tfrac1{16}\Pi_{ab}$ as entries of the projectors $B(B^{\mathsf T}B)^{-1}B^{\mathsf T}$. The average of $x^{4}$ over $G$ is $\tfrac16$ (sixteen of the $96$ elements send $e_{3}$ to $\pm e_{3}$), so degree four is not shared. (As a cross-check by another route: $Ue_{3}$ is uniform on the unit sphere of $V$, on which the fourth moment of a coordinate is $3/(6 \cdot 8) = \tfrac1{16}$.) This is (i).

\emph{Step 2 (unitary gauge; proved).} $SU(3)$ acts transitively on the unit sphere of $V$, so for each site choose $g_{x} \in SU(3)$ with $g_{x}e_{3} = \varphi_{x}$; then $\varphi_{x}\cdot U(\varphi_{y}) = e_{3}\cdot(g_{x}^{-1}Ug_{y})(e_{3})$ (the check confirms this on a sample of elements of $G$). The change of variables $U_{\ell} \mapsto g_{x}^{-1}U_{\ell}g_{y}$ preserves the Haar measure and $\chi(U_{C})$ for closed $C$, so the $\varphi$ integrals factor out and each link carries the independent weight $e^{\kappa x(U)}$.

\emph{Step 3 (the mean link; proved).} Let $M = \int Ue^{\kappa x}dU/\int e^{\kappa x}dU$. The stabiliser $H$ of $e_{3}$ in $SU(3)$ fixes $e_{4} = j(e_{3})$ and acts on $\mathrm{span}(e_{5}, \dots, e_{8})$ as $SU(2)$, with no fixed vector there. Since $x(hUh') = x(U)$ for $h, h' \in H$, $M = hMh'$: with $h' = 1$ the image of $M$ lies in the $H$-fixed vectors $\mathrm{span}(e_{3}, e_{4})$; with $h = 1$, $M(h'v - v) = 0$, and the vectors $h'v - v$ span $\mathrm{span}(e_{5}, \dots, e_{8})$, so $M$ vanishes there. $M$ commutes with $j$, so on $\mathrm{span}(e_{3}, e_{4})$ it is $a + bj$. The reflection $\sigma$ reversing $e_{4}$, $e_{6}$, $e_{8}$ fixes $\mathrm{Re}\,\Omega$ and $e_{3}$ and sends $J$ to $-J$, so $U \mapsto \sigma U\sigma$ maps $SU(3)$ onto itself, preserves the Haar measure and $x$, and gives $M = \sigma M\sigma$, hence $b = 0$. So $M = c(\kappa)\Pi$ with $c = e_{3}\cdot M(e_{3}) = \int xe^{\kappa x}/\int e^{\kappa x}$, and the mean of $U^{-1}$ is $M^{\mathsf T} = c\Pi$. The check confirms $M = (\tfrac{\kappa}{6} - \tfrac{\kappa^{3}}{288})\Pi + O(\kappa^{5})$ entry by entry from the moments of Step 1: $c = \kappa m_{2} + \kappa^{3}(\tfrac16m_{4} - \tfrac12m_{2}^{2}) + O(\kappa^{5})$ with $m_{2} = \tfrac16$, $m_{4} = \tfrac1{16}$, and $\tfrac1{96} - \tfrac1{72} = -\tfrac1{288}$. Since $Ue_{3}$ is uniform on the sphere, $x$ and $-x$ have the same distribution, so the numerator of $c$ is $\int_{x > 0}x(e^{\kappa x} - e^{-\kappa x})\,dU > 0$ for $\kappa > 0$.

\emph{Step 4 (the frozen-triplet loop; proved).} For $C$ using $P$ distinct links once each, the links are independent after Step 2, and $\chi$ is linear, so $\langle\chi(U_{C})\rangle = \tfrac16\mathrm{tr}((c\Pi)^{P}) = \tfrac16c^{P}\mathrm{tr}\,\Pi = \tfrac13c^{P}$, using $\Pi^{P} = \Pi$ and $\mathrm{tr}\,\Pi = 2$ (checked for $P = 4, 6, 8$). At $\kappa = 0$, $c = 0$ and every such loop vanishes, as gauge-variant link averages do. For the weak doublet the stabiliser is trivial and the mean link is a scalar; for the triplet it is the projector onto one $J$-complex direction, the two others being acted on by the unbroken $SU(2)$. This is (ii).

\emph{Step 5 (Wilson quarks; proved).} For each flavour, the Grassmann integral of $\exp(-\bar\psi(1 - \kappa H)\psi)$ is $\det(1 - \kappa H)$ on spinor-colour space, with spinors the minimal left ideal $\Cl(4,0)f$, $f = \tfrac12(1 + d_{1}d_{2}d_{3}d_{4})$ (eight real dimensions), made complex by right multiplication by $d_{1}d_{2}$, which commutes with the left action and squares to $-1$, and colour the $J$-complex space $V$, the two complex units identified (the tensor product is over $\mathrm{span}\{1, j\}$). The real trace of left multiplication by $x$ on the ideal is $8\langle x\rangle_{0}$ (every basis blade other than $1$ anticommutes with some vector and is traceless), and for the products of hop factors used here the trace of left multiplication by $x$ composed with right multiplication by $d_{1}d_{2}$ vanishes (checked), so their complex spin trace is real and equals $4\langle x\rangle_{0}$. For small $\kappa$ on a finite lattice $\ln\det(1 - \kappa H) = -\sum_{n \ge 1}\tfrac{\kappa^{n}}{n}\mathrm{Tr}\,H^{n}$, and $\mathrm{Tr}\,H^{n}$ is the sum over closed walks of length $n$ of the spin trace times the colour trace of the products of hop factors; a walk that reverses a step gives $(1 - d_{\mu})(1 + d_{\mu}) = 1 - d_{\mu}^{2} = 0$. At $\beta = 0$, $\langle\chi(U_{C})\rangle = \int\chi(U_{C})\det(1 - \kappa H)^{n_{f}}\prod dU/\int\det(1 - \kappa H)^{n_{f}}\prod dU$. If a link of $C$ is traversed by none of the walks of a term, that term is linear in it and integrates to zero; so the first nonzero order is $\kappa^{P}$, from one closed walk of length $P$ covering the $P$ links of $C$, which is the boundary in one of its two orientations, counted from each of its $P$ starting points. Its contribution to $n_{f}\ln\det$ is $-n_{f}\kappa^{P}\bigl(s_{+}\mathrm{tr}_{J}(U_{C}) + s_{-}\mathrm{tr}_{J}(U_{C}^{-1})\bigr)$, with $s_{\pm}$ the spin traces of the two orientations and $\mathrm{tr}_{J}$ the $J$-complex colour trace, $\mathrm{tr}_{J}(U) + \mathrm{tr}_{J}(U^{-1}) = \mathrm{tr}\,U$. Along a side, $(1 \mp d_{\mu})^{2} = 2(1 \mp d_{\mu})$, so the product round an $R \times T$ rectangle is $2^{P - 4}(1 - d_{\mu})(1 - d_{\nu})(1 + d_{\mu})(1 + d_{\nu})$, whose scalar part is $2^{P - 4}(1 - 1 - 1 + (d_{\mu}d_{\nu})^{2}) = -2^{P - 3}$; so $s_{\pm} = -2^{P - 1}$ (the check multiplies the factors in $\Cl(4,0)$ for all six planes, $R, T \le 3$, both orientations). The order-$\kappa^{P}$ term of the weight is therefore $n_{f}2^{P - 1}\kappa^{P}\,\mathrm{tr}\,U_{C}$ (the check sums all closed walks of length $P$ on the $1 \times 1$ and $2 \times 1$ patches with links in $G$ and recovers $-2^{P - 1}\mathrm{tr}\,U_{C}$ for the walk sum), and the denominator is $1 + O(\kappa)$. With $U_{C}$ Haar distributed, $\int\chi(U)\,\mathrm{tr}\,U\,dU = \tfrac16\int(\mathrm{tr}\,U)^{2}dU = \tfrac26$ (degree two, the dimension of the invariants; also over $G$), so the leading term is $n_{f}2^{P - 1}\kappa^{P}\cdot\tfrac13 = \tfrac{n_{f}}{6}(2\kappa)^{P}$. This is (iii).

\emph{Step 6 (the comparison; argued).} At small $\beta > 0$ and small $\kappa > 0$ the leading terms of a large $R \times T$ loop are of order $(2\kappa)^{2(R + T)}$ (or $c^{2(R + T)}$) and $(\beta/18)^{RT}$, the leading area-law coefficient of the fundamental loop (from the gluing factor $\tfrac13$ and the weight $\beta/6$ per plaquette); the first dominates as the loop grows. This compares leading terms only and is not a bound on the full expectation. With triplets the fundamental Wilson loop is no order parameter of confinement, the colour analogue of \claimref{synthesis.non-abelian-gauge-fixing-has-gribov-copies-and-the-weak-rotor-lattice-with-doublets-has-a-perimeter-law}(iv); for scalars in the fundamental representation the absence of a phase boundary is Fradkin and Shenker's result (imported in the store's Fact on Singer's gauge slice, Neuberger's lattice BRST and Fradkin-Shenker complementarity, clause (iii), cited here in prose), and for quarks the same reading is argued, not proved. The series' colour sector has quark triplets, $n_{g}$ generations, an input of the stored one-loop running coefficients ($b_{3} = -11 + \tfrac43n_{g}$ there; $n_{g} = 3$ at the imported values); the Yang-Mills mass-gap problem is posed for the pure gauge field and is not addressed.

\emph{Status.} (i) computed exactly; (ii) and (iii) proved, with the expansions and walk sums checked exactly; the comparison argued. Standard lattice gauge theory recomputed in the colour block and in $\Cl(4,0)$; transport-absent.
