synthesis.curved-field-vacuum-polarisati.formal:
Units $\hbar = c = 1$. Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a smooth gravitational field on four-dimensional flat spacetime with vanishing torsion (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), $D = \hb^{T}(\partial_{a})D_{a}$ its covariant vector derivative, $\mathcal{R}$ its curvature operator, $\mathcal{R}(b) = \partial_{a}\cdot\mathcal{R}(a\wedge b)$ the Ricci vector and $\mathcal{R}_{0} = \partial_{a}\cdot\mathcal{R}(a)$ the scalar. The result is conditional on Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-local-covariance-with-scaling-of-time-ordered-products}, which is cited from memory; its sources treat the time-ordered products of a scalar field, and its use for the current of the Dirac field is part of the import. It concerns the difference of two extensions and does not show that a transverse one exists. The stored kernel it refers to is the trace form of the parametrix, not a state's current two-point function. By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.protraction-identity-of-the-curvature-operator-from-vanishing-torsion}(iii), the field being torsion-free, its curvature operator obeys the protraction identity $\partial_{a}\wedge\mathcal{R}(a\wedge b) = 0$ and its Ricci map is symmetric; the cited curved-field theorem cites the same clause. For a physical vector field $A$ write
\[
K_{1}A = \nabla^{2}A, \qquad K_{2}A = D\,(D\cdot A), \qquad K_{3}A = m^{2}A, \qquad K_{4}A = \mathcal{R}_{0}\,A, \qquad K_{5}A = \mathcal{R}(A),
\]
with $\nabla^{2}A = \sum_{k} Q(\gamma_{k})\bigl[(\gamma_{k}\cdot D)(\gamma_{k}\cdot D)A - ((\gamma_{k}\cdot D)\gamma_{k})\cdot D\,A\bigr]$ the rough Laplacian on an orthonormal physical frame $\{\gamma_{k}\}$. A \emph{local term for two vector slots of degree of divergence $2$} is a kernel $(a, x; b, x') \mapsto a\cdot K_{x}\bigl(b\,\delta(x, x')\bigr)$ with $K$ a differential operator of order at most $2$ on physical vector fields of the form that Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-local-covariance-with-scaling-of-time-ordered-products}(iii) gives to the difference of two extensions that are local and covariant with almost homogeneous scaling: the coefficient of the derivatives of order $j$ is a polynomial with constant coefficients in $\mathcal{R}$, its covariant derivatives and the mass $m$, of dimension $2 - j$, covariant under the rotation gauge.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The list; proved given the form of the cited Fact, the protraction identity being Theorem \claimref{synthesis.protraction-identity-of-the-curvature-operator-from-vanishing-torsion}(iii); the dimensions of the invariant spaces by exact rank. That the coefficients are rotor-invariant tensors of the slots is the proof's reading of ``local and covariant'' in the Fact.)} Every such term is $K = \sum_{i=1}^{5}c_{i}K_{i}$ with real constants $c_{i}$: five constants in place of the $15$ coefficient functions of the point per index pair of clause (iv) of the cited theorem. The count: no Lorentz-invariant tensor has three vector slots, so there is no term $m\,D$; with four vector slots there are four invariants, two symmetric in the derivative pair ($K_{1}$, $K_{2}$ up to lower order) and two antisymmetric, which multiply commutators of covariant derivatives and are curvature terms without derivatives; the invariant bilinear forms in $(a, b)$ that are linear in a map of bivectors number $6$ for all maps, $3$ on symmetric maps, $2$ on maps obeying the protraction identity, namely $a\cdot\mathcal{R}(b)$ and $(a\cdot b)\,\mathcal{R}_{0}$, and $0$ on maps that also have vanishing Ricci vector. So the Weyl part of the curvature operator cannot occur in the difference of two extensions, and no parity-odd term occurs although invariance is imposed for the connected group only.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Transversality; proved.)} On every torsion-free field, $D\wedge D\chi = 0$ for scalar fields $\chi$ and
\[
D\cdot(D\wedge A) = \nabla^{2}A - D\,(D\cdot A) + \mathcal{R}(A)
\]
in the store's sign of the curvature operator. The condition $K(D\chi) = 0$ for every scalar $\chi$, on every torsion-free field and for every mass, holds exactly when $(c_{1}, c_{2}, c_{3}, c_{4}, c_{5}) = c\,(1, -1, 0, 0, 1)$, that is
\[
K A = c\;D\cdot(D\wedge A),
\]
the divergence of the field strength of $A$. On the flat field this is $c\,(\nabla^{2}A - \nabla(\nabla\cdot A))$, the transverse term $c\,T(\delta)$ of clause (iii) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.one-loop-vacuum-polarisation-extends-without-a-regulator-and-ward-preserving-extensions-differ-only-by-the-renormalisation-constants} up to the sign convention of $T$: the constant $Z_{3}$. A photon mass term ($c_{3}$) and the terms $c_{4}$, $c_{5}$ do not occur in the difference of two transverse extensions; the Ricci term occurs only inside $D\cdot(D\wedge A)$, the Maxwell operator of the field, where it is the minimal coupling. Nothing is said here about the finite dependence of the kernel itself on the curvature.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(What this gives for the stored clause; proved given the two imported Facts and the hypothesis that the degree of divergence is $2$.)} Assume, as argued in clause (iv) of the cited curved-field theorem from Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extension-theorem-and-ward-preserving-time-ordered-products}(ii) and (vi), that the time-ordered one-loop vacuum-polarisation kernel on the field has degree of divergence $2$. If transverse local covariant extensions exist, then any two extensions of it that are local and covariant with almost homogeneous scaling and transverse in one slot differ by $c\,a\cdot D\cdot(D\wedge(b\,\delta))$ with one real constant $c$, the same on every torsion-free field: the freedom is the flat $Z_{3}$, and the coefficient of the Ricci term relative to the Laplacian is fixed.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Existence of a transverse extension; argued, not proved.)} Suppose in addition that the failure of transversality of a local covariant extension, the map $\chi \mapsto \bar\Pi(D\chi)$, is itself a local term of the form of the cited Fact with dimension $3$, and that the kernel is symmetric under exchange of its two slots; neither is part of the stored Facts. The candidates are $D(D\cdot D\chi)$, $m^{2}D\chi$, $\mathcal{R}_{0}D\chi$, $\mathcal{R}(D\chi)$ and $(D\mathcal{R}_{0})\chi$. The first four are $K_{2}$ to $K_{5}$ applied to $D\chi$ and are removed by subtracting local terms of (i); the fifth gives a double divergence $\int\chi\,(D\mathcal{R}_{0})\cdot D\psi$ that is not symmetric in $(\chi, \psi)$ and is excluded by the symmetry. Under these two suppositions a transverse local covariant extension exists. What is missing in the store is a statement that the divergence of a local covariant time-ordered product of currents is of this local form (the literature's Ward identity or principle of perturbative agreement on a gravitational field; Zahn, arXiv:1210.4031 and arXiv:1311.7661, for the charged Dirac field in gauge backgrounds, read at the level of the abstracts only). Clause (iv) of the cited curved-field theorem therefore stays argued.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.curved-field-vacuum-polarisati.technical: The stored curved-field result found that, at each point, the vacuum polarisation on a gravitational field has the same fifteen undetermined local terms per pair of indices as on flat spacetime, but with coefficients that could vary from point to point, and it cited the imported local-covariance Fact for their reduction to constants without carrying the reduction out. This result carries it out, conditionally. The Fact is cited from memory and its sources prove it for a scalar field; its use for the electron's current is part of the import. The Fact says each coefficient is a constant-coefficient polynomial in the curvature operator, its derivatives and the mass, of a fixed dimension, and the construction is covariant under local rotations; so each coefficient is a Lorentz-invariant tensor, and the invariant tensors can be counted exactly as the common kernel of the Lorentz generators acting through the algebra. With two derivatives there are two terms, the rough Laplacian and the gradient of the divergence; with one derivative none, because no invariant has three vector slots; with no derivative the mass squared, and two terms linear in the curvature, the Ricci map and the scalar curvature, the Weyl part admitting no invariant. The count of curvature terms uses the protraction identity, a stored theorem for torsion-free fields: on symmetric maps without it there is a third invariant. That is five constants. Requiring that two extensions both obey the Ward identity makes their difference annihilate gradients. For a torsion-free field the curl of a gradient vanishes and the divergence of the field strength equals the Laplacian minus the gradient of the divergence plus the Ricci map, in the store's sign; an exact computation on a sample field shows the four other directions fail independently, so the transverse terms are the multiples of the divergence of the field strength. Given the imported Facts and the flat degree of divergence, if transverse local covariant extensions exist, two of them differ by the one constant of flat spacetime, which multiplies the Maxwell operator of the field; its Ricci term is the minimal coupling, and no independent coupling to curvature is free. Whether a transverse local covariant extension exists on a gravitational field is not proved here; it is argued under two further suppositions that the store does not hold, so the argued clause of the stored curved-field result stays argued.
synthesis.curved-field-vacuum-polarisati.lay: The effect by which a photon briefly becomes an electron and positron pair has an infinite part that a rule must fix, and the rule leaves some quantities free. On flat spacetime the free quantities reduce to one number, which is absorbed into the measured electric charge. On a gravitational field the collection had shown only that the free quantities are of the same kind at each point, and had relied on a theorem from the literature, taken as an imported fact and quoted from memory, to say they are the same everywhere. This result works out what that theorem leaves, given that imported theorem and assuming gravity without the twisting that spinning matter would source. The answer is five numbers: two that already exist on flat spacetime, a possible photon mass, and two couplings of the photon to curvature. Demanding that electric charge be conserved, for both of two competing rules, removes four of them. If two charge-conserving rules exist, they differ only by the single number of flat spacetime; that number multiplies the ordinary wave operator of light on the gravitational field, and no separate coupling of light to curvature is left free. The theorem relied on was proved for a simpler kind of field than the electron's. The tidal part of gravity, the only part present in empty space, cannot appear among the free quantities at all. The result does not show that a charge-conserving rule exists on a gravitational field; that is argued under extra assumptions and is known in the literature, not derived here, so the open point in the collection's earlier result stays open.

proofs.main:
\begin{proof}
\emph{(i).} By Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-local-covariance-with-scaling-of-time-ordered-products}(iii) with $\omega = 2$, the coefficient of the derivatives of order $j$ in $K$ is a polynomial with constant coefficients in $\mathcal{R}$, its covariant derivatives and $m$, of dimension $2 - j$, where $\mathcal{R}$ has dimension $2$ and each covariant derivative and $m$ dimension $1$. The construction is covariant under the rotation gauge (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}(e)), under which the slot vectors $a$, $b$, the derivative directions and $\mathcal{R}$ rotate together and the constants do not change; so each coefficient is a multilinear function of its vector slots, and of $\mathcal{R}$ where it occurs, invariant under rotors, hence annihilated by the action of every bivector $J$ (this is the reading made here of ``local and covariant'' in the Fact, which is cited from memory and sourced for scalar fields), $v \mapsto J\times v$ on vectors and $M \mapsto J\times M(\cdot) - M(J\times\cdot)$ on maps of bivectors. The bivectors $\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}$, $\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}$, $\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$ generate the Lorentz algebra under the commutator product, so invariance under these three suffices; the check computes the dimension of each invariant space as the corank of the three generators acting on the tensor product, exactly.

\emph{Order $2$:} dimension $0$, so the coefficient is an invariant of four vector slots $(a, b; u, v)$, $u, v$ the derivative directions. The space has dimension $4$; the part symmetric in $(u, v)$ has dimension $2$, spanned by $(a\cdot b)(u\cdot v)$ and $(a\cdot u)(b\cdot v) + (a\cdot v)(b\cdot u)$, which give $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ up to the order of the derivatives; the antisymmetric part has dimension $2$ and multiplies $[u\cdot D, v\cdot D]$, which on a torsion-free field is the action of the field strength, a term of order $0$ linear in $\mathcal{R}$. Changing the order of two covariant derivatives in $K_{1}$ or $K_{2}$ likewise adds terms of order $0$ linear in $\mathcal{R}$, and of order $1$ none, the torsion being zero. \emph{Order $1$:} dimension $1$; the only quantity of dimension $1$ is $m$, and the coefficient would be $m$ times an invariant of three vector slots, of which there is none. \emph{Order $0$:} dimension $2$: $m^{2}$ times the one invariant $a\cdot b$ of two vector slots, giving $K_{3}$, and terms linear in $\mathcal{R}$; derivatives of $\mathcal{R}$ have dimension at least $3$. The bilinear forms in $(a, b)$ linear in a map $M$ of bivectors and invariant form a space of dimension $6$; on symmetric maps $3$; on the maps with $\partial_{a}\wedge M(a\wedge c) = 0$, where $\mathcal{R}$ lies by Theorem \claimref{synthesis.protraction-identity-of-the-curvature-operator-from-vanishing-torsion}(iii), dimension $2$. The forms $a\cdot M(b)$ and $(a\cdot b)\,\partial_{c}\cdot M(c)$ are invariant and are independent (the check evaluates them on a map of Ricci type), so they span, giving $K_{5}$ and $K_{4}$. On the maps that in addition have $\partial_{a}\cdot M(a\wedge c) = 0$ the dimension is $0$. The identification of maps with tensors in the check uses the invariant form $\langle AB\rangle_{0}$ on bivectors, which is nondegenerate, so the space of invariant forms on a subspace of maps has the dimension of the invariant tensors in that subspace times the two vector slots. This gives the list. The invariance used is that of the connected group; a parity-odd term would appear as an invariant in these counts and none survives.

\emph{(ii).} For a scalar $\chi$, $D\chi = g^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\chi$ with $g^{\mu} = \hb^{T}(e^{\mu})$, and $D\wedge D\chi = (D\wedge g^{\mu})\,\partial_{\mu}\chi + g^{\nu}\wedge g^{\mu}\,\partial_{\nu}\partial_{\mu}\chi = 0$, the first term by the torsion equation of the definition, clause (f), the second by symmetry. The identity $D\cdot(D\wedge A) = \nabla^{2}A - D(D\cdot A) + \mathcal{R}(A)$ is the classical Weitzenb\"ock formula for vector fields; in the store's conventions it reads as follows. Both sides are covariant under the rotation gauge, so fix a point and a gauge with $\Omega = 0$ there. Write $D_{k} = \gamma_{k}\cdot D = D_{\hb(\gamma_{k})}$ for an orthonormal physical frame $\{\gamma_{k}\}$ of constant vectors, so that $D = \gamma^{k}D_{k}$ and $D_{k}\gamma_{l} = \Omega(\hb(\gamma_{k}))\times\gamma_{l} = 0$ at the point. There
\[
D\cdot(D\wedge A) = \sum_{k,l}\gamma^{k}\cdot\bigl(\gamma^{l}\wedge D_{k}D_{l}A\bigr) = \sum_{k,l}\bigl[(\gamma^{k}\cdot\gamma^{l})\,D_{k}D_{l}A - \gamma^{l}\,\bigl(\gamma^{k}\cdot D_{k}D_{l}A\bigr)\bigr] .
\]
The first sum is $\sum_{k}Q(\gamma_{k})D_{k}D_{k}A$, which is $\nabla^{2}A$ at the point, the correction term $((\gamma_{k}\cdot D)\gamma_{k})\cdot D A$ of the rough Laplacian vanishing there. In the second, $D_{k}D_{l} = D_{l}D_{k} + [D_{k}, D_{l}]$; $\sum_{k}\gamma^{k}\cdot D_{l}D_{k}A = D_{l}(D\cdot A)$ at the point, so that part is $-D(D\cdot A)$. The commutator of the derivatives along the background vector fields $\hb(\gamma_{k})$, $\hb(\gamma_{l})$ is the field strength on their plane plus the derivative along their Lie bracket, whose physical image is $D_{k}\gamma_{l} - D_{l}\gamma_{k}$ by the torsion equation and vanishes at the point; so by clause (c) of the definition $[D_{k}, D_{l}]A = R(\hb(\gamma_{k}\wedge\gamma_{l}))\times A = -\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{k}\wedge\gamma_{l})\cdot A$. With $(B\cdot A)\cdot c = -(B\cdot c)\cdot A$ for a bivector $B$, $\gamma^{k}\cdot\bigl(\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{k}\wedge\gamma_{l})\cdot A\bigr) = \bigl(\gamma^{k}\cdot\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{k}\wedge\gamma_{l})\bigr)\cdot A = \mathcal{R}(\gamma_{l})\cdot A$, and the remaining term is $+\sum_{l}\gamma^{l}\,(\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{l})\cdot A) = \mathcal{R}(A)$, the Ricci map being symmetric by Theorem \claimref{synthesis.protraction-identity-of-the-curvature-operator-from-vanishing-torsion}(iii). The sign of this term is the point of convention; the check verifies the identity exactly on a torsion-free polynomial field with a generic vector field, in the store's sign and not the opposite one, with the library whose curvature sign is that of the definition. Hence $K(D\chi) = 0$ for $K = c\,(K_{1} - K_{2} + K_{5})$, on every torsion-free field.

Conversely let $K = \sum c_{i}K_{i}$ with $K(D\chi) = 0$ for all $\chi$, all torsion-free fields and all masses. The constants do not depend on the field or the mass, so the conditions from any one field and any values of the mass are necessary. The check evaluates $K_{i}(D\chi)$ at a point of one polynomial torsion-free field, with its curvature jet exact, for two cubic scalars $\chi$ and two values of $m^{2}$: the resulting linear system in $(c_{1}, \dots, c_{5})$ has rank $4$ and its solutions are the multiples of $(1, -1, 0, 0, 1)$. With the first half this proves the statement. On the flat field $\mathcal{R} = 0$ and $D = \nabla$, so $K A = c\,(\nabla^{2}A - \nabla(\nabla\cdot A))$; contracted with $a$ and applied to $b\,\delta$ this is $-c\,a\cdot T(\delta)(b)$ with $T(f)(a) = (a\cdot\nabla)\nabla f - a\nabla^{2}f$ the transverse operator of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.one-loop-vacuum-polarisation-extends-without-a-regulator-and-ward-preserving-extensions-differ-only-by-the-renormalisation-constants}, whose clause (iii) finds the transverse differences of degree at most $2$ to be the multiples of this term.

\emph{(iii).} The hypothesis is the degree of divergence $2$ that clause (iv) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.vacuum-polarisation-kernel-on-a-gravitational-field-has-the-flat-leading-part-and-no-weyl-term-of-degree-four} argues. Under it, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extension-theorem-and-ward-preserving-time-ordered-products}(ii) gives that two extensions differ by derivatives of $\delta$ of order at most $2$, and Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-local-covariance-with-scaling-of-time-ordered-products}(iii) that for local covariant extensions with almost homogeneous scaling the difference is a local term in the sense of the statement; by (i) it is $\sum c_{i}K_{i}$. Whether transverse extensions exist is not shown (clause (iv) is an argument). If two exist and both are transverse in one slot, their difference $\Delta$ satisfies $\Delta(D\chi) = 0$ for every test scalar $\chi$ (transversality in the slot of $b$, integrated by parts onto $\chi$), on every field, and (ii) applies. The constants are those of the Fact, the same on every torsion-free field, so $c$ is the flat constant.

\emph{(iv) (argued).} The map $\chi \mapsto \bar\Pi(D\chi)$ vanishes off the diagonal when the unextended kernel is transverse there, so it is supported on the diagonal; that it is a polynomial in the curvature with constant coefficients and of dimension $3$ (one more than the kernel's local terms, from the extra derivative) is the supposition. The count as in (i): three derivatives on $\chi$ with one free vector slot, the invariants of four vector slots symmetrised give $D(D\cdot D\chi)$ up to lower order; one derivative on $\chi$ with $m^{2}$, $\mathcal{R}_{0}$ or the Ricci map; no derivative on $\chi$ with a vector of dimension $3$ built from the curvature, which is $D\mathcal{R}_{0}$ or the divergence of the Ricci map, equal to half of it by the contracted second Bianchi identity (classical, not stored); two derivatives with $m$ times an invariant of three vector slots, none. Subtracting $\sum_{i\geq 2}c_{i}K_{i}$ from $\bar\Pi$ changes the first four coefficients independently, by the rank computation of (ii). For the fifth, symmetry of the kernel makes $(\chi, \psi) \mapsto \int\psi\,D\cdot\bar\Pi(D\chi)$ symmetric; the first four terms are symmetric after integration by parts, and $\int\chi\,(D\mathcal{R}_{0})\cdot D\psi - \int\psi\,(D\mathcal{R}_{0})\cdot D\chi$ is not zero for $\psi = 1$ near the support of $\chi$ unless $\int\chi\,D\cdot D\mathcal{R}_{0} = 0$ for all $\chi$. This is an argument, not a proof: the supposition on the form of the divergence is the content of the literature's Ward identity on a gravitational field.
\end{proof}

synthesis.density-modes-bosonise-only-al.formal:
Let the modes $a_{k,\alpha}$ carry a momentum $k$ in a finite window $W \subset \mathbb{Z}^{d}$ and a channel $\alpha$ in a finite set of $c$ channels; each mode is a tower plane, $a^{*} = v$, $a = w$ (Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}), $v^{*} = w$, numbers in $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ with $J$ the kernel bivector. For a channel array $M$ and a shift $m \in \mathbb{Z}^{d}$ let $\rho_{m}(M) = \sum_{k, k+m \in W}a_{k}^{*}Ma_{k+m}$, with $a_{k}^{*}Ma_{l} = \sum_{\alpha,\beta}M_{\alpha\beta}a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{l,\beta}$, so $\rho_{m}(M)^{*} = \rho_{-m}(M^{*})$; $\rho_{q} = \rho_{q}(\id)$, $n(S) = \sum_{k\in S}a_{k}^{*}a_{k}$, and $E_{-}(q) = (W \cap (W - q)) \setminus (W + q)$, $E_{+}(q) = (W \cap (W + q)) \setminus (W - q)$ the entry and exit strips.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Window identity.)} For all shifts $m, l$ and arrays $M, M'$, exactly,
\[
[\rho_{m}(M), \rho_{l}(M')] = \sum_{k, k+m, k+m+l \in W}a_{k}^{*}MM'a_{k+m+l} - \sum_{k, k+l, k+l+m \in W}a_{k}^{*}M'Ma_{k+l+m} .
\]
In particular $[\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M')^{*}] = \sum_{k \in W\cap(W-q)}a_{k}^{*}MM'^{*}a_{k} - \sum_{k \in W\cap(W+q)}a_{k}^{*}M'^{*}Ma_{k}$ and $[\rho_{q}, \rho_{q}^{*}] = n(E_{-}(q)) - n(E_{+}(q))$, with $|E_{-}(q)| = |E_{+}(q)|$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Uniform seas.)} If a state has the same total occupation $\omega(a_{k}^{*}a_{k})$ at every momentum of $E_{-}(q) \cup E_{+}(q)$, then $\omega([\rho_{q}, \rho_{q}^{*}]) = 0$. This holds at every $q$ and on every window for the sea that fills one channel state per momentum (the lower band of a two-channel $h(k)$, in particular the relativistic sea in any dimension and the $1 + 1$ Dirac sea of both chiralities), and, for a given $q$, for a sea contained in $W \cap (W - q) \cap (W + q)$ (for $d = 1$, $N = 3$, the sea $\{-2, -1, 0\}$ gives $0, 1, 1$ at $q = 1, 2, 3$). The forms $\omega([\rho_{q}, \rho_{q'}^{*}])$, $q \ne q'$, vanish in every state diagonal in momentum; so in a uniform sea the total density modes carry no canonical pair. Channel-resolved densities $\rho_{q}(M)$ need not: each chirality of the $1 + 1$ Dirac sea gives $\pm\min(q, 2N - q)$, and $\rho_{q}(\tfrac12(1 + \sigma_{3}))$ of the sea of (iv) gives half the sum in (iv).
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Half-space sea.)} For $W = \{-N, \dots, N - 1\}^{d}$ and the sea $F = \{k : k_{1} < 0\}$ in every channel, $\omega_{F}([\rho_{q}, \rho_{q}^{*}]) = c\,\min(q_{1}, 2N - q_{1})\prod_{j \ge 2}(2N - |q_{j}|)$ for $q_{1} \ge 0$ (and its negative for $q_{1} < 0$), and the commutator acts as this number on every vector that agrees with $F$ on the strips; it vanishes for $q_{1} = 0$. Other seas with unequally occupied strips give other values (for $d = 2$, $N = 3$, one channel: the quadrant $\{k_{1} < 0, k_{2} < 0\}$ gives $3$ at $q = (1, 0)$ and $5$ at $q = (1, 1)$, the tilted half-space $\{k_{1} + k_{2} < 0\}$ gives $5$ at $q = (1, 0)$).
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The density-current term.)} For two channels, the sea of the lower band of $h(k) = \sum_{i}k_{i}\sigma_{i}$ ($\sigma_{i}$ the channel arrays representing the generators of the Pauli algebra $\Cl(3,0)$, band projector $\tfrac12(1 - \hat k)$, $\hat k = k/|k|$), the cube $W = \{-N, \dots, N - 1\}^{d}$ and $q = (0, \dots, 0, q)$, $1 \le q < N$: $\omega([\rho_{q}, \rho_{q}(\sigma_{3})^{*}]) = S := \sum_{k\in E_{-}\cup E_{+}}|k_{d}|/|k|$, a sum over $2q(2N)^{d-1}$ strip points; $\omega([\rho_{q}(P_{+}), \rho_{q}(P_{+})^{*}]) = S/2$ for $P_{+} = \tfrac12(1 + \sigma_{3})$, while $\omega([\rho_{q}, \rho_{q}^{*}]) = 0$ by (ii). $S = 2q$ for $d = 1$ ($h = k\sigma_{3}$), and $S \in (4qN(N - q), 8qN^{2}]$ for $d = 3$.
\end{enumerate}
Clauses (i) to (iv) are proved. \emph{Reading (argued).} Density modes with a sharp central value on the sea arise for a sea that is a half-space in one direction, as on a null generator, whose modes have no transverse dispersion (there each transverse mode carries the one-dimensional chiral boson, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(vi) on the band), and, approximately, on each patch of a Fermi surface; other seas with unequal strip occupations (quadrants, tilted or edge-crossing seas) give nonzero but different values, and the spin-resolved densities of the $3 + 1$ relativistic sea have a nonzero mean form at the cut-off, $S/2$, with a relative mean-square defect that in floating-point evaluation decreases like $N^{-2}$ ($N = 2, \dots, 8$, not part of the proof). The total density modes of the $3 + 1$ relativistic sea carry no canonical pair; the growth $(2N)^{d-1}$ of $S$ is the transverse mode count, the value per transverse momentum being of order $q$, as in $d = 1$. So the series' exact bosons are per generator, sharp on each generator's half-space sea; whether propagating $3 + 1$ bosons arise is not addressed.
synthesis.density-modes-bosonise-only-al.technical: Put fermion modes on a finite window of momenta in $d$ dimensions, each a tower plane, with finitely many channels per momentum, and form the densities $\rho_{m}(M) = \sum_{k}a_{k}^{*}Ma_{k+m}$ for any shift $m$. (i) Exactly, $[\rho_{m}(M), \rho_{l}(M')]$ is the sum of $a_{k}^{*}MM'a_{k+m+l}$ over $k$ with $k + m$ and $k + m + l$ in the window minus the sum of $a_{k}^{*}M'Ma_{k+l+m}$ over $k$ with $k + l$ and $k + l + m$ in the window; for the plain density with equal shifts this is the number in an entry strip minus the number in an exit strip of the same size. (ii) So the form of the total density vanishes in any state with the same total occupation all over the strips: the relativistic sea, which fills one state per momentum in any dimension, and the $1 + 1$ Dirac sea of both chiralities at every $q$; and, for the $q$ at hand, a Fermi sea clear of the strips. Forms between unequal shifts vanish in momentum-diagonal states, so the total density modes of a uniform sea carry no canonical pair. Channel-resolved densities can: each chirality of the $1 + 1$ sea gives $\pm\min(q, 2N - q)$. (iii) A sea filling the half-space $k_{1} < 0$ gives the sharp one-dimensional value $\min(q_{1}, 2N - q_{1})$ times the transverse overlap and the channel number, and nothing for transverse $q$; quadrant and tilted seas give other nonzero values. (iv) For the two-component relativistic sea the density-current form is $S = \sum|k_{d}|/|k|$ over the strips, and the spin-resolved density has form $S/2$: $S = 2q$ in one dimension, between $4qN(N - q)$ and $8qN^{2}$ in three, the factor $(2N)^{2}$ being the transverse mode count. Reading (argued): densities with a sharp central value come from a half-space sea, as on each horizon generator (one chiral boson per transverse mode) and approximately on Fermi-surface patches; total densities of the $3 + 1$ relativistic sea carry no canonical pair; propagating $3 + 1$ bosons are not addressed.
synthesis.density-modes-bosonise-only-al.lay: In one dimension, ripples in a sea of fermions behave exactly like bosons, and the graph uses this on the light rays that make up a horizon. This result checks what happens in more dimensions on finite pieces of momentum space. The boson behaviour comes from the edge of the sea, and it is sharp for a sea filled on one side of a single direction. In a sea of the kind that fills ordinary three-dimensional space, the total density ripples have no boson behaviour on any finite piece of it; ripples of one spin component do, on average, through the edge of the momentum range, but not sharply. Light rays on a horizon have exactly one direction of motion, so there the boson behaviour holds sharply for each ray separately; whether bosons moving through three-dimensional space arise is not settled here.

proofs.main:
\emph{Preliminaries.} By Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors} the modes $a_{x}^{*} = v_{x}$, $a_{x} = w_{x}$, $x = (k, \alpha)$, satisfy $\{a_{x}, a_{y}^{*}\} = \delta_{xy}$, $\{a_{x}, a_{y}\} = 0$, $v_{x}^{*} = w_{x}$. Hence $[a_{x}^{*}a_{y}, a_{z}^{*}a_{u}] = \delta_{yz}a_{x}^{*}a_{u} - \delta_{ux}a_{z}^{*}a_{y}$, and for coefficient arrays $A, B$ on the one-particle labels the bilinear elements $\hat A = \sum A_{xy}a_{x}^{*}a_{y}$ satisfy $[\hat A, \hat B] = \widehat{[A, B]}$ and $(\hat A)^{*} = \widehat{A^{*}}$ (coefficients in $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$, which commutes with the modes since every plane generator anticommutes with both kernel generators, Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}). The density with channel array $M$ and shift $m$ is $\rho_{m}(M) = \widehat{S_{m}\otimes M}$, $(S_{m})_{k,k+m} = 1$ when $k, k + m \in W$ and zero otherwise; $S_{m}^{T} = S_{-m}$, so $\rho_{m}(M)^{*} = \rho_{-m}(M^{*})$.

\emph{(i).} $[S_{m}\otimes M, S_{l}\otimes M'] = S_{m}S_{l}\otimes MM' - S_{l}S_{m}\otimes M'M$, and $(S_{m}S_{l})_{k,k+m+l} = 1$ exactly when $k, k + m, k + m + l \in W$, $(S_{l}S_{m})_{k,k+l+m} = 1$ exactly when $k, k + l, k + l + m \in W$, all other entries zero. This is the general identity. For $m = q$, $l = -q$ and $M'$ replaced by $M'^{*}$, $S_{q}S_{-q}$ and $S_{-q}S_{q}$ are the diagonal projections onto $W \cap (W - q)$ and $W \cap (W + q)$, which gives the equal-shift form; for one channel and $d = 1$ it is Theorem \claimref{hawking.current-commutator-exactly-edge-split}. Translation by $q$ is a bijection of $W \cap (W - q)$ onto $W \cap (W + q)$, so the two sets have the same size; removing their intersection gives $|E_{-}(q)| = |E_{+}(q)|$. For $M = M' = \id$ the common part cancels and $[\rho_{q}, \rho_{q}^{*}] = n(E_{-}(q)) - n(E_{+}(q))$, so for every state $\omega$, $\omega([\rho_{q}, \rho_{q}^{*}]) = \sum_{E_{-}(q)}\bar n_{k} - \sum_{E_{+}(q)}\bar n_{k}$ with $\bar n_{k} = \omega(n_{k})$, the total occupation of momentum $k$.

\emph{(ii).} If $\bar n_{k} = c$ on $E_{-}(q) \cup E_{+}(q)$, the value is $c(|E_{-}(q)| - |E_{+}(q)|) = 0$. For $q \ne q'$, (i) with $m = q$, $l = -q'$ writes $[\rho_{q}, \rho_{q'}^{*}]$ as a sum of bilinears $a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k+q-q',\beta}$ with $k \ne k + q - q'$, whose expectation vanishes in every state diagonal in momentum ($\omega(a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{l,\beta}) = 0$ for $k \ne l$), as are all the seas below. A state that fills, at each momentum, one mode $c_{k}^{*} = \sum_{\alpha}u_{k,\alpha}a_{k,\alpha}^{*}$ ($u_{k}$ a unit channel vector) and leaves its orthogonal complement empty has $\bar n_{k} = |u_{k}|^{2} = 1$ at every $k$; this is the lower-band sea of any two-channel $h(k)$ with nondegenerate bands at the strip momenta, in particular the relativistic sea of a two-component field in any dimension, and the $1 + 1$ Dirac sea of $h(k) = k\sigma_{3}$ (channel $1$ filled for $k < 0$, channel $2$ for $k \ge 0$). A sea $F$ with $F \subset W \cap (W - q) \cap (W + q)$ meets neither strip, so $\bar n = 0$ there; this condition depends on $q$ (for $d = 1$, $N = 3$, $F = \{-2, -1, 0\}$ the values at $q = 1, 2, 3$ are $0, 1, 1$). In the uniform cases $\omega([\rho_{q}, \rho_{q}^{*}]) = 0$ at every $q$ and on every window, and for the bounded sea at every $q$ for which it is clear of the strips; with the vanishing forms at $q \ne q'$, the total density modes carry no canonical pair in those states. For the $1 + 1$ Dirac sea one channel alone, $\rho_{q}(E_{11})$, has the value $\min(q, |I| - q)$ on a window $I$ of $|I|$ momenta (centred so that half are negative), and the other channel the opposite value: the two chiralities cancel in the total, while each channel-resolved density alone carries the one-dimensional value.

\emph{(iii).} For $W = \{-N, \dots, N - 1\}^{d}$, $q_{1} \ge 0$, and $F = \{k_{1} < 0\}$ in each of $c$ channels: $W \cap (W \mp q)$ is a product of intervals, and in each transverse direction $j$ both have $2N - |q_{j}|$ points; in the first direction, $\{k_{1} : k_{1}, k_{1} + q_{1} \in I\}$ contains $\min(N, 2N - q_{1})$ negative values and $\{k_{1} : k_{1}, k_{1} - q_{1} \in I\}$ contains $\max(N - q_{1}, 0)$, whose difference is $\min(q_{1}, 2N - q_{1})$. Multiplying gives the value, $0$ when $q_{1} = 0$; $q_{1} < 0$ follows by $\rho_{q}^{*} = \rho_{-q}$. On a vector that agrees with $F$ on $E_{-}(q) \cup E_{+}(q)$ the operator $n(E_{-}) - n(E_{+})$ acts as this number. Along a single null generator ($d = 1$) with the window centred at $0$ this is the edge-clean value of Theorem \claimref{hawking.current-commutator-exactly-edge-split}. A half-space is not needed for a nonzero value: by (i) any sea with unequally occupied strips gives one; counting on $W = \{-3, \dots, 2\}^{2}$ gives $3$ at $q = (1, 0)$ and $5$ at $q = (1, 1)$ for the quadrant $\{k_{1} < 0, k_{2} < 0\}$, and $5$ at $q = (1, 0)$ for $\{k_{1} + k_{2} < 0\}$. What singles out the half-space is that its value depends on $q$ only through $q_{1}$ and the overlaps, and is a scalar on the sea.

\emph{(iv).} With $M = \id$ and $M' = \sigma_{3}$ in (i), $[\rho_{q}, \rho_{q}(\sigma_{3})^{*}] = s_{3}(E_{-}(q)) - s_{3}(E_{+}(q))$ (the common part again cancels), $s_{3}(S) = \sum_{k\in S}a_{k}^{*}\sigma_{3}a_{k}$. In the sea of (ii) the one-particle density at $k$ is the projection onto $u_{k}$, $\omega(a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k,\beta}) = \bar u_{k,\alpha}u_{k,\beta}$, so $\omega(a_{k}^{*}Xa_{k}) = \langle u_{k}, Xu_{k}\rangle$. In the Pauli algebra $\Cl(3,0)$, where the channel arrays $\sigma_{i}$ represent the generators $e_{i}$ and half the matrix trace is the scalar part, the lower band of $h(k) = \sum_{i}k_{i}e_{i}$ is the projector $P_{-} = \tfrac12(1 - \hat k)$, $\hat k = k/|k|$: $Q(\hat k) = 1$ gives $P_{-}^{2} = P_{-}$ and $\hat kP_{-} = -P_{-}$, and $2\langle P_{-}e_{i}\rangle_{0} = -\hat k_{i}$. So $\omega(a_{k}^{*}\sigma_{3}a_{k}) = -k_{3}/|k|$. For $q = (0, \dots, 0, q)$ with $1 \le q < N$, the strip $E_{-}$ is the bottom $q$ layers in the last direction ($k_{3} < 0$) and $E_{+}$ the top $q$ layers ($k_{3} \ge N - q > 0$), $2q(2N)^{d-1}$ points in all, none at $k = 0$, and
\[
\omega([\rho_{q}, \rho_{q}(\sigma_{3})^{*}]) = \sum_{k\in E_{-}\cup E_{+}}\frac{|k_{3}|}{|k|} .
\]
For $P_{+} = \tfrac12(1 + \sigma_{3})$, normal with $P_{+}^{2} = P_{+}$, (i) gives $[\rho_{q}(P_{+}), \rho_{q}(P_{+})^{*}] = \sum_{E_{-}}a_{k}^{*}P_{+}a_{k} - \sum_{E_{+}}a_{k}^{*}P_{+}a_{k}$, with $\omega(a_{k}^{*}P_{+}a_{k}) = \tfrac12(1 - k_{3}/|k|)$; since $|E_{-}| = |E_{+}|$ the constant parts cancel and the value is $S/2$. For $d = 1$ every term of $S$ is $1$: $S = 2q$. For $d = 3$, $|k_{3}| \ge N - q$ on both strips and $|k|^{2} \le 3N^{2} < 4N^{2}$, so each term lies in $((N - q)/(2N), 1]$ and the sum lies in $(4qN(N - q), 8qN^{2}]$. The factor $(2N)^{d-1}$ counts the transverse momenta of the strips: per transverse momentum the value lies in $(q(N - q)/N, 2q]$, of order $q$ as in $d = 1$.

\emph{Checks.} The exact check verifies (i) in the algebra on a $2\times3$ window with one channel and a $2\times2$ window with two channels ($M = \id$, $M' = \id, \sigma_{3}, \sigma_{1}$), the general form with unequal shifts of both signs and $J$-valued arrays on the $2\times2$ two-channel window, and $|E_{-}| = |E_{+}|$ by counting for boxes in $d = 1, 2, 3$ and an irregular window; (ii) in the algebra for the $1 + 1$ Dirac sea and a sea with a rotated channel state on four momenta ($q = 1, 2, 3$), one channel alone giving $\min(q, 4 - q)$, and by counting for a bounded sea and uniform filling in $d = 3$, the $q$-dependence of the bounded-sea hypothesis ($0, 1, 1$), and a vanishing form at $q \ne q'$; (iii) by counting for $N = 2, 3$, $d = 2, 3$, every $q$, and in the algebra on a $4\times2$ window, and the quadrant and tilted counterexamples; (iv) the value $2q$ and the spin-resolved value $q$ in the algebra for $d = 1$ on six momenta ($q = 1, 2$), the Pauli projector at three rational unit vectors, and for $d = 3$, $N = 2, 3, 4$, the strip count and the two termwise bounds as integer inequalities.

synthesis.deposit-over-the-conformal-vac.formal:
Units $\hbar = c = 1$. \emph{Hypothesis:} the descended field near the descent is the Weyl-flat gravitational field on flat spacetime $\hb(b) = b/a(t)$, $t = x\cdot e_{0}$ the conformal time, $a$ smooth and positive on the collar where the deposit is set (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}; derived metric $a(t)^{2}$ times the flat one, a Robertson-Walker field, read through Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}), as for a descent of radiation type. Let $\psi$ be the massless Dirac field of Proposition \claimref{field-theory.second-quantisation} on it, $\chi = a^{3/2}\psi$ the conformally rescaled field, which solves the flat massless Dirac equation, and $\omega_{c}$ the conformal vacuum, the flat massless vacuum of $\chi$. A \emph{diagonal homogeneous deposit} is a gauge-invariant quasi-free state $\omega$ diagonal in the plane-wave quasi-particle modes of $\omega_{c}$ (no particle-antiparticle pair coherence, no coherence between momenta or helicities), with particle and antiparticle occupations $n_{+}(p), n_{-}(p) \in [0, 1]$ per comoving momentum $\vec p$ and helicity, $p = |\vec p|$; write $M_{k} = 2\int d^{3}p\,p^{k}\,(n_{+} + n_{-})$ and $R^{(\pm)} = \mathcal{G}_{\omega}^{(\pm)} - \mathcal{G}_{\omega_{c}}^{(\pm)}$ for the remainders of both orderings (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}(b)).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Reference; standard.)} $\omega_{c}$ is Hadamard.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Criterion; the standard flat criterion carried by conformal covariance; the converse given the moment lemma.)} If $M_{k} < \infty$ for every $k$, both remainders are smooth on $M \times M$ and $\omega$ is Hadamard. Conversely, if $\omega$ is Hadamard, every $M_{k}$ is finite. More precisely, $M_{0}, \dots, M_{j} < \infty$ gives remainders of class $C^{j}$, and a remainder of class $C^{2m+1}$ along a timelike line gives $M_{2m+1} < \infty$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The thermal deposit; proved.)} For the Fermi-Dirac profile $n_{\pm} = (e^{p/T} + 1)^{-1}$ (Theorem \claimref{hawking.i-state}; $T = a_{d}T_{d}$ comoving), $M_{k} \le 16\pi\,(k + 2)!\,T^{k + 3}$ for every $k$, so the thermal deposit is Hadamard; so is every diagonal deposit whose profile is bounded by $C_{N}(1 + p/T)^{-N}$ for every $N$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The shot-noise data do not decide it; proved.)} The profile $n_{\pm} = (1 + p/T)^{-6}$ has finite number, mean energy $\tfrac32 T$ and energy spread $c = \langle\omega^{2}\rangle/\langle\omega\rangle^{2} = \tfrac83$, so the shot term of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.quasi-free-deposit-is-vacuum-plus-shot-noise}(iv) is finite, while $M_{k} = \infty$ for every $k \ge 3$: its remainders are of class $C^{2}$ and not of class $C^{3}$ along a timelike line, and it is not Hadamard.
\item[(v)] \emph{(A finite number alone, Hadamard or not; proved.)} If $M_{0} < \infty$, then $|R^{(\pm)}(x, y)| \le (2\pi)^{-3}M_{0}\,a(x)^{-3/2}a(y)^{-3/2}$, a bounded remainder, so at every point $x_{0}$ the scaling limit of $\omega$ (weight $\tfrac32$ per leg) equals that of $\omega_{c}$, the flat massless vacuum in the local inertial coordinates $a(t_{0})(x - x_{0})$, even when $\omega$ is not Hadamard.
\end{enumerate}
So under the hypothesis the stored thermal deposit is a Hadamard state on the descent's collar; the number of quanta controls the scaling limit, the first two moments the shot noise, and the whole ultraviolet tail the Hadamard class.
synthesis.deposit-over-the-conformal-vac.technical:
The question is whether the state the descent deposits on the fields is a Hadamard state, the class on which a renormalised stress tensor exists and which the horizon premises need. The store describes the deposit as the vacuum plus quanta, with a bound on its fluctuations in terms of the number of quanta and their energy spread.

The result assumes that the descended field near the descent is of Robertson-Walker form with a smooth scale factor, as for a descent of radiation type; a kink in the scale factor would make the Hadamard condition undefined there. It treats the massless Dirac field, which is conformally the flat one, so the conformal vacuum is Hadamard, and deposits diagonal in that vacuum's particle modes, with no particle-antiparticle pair coherence. Such a deposit is Hadamard exactly when every moment of its occupation profile is finite. This is the standard flat-space criterion, carried over by conformal covariance: sufficiency by differentiating under the integral, necessity because odd time derivatives at coincidence weigh particles and antiparticles with the same sign, so their finiteness forces the moments.

The thermal profile decays exponentially and has every moment, so the thermal deposit is Hadamard. A profile falling as the sixth inverse power has a finite shot term, the kind of data the stored bound uses, yet infinite moments from the third on: it is twice but not three times differentiable at coincidence and not Hadamard. So the number of quanta does not decide the Hadamard property. A finite number alone still makes the remainder bounded, so the deposit looks like the vacuum at short distances even when it is not Hadamard. Transport-absent.
synthesis.deposit-over-the-conformal-vac.lay: When the universe's earlier phase handed its contents to the later one, it left the quantum fields in some state. Physics in a gravitational field needs that state to be of a particular well-behaved kind, called Hadamard, which roughly means it looks like empty space at very short distances in a smooth way. This result shows, for massless spin-one-half particles and assuming the young universe was uniform and expanding smoothly, that a thermal hand-over, the kind the series uses, is of that kind. It also shows that the series' earlier calculation of how much the hand-over can disturb things, which uses only how many particles there are and how their energies spread, cannot settle the question: what matters is how fast the number of particles falls off at high energy.
flags: massless Dirac field only: a massive field has no conformal vacuum; no massive analogue of the moment criterion is claimed

deposit diagonal in the plane-wave quasi-particle modes of the conformal vacuum, occupations independent of helicity; particle-antiparticle pair coherences, helicity coherences and coherences between momenta are not treated

descended field of Robertson-Walker form with smooth positive scale factor near the descent (as for a descent of radiation type): a stated hypothesis, not derived; on the Kasner branch the field is Weyl-curved and the result does not apply

proofs.main:
Units $\hbar = c = 1$; $\Cl(1,3)$ with $e_{0}^{2} = 1$, $e_{i}^{2} = -1$; the unit imaginary is $I_{4} = e_{0}e_{1}e_{2}e_{3}$ ($I_{4}^{2} = -1$, checked). Matrix forms are parenthetical readings of left multiplication.

\emph{Set-up.} The field $\hb(b) = b/a(t)$ has $\hb^{-1}(b) = a\,b$, so its derived metric is $g(u, v) = a^{2}\,u\cdot v$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}(i)), conformally flat, so the Weyl part of its field strength vanishes (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-conformal-covariance-of-massless-fields-and-local-conformal-flatness}(a)); $a$ is smooth and positive on the collar by hypothesis. The massless Dirac equation is conformally covariant with weight $\tfrac32$: $\psi = a^{-3/2}\chi$ solves it on $(\hb, \Omega)$ exactly when $\chi$ solves the flat massless equation (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-conformal-covariance-of-massless-fields-and-local-conformal-flatness}(b); the conformal transfer of null geodesics and wave-front sets is proved for every conformal factor in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.weyl-flat-fields-need-no-scaling-limit-premise-and-robertson-walker-generators-see-the-schwarzian}(i)), and the map is unitary for the conserved current, so the CAR algebras of $\psi$ and $\chi$ are identified. The flat massless vacuum of $\chi$ has (matrix reading, as in the stored kernels of Proposition \claimref{field-theory.second-quantisation}; the phases are numbers read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$) $\omega_{c}(\chi(x)\chi^{\dagger}(y)) = \int\frac{d^{3}p}{(2\pi)^{3}}\Lambda_{+}(\hat p)\,e^{-I_{4}p\cdot(x - y)}$ and the other ordering with $\Lambda_{-}$, where $p = |\vec p|(e_{0} + \hat p)$ is the null momentum, $\hat p$ the unit spatial vector ($\hat p^{2} = -1$) and $\Lambda_{\pm}(\hat p) = \tfrac12(1 \pm \hat p e_{0})$. The check verifies on Pythagorean directions that $(\hat p e_{0})^{2} = 1$, that $\Lambda_{\pm}$ are idempotent, complementary, mutually annihilating and self-adjoint for the Dirac adjoint ($e_{0}\tilde\Lambda e_{0} = \Lambda$), with scalar part $\tfrac12$, that $\Lambda_{+} = pe_{0}/(2p_{0})$ and $p\Lambda_{+} = 0$ on the null shell: orthogonal projectors of norm one onto the solutions.

\emph{The deposit's remainder.} In the quasi-particle modes of $\omega_{c}$ (annihilators $a_{\vec p}$ for particles, $b_{\vec p}$ for antiparticles), the deposit has $\omega(a^{\dagger}a) = n_{+}$ and $\omega(bb^{\dagger}) = 1 - n_{-}$ mode by mode, with no coherences and no pairing (gauge invariance and diagonality). Hence each remainder is a superposition of plane waves,
\[
R^{(\pm)}(x, y) = a(x)^{-3/2}a(y)^{-3/2}\sum_{h}\int\frac{d^{3}p}{(2\pi)^{3}}\Bigl(\epsilon^{\pm}_{+}\,n_{+}(p)\,\Pi_{+}\,e^{-I_{4}p\cdot(x - y)} + \epsilon^{\pm}_{-}\,n_{-}(p)\,\Pi_{-}\,e^{+I_{4}p\cdot(x - y)}\Bigr),
\]
summed over the helicities $h$, with signs $\epsilon = \pm 1$ fixed by the ordering and projector weights $\Pi_{\pm}$ of the form $\Lambda_{\pm}(\pm\hat p)$ (times a helicity projector), of norm one. The factor $a(x)^{-3/2}a(y)^{-3/2}$ is smooth and nonvanishing, so smoothness and boundedness of $R^{(\pm)}$ are those of the integral.

\emph{(i)} This is standard, and is proved for every conformal factor in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.weyl-flat-fields-need-no-scaling-limit-premise-and-robertson-walker-generators-see-the-schwarzian}(i): the flat null lines with affine parameter $\tilde\lambda$, $d\tilde\lambda = a^{2}d\lambda$, are the affine null geodesics of the derived metric (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}(iii)) and carry the flat covectors, so the relation $\sim$ and the sets $C^{\pm}$ of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition} are the same for the derived metric and the flat one. The flat massless vacuum satisfies $\mathrm{WF}'(\mathcal{G}^{(\pm)}) = C^{\pm}$ (Fact (b) for the flat field), and multiplication by the smooth nonvanishing $a(x)^{-3/2}a(y)^{-3/2}$ does not change a wave-front set (standard). So $\omega_{c}$ is Hadamard on $(\hb, \Omega)$.

\emph{(ii), sufficiency.} This is the standard flat-space criterion (rapid decrease of the occupation numbers), carried to the descended field by conformal covariance; the argument is recorded for completeness. For a null momentum $|p_{\mu}| \le p$ in every component, so every derivative of order $j$ of the integrand in $(x, y)$ is bounded by $p^{j}(n_{+} + n_{-})$ times a constant; if $M_{0}, \dots, M_{j} < \infty$ (the factor 2 in $M_{k}$ counts the helicities), dominated convergence gives remainders of class $C^{j}$, and if every $M_{k}$ is finite they are smooth. A smooth kernel has empty wave-front set, so $\mathrm{WF}'(\mathcal{G}^{(\pm)}_{\omega}) = \mathrm{WF}'(\mathcal{G}^{(\pm)}_{\omega_{c}}) = C^{\pm}$ and $\omega$ is Hadamard by (i).

\emph{(ii), necessity.} Suppose $\omega$ is Hadamard; by Fact (b) its remainders relative to the Hadamard $\omega_{c}$ are smooth. Restrict the ordering $\omega(\chi^{\dagger}(y)\chi(x))$ to a timelike line $x = y + \tau e_{0}$ and take the scalar part of the spin trace: $\phi(\tau) = \int e^{-I_{4}\nu\tau}\,d\mu(\nu)$ in the frequency $\nu$, where particles sit at $\nu = p$ with weight $+n_{+}$ and antiparticles at $\nu = -p$ with weight $-n_{-}$ (the sign of reordering $bb^{\dagger}$ against the vacuum), both times the positive spin trace. The measure $\mu$ is signed, but $\nu\,d\mu$ is positive: $p \cdot n_{+} \ge 0$ and $(-p)(-n_{-}) \ge 0$, and for every odd power $\nu^{2m+1}d\mu$ weighs particles and antiparticles alike by $p^{2m + 1}n_{\pm}$ (checked, with the even powers shown to mix signs). So $I_{4}\phi'$ is the Fourier transform of the positive tempered measure $\nu\,d\mu$. A positive tempered measure whose Fourier transform is continuous near $0$ is finite, and if the transform is of class $C^{2m}$ near $0$ the measure has a finite moment of order $2m$ (Bochner's theorem and the moment lemma for characteristic functions, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-bochner-theorem-moment-lemma-and-whitney-even-functions}(a), (b); the step uses that $(z + z^{-1} - 2)^{m} = (-1)^{m}|z - 1|^{2m}$ for unit $z = c + sI_{4}$, so the $2m$-th symmetric differences at coincidence are of one sign, checked on Pythagorean phases). Hence a remainder of class $C^{2m+1}$ along the line, for which $I_{4}\phi'$ is of class $C^{2m}$, gives $\int p^{2m + 1}(n_{+} + n_{-})\,d^{3}p < \infty$, that is $M_{2m+1} < \infty$, and smoothness gives every odd moment; the even ones follow from $p^{2m} \le 1 + p^{2m+1}$ and $n_{\pm} \le 1$ on $p < 1$.

\emph{(iii)} The thermal deposit has the Fermi-Dirac occupations of Theorem \claimref{hawking.i-state} in the comoving momenta. With $y = e^{-p/T} \in (0, 1]$, $n_{\mathrm{FD}} = y/(1 + y) \le y$ (checked on samples), and $\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{k}e^{-x}dx = k!$: the antiderivative is $-e^{-x}P_{k}(x)$ with $P_{k} = \sum_{j \le k}\tfrac{k!}{j!}x^{j}$, and $P_{k} - P_{k}' = x^{k}$, an exact polynomial identity (checked for $k \le 15$, with the factorials $0!, \dots, 7!$ and the bounds $16(k+2)!$ for $k \le 3$ asserted). So $M_{k} \le 2\cdot 2\cdot 4\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}p^{k + 2}e^{-p/T}dp = 16\pi(k + 2)!\,T^{k + 3}$ (two helicities, particles and antiparticles), finite for every $k$; by (ii) the thermal deposit is Hadamard. The exact moments are $16\pi(k + 2)!\,\eta(k + 3)T^{k+3}$ with $1 - 2^{-s} \le \eta(s) \le 1$ (alternating series, standard). The same bound holds whenever $n_{\pm} \le C_{N}(1 + p/T)^{-N}$ for every $N$.

\emph{(iv)} For $n = (1 + p/T)^{-6}$, substitute $q = u/(1 + u)$, $u = p/T$: $\int_{0}^{\infty}u^{2 + k}(1 + u)^{-6}du = \int_{0}^{1}q^{2 + k}(1 - q)^{2 - k}dq$, which is $\tfrac{1}{30}$, $\tfrac{1}{20}$, $\tfrac15$ for $k = 0, 1, 2$ (exact polynomial integrals, checked). So the number density, the mean energy $\tfrac{1/20}{1/30}T = \tfrac32 T$ and the energy spread $c = \tfrac{(1/5)(1/30)}{(1/20)^{2}} = \tfrac83$ are finite, and the shot term $(3c_{k}k^{3}/2\pi^{2}\bar n)^{1/2}$ of Proposition \claimref{synthesis.quasi-free-deposit-is-vacuum-plus-shot-noise}(iv) is finite ($c_{k} \le c(1 + k/\langle\omega\rangle)^{2}$ as there). For $k = 3$ the integrand is $q^{5}(1 - q)^{-1}$; on the piece $[1 - 2^{1 - j}, 1 - 2^{-j}]$ of length $2^{-j}$, $(1 - q)^{-1} \ge 2^{j - 1}$ and $q^{5} \ge (1 - 2^{1 - j})^{5}$, so each piece contributes at least $\tfrac12(1 - 2^{1-j})^{5} \ge \tfrac{1}{10}$ for $j \ge 3$ and the integral diverges (checked over forty pieces); since $u^{2 + k} \ge u^{5}$ for $u \ge 1$, every $M_{k}$ with $k \ge 3$ is infinite. By (ii) the remainders are of class $C^{2}$ and, since $M_{3} = \infty$, not of class $C^{3}$ along a timelike line; the deposit is not Hadamard. So the number of quanta and their energy spread, the data of the stored shot-noise bound, do not decide the Hadamard property. The profile is a valid occupation, $0 < n \le 1$.

\emph{(v)} With $\|\Pi_{\pm}\| = 1$, $|R^{(\pm)}(x, y)| \le a(x)^{-3/2}a(y)^{-3/2}(2\pi)^{-3}\sum_{h}\int d^{3}p\,(n_{+} + n_{-}) = (2\pi)^{-3}M_{0}\,a(x)^{-3/2}a(y)^{-3/2}$, the stated bound, finite when $M_{0}$ is, whether or not the higher moments are. Under the scaling about $x_{0}$ with weight $\tfrac32$ per leg, $(S_{l}R)(x, y) = l^{3}R(x_{0} + lx, x_{0} + ly)$, a remainder bounded by $C$ near $x_{0}$ is bounded by $l^{3}C \to 0$. The scaling limit of $\omega_{c}$ is the flat massless vacuum in the local inertial coordinates $a(t_{0})(x - x_{0})$: its kernel is $a(x)^{-3/2}a(y)^{-3/2}$ times the flat one, which is homogeneous of degree $-3$ (standard; computed in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.weyl-flat-fields-need-no-scaling-limit-premise-and-robertson-walker-generators-see-the-schwarzian}(i)). So the scaling limit of $\omega$ is the same, even when $\omega$ is not Hadamard; for Hadamard states this is that result's clause (i).

synthesis.electron-positron-to-muon-pair.technical:
With the conventions of one-loop electrodynamics in the spacetime algebra, the scattering of an electron and a positron into a muon pair is computed through the reduction formula. On shell, the propagator residue $p + m$ is twice the mass times an idempotent of trace two, so the spin sums of the external states are the real multivectors $p + m$ (particles) and $p - m$ (antiparticles); no imaginary unit enters.

At tree level the spin-averaged squared amplitude is the product of two Clifford traces, which reproduces the standard form exactly; for massless leptons it gives the $1 + \cos^{2}\theta$ distribution and $\sigma = 4\pi\alpha^{2}/(3s)$, and with the muon mass the threshold factor $\beta(3 - \beta^{2})/2$ (checked exactly at rational speeds, including threshold-free and massless limits).

At one loop the vacuum-polarisation insertion on the s-channel photon multiplies the tree amplitude by $1/(1 - \hat\Pi(s))$, the longitudinal part dropping between on-shell currents. Its absorptive part, the integral of $x(1-x)$ over the window where $x(1-x)s > m^{2}$, is $(\alpha/3)\beta(3 - \beta^{2})/2$ in size, which is exactly $s\sigma_{\mathrm{tree}}/(4\pi\alpha)$ for producing that fermion: the s-channel optical-theorem relation for the photon self-energy. The loop has no internal photon and the subtracted function does not depend on the regulator. At high energy the insertion is $(\alpha/(3\pi))(\ln(s/m^{2}) - 5/3)$, the running of the coupling, and under the Krein-form premise $Z_{1} = Z_{2}$ makes the charge renormalisation $Z_{3}^{1/2}$ alone. These are standard results, recomputed. Vertex and box corrections and soft-photon emission are not computed.
synthesis.electron-positron-to-muon-pair.lay: The series' algebra of spacetime now reproduces a standard textbook scattering prediction: an electron and a positron annihilate into a muon and an antimuon. The incoming and outgoing particles are fixed by algebraic projections built from their momenta, each picking out the particle's two spin states, and the rate comes out as the textbook formula, with the characteristic angular pattern and the suppression near the energy threshold for making the muons. At the next order the photon in the middle is dressed by virtual pairs; the part of this dressing that corresponds to real pairs being produced matches the rate computed at the first order exactly, one instance of the rule that probabilities add up to one, and the rest is the slow growth of the electric force with energy. Reading that growth as a change of the charge itself assumes the series' premise that the photon's states carry the standard indefinite measure.

proofs.main:
\emph{Conventions.} $\Cl(1,3)$ with signature $(+,-,-,-)$; vectors $p = p^{\mu}\gamma_{\mu}$, $\gamma^{\mu}$ the reciprocal frame; the matrix trace is $4\langle\cdot\rangle_{0}$ and the units of the Feynman rules, the field theory's unit $I_{4}$, are coefficients collected outside the product (the right unit) (\claimref{synthesis.one-loop-qed-in-the-spacetime-algebra}(1), (5)). The vertex is $\gamma^{\mu}$ with the coupling of \claimref{field-theory.coupled-system-tree-level}; the free Dirac fields and their two spin states per momentum are those of \claimref{field-theory.second-quantisation}. The s-channel photon at tree level couples conserved currents, so the stored photon suffices there. The polarisation loop inside the photon line is a fermion loop with no internal photon; the stored result computes it with Pauli-Villars fermions (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-one-loop-integrals-and-pauli-villars-regulators}), and the subtracted function $\hat\Pi$ used here does not depend on the regulator (a regulator-free construction with no Krein form is \claimref{synthesis.one-loop-vacuum-polarisation-extends-without-a-regulator-and-ward-preserving-extensions-differ-only-by-the-renormalisation-constants}(ii)). Only the charge-renormalisation sentence of Step 5 uses loops with an internal photon, and so the Krein-form premise \claimref{synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-inner-product-for-gauge-fields}.

\emph{Step 1 (LSZ).} Let $Q(p) = m^{2}$. Then $p^{2} = m^{2}$ as multivectors, so $(p + m)^{2} = p^{2} + 2mp + m^{2} = 2m(p + m)$, $(p - m)^{2} = -2m(p - m)$ and $(p + m)(p - m) = p^{2} - m^{2} = 0$; $\langle p\rangle_{0} = 0$ gives $4\langle p \pm m\rangle_{0} = \pm 4m$. So for $m \neq 0$, $P_{\pm} = (m \pm p)/(2m)$ are complementary idempotents with $4\langle P_{\pm}\rangle_{0} = 2$: each projects the spinor module onto a two-dimensional space, the two spin states. Off shell $(p - m)S(p) = 1$ with $S(p) = (p + m)/(Q(p) - m^{2})$, and $(Q(p) - m^{2})S(p) = p + m$, the residue at the pole. The reduction formula \cite{LSZ1955} (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-lsz-reduction-ward-identity-and-the-second-qed-beta-coefficient}(i); Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-one-loop-integrals-and-pauli-villars-regulators}(v)) writes an S-matrix element as the amputated Green function at the poles times $Z_{2}^{1/2}$ per external fermion; at tree level $Z_{2} = 1$. Summed over spins, an outgoing particle and an incoming particle contribute $p + m$ (the residue), an incoming antiparticle and an outgoing antiparticle $p - m$ (the residue of $S(-p)$ up to sign). For $m = 0$ the residue $p$ is nilpotent ($p^{2} = 0$) and $4\langle\cdot\rangle_{0}$ of $p$ times anything is the massless spin sum. The check verifies these identities at three rational on-shell momenta (masses $4$, $12$, $0$) and the residue at an off-shell momentum.

\emph{Step 2 (tree amplitude).} With $q = p_{1} + p_{2}$, the amplitude is $M = \frac{e^{2}}{s}\,[\bar v(p_{2})\gamma^{\mu}u(p_{1})][\bar u(p_{3})\gamma_{\mu}v(p_{4})]$ (units collected in front). Squaring and summing over spins by Step 1, $\tfrac14\sum|M|^{2} = \tfrac{e^{4}}{4s^{2}}T_{e}^{\mu\nu}T_{\mu\nu}^{\mu}$ with $T_{e}^{\mu\nu} = 4\langle(p_{2} - m_{e})\gamma^{\mu}(p_{1} + m_{e})\gamma^{\nu}\rangle_{0}$, $T^{\mu}_{\mu\nu} = 4\langle(p_{3} + m_{\mu})\gamma_{\mu}(p_{4} - m_{\mu})\gamma_{\nu}\rangle_{0}$. Expanding $4\langle abcd\rangle_{0} = 4[(a\cdot b)(c\cdot d) - (a\cdot c)(b\cdot d) + (a\cdot d)(b\cdot c)]$ and $4\langle ab\rangle_{0} = 4a\cdot b$ gives the standard form of clause (2); the check computes the two traces and their contraction exactly at three rational configurations (both masses, electron massless, both massless) and compares with the standard form, with a control (the particle residue in place of the positron's fails). Massless kinematics in the centre-of-mass frame, $p_{1} = E(\gamma_{0} + \gamma_{3})$, $p_{3} = E(\gamma_{0} + \sin\theta\,\gamma_{1} + \cos\theta\,\gamma_{3})$, give $\tfrac14\sum|M|^{2} = e^{4}(1 + \cos^{2}\theta)$ (checked at five rational angles; a polynomial of degree two in $\cos\theta$ is fixed by three). With $d\sigma/d\Omega = \tfrac{1}{64\pi^{2}s}\tfrac{|p_{3}|}{|p_{1}|}\tfrac14\sum|M|^{2}$ (standard two-body phase space \cite{PeskinSchroeder1995}) and $e^{2} = 4\pi\alpha$: $d\sigma/d\Omega = \tfrac{\alpha^{2}}{4s}(1 + \cos^{2}\theta)$ and $\sigma = 2\pi\tfrac{\alpha^{2}}{4s}\int_{-1}^{1}(1 + c^{2})\,dc = \tfrac{4\pi\alpha^{2}}{3s}$. For $m_{e} = 0$ and muon speed $\beta$ ($m_{\mu} = \tfrac{\sqrt s}{2}(1 - \beta^{2})^{1/2}$) the trace result is a polynomial of degree two in $c = \cos\theta$; it is fixed by $c = -1, 0, 1$, checked at $c = 3/5$, and $\sigma\,s/(\pi\alpha^{2}) = \tfrac{\beta}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}\tfrac{|M|^{2}}{e^{4}}dc = \tfrac43\cdot\tfrac{\beta(3 - \beta^{2})}{2}$ at $\beta = \tfrac35, \tfrac45, \tfrac{12}{13}, 1$, exactly. Since both sides are polynomials in $\beta$ of degree three after multiplying by $s^{2}$ and fixing $s$, four values of $\beta$ establish the identity at that $s$, and both scale as $1/s$.

\emph{Step 3 (one loop: the insertion).} The photon two-point function with polarisation insertions is, in a covariant gauge (the unit of the Feynman rules the field theory's unit $I_{4}$, numbers read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$), $\frac{-I_{4}}{q^{2}(1 - \hat\Pi(q^{2}))}\bigl(g_{\mu\nu} - \frac{q_{\mu}q_{\nu}}{q^{2}}\bigr) + (\text{gauge part})\frac{q_{\mu}q_{\nu}}{q^{4}}$, by transversality of the stored polarisation (\claimref{synthesis.one-loop-qed-in-the-spacetime-algebra}(2)). Between on-shell currents every $q_{\mu}$ term vanishes: $4\langle(p_{2} - m)\,q\,(p_{1} + m)\gamma^{\nu}\rangle_{0} = 0$ for $q = p_{1} + p_{2}$, because $(p_{2} - m)(p_{1} + p_{2})(p_{1} + m) = (p_{2} - m)[(p_{1} - m) + (p_{2} + m)](p_{1} + m) = 0$ by Step 1; the check verifies this for both currents and every $\nu$, with the control $q = p_{1} - p_{2}$, which does not drop. So the s-channel amplitude is $M_{\mathrm{tree}}/(1 - \hat\Pi(s))$, with $\hat\Pi(s) = \Pi(s) - \Pi(0)$ the on-shell subtracted function of the stored result: $\hat\Pi(s) = -\tfrac{2\alpha}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}x(1 - x)\ln\frac{m^{2}}{m^{2} - x(1-x)s - I_{4}0}dx$ (\cite{PeskinSchroeder1995}, sec. 7.5, eqs. (7.90) to (7.92); the regulator scale cancels in the subtraction).

\emph{Step 4 (absorptive part and the optical theorem).} For $s > 4m^{2}$ the argument $m^{2} - x(1-x)s$ is negative exactly on the window $x_{-} < x < x_{+}$, $x_{\pm} = (1 \pm \beta)/2$, since $x_{\pm}(1 - x_{\pm}) = (1 - \beta^{2})/4 = m^{2}/s$ (checked). There $\ln\frac{m^{2}}{A - I_{4}0} = \ln\frac{m^{2}}{|A|} + I_{4}\pi$ ($\mathrm{Im}$ the coefficient of $I_{4}$), so $\mathrm{Im}\,\hat\Pi(s + I_{4}0) = -2\alpha\int_{x_{-}}^{x_{+}}(x - x^{2})dx = -\tfrac{\alpha}{6}\beta(3 - \beta^{2})$, exactly (checked at four rational $\beta$; the integral is the polynomial $\beta(3 - \beta^{2})/12$). By Step 2, $s\,\sigma_{\mathrm{tree}}(e^{+}e^{-} \to f\bar f)/(4\pi\alpha) = \tfrac{\alpha}{4}\cdot\tfrac43\cdot\tfrac{\beta(3 - \beta^{2})}{2} = \tfrac{\alpha}{6}\beta(3 - \beta^{2})$, the same. This is the s-channel optical-theorem relation for the photon self-energy: the discontinuity of the one-loop photon line is the phase-space integral of the squared tree amplitude for producing the pair (\cite{PeskinSchroeder1995}, sec. 7.3; argued here, the two sides computed). Full unitarity of the S-matrix at order $e^{4}$ also involves $e^{+}e^{-} \to \gamma\gamma$, the t-channel and box cuts, which are not computed.

\emph{Step 5 (large $s$ and the charge).} For $s \gg m^{2}$, $\ln\frac{m^{2}}{|m^{2} - x(1-x)s|} = -\ln\frac{s}{m^{2}} - \ln(x(1-x)) + O(m^{2}/s)$, so $\mathrm{Re}\,\hat\Pi = \tfrac{2\alpha}{\pi}[\tfrac16\ln\tfrac{s}{m^{2}} + J]$ with $J = \int_{0}^{1}x(1-x)\ln(x(1-x))\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{1}(x - x^{2})\ln x\,dx = 2(-\tfrac14 + \tfrac19) = -\tfrac{5}{18}$, by $\int_{0}^{1}x^{n}\ln x\,dx = -1/(n+1)^{2}$: $\mathrm{Re}\,\hat\Pi = \tfrac{\alpha}{3\pi}(\ln\tfrac{s}{m^{2}} - \tfrac53)$ (the rationals checked). In multiplicative renormalisation the charge is $e = Z_{1}^{-1}Z_{2}Z_{3}^{1/2}e_{0}$ (the vertex counterterm $Z_{1}$, the fermion field factor $Z_{2}^{1/2}$ on either side of the vertex, which LSZ supplies on external legs, and the photon field factor $Z_{3}^{1/2}$); under the Krein-form premise, with $Z_{1} = Z_{2}$ (\claimref{synthesis.one-loop-qed-in-the-spacetime-algebra}(4); Ward's identity, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-lsz-reduction-ward-identity-and-the-second-qed-beta-coefficient}(ii)) the fermion factors cancel and $e = Z_{3}^{1/2}e_{0}$, so the insertion is the running coupling $\alpha(s) = \alpha/(1 - \mathrm{Re}\,\hat\Pi(s))$ at this order (argued). Not computed: the vertex and box corrections and real soft-photon emission, whose infrared divergences cancel only in the inclusive rate.

\emph{Status.} Clause (1) proved (algebra); clause (2) computed exactly (an identity of polynomials, sampled at rational kinematics) with the phase-space formula imported; clause (3) computed for the absorptive part and the constant, argued for the optical-theorem reading and the charge renormalisation. All standard (LSZ 1955; Peskin and Schroeder secs. 5.1, 7.3, 7.5), recomputed in the spacetime algebra. Transport-absent; the spacetime algebra is convenient.
