synthesis.helicity-one-pair-modes-on-a-n.formal:
Let the modes on one null generator carry a generator momentum $k$ in the window $I = \{-N, \dots, N - 1\}$ and a channel $\alpha$ in a finite set; each mode $(k, \alpha)$ is a tower plane with $a_{k,\alpha}^{*} = v$, $a_{k,\alpha} = w$ (Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}), with the adjoint $*$ ($v^{*} = w$). Numbers are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$, $J = g_{1}g_{2}$ the kernel bivector, which commutes with every mode, $J^{2} = -1$, $J^{*} = -J$. For a channel matrix $M$ with entries in $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ ($M^{*}$ its conjugate transpose) and $q \ge 0$ let $\rho_{q}(M) = \sum_{k, k+q \in I}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}M_{\alpha\beta}a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k+q,\beta}$. The transverse rotation by $\theta$ about the generator is the mode rotation $U(\theta) = \exp(\theta J\sum_{k,\alpha}w_{\alpha}n_{k,\alpha})$ of \claimref{synthesis.ladder-bosons-inherit-spin-statistics-from-the-single-modes}(i), which acts by $a_{k,\alpha} \mapsto e^{-\theta w_{\alpha}J}a_{k,\alpha}$, with real weights $w_{\alpha}$, $W = \mathrm{diag}(w_{\alpha})$; the two chirality channels of a Dirac species have $w = \pm\tfrac12$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.light-ray-good-part-of-a-spinor-is-two-chirality-arrays}(iv)). $\rho_{q}(M)$ has helicity $h$ if the rotation multiplies it by $e^{h\theta J}$. The chiral sea $\Omega$ has every channel filled for $k < 0$ and empty for $k \ge 0$; a vector is edge-clean at depth $q$ if the lowest $q$ momenta are filled and the highest $q$ empty in every channel.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Window identity; the case $d = 1$, equal shifts, of \claimref{synthesis.density-modes-bosonise-only-along-one-null-direction}(i), the level-one $\mathfrak{u}(n)$ current algebra on a window.)} $[\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M')^{*}] = \sum_{k, k+q \in I}a_{k}^{*}MM'^{*}a_{k} - \sum_{k, k-q \in I}a_{k}^{*}M'^{*}Ma_{k}$ exactly, with $a_{k}^{*}Xa_{k} = \sum X_{\alpha\beta}a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k,\beta}$; on edge-clean vectors it acts as $q\operatorname{tr}(M'^{*}M) + \rho_{0}([M, M'^{*}])$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Normality.)} For $N > q$, $[\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M')^{*}]$ is a scalar on the edge-clean vectors if and only if $[M, M'^{*}] = 0$; so $\rho_{q}(M)$ is a canonical boson there (value $q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M)$) if and only if $M$ is normal.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Helicity.)} $\rho_{q}(M)$ has helicity $h$ if and only if $[W, M] = hM$. For $h \ne 0$ such an $M$ is nilpotent, hence, if nonzero, not normal: a pair mode of helicity $\pm1$ is never a canonical boson on the edge-clean vectors, its commutator there carrying the operator $\rho_{0}([M, M^{*}])$ (for $M = E_{+-}$ the difference of the channel numbers). If $\rho_{q}(M_{1}), \rho_{q}(M_{2})$ rotate as a vector ($J[W, M_{1}] = M_{2}$, $J[W, M_{2}] = -M_{1}$) and $[M_{i}, M_{j}^{*}] = 0$ for all $i, j$, then $M_{1} = M_{2} = 0$: no two pair modes with central mutual commutators form a rotation doublet. Normal helicity-zero modes (the channel densities among them) are canonical bosons.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Quasi-spin.)} Let $M^{2} = 0$, $r = \operatorname{rank}M$, $N \ge q \ge 1$, $B = \rho_{q}(M)^{*}$. Then $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = (p!)^{2}e_{p}(x)$, $x$ the $qr$ numbers $\sigma_{s}^{2}$ (singular values of $M$, each repeated $q$ times), so $B^{p}\Omega = 0$ for $p > qr$ and $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} < p!\,|B\Omega|^{2p}$ for $p \ge 2$. For $M = E_{+-}$: $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = (p!)^{2}\binom{q}{p}$ and $[\rho_{q}(M), B]B^{p}\Omega = (q - 2p)B^{p}\Omega$, the quasi-spin of $q$ sites.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Positivity.)} For every state $\omega$ of the tower and every $X$ with $\omega(X^{*}X) = 0$, $\omega([X, X^{*}]) = \omega(XX^{*}) \ge 0$. On the chiral sea every $\rho_{q}(M)$, $q \ge 1$, annihilates $\Omega$ and $\omega_{\Omega}([\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M)^{*}]) = q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M)$; on the reversed sea the value is $-q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M)$ and $\rho_{q}(M)^{*}$ annihilates. So, for the tower's positive adjoint, no pair mode of a tower state annihilates the state with a negative commutator, as the timelike polarisation of (K1) in Premise \claimref{synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-inner-product-for-gauge-fields} would. The first sentence holds for every element $X$ of every algebra with a positive state; it is the reason Gupta and Bleuler need an indefinite form, not a property of pair modes. With a Krein adjoint $\eta X^{*}\eta$, $\eta$ a self-adjoint involution, a pair mode can be the timelike mode: on two modes with $\eta = 1 - 2n_{2}$, $X = a_{1}^{*}a_{2}$ and $\Omega$ the vector with mode $1$ filled and mode $2$ empty, $X\Omega = 0$, $\eta X^{*}\eta = -X^{*}$ and $[X, \eta X^{*}\eta]\Omega = -\Omega$.
\end{enumerate}
Clauses (i) to (v) are proved. \emph{Reading (argued).} On the window restriction of the null vacuum, the chiral sea (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(vi)), the exact pair bosons are helicity-zero density waves; a helicity-one quantum about the generator built from pairs is a quasi-spin, of finite capacity $qr$, canonical only in the contraction over many two-level sites, with the channel-number difference as the obstruction operator; for transversally smeared flip modes over many generators that contraction is the mean-square statement of \claimref{synthesis.null-plane-photon-data-and-the-pair-currents-of-the-generators}(v). So the tower gives the photon's canonical relations from pairs at most as a contraction, and no pair mode is the timelike mode of (K1) for the tower's positive adjoint; with a Krein adjoint $\eta X^{*}\eta$ (as (KF) and \claimref{synthesis.self-adjoint-brst-charge-needs-a-krein-form-and-the-tower-supplies-the-ghosts} construct it) a pair mode can be, so (v) does not exclude (KF). The stored elementary photon (\claimref{field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes}) and (KF) are unchanged.
synthesis.helicity-one-pair-modes-on-a-n.technical: Take the modes on one null generator, labelled by a generator momentum $k$ in the window $I = \{-N, \dots, N - 1\}$ and a channel in a finite set, each a tower plane, with numbers in $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ ($J$ the kernel bivector, commuting with every mode). Pair modes are $\rho_{q}(M) = \sum_{k}a_{k}^{*}Ma_{k+q}$ for a channel matrix $M$; the rotation about the generator multiplies channel $\alpha$ by $e^{-\theta w_{\alpha}J}$, with weights $\pm\tfrac12$ for the two chirality channels of a Dirac species. (i) Exactly, $[\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M')^{*}]$ is the sum of $a_{k}^{*}MM'^{*}a_{k}$ over $k$ with $k + q$ in the window minus the sum of $a_{k}^{*}M'^{*}Ma_{k}$ over $k$ with $k - q$ in the window; on vectors whose lowest $q$ momenta are filled and highest $q$ empty it is $q\operatorname{tr}(M'^{*}M) + \rho_{0}([M, M'^{*}])$. (ii) With a bulk momentum present, that is a scalar exactly when $[M, M'^{*}] = 0$, so $\rho_{q}(M)$ is a canonical boson exactly when $M$ is normal. (iii) Helicity $h$ means $[W, M] = hM$; for $h = \pm1$ the matrix is nilpotent and so, if nonzero, not normal: the commutator keeps the channel-number difference. Two linear polarisations rotating into each other cannot both be canonical with central mutual commutators, since $M_{1} \mp JM_{2}$ would be normal and nilpotent. Normal helicity-zero modes, such as the channel densities, are exact bosons. (iv) On the chiral sea a nilpotent mode of rank $r$ at momentum $q$ is a quasi-spin of $qr$ two-level sites: $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = (p!)^{2}e_{p}$, strictly below the Bose value for $p \ge 2$ and zero beyond $qr$ quanta; for the flip $E_{+-}$ the normalised commutator on $p$ quanta is $1 - 2p/q$. (v) A mode that annihilates a positive state has a nonnegative commutator in it, so for the positive adjoint no pair mode is the timelike Gupta-Bleuler mode that the Krein premise (KF) uses; this holds for every algebra with a positive state, and with a Krein adjoint $\eta X^{*}\eta$ a pair mode can be that mode, so (KF) is not excluded. Reading (argued): the null vacuum's exact pair bosons are helicity-zero density waves; helicity-one pair quanta exist only as the contraction of a quasi-spin over many sites (for smeared flip modes over many generators, the mean-square statement of \claimref{synthesis.null-plane-photon-data-and-the-pair-currents-of-the-generators}(v)); the elementary photon and (KF) stay as stored.
synthesis.helicity-one-pair-modes-on-a-n.lay: The graph already shows that ripples in the density of the fermions filling a light ray behave exactly like bosons. This result asks whether such ripples could be photons, which spin about their direction of motion (helicity one). On a single light ray the answer is no: the ripples that are exactly bosons do not spin, and the ripples that do spin behave like a finite collection of two-state switches, which fill up after a few quanta and only approach boson behaviour when very many of them are pooled. The indefinite bookkeeping that standard photon quantisation uses for its unphysical time-like polarisation also cannot come from these ripples with the fermions' own positive bookkeeping, because every state of the fermions has positive probabilities; an indefinite bookkeeping can still be imposed on them, as the standard construction does.

proofs.main:
\emph{Preliminaries.} The window identity (i) is the case $d = 1$ with equal shifts of the strip identity of \claimref{synthesis.density-modes-bosonise-only-along-one-null-direction}(i), the level-one $\mathfrak{u}(n)$ current algebra on a window; it is proved again here in the form used. The unit $J$ is the one justified by \claimref{synthesis.kernel-bivector-is-the-unit-of-hermitian-boson-fields-on-the-tower}, and the rotation in (iii) is the mode rotation of \claimref{synthesis.ladder-bosons-inherit-spin-statistics-from-the-single-modes}(i). By Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors} the modes $a_{x}^{*} = v_{x}$, $a_{x} = w_{x}$ ($x = (k, \alpha)$) satisfy $\{a_{x}, a_{y}^{*}\} = \delta_{xy}$, $\{a_{x}, a_{y}\} = 0$, and $v_{x}^{*} = w_{x}$. $J = g_{1}g_{2}$ has $J^{2} = -g_{1}^{2}g_{2}^{2} = -1$ and $J^{*} = (-g_{2})(-g_{1}) = g_{2}g_{1} = -J$; every plane generator anticommutes with $g_{1}$ and with $g_{2}$ (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}), so $J$ commutes with every mode, and $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ is a field ($\cong \C$, conjugation $J \mapsto -J$) commuting with the mode algebra. Channel vectors and matrices have entries in it, with the positive Hermitian form $\langle u, u'\rangle = \sum_{\alpha}\bar u_{\alpha}u'_{\alpha}$; for a channel vector $u$ the element $c_{k}(u) = \sum_{\alpha}\bar u_{\alpha}a_{k,\alpha}$ is a mode, and orthonormal $u$'s give modes obeying the same relations. For a matrix $A$ on the one-particle index set (momenta of $I$ times channels) write $\hat A = \sum_{x,y}A_{xy}a_{x}^{*}a_{y}$. From the relations, $[a_{x}^{*}a_{y}, a_{z}^{*}a_{u}] = \delta_{yz}a_{x}^{*}a_{u} - \delta_{ux}a_{z}^{*}a_{y}$, hence
\[
[\hat A, \hat B] = \widehat{[A, B]}, \qquad (\hat A)^{*} = \widehat{A^{*}} ,
\]
the second because $(c\,a_{x}^{*}a_{y})^{*} = \bar c\,a_{y}^{*}a_{x}$. Now $\rho_{q}(M) = \widehat{S_{q}\otimes M}$, where $S_{q}$ is the partial shift with $(S_{q})_{k,k+q} = 1$ for $k, k + q \in I$ and zero otherwise, and $\rho_{q}(M')^{*} = \widehat{S_{q}^{T}\otimes M'^{*}}$.

\emph{(i).} $[S_{q}\otimes M, S_{q}^{T}\otimes M'^{*}] = S_{q}S_{q}^{T}\otimes MM'^{*} - S_{q}^{T}S_{q}\otimes M'^{*}M$, and $S_{q}S_{q}^{T}$, $S_{q}^{T}S_{q}$ are the diagonal projections onto $\{k : k + q \in I\}$ and $\{k : k - q \in I\}$. This is the window identity. Write the first set as $I$ minus the top $q$ momenta and the second as $I$ minus the bottom $q$:
\[
[\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M')^{*}] = \rho_{0}([M, M'^{*}]) - \sum_{k\ \mathrm{top}}a_{k}^{*}MM'^{*}a_{k} + \sum_{k\ \mathrm{bottom}}a_{k}^{*}M'^{*}Ma_{k} .
\]
On an edge-clean vector every top mode is empty, so $a_{k,\beta}$ annihilates it for $k$ in the top $q$; every bottom mode is filled, so $a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k,\beta}$ acts on it as $\delta_{\alpha\beta}$. The last sum therefore acts as $q\operatorname{tr}(M'^{*}M)$. For $M = M'$ and a single channel this is the edge identity of Theorem \claimref{hawking.current-commutator-exactly-edge-split}.

\emph{(ii).} If $[M, M'^{*}] = 0$ the value on edge-clean vectors is the scalar $q\operatorname{tr}(M'^{*}M)$. Conversely let $X = [M, M'^{*}] \ne 0$; $\operatorname{tr}X = 0$. Since $N > q$ there is a bulk momentum $k_{0}$ (neither top nor bottom). Let $\psi_{0}$ be the edge-clean vector in which every momentum other than $k_{0}$ is filled in every channel or empty in every channel, and $k_{0}$ is empty, and consider $c_{k_{0}}(u)^{*}\psi_{0}$, one particle at $k_{0}$ in the channel state $u$. At a filled momentum $a_{k}^{*}Xa_{k}$ acts as $\operatorname{tr}X = 0$, at an empty one as $0$, and at $k_{0}$ it maps $c_{k_{0}}(u)^{*}\psi_{0}$ to $c_{k_{0}}(Xu)^{*}\psi_{0}$. If $\rho_{0}(X)$ were a scalar on all edge-clean vectors, every $u$ would be an eigenvector of $X$ with one eigenvalue, so $X$ would be a multiple of the identity matrix, and $\operatorname{tr}X = 0$ makes it zero. So $[\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M')^{*}]$ is a scalar on the edge-clean vectors if and only if $[M, M'^{*}] = 0$; for $M = M'$, if and only if $M$ is normal.

\emph{(iii).} The rotation $a_{k,\alpha} \mapsto e^{-\theta w_{\alpha}J}a_{k,\alpha}$ preserves the relations (the factors are unit elements of $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ commuting with the modes), and $(e^{-\theta w_{\alpha}J}a_{k,\alpha})^{*} = a_{k,\alpha}^{*}e^{\theta w_{\alpha}J}$, so $a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k+q,\beta} \mapsto e^{\theta(w_{\alpha} - w_{\beta})J}a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k+q,\beta}$ and $\rho_{q}(M) \mapsto \rho_{q}(e^{\theta JW}Me^{-\theta JW})$. This equals $e^{h\theta J}\rho_{q}(M)$ for every $\theta$ exactly when every nonzero entry has $w_{\alpha} - w_{\beta} = h$, that is $[W, M] = hM$. Then a nonzero entry of $M^{n}$ needs $w_{\alpha} - w_{\beta} = nh$, impossible once $n|h|$ exceeds the spread of the weights: $M$ is nilpotent. A normal nilpotent matrix is zero: normality gives $|Mx|^{2} = \langle x, M^{*}Mx\rangle = \langle x, MM^{*}x\rangle = |M^{*}x|^{2}$, so $\ker M = \ker M^{*} = (\operatorname{im}M)^{\perp}$; if $M^{2}x = 0$ then $Mx \in \ker M \cap \operatorname{im}M = 0$, so $\ker M^{2} = \ker M$, and by induction $\ker M^{n} = \ker M$, which is everything. Hence for $h \ne 0$ and $M \ne 0$, $[M, M^{*}] \ne 0$ and by (ii) $\rho_{q}(M)$ is not a canonical boson on the edge-clean vectors; its commutator there is $q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M) + \rho_{0}([M, M^{*}])$. For the two chirality channels of a Dirac species the weights are $\pm\tfrac12$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.light-ray-good-part-of-a-spinor-is-two-chirality-arrays}(iv)), so the helicity-one matrices are the multiples of $E_{+-}$ and the helicity-minus-one matrices those of $E_{-+}$; for $M = E_{+-}$, $[M, M^{*}] = E_{++} - E_{--}$ and $\rho_{0}([M, M^{*}])$ is the difference of the numbers in the two channels.
For the doublet, the rotation acts as $\rho_{q}(M_{1}) \mapsto \cos\theta\,\rho_{q}(M_{1}) + \sin\theta\,\rho_{q}(M_{2})$, $\rho_{q}(M_{2}) \mapsto -\sin\theta\,\rho_{q}(M_{1}) + \cos\theta\,\rho_{q}(M_{2})$ exactly when $J[W, M_{1}] = M_{2}$ and $J[W, M_{2}] = -M_{1}$ (differentiate at $\theta = 0$; conversely the linear system integrates to the rotation). Put $M_{\pm} = M_{1} \mp JM_{2}$. Then $J[W, M_{\pm}] = M_{2} \pm JM_{1} = \pm J M_{\pm}$, so $[W, M_{\pm}] = \pm M_{\pm}$, and $M_{\pm}$ is nilpotent. If $[M_{i}, M_{j}^{*}] = 0$ for $i, j \in \{1, 2\}$ then $[M_{\pm}, M_{\pm}^{*}] = [M_{1} \mp JM_{2}, M_{1}^{*} \pm JM_{2}^{*}]$ is a combination of the $[M_{i}, M_{j}^{*}]$ and vanishes, so $M_{\pm}$ is normal and nilpotent, hence zero, and $M_{1} = \tfrac12(M_{+} + M_{-}) = 0$, $M_{2} = \tfrac{J}{2}(M_{+} - M_{-}) = 0$.
A matrix with $[W, M] = 0$ that is normal gives, by (ii), the scalar $q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M)$ on edge-clean vectors; the channel densities $E_{\alpha\alpha}$ are such.

\emph{(iv).} Let $M^{2} = 0$, $r = \operatorname{rank}M$, and $N \ge q$. Write $M^{*} = \sum_{s=1}^{r}\sigma_{s}t_{s}u_{s}^{*}$ with $\sigma_{s} > 0$ and orthonormal families $(u_{s})$, $(t_{s})$ (the singular value decomposition over $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$); $M^{*2} = 0$ gives $\sigma_{s}\sigma_{r'}\langle u_{s}, t_{r'}\rangle = 0$, so every $u_{s}$ is orthogonal to every $t_{r'}$. Then $B = \rho_{q}(M)^{*} = \sum_{k}\sum_{s}\sigma_{s}\,c_{k+q}(t_{s})^{*}c_{k}(u_{s})$, the sum over $k, k + q \in I$. Apply $B$ repeatedly to $\Omega$. A term with $k + q < 0$ vanishes on every vector reached, since its target mode $c_{k+q}(t_{s})$ is filled: modes at negative momenta change only in the directions $u_{s'}$, which are orthogonal to every $t_{s}$; a term with $k \ge 0$ vanishes, since the only filled modes at momenta $\ge 0$ lie in the span of the $t$'s, orthogonal to $u_{s}$. The remaining terms have $k \in \{-q, \dots, -1\}$ and define $\sigma_{k,s}^{+} = c_{k+q}(t_{s})^{*}c_{k}(u_{s})$ on $qr$ distinct sites $(k, s)$: they commute pairwise (even elements of distinct modes) and square to zero, and the vectors $\prod_{(k,s)\in S}\sigma_{k,s}^{+}\Omega$ for distinct sets $S$ are orthonormal. Hence $B^{p}\Omega = p!\sum_{|S| = p}\prod_{(k,s)\in S}\sigma_{s}\sigma_{k,s}^{+}\Omega$ and
\[
|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = (p!)^{2}e_{p}(x), \qquad x = (\sigma_{s}^{2})_{(k,s)}, \qquad |B\Omega|^{2} = e_{1}(x) = q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M),
\]
with $e_{p}$ the elementary symmetric polynomial: zero for $p > qr$. Expanding $e_{1}(x)^{p}$, the products with distinct indices give $p!\,e_{p}(x)$ and for $p \ge 2$ the products $x_{i}^{p} > 0$ are extra, so $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} < p!\,|B\Omega|^{2p}$ for $p \ge 2$, whereas a canonical boson has equality. For $M = E_{+-}$, $r = 1$, $x = (1, \dots, 1)$ ($q$ entries), $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = (p!)^{2}\binom{q}{p}$. On the same vectors the terms of $\rho_{q}(M) = B^{*}$ outside the sites vanish by the same occupancy argument, and $[\sigma_{k}^{-}, \sigma_{k}^{+}] = 1 - 2\sigma_{k}^{+}\sigma_{k}^{-}$ on the two states of a site, so $[\rho_{q}(M), B]B^{p}\Omega = (q - 2p)B^{p}\Omega$: the normalised commutator is $1 - 2p/q$, the quasi-spin of $q$ sites of Proposition \claimref{field-theory.how-close-tower-comes-ccr} (there with $n$ pairs). For the same-channel density at $q = 1$, $D = \rho_{1}(E_{++})^{*}$, the moves $k \to k + 1$ chain, and $|D^{2}\Omega|^{2} = 2 = 2!\,|D\Omega|^{4}$ (computed on the window $N = 2$).

\emph{(v).} $\omega([X, X^{*}]) = \omega(XX^{*}) - \omega(X^{*}X) = \omega(XX^{*}) \ge 0$ when $\omega(X^{*}X) = 0$, by positivity of $\omega$. For $q \ge 1$, $\rho_{q}(M)\Omega = 0$: each term removes a particle at $k + q$ and adds one at $k < k + q$, impossible in the sea since $k + q < 0$ forces $k < 0$, filled. By (i) on the edge-clean vector $\Omega$ (here $N \ge q$), $\omega_{\Omega}([\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M)^{*}]) = q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M) + \omega_{\Omega}(\rho_{0}([M, M^{*}]))$, and $\omega_{\Omega}(\rho_{0}(X)) = N\operatorname{tr}X = 0$; the reversed sea (filled for $k \ge 0$) is edge-clean for the reflected window and gives $-q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M)$, with $\rho_{q}(M)^{*}$ annihilating it. The timelike mode of the Gupta-Bleuler form in (K1) of Premise \claimref{synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-inner-product-for-gauge-fields} annihilates the vacuum and has $[a_{0}, a_{0}^{\dagger}] = -1$, which the first sentence excludes for every pair mode and every state of the tower, for the positive adjoint $*$. The first sentence uses only $\omega(Y^{*}Y) \ge 0$, so it holds for every element of every algebra with a positive state: it is why Gupta and Bleuler need an indefinite form. With a Krein adjoint $X^{\dagger} = \eta X^{*}\eta$ the conclusion fails for pair modes: on two modes take $\eta = 1 - 2n_{2}$ (self-adjoint, $\eta^{2} = 1$), $X = a_{1}^{*}a_{2}$ and $\Omega$ with mode $1$ filled and mode $2$ empty. Then $X\Omega = 0$; $\eta$ anticommutes with $a_{2}, a_{2}^{*}$ and commutes with $a_{1}, a_{1}^{*}$, so $X^{\dagger} = \eta a_{2}^{*}a_{1}\eta = -a_{2}^{*}a_{1} = -X^{*}$ and $[X, X^{\dagger}]\Omega = -[X, X^{*}]\Omega = -(n_{1} - n_{2})\Omega = -\Omega$. So (v) does not exclude Premise (KF), whose form is of this kind (as in \claimref{synthesis.self-adjoint-brst-charge-needs-a-krein-form-and-the-tower-supplies-the-ghosts}(ii)).

\emph{Checks.} The exact check verifies (i) on the window $N = 2$ with two channels for $q = 1, 2$ and nine pairs of six matrices (real and with $J$ entries, normal and nilpotent); (ii) at $q = 1$ on the edge-clean projector, including the values $q \pm 1$ of the helicity-one mode on two edge-clean states; (iii) the weights $\pm\tfrac12$, the doublet $M_{1} = E_{+-} + E_{-+}$, $M_{2} = J(E_{+-} - E_{-+})$ with $[M_{1}, M_{2}^{*}] \ne 0$, five integer helicity-one matrices on four channels, and the rotation at the half angle with $(\cos, \sin) = (\tfrac{12}{13}, \tfrac{5}{13})$; (iv) $q = 1, 2$, the Cartan comparison, a rank-one nilpotent rational $M$, and a rank-two helicity-one $M$ on four channels ($K = [[1, J], [0, 2]]$ in the block from the weight $-\tfrac12$ to the weight $+\tfrac12$ channels, $q = 1$: $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = 1, 6, 16, 0$); (v) $q = 1, 2$ on the sea and the reversed sea, and the Krein counter-model on two modes.

\item[(iv)] \emph{(The lift locus; a corollary of stored clauses.)} In the setting of Theorems \claimref{synthesis.rung-field-on-the-lift-locus} and \claimref{synthesis.rung-field-d-term-action-and-tree-masses-on-the-lift-locus}, put $\phi_{1} = \alpha$ and $\phi_{2} =  ar{ eta}$, read in $\Cl(3,0)^{+}$ by $(z_{1}, z_{2}) \mapsto z_{1} + e_{01}z_{2}$ with $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$ read as $\mathrm{span}\{1, e_{12}\}$ acting on the right; then the slot $U(2)$ acts on both as on a doublet, the span$\{1, e_{12}\}$ part of $\widetilde{\phi}_{2}\phi_{1}$ is $\phi_{2}^{\dagger}\phi_{1} = \alpha^{\mathsf T} eta = Q(c)$, and $\mathsf{N}^{2} - m^{2} = N_{1}N_{2}$. On the null-lift locus $Q(c) = -H^{2}$, so $K = H^{4}$ and $N_{1}N_{2} = H^{4} + K' \ge H^{4}$: the Goldstone rank is $3$ exactly on the boundary $\mathsf{N}^{2} - m^{2} = H^{4}$, the charge-preserving orbits, and $4$ in the interior, and never $0$, so the rung field on the locus has no unbroken electroweak phase; the D-term vacuum of the stored theorem lies on the boundary. This restates, in doublet language, the stabilisers of the lift-locus theorem (1) (a circle on the boundary orbits, trivial inside) and the D-term theorem (1), (2).
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.higgs-sector-brst-does-not-fix.technical: The scalar part of the BRST differential, the gauge transformation of the two doublets with the gauge parameter replaced by the ghost, squares to zero for every field value: it only needs the doublets to carry a representation of the gauge algebra, so no condition on the vacuum enters there. A condition does enter one step later. The stored positivity result quantises the free theory about a vacuum, with its free BRST charge, and that free charge is a symmetry of the free action only if the vacuum is a stationary point of the potential: off such a point the linear term of the potential spoils the invariance of the quadratic action, because the doublets carry no invariant direction. The second finding is that the BRST construction cannot choose the breaking pattern. Two doublets break the electroweak factor to the photon's $\uu(1)$ exactly when they are aligned, and break it completely otherwise. Two simple gauge-invariant potentials, differing only in the sign of the term measuring alignment, have their lowest points on the neutral pattern (three massive vectors) and on a charge-breaking one (four massive vectors, a massive photon), and the BRST machinery, gauge fixing and positivity of physical states work equally in both. So the neutral pattern must come from the potential. On the rung field's constrained surface, the two doublets have a fixed nonzero inner product, so they always break the symmetry, the photon is massless exactly on the boundary of the orbit space found earlier, and the stored D-term potential puts its vacuum on that boundary.
synthesis.higgs-sector-brst-does-not-fix.lay: The Higgs field gives the W and Z bosons their mass while leaving the photon massless. The series has two Higgs-like fields, and earlier work assumed the way they settle leaves the photon massless, then checked that the quantum bookkeeping of the forces (the BRST method, which removes unphysical states) works. This result asks whether that bookkeeping could itself force the photon to stay massless. It cannot: the bookkeeping works just as well when the fields settle in a way that gives the photon a mass, as an explicit pair of examples shows, differing only in the sign of one number in the energy of the fields. It does demand that the fields sit at a balanced point of their energy. So which pattern nature picks has to come from the energy of the fields; on the constrained version of the series' field with its simplest energy, it does pick the massless photon.

synthesis.imported-adler-bell-jackiw-axi.formal:
Units $\hbar = c = 1$, signature $(+,-,-,-)$, $\alpha = e^{2}/(4\pi)$. Numbers, the bilinears $j^{5}_{\mu}$ and $j^{5}$ among them, are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$, the field theory's unit (on Clifford products the right unit $x \mapsto xI_{4}$), and $\gamma_{5}$ is the chirality $x \mapsto I_{4}xI_{4}$ of the store's one-loop electrodynamics (the left $I_{4}$ inside the product, the right one the unit); the sources write $i$ for $I_{4}$. For a Dirac fermion of mass $m$ and charge $e$ coupled to the electromagnetic field $F$, with the axial current $j^{5}_{\mu} = \bar\psi\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}\psi$ and the pseudoscalar density $j^{5} = \bar\psi\gamma_{5}\psi$ (index reading of the sources), the one-loop triangle graph with one axial and two vector vertices cannot be made to conserve the vector current and to satisfy the naive axial Ward identity at once; keeping the vector current conserved,
\[
\partial^{\mu}j^{5}_{\mu} = 2I_{4}m\,j^{5} + \frac{\alpha}{4\pi}\,\epsilon_{\xi\sigma\tau\rho}F^{\xi\sigma}F^{\tau\rho}
\]
\cite{Adler1969} (in the form of \cite{Adler2004}, eq. (1), with bare $m$ and $\alpha$). The anomalous term is proportional to $E\cdot B$, the pseudoscalar part of the square of the field-strength bivector. In the $\sigma$-model the same term removes the conflict between partial conservation of the axial current and the observed rate of $\pi^{0} \to \gamma\gamma$ \cite{BellJackiw1969}.
synthesis.imported-adler-bell-jackiw-axi.technical: The axial anomaly is the failure of the classical conservation law of the axial current of a massless fermion in the quantum theory. Adler computed the triangle graph with one axial and two vector vertices in spinor electrodynamics and showed that, when the vector current is kept conserved (as gauge invariance requires), the divergence of the axial current acquires a term proportional to the electromagnetic field contracted with its dual, $E\cdot B$, with coefficient $\alpha/(4\pi)$ in the normalisation $\epsilon FF$. Bell and Jackiw found the same term in the $\sigma$-model and showed that it accounts for the decay of the neutral pion into two photons, which the naive current algebra forbids.
synthesis.imported-adler-bell-jackiw-axi.lay: Some symmetries of the classical equations of particle physics do not survive in the quantum theory. The best known case concerns the difference between left-handed and right-handed particles: in 1969 Adler, and Bell and Jackiw, found that quantum effects of light break this balance by an amount set by the electric and magnetic fields together, and that this explains why a neutral pion decays into two photons. The series takes this result from the literature.

synthesis.imported-bochner-theorem-momen.technical: Three classical lemmas of analysis. Bochner's theorem says that the functions of one real variable that are continuous and positive definite are exactly the Fourier transforms of finite positive measures. The moment lemma of probability theory says that smoothness of such a transform at the origin controls the measure's tail: a derivative of even order $2k$ at the origin forces the moment of order $2k$ to be finite. Whitney's theorem says that a smooth even function of one variable is a smooth function of the square of that variable, and so a smooth odd one is the variable times such a function.
synthesis.imported-bochner-theorem-momen.lay: These are three standard results of mathematical analysis. One says which functions arise as averages of waves with positive weights; another says that if such an average is smooth at its centre, the weights must fall off fast at high frequencies; the third says that a smooth function that is symmetric about zero can be written as a smooth function of the square of its argument. They are taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-brst-kugo-ojima-stroc.technical: These are the standard foundations of the covariant quantisation of gauge fields. Becchi, Rouet and Stora, and independently Tyutin, found that the gauge-fixed action with ghosts keeps a nilpotent fermionic symmetry, now called BRST, whose charge defines the physical states as a cohomology. Kugo and Ojima showed that when this charge is self-adjoint for an indefinite inner product, the unphysical modes (timelike and longitudinal photons, ghosts and antighosts) pair into quartets of zero norm, so the physical states have positive norm and the physical scattering is unitary. Strocchi proved that the indefinite metric cannot be avoided: on a positive-metric space a local covariant vector potential satisfying Maxwell's equations has trivial field strength. Gribov showed that the usual non-abelian gauge conditions do not pick a unique representative of each gauge orbit beyond small fields, so the ghost construction is a perturbative tool.
synthesis.imported-brst-kugo-ojima-stroc.lay: Force fields such as light and the gluons carry a redundancy: many mathematical descriptions give the same physics. Removing it while keeping the equal treatment of space and time is done with fictitious ghost particles and a bookkeeping symmetry found in the 1970s. That bookkeeping works only if some unphysical states are allowed negative or zero length, which then cancel in groups of four; a theorem of Strocchi shows there is no way around this, and Gribov showed that for the gluons the usual way of removing the redundancy fails for very strong fields. The series takes these results from the literature.

synthesis.imported-conformal-covariance-.technical: Two classical facts of conformal geometry. First, a four-dimensional gravitational field whose Weyl curvature vanishes is, near each point, a rescaling of the flat field by a smooth positive factor (Weyl and Schouten; in four or more dimensions the Weyl tensor is the complete local obstruction to conformal flatness). Second, the massless fields of the standard model are conformally covariant in four dimensions: under a rescaling of the metric by $\varphi^{2}$ a solution of the massless Dirac equation is carried to a solution by the factor $\varphi^{-3/2}$, a conformally coupled massless scalar by $\varphi^{-1}$, and the Maxwell and Yang-Mills equations are unchanged. The maps preserve the conserved current or symplectic form, so the quantum field algebras are identified. Together they let the conformal vacuum of a Weyl-flat field be the flat vacuum, rescaled.
synthesis.imported-conformal-covariance-.lay: Some gravitational fields are, up to a change of scale from place to place, the same as empty flat space: exactly those in which gravity stretches but does not distort shapes. Massless particles, such as light and massless electrons, cannot tell a change of scale apart, so on such fields their physics is that of flat space, rescaled. These are classical results, taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-dimensional-regularis.formal:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Dimensional regularisation.)} Loop integrals are continued in the spacetime dimension $D$ and their divergences appear as poles at $D = 4$; the continuation preserves Lorentz invariance and, for vector-like gauge theories, gauge invariance \cite{tHooftVeltman1972}.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The BMHV $\gamma_{5}$.)} In the scheme of 't Hooft and Veltman and of Breitenlohner and Maison the vectors of the algebra continued to dimension $D$ split as $a = \bar a + \hat a$ into a part in the four spacetime directions and an orthogonal $(D-4)$-dimensional (evanescent) part, so that $Q(a) = Q(\bar a) + Q(\hat a)$ and $\bar a\hat b = -\hat b\bar a$ (the frame vectors $\gamma^{\mu} = \bar\gamma^{\mu} + \hat\gamma^{\mu}$), and the chirality element $\gamma_{5}$ is the four-dimensional pseudoscalar $I_{4} = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$ acting by left multiplication inside the Clifford product, with the field's unit outside it as the right unit, $\gamma_{5}x = I_{4}\,x\,I_{4}$ (conventions, chiral loops): it anticommutes with left multiplication by every $\bar a$ and commutes with left multiplication by every $\hat a$, since $I_{4}$ anticommutes with the four spacetime vectors and commutes with every vector orthogonal to them. In chiral gauge theories this breaks BRST invariance; the singular and evanescent counterterms are not gauge invariant, and finite counterterms restore the symmetry; at one loop the renormalisation group equations are unchanged \cite{BreitenlohnerMaison1977, BeluscaMaito2020}.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The obstruction.)} No element $\gamma_{5}$ that anticommutes with every vector of the algebra continued to $D \neq 4$ is compatible with a cyclic trace $\mathrm{Tr}$ and $\mathrm{Tr}(\gamma_{5}\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{\nu}\gamma^{\rho}\gamma^{\sigma}) \neq 0$ \cite{BreitenlohnerMaison1977}; in four dimensions the trace is four times the scalar part, and $\mathrm{Tr}(\gamma_{5}abcd)$ is $4\langle I_{4}abcd\rangle_{0}$ with the unit in front.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The $d$-dimensional integral rules.)} On the Euclidean section, with measure $d^{d}\ell/\pi^{d/2}$, $d = 4 - 2\epsilon$: integrals are invariant under shifts of the loop momentum, $\int d^{d}\ell\,f(\ell + p) = \int d^{d}\ell\,f(\ell)$ \cite{Weinzierl2010}; scale-free integrals vanish, $\int d^{d}\ell\,Q(\ell)^{-a} = 0$, and so do integrals of total derivatives, which gives the integration-by-parts identities, among them the triangle rule \cite{ChetyrkinTkachov1981, Grozin2003, KotikovTeber2018}; the radial integral is $\int\frac{d^{d}\ell}{\pi^{d/2}}\,\frac{Q(\ell)^{r}}{(Q(\ell) + \Delta)^{N}} = \frac{\Gamma(r + d/2)\,\Gamma(N - r - d/2)}{\Gamma(d/2)\,\Gamma(N)}\,\Delta^{d/2 + r - N}$, and under the integral $\ell^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots\ell^{\alpha_{2r}} \to Q(\ell)^{r}\{\delta^{r}\}/(d(d+2)\cdots(d + 2r - 2))$, $\{\delta^{r}\}$ the sum over the pairings of the indices (symmetric integration); the Minkowski forms follow by the Wick rotation. The massless one-loop bubble is
\[
\int\frac{d^{d}k}{\pi^{d/2}}\,\frac{1}{Q(k)^{a_{1}}\,Q(k - q)^{a_{2}}} = G(a_{1}, a_{2})\,Q(q)^{d/2 - a_{1} - a_{2}}, \qquad G(a_{1}, a_{2}) = \frac{\Gamma(a_{1} + a_{2} - d/2)\,\Gamma(d/2 - a_{1})\,\Gamma(d/2 - a_{2})}{\Gamma(a_{1})\,\Gamma(a_{2})\,\Gamma(d - a_{1} - a_{2})}
\]
\cite{Grozin2003, KotikovTeber2018}, and the two-loop massless self-energy integral with five lines of unit index, $\int\int\frac{d^{d}k\,d^{d}l}{\pi^{d}}\,\frac{1}{Q(k)Q(k - q)Q(l)Q(l - q)Q(k - l)}$, equals $6\zeta_{3}/Q(q) + O(\epsilon)$ \cite{ChetyrkinTkachov1981, KotikovTeber2018}.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Two loops in the abelian chiral theory.)} For an abelian gauge theory with right-handed fermions of charges $\mathcal{Y}_{R}$ and $\mathrm{Tr}\,\mathcal{Y}_{R}^{3} = 0$, the BMHV scheme is consistent at two loops: the finite symmetry-restoring counterterms through two loops have the same form as at one loop, restoring the Ward identities, the one-loop ones being $\frac{\hbar}{16\pi^{2}}\int\bigl[-\frac{e^{2}}{6}\mathrm{Tr}(\mathcal{Y}_{R}^{2})\,\bar A\cdot\bar\partial^{2}\bar A + \frac{e^{4}}{12}\mathrm{Tr}(\mathcal{Y}_{R}^{4})\,(\bar A^{2})^{2} + (\text{a fermion term proportional to } 5 + \xi)\bigr]$; ultraviolet-divergent evanescent counterterms are needed in addition \cite{BeluscaMaito2021}.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.imported-dimensional-regularis.technical:
Dimensional regularisation continues loop integrals to a non-integer number of dimensions, so divergences become poles at four dimensions; it keeps Lorentz and vector-like gauge invariance. The chirality element $\gamma_{5}$ is intrinsically four-dimensional: in the spacetime algebra it is the pseudoscalar $I_{4}$, with the field's unit outside the product. No continuation keeps it anticommuting with every vector while traces stay cyclic and the four-dimensional epsilon trace survives. The standard consistent choice, due to 't Hooft and Veltman and to Breitenlohner and Maison, splits each vector into a four-dimensional part, with which $\gamma_{5}$ anticommutes, and an evanescent part, with which it commutes; in geometric algebra this is what the four-dimensional pseudoscalar $I_{4}$ does by itself, since it anticommutes with the spacetime vectors and commutes with the vectors orthogonal to them. In chiral gauge theories this breaks the BRST symmetry, and finite counterterms are needed to restore it; for an abelian theory with right-handed fermions their form at two loops is the same as at one loop (Belusca-Maito and collaborators, 2021).

The rules that make dimensionally continued integrals computable are also standard. Integrals do not change when the loop momentum is shifted, integrals with no scale and integrals of total derivatives vanish, and the last gives the integration-by-parts identities of Chetyrkin and Tkachov, which reduce massless multi-loop integrals to a few masters. The one-loop radial integral and the massless bubble are ratios of Gamma functions; under the integral, products of loop momenta are replaced by symmetric combinations of the metric over $d(d+2)\cdots$; and the two-loop self-energy integral with five unit lines is $6\zeta_{3}$ at four dimensions.
synthesis.imported-dimensional-regularis.lay: One standard way of taming the infinities of quantum corrections pretends that spacetime has a slightly non-integer number of dimensions. The quantity that distinguishes left-handed from right-handed particles exists only in four dimensions, so the method has to give up one of its properties; the standard choice keeps it consistent at the cost of extra corrections in theories, like the weak force, that treat left and right differently. The method comes with a small set of rules for doing the resulting integrals, which reduce complicated calculations to a few standard ones.

synthesis.imported-dimock-dirac-car-alge.technical: Before one can ask for a quantum state of the Dirac field in a gravitational field, the field itself, as an algebra of operators, has to exist. Dimock showed that on every spacetime with a well-posed initial-value problem (globally hyperbolic) the free Dirac field exists, with anticommutators that vanish at spacelike separation, and that its algebras of local observables satisfy the standard axioms of algebraic quantum field theory in a form adapted to curved backgrounds. In the store's language: on every gravitational field with a globally hyperbolic derived metric the Dirac CAR algebra exists; what is not fixed is a state, which is a separate datum. The same construction shows that the anticommutator of two smeared fields is the conserved inner product (the flux of the current through any instant) of the classical solutions they define, and that the causal propagator rebuilds every solution from its values at one instant.
synthesis.imported-dimock-dirac-car-alge.lay: The rules of quantum field theory for electrons and similar particles can be set up in any reasonable gravitational field: the field's operators exist and respect causality. Dimock proved this in 1982. What the construction does not provide is a choice of the quantum state, the analogue of empty space, which has to be supplied separately. This is taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-dirac-hadamard-form-p.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric is smooth and globally hyperbolic, read on several charts where its global structure needs them, and let $\psi$ be the free Dirac field of mass $m \ge 0$ on it, quantised by the canonical anticommutation relations, with the two two-point functions $\mathcal{G}^{(\pm)}$ of a quasi-free state $\omega$ and the sets $C^{(\pm)}$ of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}(b).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \emph{(Equivalence; Sahlmann and Verch, Thm.~5.8.)} $\omega$ satisfies the wave front set condition $\mathrm{WF}'(\mathcal{G}^{(\pm)}) = C^{(\pm)}$ exactly when its two-point functions have the Hadamard form, in the sense defined there through the squared Dirac operator (the Dirac operator applied to a Hadamard parametrix of its square, plus a smooth kernel). The source poses its CAR results for Majorana spinors; for the Dirac field of four dimensions the class of Hadamard states is treated by Sanders, who fills gaps in the earlier equivalence arguments. The statement of Thm.~5.8 is taken from the source's abstract and introduction, not read against its text.
\item[(b)] \emph{(Propagation; Kratzert, Hollands, Sahlmann and Verch, Sec.~5.2.)} If the two-point functions of $\omega$ have the Hadamard form on an open neighbourhood of one Cauchy surface, they have it on the whole field: Cauchy evolution preserves the Hadamard form of the Dirac field. The argument rests on the propagation of singularities (of polarisation sets) for the Dirac operator, the polarisation set of a Hadamard Dirac two-point function being computed by Kratzert.
\item[(c)] \emph{(Adiabatic states; Hollands.)} On a Robertson-Walker field (spatial sections flat or curved) with smooth scale factor, a homogeneous isotropic gauge-invariant quasi-free state of the massive Dirac field that is adiabatic of infinite order is Hadamard.
\item[(d)] \emph{(Scaling limits; Sahlmann and Verch, Prop.~5.6, Lemma~5.7, Def.~5.3; added in version 2.)} Posed for Majorana spinors on a globally hyperbolic spacetime of dimension $n = 3, 4, 9, 10 \bmod 8$, with Dirac operator $\slashed{\nabla} + I_{5}m$, $m \ge 0$ (a constant, or a bundle map), where the scalar unit of the source's complex spinor bundle, which commutes with the Clifford action of every vector, is read as the central pseudoscalar $I_{5} = I_{4}e$ of the odd extension $\Cl(2,3)$ (\claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}), and a state Hadamard when near a Cauchy surface its two-point function is $\omega_{2}(f\otimes f') = w(Df\otimes f')$ with $w$ of Hadamard form for the squared operator. Let $\omega$ be a quasi-free Hadamard state, $p$ a point, $\xi_{p}$ normal coordinates at $p$, $\delta_{\lambda}(q) = \xi_{p}(\lambda\,\xi_{p}^{-1}(q))$ the dilations, lifted to the bundle, and $\alpha = \tfrac{n}{2} + \tfrac12$ ($\tfrac52$ in four dimensions) the weight of the dilated test sections. Then, as $\lambda \to 0$, the two-point function of $\omega$ on the dilated test sections converges to $G^{(1)}_{\eta}((\gamma^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\Theta R_{*}f)R_{*}f')$, where $G^{(1)}_{\eta}$ is the leading Hadamard distribution of the flat metric in the normal coordinates (with no mass term), $R$ identifies the fibres with $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{5}\}^{r}$ through the normal coordinates and a frame, and $\Theta$ is the matrix at $p$ of the Dirac conjugation composed with charge conjugation: the scaling limit of $\omega$ at $p$ is the two-point function of the massless Dirac field on Minkowski space, whatever the mass and the curvature. The limit distributions contain $(p, \xi; p, -\xi)$ in their wave front sets for every $(p, \xi)$ in the set $N^{-}$ of the source (Lemma~5.7).
\end{enumerate}
Not part of this Fact: the converse of (c) (that a homogeneous Hadamard state is adiabatic of infinite order); the transcription of (d) from Majorana to Dirac spinors and from normal-coordinate to other dilations, which the results that use (d) carry out themselves; the source's proof of (d) (its Appendix A.5). \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Kratzert2000}; \cite{Hollands2001}; \cite[Sec.~5.2, Thm.~5.8, Def.~5.3, Prop.~5.6, Lemma~5.7]{SahlmannVerch2001}; for the Dirac equivalence also \cite{Sanders2010}.
synthesis.imported-dirac-hadamard-form-p.technical: For the scalar field the store imports that a two-point function of Hadamard form near one instant has that form everywhere. This Fact supplies the same for the Dirac field. For quasi-free states of the free Dirac field on a globally hyperbolic gravitational field, the wave front set form of the Hadamard condition, imposed on both orderings of the two-point function, is equivalent to the Hadamard form defined through the squared Dirac operator (Sahlmann and Verch), and the Hadamard form propagates by Cauchy evolution from a neighbourhood of one Cauchy surface to the whole field; the propagation rests on the propagation of singularities for the Dirac operator, with the polarisation set of a Hadamard Dirac two-point function computed by Kratzert. On Robertson-Walker fields, Hollands showed that the homogeneous Dirac states adiabatic of infinite order, those that agree with the adiabatic expansion of the mode equation to every order in the inverse momentum, are Hadamard. Only that direction is imported; the converse is not. Sahlmann and Verch also determine the short-distance scaling limit of such states: scaled towards a point in normal coordinates, a quasi-free Hadamard state tends to the vacuum two-point function of the massless Dirac field on Minkowski space, whatever the mass and the curvature. Their results for the anticommutation relations are posed for Majorana spinors; Sanders treats the Hadamard states of the four-dimensional Dirac field and fills gaps in the earlier equivalence arguments.
synthesis.imported-dirac-hadamard-form-p.lay: Physicists require that a reasonable quantum state of a field, looked at closely enough, resembles empty space. For electrons and the other particles of spin one half, these results show that it is enough to check this at one moment: the equations of motion then keep it true at every other moment. They also show that in a uniformly expanding universe a standard recipe for building states, which follows the expansion smoothly to every order, gives states of this regular kind, and that close up such a state looks exactly like the empty state of massless particles in flat space. These are taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extens.technical: Causal perturbation theory, due to Epstein and Glaser, builds the time-ordered products of an interacting quantum field theory order by order from causality alone. At each order the product is already determined away from the points where all arguments coincide; the ultraviolet problem is only how to extend a distribution across that set, and no regulator is introduced. Brunetti and Fredenhagen put the extension step in a local form ordered by the scaling degree: a distribution of scaling degree below the dimension has one extension of the same degree, and at or above the dimension extensions exist and differ by finitely many derivatives of the delta function, the local counterterms. For electrodynamics Scharf showed in this framework that the free normalisation can be chosen so that gauge invariance, and with it the Ward identities, hold at every order (a later proof by Grigore repairs a step that rests on reduction formulae). Duetsch and Fredenhagen constructed the local algebras of interacting fields and implemented the BRST symmetry of electrodynamics by a local Kugo-Ojima operator, with the positivity of the physical states preserved. Hollands extended the construction to Yang-Mills theory on any globally hyperbolic gravitational field, with Ward identities that keep the interacting BRST charge nilpotent. Clause (vi) records the rules by which the scaling degree of a one-loop kernel on a gravitational field is counted: an inverse power of the Synge function with the Feynman prescription has twice that power as its degree, a smooth factor vanishing on the diagonal lowers the degree by its order of vanishing, degrees add at most under the products that occur, and the Hadamard series can be cut after any number of terms with a remainder as differentiable as the number of terms kept. These four are cited from memory.
synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extens.lay: The infinities of quantum field theory can be avoided without any artificial cut-off. Epstein and Glaser showed that the calculation can be built up step by step from the requirement that cause precedes effect; the only freedom left at each step is how to treat the points where particles meet, and that freedom is a short list of constants. Later work showed that this freedom can be used to keep the conservation of electric charge exact at every step, constructed the local quantities of the theory directly, and extended the construction to the force fields of the strong and weak interactions, on flat spacetime and in gravitational fields. The series takes these results from the literature.

synthesis.imported-fewster-lang-spin-pro.formal:
Let a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) have an ultrastatic derived metric on a slab, the product of a time interval $(-T/2, T/2)$ with a compact spatial section $\Sigma$, oriented and globally hyperbolic, and consider the quantised free Dirac field of mass $m$ on it. Weight the spacetime spin product $\int\bar{\psi}\phi$ of two solutions by a nonnegative integrable function $f$ of time; on the space of solutions with the conserved-current inner product it is represented by a bounded self-adjoint operator, and the positive spectral projection of that operator defines a gauge-invariant, pure, quasi-free state, the state extracted from the fermionic projector of Finster and Reintjes \cite{FinsterReintjes2015}, the Dirac analogue of the Sorkin-Johnston state of a scalar field \cite{FewsterLang2015}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For the sharp weight, $f$ the indicator function of the slab, the state fails to be Hadamard for generic lifetimes $T$ (\cite{FewsterLang2015}, Thm.~3.4).
\item[(ii)] For $f$ smooth, compactly supported in the slab, nonnegative and not identically zero, the resulting softened state is Hadamard (\cite{FewsterLang2015}, Thm.~3.5).
\item[(iii)] The Hadamard condition of these states is tied to the finiteness of the fluctuations of Wick polynomials \cite{FewsterLang2015}.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Beyond one flat chart:} the compactness of the spatial section $\Sigma$ is a global ingredient of the setting of the theorems.
synthesis.imported-fewster-lang-spin-pro.technical: On a short stretch of time, a slab, one can build a state of the Dirac field from the field alone: weight the spin product of two solutions over spacetime, compare it with the conserved charge product, and keep the positive part. Fewster and Lang showed that this state, the finite-time form of Finster and Reintjes's fermionic projector and the Dirac analogue of the Sorkin-Johnston state, is pure and quasi-free, but on an ultrastatic slab with compact spatial sections it is generically not Hadamard if the weight is sharp in time; softened with a smooth weight that vanishes near the ends of the slab, it is Hadamard.
synthesis.imported-fewster-lang-spin-pro.lay: A natural way to pick out a quantum state of the electron field, using only the field's own structure over a finite stretch of time, gives a state that is too rough at short distances when the stretch has sharp ends. Fewster and Lang proved this, and showed that smoothing the ends repairs it. The series uses their result when testing whether that construction could select the state left behind by the descent.

synthesis.imported-free-field-spin-stati.technical: The free massless field's vacuum correlation is $-1/(4\pi^{2})$ over the spacetime interval with a small imaginary shift fixing the analytic continuation; at spacelike separation it is real and even. Pauli used this to show that a free field of integer spin must commute and one of half-integer spin must anticommute at spacelike separation if the state space has positive norm, the free-field form of the spin-statistics connection. Guido and Longo proved an algebraic version for interacting fields: if the vacuum's modular flow on each wedge is the wedge's boost (modular covariance), and the net has the Reeh-Schlieder property and normal commutation relations, then the operator grading Bose and Fermi fields is the rotation by $2\pi$; positive energy follows and need not be assumed.
synthesis.imported-free-field-spin-stati.lay: Particles of whole-number spin behave as bosons and those of half-number spin as fermions. For free particles this follows from a short argument of Pauli using the standard formula for how a field's values at two points are correlated. For interacting fields Guido and Longo proved it from a property of the vacuum: that its natural flow in each wedge of spacetime is the geometric boost. The series takes these results as given.

synthesis.imported-hadamard-parametrix-o.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on four-dimensional flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric $g$ is smooth and globally hyperbolic on a region $U$ of its invertible region, $N \subset U$ geodesically convex, $\sigma$ the Synge function of $g$ on $N\times N$ ($\sigma = \tfrac12 Q(x - x')$ on the flat field) and $\Delta$ its Van Vleck determinant.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \emph{(Bundle parametrix; Friedlander; B\"ar, Ginoux and Pf\"affle, Ch.~2.)} A normally hyperbolic operator $P$ on a vector bundle over $N$ (principal part that of the d'Alembertian of $g$) is, uniquely, the d'Alembertian of a connection $\nabla^{P}$ plus a zero-order term. Its Hadamard coefficients are the unique sections fixed by transport equations along the geodesics from $x'$ with the identity at coincidence, and the leading one is $\Delta^{1/2}(x, x')\,\Pi(x, x')$, $\Pi(x, x')$ the parallel transport of $\nabla^{P}$ along the geodesic from $x'$ to $x$. In four dimensions the Hadamard parametrix of $P$ is, up to its normalising constant, $U/\sigma + V\log\sigma + W$ with $U = \Delta^{1/2}\Pi$ and $V$, $W$ smooth.
\item[(b)] \emph{(The squared Dirac operator; Lichnerowicz.)} Let $\psi$ be the free Dirac field of mass $m \ge 0$ on $(\hb, \Omega)$, with covariant derivative $D_{a}\psi = a\cdot\nabla\psi + \tfrac12\Omega(a)\psi$ and Dirac operator $D = g^{\mu}D_{e_{\mu}}$, $g^{\mu} = \hb^{T}(e^{\mu})$; on massive lines the field theory's unit stands outside the Clifford product, as the right unit $R_{I_{4}}: \psi \mapsto \psi I_{4}$. The squared operator $(R_{I_{4}}D - m)(R_{I_{4}}D + m) = -(D^{2} + m^{2})$ is normally hyperbolic, and by the Lichnerowicz formula ($D^{2}$ is the d'Alembertian of the spin connection plus a multiple of the scalar curvature) its connection $\nabla^{P}$ is the spin connection. So $\Pi(x, x')$ is left multiplication by the rotor $R$ of the geodesic $\gamma$ from $x'$ ($t = 0$) to $x$ ($t = 1$), $\dot R = -\tfrac12\Omega(\dot\gamma)R$, $R = 1$ at $t = 0$ (parallel transport, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}(ii)), and the leading Hadamard coefficient of the squared Dirac operator is $U = \Delta^{1/2}R$.
\item[(c)] \emph{(The $I_{5}0$ prescription; Kay and Wald; Sahlmann and Verch, Sec.~5.1.)} The distributions $1/\sigma$ and $\log\sigma$ of the Hadamard form are the $\epsilon \to 0^{+}$ limits of their regularisations by $\epsilon(t(x) - t(x'))$ and $\epsilon^{2}$, the infinitesimal shift being that of a spacetime vector, so that its unit is the central pseudoscalar $I_{5} = I_{4}e$ of the odd extension $\Cl(2,3)$, which commutes with every vector, and the regularised $\sigma$ a number of $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{5}\}$ (on the flat field $\tfrac12 Q(x - x' - \epsilon I_{5}e_{0})$, \claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}), for a time function $t$ (a smooth function with future-directed timelike unit gradient), as in the source; the Hadamard form so defined, for the scalar field and for vector-valued fields such as the Dirac field, does not depend on the choice of time function. This concerns the bulk distributions on $N\times N$.
\item[(d)] \emph{(Fundamental solutions in four dimensions; Friedlander; B\"ar, Ginoux and Pf\"affle, Ch.~2; for scalar and vector fields Poisson, Secs.~4.3.2, 4.4.2.)} On a geodesically convex, causally convex domain $N$ (a causal domain), with $\sigma$ positive on timelike separation, a time function $t$, and $P$ normalised so that its principal part is $(g^{\mu}\cdot g^{\nu})\,\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}$, the square of the physical gradient $\hb^{T}(\nabla) = g^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}$ at principal order (in components $g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}$; on the flat field the d'Alembertian $\partial_{t}^{2} - \nabla^{2}$), the retarded and advanced fundamental solutions of $P$ ($PG_{\pm} = \delta$, $G_{\pm}(\cdot, x')$ supported in $J^{\pm}(x')$) are
\[
G_{\pm}(x, x') = \frac{1}{4\pi}\,\theta\bigl(\pm(t(x) - t(x'))\bigr)\bigl[U(x, x')\,\delta(\sigma) + V(x, x')\,\theta(\sigma)\bigr],
\]
with $U = \Delta^{1/2}\Pi$ the leading coefficient of (a) and $V$ smooth on $N\times N$; on the flat field $\tfrac{1}{4\pi}\theta(t)\delta(\sigma) = \theta(t)\delta(t - r)/(4\pi r)$. For the squared Dirac operator $D^{2} + m^{2}$ of (b), $U = \Delta^{1/2}R$.
\end{enumerate}
Not part of this Fact: the higher Hadamard coefficients, the covariant expansion of $\Delta$, the coefficient of the curvature term in the Lichnerowicz formula, the normalising constant of the parametrix, and restrictions of the regularised distributions of (c) to null hypersurfaces, which depend on the time function by smooth kernels. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Friedlander1975}; \cite[Ch.~2]{BarGinouxPfaffle2007}; \cite[Secs.~3.5, 5.1]{SahlmannVerch2001}; \cite{KayWald1991}; \cite{Radzikowski1996}; for the transport equations \cite[Def./Prop.~2.10]{Ronge2026}; for the spinor coefficient in two dimensions \cite[Eq.~(52)]{Lewis2020}; for (d) in the scalar and vector cases \cite[Secs.~4.3.2, 4.4.2]{Poisson2004}.
synthesis.imported-hadamard-parametrix-o.technical: The Hadamard condition says that at short distances the two-point function of a state looks like the vacuum's, and it is written with an explicit singular term built from the squared geodesic distance $\sigma$ between the two points. For a field with several components, the coefficient of the leading singular term is a matrix: the square root of the Van Vleck determinant, which measures how geodesics from a point spread, times the parallel transport of the field's connection along the geodesic joining the two points. For the Dirac field the relevant operator is the square of the Dirac operator, whose connection is the spin connection, so in Gauge Theory Gravity the transport is left multiplication by the rotor that solves $\dot R = -\tfrac12\Omega(\dot\gamma)R$ along the geodesic. The singular terms carry an infinitesimal imaginary shift fixed by a time function, and the resulting Hadamard form is the same for every time function. In four dimensions the retarded and advanced solutions of the squared operator have the same coefficient: a delta function on the light cone with that coefficient, plus a smooth tail inside the cone. These are standard results taken from the literature.
synthesis.imported-hadamard-parametrix-o.lay: Physicists describe the regular states of a quantum field by the exact way its correlations blow up when two points come together. For the electron field, the strength of that blow-up is set by two pieces of geometry: how quickly straight paths from a point spread out, and how the electron's spin is carried along the path joining the two points. The rule also does not depend on which way of slicing space-time into moments is used to state it, and the same two pieces of geometry fix how a disturbance of the field spreads along the light cone. These are taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-hadamard-stress-tenso.formal: Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric is the Reissner-Nordstr\"om-de Sitter metric of a charged hole with positive cosmological constant, and let $\phi$ be a free real scalar field on it. For every state of $\phi$ that is Hadamard (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}(a)) in the domain of dependence of an initial Cauchy surface, the expected renormalised stress tensor along a radial null geodesic crossing the Cauchy horizon of the hole's interior satisfies $\langle T_{VV}\rangle \sim C/V^{2}$ as $V \to 0$, where $V$ is an affine parameter vanishing at the Cauchy horizon and $C$ is independent of the state and generically nonzero. This divergence is stronger than that of the classical field. \emph{Beyond one flat chart:} the statement concerns the maximal extension of the field through the hole's interior to its Cauchy horizon, read on several charts. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{HollandsWaldZahn2020}.
synthesis.imported-hadamard-stress-tenso.technical: A charged black hole in a universe with a positive cosmological constant has, inside, a Cauchy horizon beyond which the future is no longer fixed by the initial data. Classically, perturbations may stay mild there. Hollands, Wald and Zahn showed that a quantum scalar field in any regular (Hadamard) state behaves worse: its expected energy density, measured along a light ray falling through the Cauchy horizon, diverges as the inverse square of the affine distance to it, with a coefficient that does not depend on the state and is generically nonzero. They argue that this makes the Cauchy horizon a strong curvature singularity. For a state set on a collar of an earlier surface, the propagation of the Hadamard form reaches only the domain of dependence of that collar, and at such a Cauchy horizon its stress tensor diverges.
synthesis.imported-hadamard-stress-tenso.lay: Inside a charged black hole there is a boundary beyond which the laws of physics no longer predict what happens from the past. Hollands, Wald and Zahn showed that the energy of a quantum field becomes infinite as one approaches that boundary, whatever regular state the field starts in, which suggests the boundary is destroyed and replaced by a singularity. This is taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: S. Hollands, R. M. Wald and J. Zahn, Quantum instability of the Cauchy horizon in Reissner-Nordstrom-deSitter spacetime, Class. Quantum Grav. 37 (2020), 115009; arXiv:1912.06047.

synthesis.imported-haefner-nicolas-dirac.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on four-dimensional flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric $g$ is smooth on a region $U$ of its invertible region, $p_{0} \in U$, and $\mathcal{O} \subset U$ a geodesically convex, globally hyperbolic neighbourhood of $p_{0}$ with a time function $t$, $t(p_{0}) = 0$, and slices $\Sigma_{T} = \{t = T\}$. Let $\mathcal{C}^{+}_{0}$ be the future light cone of $p_{0}$, with its vertex blown up, and $D_{T} = J^{+}(p_{0})\cap\{0 \le t \le T\}$ for $T > 0$ small enough. Consider the Dirac field of mass $m \ge 0$ on $\mathcal{O}$ (an electromagnetic potential is allowed in the source). Then (H\"afner and Nicolas):
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \emph{(Flux identity; Eq.~(14).)} For a smooth solution $\Psi$ with data on $\Sigma_{T}$, the flux of the conserved Dirac current through $\Sigma_{T}$ equals its flux through $\mathcal{C}^{+}_{0}\cap D_{T}$: $\int_{\Sigma_{T}}|\Psi|^{2}\,d\sigma_{\Sigma_{T}} = \int_{\mathcal{C}^{+}_{0}}(|\Psi_{1}|^{2} + |\Psi_{4}|^{2})\,d\sigma_{\mathcal{C}^{+}_{0}}$, where $\Psi_{1}$, $\Psi_{4}$ are the components of $\Psi$ on the cone, in a spin frame adapted to it, that the flux through the cone sees.
\item[(b)] \emph{(Theorem 1, with the abstract.)} The trace operator $\Gamma$, which takes data on $\Sigma_{T}$ to the pair $(\Psi_{1}, \Psi_{4})$ on the cone, extends to an isometry from $L^{2}$ data on $\Sigma_{T}$ to $L^{2}(\mathcal{C}^{+}_{0}, d\sigma)\otimes\mathbb{C}^{2}$; the characteristic Cauchy problem on the cone has, for $L^{2}$ data, a unique solution in the future of the cone within $D_{T}$, so $\Gamma$ is unitary.
\item[(c)] \emph{(Theorem 2.)} $\Gamma$ is an isomorphism from $H^{1}(\Sigma_{T})$ onto the space of cone data whose $(\Psi_{1}, \Psi_{4})$ and their derivatives along the null tetrad are square integrable.
\end{enumerate}
Not part of this Fact: null hypersurfaces other than light cones near their vertex, the part of the cone beyond $t = T$, and any statement about states. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{HafnerNicolas2011}, Def.~3.6, Def.~4.2, Eq.~(14), Theorems 1 and 2.
synthesis.imported-haefner-nicolas-dirac.technical: On a null hypersurface the Dirac field is determined by only half of its components, the ones that the flow of the conserved current through the hypersurface sees. Häfner and Nicolas proved, for the light cone of a point in an arbitrary spacetime, close enough to the vertex, that these two components on the cone carry exactly the same norm as the full field on a spacelike slice (the current is conserved, so what flows through the slice flows through the cone), and that every square-integrable choice of them comes from exactly one solution. The trace on the cone is therefore unitary, which is the statement that the field restricted to the light rays of the cone obeys the canonical anticommutation relations. They also identify the cone data that give solutions with one square-integrable derivative. The field may be massive. This is a standard result taken from the literature, for light cones near the vertex only.
synthesis.imported-haefner-nicolas-dirac.lay: Along a sheet of light rays the electron field is fixed by only half of its parts. For the light cone of a point, close to its tip, in any gravitational field, mathematicians proved that those parts carry exactly the same information as the whole field at an instant, with nothing lost and nothing extra. This is taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-heat-kernel-coefficie.technical: The heat kernel of a second-order operator of Laplace type has a small-time expansion whose coefficients are integrals of local invariants: the endomorphism part $E$, the curvature $\Omega$ of the connection and the curvature of the manifold. Vassilevich labels them by the power $t^{(k-n)/2}$, so the coefficient that carries $E^{2}$ and $\Omega^{2}$ is his $a_{4}$; DeWitt labels by integer powers and calls it $a_{2}$. On a flat background its field-strength part is $\tfrac12E^{2} + \tfrac1{12}\Omega^{2}$, and it multiplies the logarithm of the cut-off in the one-loop determinant. In the background-field gauge of Abbott the gauge fixing respects the gauge symmetry of the background, so the one-loop effective action is a gauge-invariant function of the background field strength, and the coefficient of its square gives the running of the coupling; each field contributes the determinant of its one-loop operator, weighted by its statistics and by whether it is real or complex, with the Faddeev-Popov ghosts entering as a complex scalar with fermionic sign.
synthesis.imported-heat-kernel-coefficie.lay: How strongly the forces of nature act changes with the energy at which they are probed, and the rate of change at the first quantum level can be read from a standard expansion that describes how heat would spread on the space of field configurations. Combined with a standard way of fixing the redundancy of force fields that keeps their symmetry visible, the expansion gives each kind of particle's contribution to the running. These are textbook results that the series takes as given.

synthesis.imported-kuckert-modular-pct-s.technical: Kuckert's theorem derives the spin-statistics connection of a theory of local observables from a weak modular assumption: the modular conjugation of each wedge, defined by the vacuum, acts on the local algebras as the wedge's spacetime reflection. With covariance under the covering group, the spectrum condition and a compact internal symmetry group, the rotation by $2\pi$ is then a product of modular conjugations of wedges turned by half that angle, trivial on observables, and on the Doplicher-Roberts field algebra it is the Bose-Fermi grading. The modular groups themselves need not act as boosts, so the assumption is weaker than full modular covariance. Borchers's theorem supplies the relation between the modular objects of an algebra and a positive-energy translation that maps the algebra into itself: the modular group dilates the translations at rate $2\pi$, and the modular conjugation reverses them.
synthesis.imported-kuckert-modular-pct-s.lay: Why particles of half-integer spin obey the exclusion rule can be proved in several ways. Kuckert showed that it follows from a symmetry property of the vacuum: the mathematical reflection that the vacuum defines for each wedge-shaped region of spacetime must act on what can be measured as the ordinary mirror reflection of that wedge. Borchers's theorem, a tool of the same theory, says how this reflection and its companion flow treat a shift along a light ray that carries the region into itself. The series uses both when asking which assumption would carry its spin and statistics results beyond approximations.

synthesis.imported-local-covariance-with.formal:
Units $\hbar = c = 1$. Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on four-dimensional flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric is smooth and globally hyperbolic, with curvature operator $\mathcal{R}$, and let the free fields on it be given with their Wick polynomials defined by subtraction of the Hadamard parametrix. For $\lambda > 0$ write $(\hb, \Omega)_{\lambda}$ for the field obtained by the constant rescaling of the displacement gauge field that multiplies the derived metric by $\lambda^{2}$, and $m \mapsto m/\lambda$ for the accompanying rescaling of the mass. The sources treat a real scalar field; the statement was written from memory and then compared with the sources at the level given under provenance:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Existence.)} Time-ordered products $T_{n}$ of Wick polynomials exist on every such field with the following properties. \emph{Locality and covariance:} $T_{n}$ on a region is a functional of the field on that region only, and an isometric embedding of one field into another that preserves the causal structure, the orientations and the spin structure carries the products of the first to those of the second. \emph{Scaling:} under $(\hb, \Omega) \mapsto (\hb, \Omega)_{\lambda}$, $m \mapsto m/\lambda$, each $T_{n}$ is multiplied by the power of $\lambda$ given by the engineering dimensions of its arguments, up to a polynomial in $\log\lambda$ whose coefficients are products of lower order with local terms (almost homogeneous scaling). \emph{Regularity:} the products obey the microlocal spectrum condition, vary continuously under smooth variations of the metric, and depend analytically on it along analytic families (the source requires both: continuity alone does not exclude local curvature terms that are not analytic). Together with causal factorisation, symmetry, unitarity and the commutation relations with the free field \cite{HollandsWald2001, HollandsWald2002}; the microlocal construction by extension of distributions is that of \cite{BrunettiFredenhagen2000}. The first source proves the existence of the local Wick polynomials and defers that of the time-ordered products to the second, which proves it for a free scalar field.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Uniqueness.)} Two prescriptions with the properties of (i) differ, at each order, by terms supported on the total diagonal that are themselves local and covariant functionals of the field with almost homogeneous scaling: sums of covariant derivatives of the delta function whose coefficients are polynomials, with constant real coefficients, in the curvature operator, its covariant derivatives and the mass, each term of the engineering dimension fixed by the scaling. The freedom at each order is therefore a finite list of constants, the same on every field \cite{HollandsWald2001}.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The form used in the store.)} For a kernel of degree of divergence $\omega$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extension-theorem-and-ward-preserving-time-ordered-products}(ii)), the extension across the diagonal can be chosen as a local and covariant functional of the field that scales almost homogeneously under the constant rescaling of the displacement gauge field with the mass rescaled inversely; and in the difference of two such extensions the coefficient of a derivative of $\delta$ of order $j \leq \omega$ is a polynomial in the curvature operator, its covariant derivatives and the mass, of dimension $\omega - j$ (the curvature operator of dimension $2$, each covariant derivative and the mass of dimension $1$), with constant coefficients. For $\omega = 2$ the dimension is $2 - j$.
\end{enumerate}
The sources prove (i) and (ii) for a real scalar field (the first states the restriction, the second's abstract says a free scalar field). For the Dirac field charged under a gauge group, in gauge and Yukawa background fields, renormalised Wick powers and time-ordered products are constructed in \cite{Zahn2012}, with the current and the stress-energy tensor conserved and the remaining ambiguity characterised, and perturbative agreement for the charged Dirac field is shown in \cite{Zahn2013}; both were read at the level of the abstract only, and whether they give (i) to (iii) in the form used here, for the current of the Dirac field on a gravitational field, was not verified. That use is therefore taken with the import and is its less well sourced part. Not part of this Fact: the Ward identity on a gravitational field, the existence of a transverse extension there, and the value of any constant. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{HollandsWald2001} (abstract and the first part of the arXiv text checked on the web on 10 November 2026: the restriction to a real scalar field, uniqueness up to finitely many parameters, the continuity and analyticity requirements, scaling with the metric and the squared mass rescaled together, existence of the time-ordered products deferred); \cite{HollandsWald2002} (abstract checked); \cite{BrunettiFredenhagen2000} for the microlocal setting; \cite{Zahn2012}, \cite{Zahn2013} (abstracts checked). Section and theorem numbers are not given because they were not verified.
synthesis.imported-local-covariance-with.technical: On flat spacetime the freedom in extending a one-loop kernel across coincident points is a short list of constants, because translation and Lorentz covariance force the coefficients of the delta-function terms to be constant invariant tensors. On a gravitational field there is no such symmetry, and the extension theorem alone leaves the coefficients free functions of the point. Hollands and Wald replaced the missing symmetry by two requirements. The construction must be local and covariant: it may use only the field in a neighbourhood of the points, and it must be the same construction on every field, so that the coefficients are built from the curvature operator and its derivatives at the point. And it must scale almost homogeneously when the displacement gauge field is rescaled by a constant with the mass rescaled inversely, so that each coefficient has a fixed dimension; analytic dependence on the field then makes it a polynomial (continuity alone would not). Curvature has dimension two and a mass dimension one, so a kernel of degree of divergence two allows a constant in front of the second derivatives of delta and, without derivatives, terms linear in the curvature operator and quadratic in the mass, each with a constant coefficient. They proved that time-ordered products with these properties exist and that any two differ in this way. The sources treat a scalar field; the store uses the statement for the current of the Dirac field, which is the less well sourced part of the import: the literature for the Dirac field (Zahn 2012, 2013, in gauge and Yukawa background fields) was read at the level of the abstracts only. The Ward identity on the field, which removes further constants, is not part of this Fact. The statement was written from memory and compared with the abstracts of the sources and the opening part of the first paper; theorem numbers were not verified.
synthesis.imported-local-covariance-with.lay: Quantum field theory leaves a small amount of freedom at the points where particles meet: on flat spacetime, a few constants. In a gravitational field the same mathematics would allow those constants to vary from place to place in an arbitrary way. Hollands and Wald showed around 2001 that two natural demands remove this: the rule must be built only from the field near the point, in the same way everywhere, and it must behave correctly when all lengths are rescaled together. Then the freedom is again a few constants, multiplying expressions made from the curvature. The collection takes this from the literature. The original papers prove it for the simplest kind of field, not for the electron's; the statement was compared with the summaries of the papers and the opening part of the first, not with their proofs.

synthesis.imported-lsz-reduction-ward-id.technical: Three standard results of quantum electrodynamics. The reduction formula of Lehmann, Symanzik and Zimmermann turns time-ordered correlation functions into scattering amplitudes: each external particle contributes a pole at its mass shell, the amplitude is the residue, and each leg carries the square root of the field's normalisation constant. Ward's identity ties the electron-photon vertex at zero momentum transfer to the momentum derivative of the electron self-energy, so the vertex and electron-field renormalisation constants are equal and only the photon field renormalises the charge. Jost and Luttinger computed the vacuum polarisation to fourth order in the charge, the second coefficient of the running of the fine-structure constant: per Dirac fermion $\mu\,d\alpha/d\mu = 2\alpha^{2}/(3\pi) + \alpha^{3}/(2\pi^{2})$.
synthesis.imported-lsz-reduction-ward-id.lay: Three classic results of the quantum theory of light and electrons: the rule that turns the theory's correlation functions into probabilities for particles to scatter; Ward's identity, which guarantees that the electron's charge is corrected only through the light field and never separately through the electron; and the second-order calculation of how the strength of the electric force grows with energy. The series takes these from the literature.
