synthesis.imported-luscher-mack-conforma.formal: Let a quantum field theory on Minkowski space (the flat gravitational field, $\hb = 1$, $\Omega = 0$; Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) satisfy the Wightman axioms and be conformally invariant, in the sense that its Euclidean Green functions are invariant under the Euclidean conformal group. Then (L\"uscher and Mack) the theory extends to the universal covering $\widetilde{M}$ of compactified Minkowski space, on which the universal covering of the conformal group $\mathrm{SO}(2,4)$ acts by a unitary representation on the state space; $\widetilde{M}$ carries the derived metric of the Einstein static field $\mathbb{R} \times S^{3}$ of unit radius, conformal to Minkowski space on the image of the embedding. The conformal energy $H = \tfrac12(P_{0} + K_{0})$, the combination of the time translation $P_{0}$ and the special conformal generator $K_{0}$ of Minkowski space, generates the time translations of $\mathbb{R} \times S^{3}$: it is the energy of the theory on the unit Einstein static field, and its spectrum is bounded below. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{LuscherMack1975}. \emph{Beyond one flat chart.} $\widetilde{M}$ and the Einstein static field are global and are read on several charts of flat spacetime, each with its own gravitational field, glued by gauge transformations; the conformal embedding of Minkowski space into one of them is stated on one chart.
synthesis.imported-luscher-mack-conforma.technical: A conformally invariant field theory on Minkowski space does not live only on Minkowski space: its natural home is the universal covering of the conformal compactification, which is the Einstein static universe, a cylinder $\mathbb{R} \times S^{3}$. L\"uscher and Mack showed that, given Euclidean conformal invariance, the Minkowski theory extends there, with the whole covering group of the conformal group acting unitarily. Under this embedding the time translation of the cylinder of unit radius is the conformal Hamiltonian $\tfrac12(P_{0} + K_{0})$ of Minkowski space, so the conformal energy of a state on Minkowski space is its energy on the unit Einstein static field.
synthesis.imported-luscher-mack-conforma.lay: Theories that look the same at every scale can be moved, without losing information, from ordinary flat spacetime onto a closed universe shaped like a cylinder whose cross-section is a three-dimensional sphere. L\"uscher and Mack showed how. On that cylinder an ordinary energy is defined, and it corresponds to a particular combination of energy and a rescaling-type symmetry in flat spacetime. This is taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: M. L\"uscher and G. Mack, Global conformal invariance in quantum field theory, Commun. Math. Phys. 41 (1975), 203--234.

synthesis.imported-one-loop-integrals-an.formal:
Signature $(+,-,-,-)$, $\ell^{2} = Q(\ell)$, units $\hbar = c = 1$. Numbers are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$, the field theory's unit (on values that are not even, such as a Dirac numerator, it is the right unit $x \mapsto xI_{4}$, a coefficient collected in front of the product).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Feynman parametrisation.)} For nonzero $D_{1}, \ldots, D_{n}$ of one sign, $\dfrac{1}{D_{1}\cdots D_{n}} = (n-1)!\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\!dx_{1}\cdots dx_{n}\,\frac{\delta(1 - \sum_{j}x_{j})}{(\sum_{j}x_{j}D_{j})^{n}}$ \cite{Weinzierl2010}.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Wick-rotated integrals.)} After the rotation $\ell_{0} = I_{4}\ell_{E,0}$ of the scalar integration variable $\ell_{0}$ in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$, which takes $\int d^{4}\ell\,f(-\ell^{2})$ to $I_{4}\int d^{4}\ell_{E}\,f(\ell_{E}^{2})$ \cite{Weinzierl2010}, for $\Delta > 0$: $\int\frac{d^{4}\ell}{(2\pi)^{4}}(\ell^{2} - \Delta)^{-3} = \frac{-I_{4}}{32\pi^{2}\Delta}$; with the Euclidean cut-off $\ell_{E}^{2} \le L$, $\int\frac{d^{4}\ell}{(2\pi)^{4}}(\ell^{2} - \Delta)^{-2} = \frac{I_{4}}{16\pi^{2}}\bigl(\ln(L/\Delta) - 1 + O(\Delta/L)\bigr)$. Terms odd in $\ell$ integrate to zero and $(a\cdot\ell)(b\cdot\ell) \to \tfrac14 Q(\ell)\,a\cdot b$ under the integral for constant vectors $a, b$ (symmetric integration; in components $\ell^{\alpha}\ell^{\beta} \to \tfrac14 Q(\ell)g^{\alpha\beta}$) \cite{PeskinSchroeder1995}.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Pauli-Villars regulators.)} Each internal line of mass $m$ is replaced by a weighted sum over fields of masses $M_{i}$ and weights $c_{i}$, $c_{0} = 1$, $M_{0} = m$, with $\sum_{i}c_{i} = \sum_{i}c_{i}M_{i}^{2} = 0$; the weights take both signs, and a field of negative weight is quantised with a negative metric. At one loop these conditions make the integrals of (ii) finite, the regularisation is Lorentz invariant and keeps the Ward identity of electrodynamics, and the physical limit is $M_{i} \to \infty$ for $i \ge 1$ \cite{PauliVillars1949}. A regulator of a single Weyl fermion is a Dirac field of mass $M_{i}$, so the scheme does not preserve chirality.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Covariant photon.)} In the covariant (Gupta-Bleuler) quantisation the photon propagator in the gauge with parameter $\xi$ is the linear map on vectors $a \mapsto \frac{-I_{4}}{k^{2} + I_{4}0}\bigl(a - (1 - \xi)\frac{(a\cdot k)\,k}{k^{2}}\bigr)$, the unit a coefficient in front (in components $\frac{-I_{4}}{k^{2} + I_{4}0}\bigl(g_{\mu\nu} - (1 - \xi)\frac{k_{\mu}k_{\nu}}{k^{2}}\bigr)$, the values $\gamma_{\mu}\cdot D(\gamma_{\nu})$ of this map $D$), $\xi = 1$ the Feynman gauge, and on-shell amplitudes between physical external states are independent of $\xi$ by the Ward identity \cite{PeskinSchroeder1995}.
\item[(v)] \emph{(On-shell external states.)} Scattering amplitudes are evaluated between on-shell spinors, $(p - m)u(p) = 0$, so between external states a Dirac line carries the projector $(p + m)/(2m)$ (LSZ reduction) \cite{PeskinSchroeder1995}.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.imported-one-loop-integrals-an.technical: These are the standard tools for computing one-loop corrections in a relativistic quantum field theory. Feynman's trick combines a product of propagator denominators into one power of a weighted sum over the simplex. The loop momentum is then shifted, the integral rotated to Euclidean signature, and terms odd in the momentum dropped while products of two momenta are replaced by a quarter of the square times the metric; the remaining integrals are elementary, finite for three denominators and logarithmically divergent for two. Pauli and Villars regulate by adding heavy copies of each field with weights of both signs, chosen so that the weights and the weighted squared masses sum to zero: this is relativistically invariant and respects the conservation of charge, but the copies of negative weight are fields of negative norm, and a regulated chiral fermion acquires a mass. In covariant quantisation the photon propagator carries a gauge parameter on which physical on-shell amplitudes do not depend, and external lines are on-shell spinors.
synthesis.imported-one-loop-integrals-an.lay: To compute the first quantum corrections in a theory such as electrodynamics, physicists use a standard toolkit: a trick for combining denominators, a rotation of the time direction into an imaginary one that turns the integrals into ordinary ones, and a way of taming their infinities with heavy auxiliary particles, some of which count negatively. These tools are textbook material; the series takes them as given.

imported_from.citation: W. Pauli and F. Villars, On the invariant regularization in relativistic quantum theory, Rev. Mod. Phys. 21 (1949), 434--444.
M. E. Peskin and D. V. Schroeder, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory, Addison-Wesley (1995), chapters 6 and 7.
S. Weinzierl, Introduction to Feynman integrals, arXiv:1005.1855, equations (50) and (61).

synthesis.imported-quasi-spin-pairing-an.technical: Kerman's quasi-spin method solves the pairing model of nuclear physics exactly if all the levels are degenerate: the pair creation and annihilation operators form an $\su(2)$, so the energies follow from the Casimir and depend only on the particle number and the seniority, the number of unpaired particles. Breaking one pair costs the pairing strength times the pair degeneracy. Nambu and Jona-Lasinio found the particle-physics analogue: a fermion that gets its mass dynamically has a scalar partner at twice its mass. Assuming the top quark is the sole constituent, this gives the classic top-condensation prediction of a Higgs at twice the top mass, which more elaborate models with several condensates bring down to the observed value.
synthesis.imported-quasi-spin-pairing-an.lay: When particles pair up, as electrons do in a superconductor and nucleons in a nucleus, it costs a definite energy to break a pair, and for the simplest model this is known exactly. Particle physicists borrowed the idea: if the Higgs boson were a bound pair of top quarks, the simplest estimate puts it at twice the top's mass, far heavier than observed, though models with several kinds of pairs can bring it down. The series takes these results as given.

synthesis.imported-renormalised-stress-t.formal: Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric is smooth and globally hyperbolic, and let $\psi$ be the free Dirac field on it, formulated as a locally covariant quantum field theory. Wick polynomials of $\psi$ are defined by point splitting with the Hadamard parametrix subtracted (the extended algebra of observables). On every Hadamard state $\omega$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-microlocal-hadamard-condition}(b)) they give an expected stress-energy tensor $\langle T_{ab}\rangle_{\omega}$, a smooth symmetric tensor field of the derived metric, which is covariantly conserved, $\nabla^{a}\langle T_{ab}\rangle_{\omega} = 0$; its trace anomaly is computed explicitly there. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{DappiaggiHackPinamonti2009}. Cited from memory, not part of the checked statement: that the trace anomaly is a local polynomial in the curvature and the mass, the same for every state; that the renormalised tensor is fixed up to local covariant terms built from the curvature and the mass; and that the difference of the tensors of two Hadamard states, the coincidence limit of a differential operator applied to their smooth difference kernel, needs no renormalisation.
synthesis.imported-renormalised-stress-t.technical: A quantum field's energy density cannot be read off its two-point function directly, since the coincidence limit is infinite; on Hadamard states the infinite part is the same universal singularity for every state and can be subtracted geometrically. Dappiaggi, Hack and Pinamonti carried this out for the Dirac field on any globally hyperbolic gravitational field, in the locally covariant framework: they defined Wick polynomials of the spinor field by subtracting the Hadamard parametrix, and with them a stress-energy tensor that is covariantly conserved on Hadamard states and so can act as the source of the gravitational field equations. Its trace is the trace anomaly, which they computed. The tensor is defined only on Hadamard states, and the remaining freedom is in local curvature terms common to all states.
synthesis.imported-renormalised-stress-t.lay: In a gravitational field the energy carried by a quantum field can be computed only for well-behaved quantum states, called Hadamard states, by removing an infinite part that is the same for all of them. For electrons and the other particles of spin one half this was worked out by Dappiaggi, Hack and Pinamonti, who showed that the resulting energy and momentum are conserved, so they can serve as the source in the equations of gravity. This is taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: C. Dappiaggi, T.-P. Hack and N. Pinamonti, The extended algebra of observables for Dirac fields and the trace anomaly of their stress-energy tensor, Rev. Math. Phys. 21 (2009), 1241--1312; arXiv:0904.0612.

synthesis.imported-schwinger-term-and-ma.technical: For fermions in one chiral band with the negative levels filled, the Fourier modes of the density do not commute: the commutator of a mode with its conjugate equals the momentum, a central term. It makes the density modes a set of boson modes, the basis of bosonisation (Tomonaga; Mattis and Lieb, who noticed the care the normal ordering needs). For any finite band the term is absent; it comes from the infinite sea. In relativistic field theory the same structure appears as Schwinger's term in the commutator of charge and current densities, which a positive-energy vacuum forces to be nonzero.
synthesis.imported-schwinger-term-and-ma.lay: In a one-dimensional sea of fermions, ripples of density behave exactly like independent bosons, a standard result of the 1950s and 1960s. The reason is a small extra term in how density ripples combine, which comes from the infinitely deep sea of filled levels; Schwinger showed the same kind of term must appear in any relativistic theory with a stable vacuum. The series takes these results as given.

synthesis.imported-singer-gauge-slice-ne.technical: These are the standard non-perturbative limits of gauge fixing and the standard phase structure of lattice gauge theories with Higgs fields. Singer showed that Gribov's observation is topological: on the three- or four-sphere no continuous condition picks one representative from every gauge orbit of a non-abelian field. Neuberger showed that a BRST gauge fixing on the lattice fails globally: summing over the Gribov copies with the signs of their Faddeev-Popov determinants gives the Euler characteristic of the compact gauge group, zero, so the partition function and every expectation value become $0/0$. Fradkin and Shenker showed that with a Higgs field in the fundamental representation the Higgs and confining regimes of a lattice gauge theory are one phase: no sharp order parameter separates them.
synthesis.imported-singer-gauge-slice-ne.lay: Describing the force fields of particle physics involves a redundancy, and the usual ways of removing it work only for weak fields. Singer proved that no smooth way of removing it works everywhere; Neuberger showed that the standard bookkeeping, done on a lattice of spacetime points, gives zero divided by zero; and Fradkin and Shenker showed that a force field with a Higgs field of the simplest kind has no sharp boundary between a regime where its charges are confined and one where its particles are massive. The series takes these results from the literature.

synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-.technical: Wilson put gauge theory on a spacetime lattice with group-valued link variables and the action built from the trace of the product around each elementary square; the theory is gauge invariant with no gauge fixing, its coupling is $\beta = 2N/g^{2}$ for $SU(N)$, and it reduces to Yang-Mills theory as the lattice spacing shrinks. Under strong coupling Wilson loops fall with the area they enclose, which is confinement of static charges. Osterwalder and Seiler proved that these lattice theories have a positive transfer matrix, so they describe quantum theories at finite spacing, and proved the strong-coupling area law rigorously. Elitzur showed that a local symmetry cannot break spontaneously on the lattice. The strong-coupling area law does not distinguish abelian from non-abelian groups: four-dimensional compact $U(1)$ also confines at strong coupling, but it is proved to have a deconfined, massless phase at weak coupling.
synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-.lay: Putting the forces of nature on a grid of points in space and time, as Wilson did in 1974, avoids the redundancy problems of their usual description and makes it possible to prove things about them. On such a grid, if the coupling is strong, a pair of test charges is held together with a force that does not weaken with distance. This is proved rigorously, but it holds for electromagnetism on a grid too, which is known to stop confining at weak coupling, so it is not by itself evidence that the real strong force confines.

synthesis.interacting-fields-of-causal-p.formal:
Units and signature of the store; $\Cl(1,3)$ with $I_{4} = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$. The attached free fields are the Dirac spinor values $\psi$ of Proposition \claimref{field-theory.second-quantisation}, on which a Lorentz rotor $R$ acts by $\psi \mapsto R\psi$; the gauge potentials and their gradients, vector values with $x \mapsto Rx\tilde R$; palatial scalars, any number of doublets; and the Faddeev-Popov ghosts $c$, $\bar c$, scalar CAR modes on tower planes (\claimref{synthesis.self-adjoint-brst-charge-needs-a-krein-form-and-the-tower-supplies-the-ghosts}, Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-tower-limit}). Their statistics are those of \claimref{synthesis.locality-of-the-attached-free-fields-fixes-their-statistics}: anticommuting spinors, commuting scalars and field strengths, anticommuting ghosts in the indefinite form; for the potential itself in Feynman gauge, which that result does not cover, we assume the Gupta-Bleuler (indefinite) form, clause (K1) of Premise \claimref{synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-inner-product-for-gauge-fields}, in which its polarisation sum is $-a\cdot b$, of degree $0$ in $k$, and it is local as a commuting field (computed in (i)). Let the interaction density $\mathcal{L}$ be a sum of the monomials (i) below, and let the interacting field of a Wick polynomial $A$ be Bogoliubov's $A_{\mathrm{int}}(x) = \frac{\delta}{I_{4}\,\delta h(x)}S(\mathcal{L})^{-1}S(\mathcal{L} + hA)\big|_{h = 0}$ (the complex unit of the free fields' Fock space is the field theory's unit $I_{4}$, numbers read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$), a formal power series, with time-ordered products that are graded symmetric and preserve the Grassmann parity, factorise causally, satisfy the Wick expansion (the free-field condition (N3) of \cite{DutschFredenhagen1999}), and, as an assumption, are covariant under a representation $U$ of the covering group of the Poincar\'e group (\cite{DutschFredenhagen1999} state covariance, (N1), for the Poincar\'e group itself; Epstein and Glaser \cite{EpsteinGlaser1973}, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extension-theorem-and-ward-preserving-time-ordered-products}; \cite{DutschFredenhagen1999}, (2.2), (2.3), (2.7)). Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The interaction density; computed.)} The rotor of the loop of four quarter turns in the plane $\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}$ is $-1$: it fixes every vector and bivector value and negates every spinor value. The vector vertex $\langle\psi\gamma_{0}\tilde\psi A\rangle_{0}$, the axial vertex $\langle\psi\gamma_{3}\tilde\psi A\rangle_{0}$, the scalar and pseudoscalar Yukawa terms and mass insertions $\langle\psi\tilde\psi\rangle_{0}\phi$, $\langle\psi\tilde\psi I_{4}\rangle_{0}\phi$, the scalar gauge couplings, the quartic, the non-abelian cubic and quartic terms, the gauge fixing $\langle\nabla A\rangle_{0}^{2}$ and the ghost terms $\langle\nabla\bar c\,\nabla c\rangle_{0}$, $\langle\nabla\bar c\,A\rangle_{0}c$ are Lorentz scalars, each with an even number of spinor factors (so $U(2\pi)$ acts on $\mathcal{L}$ as $+1$) and with as many ghost as antighost factors; nothing depends on the number of scalar doublets. The free Feynman-gauge potential has the polarisation sum $-a\cdot b$, independent of $k$ and indefinite, and the bracket factor of the stored locality result vanishes for it as a commuting field.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Wick monomials; proved.)} On a Wick monomial with $n_{\psi}$ spinor and $n_{c} + n_{\bar c}$ ghost factors, $U(2\pi)$ acts as $(-1)^{n_{\psi}}$ and the Grassmann parity is $(-1)^{n_{\psi} + n_{c} + n_{\bar c}}$; they agree if and only if $n_{c} + n_{\bar c}$ is even, in particular at ghost number zero, and two such monomials on disjoint modes anticommute exactly when both have $U(2\pi) = -1$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Interacting fields; proved given the imported axioms.)} Every order of $A_{\mathrm{int}}$ is a retarded product of copies of $\mathcal{L}$ with $A$; by parity preservation it has the Grassmann parity of $A$, and by covariance under the covering group its $2\pi$ eigenvalue is that of $A$; the interacting fields are graded-local with that parity (\cite{DutschFredenhagen1999}, Proposition 2, (2.25), for QED, where the ghosts do not couple; for a coupled ghost vertex, Yang-Mills, \cite{Hollands2008}, cited from memory), the first order following from the graded Jacobi identity for even $\mathcal{L}$ and the light-cone lemma of the proof. Hence, if the time-ordered products satisfy these conditions, then on every interacting field with an even number of ghost factors, in particular the interacting field of every Wick polynomial of ghost number zero, the statistics operator equals $U(2\pi)$ to every order: the spin-statistics connection holds in perturbation theory with no Jost-point or modular premise. Ghost fields of odd ghost count have the opposite sign, the Krein exception of the free-field result.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(What remains; argued.)} The statement concerns formal power series. Beyond perturbation theory a premise remains (the Jost point of Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-standard-field-theory}, or a modular premise, \claimref{synthesis.wedge-reflections-compose-to-the-two-pi-rotor-so-geometric-modular-conjugations-give-interacting-spin-statistics}); for electrically charged fields the nonperturbative charge classes are localised in hypercones \cite{BuchholzRoberts2014}, where a spin-statistics theorem is not supplied by the sources read.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.interacting-fields-of-causal-p.technical:
The question is whether the spin-statistics connection of interacting fields needs the Jost-point theorem. In perturbation theory it does not. Interacting fields are built from the free fields by Bogoliubov's formula, each order a retarded product of the Wick polynomial with copies of the interaction density, and causal perturbation theory proves that interacting fields are graded-local with the free grading and covariant whenever the time-ordered products are (standard: Epstein-Glaser; Dütsch-Fredenhagen for QED with spinors and ghosts; Hollands for Yang-Mills). The conditions used are graded symmetry and parity preservation, causal factorisation, the Wick expansion and covariance under the covering group, the last assumed (the standard axiom is stated for the Poincar\'e group); the free potential in Feynman gauge is taken in its indefinite form, where it is local. The series' part is the bookkeeping on its own field list, done exactly in the spacetime algebra: the rotation by $2\pi$ is the rotor $-1$, which negates spinor values and fixes vector, bivector and scalar values; every monomial of the series' interaction (vector and axial vertices, Yukawa and mass insertions with any number of doublets, scalar and non-abelian gauge couplings, gauge fixing, ghost terms) is a Lorentz scalar with an even number of spinors and as many ghosts as antighosts. So an interacting field keeps both the Grassmann parity and the $2\pi$ eigenvalue of its Wick polynomial, and the two agree exactly when the number of ghost factors is even, in particular at ghost number zero. The first-order locality step reduces, by the graded Jacobi identity for an even interaction and a light-cone lemma, to free graded locality, checked exactly on the tower's CAR modes.

So the Jost import is needed only beyond perturbation theory, where a premise remains (the Jost point or a modular premise, \claimref{synthesis.wedge-reflections-compose-to-the-two-pi-rotor-so-geometric-modular-conjugations-give-interacting-spin-statistics}); electrically charged fields add an infrared obstacle there.
synthesis.interacting-fields-of-causal-p.lay: Particles of half-integer spin obey the exclusion rule and those of whole-number spin do not. For the series' free particles this tie was already derived; the question was whether it survives interactions. In the standard step-by-step construction of interacting fields, it does: each step combines the free fields with the interaction, and every term of the series' interaction contains matter fields in pairs, so turning a field by a full circle and exchanging two fields give the same sign before and after the interaction is switched on. The bookkeeping fields used to fix gauges are the one exception, as they were for free fields, and they always appear in pairs in anything physical. What the step-by-step construction does not give is a statement about the full theory beyond that expansion; there a deeper assumption is still needed.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting and imports.} Work in $\Cl(1,3)$ with $\gamma_{0}^{2} = 1$, $\gamma_{i}^{2} = -1$ and $I_{4} = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$. A rotor $R$ ($R\tilde R = 1$, even) acts on the series' Dirac values by $\psi \mapsto R\psi$ (Proposition \claimref{field-theory.second-quantisation}), on vector values (potentials, gradients) and bivector values by $x \mapsto Rx\tilde R$, and trivially on scalar values (the components of any number of scalar doublets and the ghosts of \claimref{synthesis.self-adjoint-brst-charge-needs-a-krein-form-and-the-tower-supplies-the-ghosts}). The covering group of the Lorentz group is the rotor group; its element $-1$ is the end point of the lift of a closed loop of rotations. The free fields have the statistics of \claimref{synthesis.locality-of-the-attached-free-fields-fixes-their-statistics}: with positive norm the spinor is a CAR field and the scalars and the field strength CCR fields; the ghosts are local CAR scalars, which needs the indefinite form. The potential itself in Feynman gauge is not covered by that result; it enters as a condition (Step 2). From outside the store the proof uses only the axioms and results of causal perturbation theory (standard): time-ordered products $T$ that are multilinear, graded symmetric in their arguments and preserve the Grassmann parity (the renormalisation freedom is spanned by local terms of the parity of the product), satisfy the Wick expansion in the free fields ((N3) of \cite{DutschFredenhagen1999}), factorise causally ($T(A_{1}(x_{1})\cdots A_{n}(x_{n})) = T(A_{1}\cdots A_{k})T(A_{k+1}\cdots A_{n})$ when no $x_{j}$, $j > k$, lies in the closed causal future of an $x_{i}$, $i \le k$) and are covariant, $\mathrm{Ad}\,U(L)\,T(A_{1}(x_{1})\cdots) = T(\mathrm{Ad}\,U(L)A_{1}(x_{1})\cdots)$ \cite{DutschFredenhagen1999} ((2.2), (2.3)); there (N1) is stated for the proper orthochronous Poincar\'e group, and covariance under its covering group, with $U$ acting on spinor fields through the rotor group, is an assumption of the present result (standard for spinor fields, cited from memory); their existence \cite{EpsteinGlaser1973} (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extension-theorem-and-ward-preserving-time-ordered-products}(i)); Bogoliubov's interacting fields \cite{DutschFredenhagen1999} ((2.7)); and graded locality of interacting fields to all orders \cite{DutschFredenhagen1999} (Proposition 2 and (2.25), read: the bracket is an anticommutator only when both fields have an odd number of spinor fields or both an odd number of ghost fields, in a convention where free spinors commute with free ghosts; in their QED the ghosts do not couple); with a coupled ghost vertex (Yang-Mills) \cite{Hollands2008} (cited from memory, the relevant sections not read).

\emph{Step 1: the rotation by $2\pi$ (clause (i), first sentence).} Let $B = \gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}$, $B^{2} = -1$. The versor $q = 1 + B$ has $q\tilde q = 2$ and $q x \tilde q/2$ is the quarter turn in the plane $B$; $q^{2} = 2B$, so $q^{2}/2 = B$ is the half turn ($B\gamma_{1}\tilde B = -\gamma_{1}$, checked), and $q^{4} = (2B)^{2} = -4$. The four quarter turns compose the closed loop of rotations by $\pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2, 2\pi$; its lift to rotors, normalised by $(q\tilde q)^{2} = 4$, ends at $q^{4}/4 = -1$. The script computes $q^{4}$, its norm and the action of $U = -1$: $Ux\tilde U = x$ on five vectors and two bivectors, $U\psi = -\psi$ on three even multivectors. So $U(2\pi)$ multiplies a monomial by $(-1)^{n_{\psi}}$, $n_{\psi}$ its number of spinor factors (the conjugate $\tilde\psi$ counts as a spinor factor, $\tilde\psi \mapsto \tilde\psi\tilde R$).

\emph{Step 2: the interaction density (clause (i)).} The monomials are those of the stored results: the vector vertex $\langle J A\rangle_{0}$, $J = \psi\gamma_{0}\tilde\psi$, of the one-loop QED result (\claimref{synthesis.one-loop-qed-in-the-spacetime-algebra}, the matrix reading $\bar\psi\gamma^{\mu}\psi A_{\mu}$); the axial vertex $\langle K A\rangle_{0}$, $K = \psi\gamma_{3}\tilde\psi$ (with the vector vertex it gives the chiral couplings of the weak factor); the Yukawa terms of the doublets and their mass insertions $\langle\psi\tilde\psi\rangle_{0}\phi$, $\langle\psi\tilde\psi I_{4}\rangle_{0}\phi$; the scalar gauge couplings $\langle A\nabla\rangle_{0}\phi\phi$ and $\langle AA\rangle_{0}\phi\phi$ and the quartic $\phi^{4}$; the non-abelian cubic $\langle(\nabla \wedge A)(A \wedge A)\rangle_{0}$ and quartic $\langle(A \wedge A)(A \wedge A)\rangle_{0}$ with structure constants as scalar coefficients; the gauge fixing $\langle\nabla A\rangle_{0}^{2}$; and the ghost terms $\langle\nabla\bar c\,\nabla c\rangle_{0}$ and $\langle\nabla\bar c\,A\rangle_{0}c$ of the BRST result. The scalar content enters only through Lorentz scalars of scalar values, so the number of doublets plays no role. Each is a scalar part of a product of rotor-covariant values, hence invariant under every rotor: $\psi\gamma_{\mu}\tilde\psi \mapsto R\psi\gamma_{\mu}\tilde\psi\tilde R$, $\psi\tilde\psi \mapsto R\psi\tilde\psi\tilde R = \psi\tilde\psi$ (its scalar and $I_{4}$ parts are invariant), and $\langle R X\tilde R\rangle_{0} = \langle X\rangle_{0}$. The script evaluates every monomial on three spinors and sample vectors and scalars, before and after four exact rotors (a rotation $(3 + 4\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2})/5$, a boost $(5 + 4\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1})/3$, a rotation $(5 + 12\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3})/13$ and their product), and under $U = -1$, where the value is $(-1)^{n_{\psi}}$ times the original and nonzero; it also checks that a one-spinor scalar such as $\langle\psi\gamma_{0}A\rangle_{0}$ changes sign under $U$, so the test is not vacuous. The counts are not labelled by hand: the script computes $n_{\psi}$, $n_{c}$, $n_{\bar c}$ as the homogeneity degrees of each monomial under $\psi \mapsto 2\psi$, $c \mapsto 3c$, $\bar c \mapsto 5\bar c$, and finds $n_{\psi} \in \{0, 2\}$, $n_{c} = n_{\bar c}$; the control scalar has degree $1$. The free potential in Feynman gauge: by the Gupta-Bleuler form of the BRST result, $[a_{\mu}, a_{\nu}^{\dagger}] = -\gamma_{\mu}\cdot\gamma_{\nu}$, so its polarisation sum on test vectors is $\sum_{\mu}(-Q(\gamma_{\mu}))(a\cdot\gamma_{\mu})(\gamma_{\mu}\cdot b) = -a\cdot b$ (checked on five vectors), independent of $k$, of degree $d = 0$, and indefinite (negative on a timelike test vector). With the bracket factor $1 + \eta c(-1)^{d}$ of the stored locality result and $c = 1$ (the antiparticle sum equals the particle sum for a Hermitian field), the factor vanishes for $\eta = -1$: the potential is a local commuting field in the indefinite form, the standard Gupta-Bleuler statement (the stored result treats only the field strength at positive norm, so this is a condition of the present result, clause (K1) of Premise \claimref{synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-inner-product-for-gauge-fields}, with the degree computed).

\emph{Step 3: Wick monomials (clause (ii)).} The Grassmann parity of a Wick monomial is the parity of its number of anticommuting factors, $n_{\psi} + n_{c} + n_{\bar c}$, by the free statistics; $U(2\pi)$ acts as $(-1)^{n_{\psi}}$ by Step 1. They agree if and only if $n_{c} + n_{\bar c}$ is even; at ghost number $n_{c} - n_{\bar c} = 0$ the sum $2n_{c}$ is even. The script models the anticommuting factors as tower modes $v_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} + f_{j})$ on distinct tower planes of $\Cl(m, m)$ ($e_{j}^{2} = 1$, $f_{j}^{2} = -1$; $v_{j}^{2} = 0$, $\{v_{j}, v_{k}\} = 0$, the CAR of Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-tower-limit}), reads the Grassmann parity from the grade involution there, and computes the $2\pi$ eigenvalue separately in $\Cl(1,3)$ as the sign by which $U$ applied to each factor changes the product $\psi_{1}\gamma_{0}\psi_{2}\gamma_{0}\cdots\psi_{n_{\psi}}$ of sample spinors (nonzero); over $n_{\psi} \le 3$, $n_{c}, n_{\bar c} \le 2$ the two disagree on exactly the $16$ monomials with $n_{c} + n_{\bar c}$ odd. For ghost-even monomials on disjoint modes the script checks that they anticommute exactly when both have $U(2\pi) = -1$ and commute otherwise. In the convention of \cite{DutschFredenhagen1999}, where spinors commute with ghosts, the bracket sign is $(-1)^{n_{\psi}(A)n_{\psi}(B) + n_{gh}(A)n_{gh}(B)}$; for fields of even ghost count it is $(-1)^{n_{\psi}(A)n_{\psi}(B)}$ in both conventions.

\emph{Step 4: interacting fields keep parity and spin (clause (iii), first part).} The $n$-th order of $A_{\mathrm{int}}(x)$ is $\tfrac{I_{4}^{n}}{n!}\int R(\mathcal{L}(y_{1})\cdots\mathcal{L}(y_{n}); A(x))\,g(y_{1})\cdots g(y_{n})$, a retarded product, a finite combination of time-ordered and anti-time-ordered products of the same factors. By the causal Wick expansion its terms are Wick monomials obtained from the product $\mathcal{L}^{n}A$ by contracting pairs of a field with its conjugate (a $\psi$ with a $\tilde\psi$, a $c$ with a $\bar c$, two bosons), which changes $n_{\psi}$ and $n_{c} + n_{\bar c}$ by even numbers; local renormalisation terms have the Grassmann parity of the product by the parity condition. Since each copy of $\mathcal{L}$ is even (Step 2), every term has the Grassmann parity of $A$. (No conservation of ghost number by the time-ordered products is needed: the result uses only the Grassmann parity and the $2\pi$ eigenvalue, whose ratio is the ghost parity.) By covariance, $\mathrm{Ad}\,U(2\pi)$ acts on the retarded product as on the product of its arguments, that is by $(+1)^{n}(-1)^{n_{\psi}(A)}$. So $A_{\mathrm{int}}$ has the Grassmann parity and the $U(2\pi)$ eigenvalue of $A$, and by Step 3 they agree when $A$ has an even ghost count, in particular when $A$ has ghost number zero. The script checks in the tower model that for an even element $\mathcal{L}$ (spinor and ghost bilinears) the graded commutator $[\mathcal{L}, A]$ has the grade and the spinor-mode sign of $A$, and that $\mathcal{L}$ is fixed by the spinor-mode sign flip.

\emph{Step 5: graded locality (clause (iii), second part).} To all orders this is \cite{DutschFredenhagen1999} (2.25) for QED and \cite{Hollands2008} (cited from memory) with coupled ghosts. At first order it follows from the free statistics, and we give the step since it shows where evenness of $\mathcal{L}$ enters. Write $[X, Y\} = XY - (-1)^{|X||Y|}YX$ for homogeneous $X$, $Y$. With the first-order retarded product $R(\mathcal{L}(y); A(x)) = \theta(x^{0} - y^{0})[A(x), \mathcal{L}(y)]$ (up to a constant), for $x$ and $z$ spacelike separated the first-order part of $[A_{\mathrm{int}}(x), B_{\mathrm{int}}(z)\}$ is a multiple of $\int g(y)\bigl(\theta(x^{0} - y^{0})[[A(x), \mathcal{L}(y)], B(z)\} + \theta(z^{0} - y^{0})[A(x), [B(z), \mathcal{L}(y)]\}\bigr)dy$. For $\mathcal{L}$ even, $\mathrm{ad}_{\mathcal{L}}$ is an even derivation of the graded commutator: $[\mathcal{L}, [A, B\}] = [[\mathcal{L}, A], B\} + [A, [\mathcal{L}, B]\}$ (graded Jacobi; checked for all pairs of five homogeneous elements in $\Cl(6, 6)$; with an odd $\mathcal{L}$ the identity needs the sign $(-1)^{|\mathcal{L}||A|}$ on the second term and the even form fails, both checked). Where both step functions are $1$ the integrand is $-[\mathcal{L}(y), [A(x), B(z)\}] = 0$, since free fields at spacelike separation graded-commute. Where only the first is $1$, $y^{0} > z^{0}$ and $[A(x), \mathcal{L}(y)] \neq 0$ only for $y$ in the causal past $J^{-}(x)$; then $y$ is spacelike to $z$ (the light-cone lemma: $y \in J^{+}(z)$ would give $x \in J^{+}(z)$, and $y \in J^{-}(z)$ contradicts $y^{0} > z^{0}$; the script confirms it on a rational grid of trial points for three spacelike pairs, and finds grid points in $J^{-}(x) \cap J^{-}(z)$ with $y^{0} \le z^{0}$, so the hypothesis $y^{0} > z^{0}$ is needed), so $B(z)$ graded-commutes with $A(x)$ and with $\mathcal{L}(y)$ and hence, by the Jacobi identity, with $[A(x), \mathcal{L}(y)]$. The last case is symmetric. So the first-order bracket vanishes. Together with Step 4, on interacting fields of even ghost count the statistics grading is $U(2\pi)$ to every order; a ghost field of odd ghost count has grading $-U(2\pi)$, the Krein case of the free-field result.

\emph{Step 6: scope (clause (iv)).} The statement is about formal power series in the coupling; the interacting local algebras exist without the adiabatic limit \cite{DutschFredenhagen1999}, but convergence and a nonperturbative vacuum are not addressed. The free-field input is the store's result for massless fields; the series' masses come from Yukawa couplings to the rung field and its vacuum value, which are even two-spinor insertions covered by Step 2, so the expansion can be posed around massless free fields (massive free Dirac locality is standard, cited from memory). Gauge anomalies and the positivity of the physical quotient (\cite{DutschFredenhagen1999}, Theorem 4) are not used: statistics and covariance do not depend on the Ward identities. Beyond perturbation theory the spin-statistics connection rests on a premise: the Jost-point theorem of Wightman's framework (Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-standard-field-theory}) or a modular premise (\claimref{synthesis.wedge-reflections-compose-to-the-two-pi-rotor-so-geometric-modular-conjugations-give-interacting-spin-statistics}). synthesis.kasner-field-is-weyl-flat-only.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric is the four-dimensional diagonal Kasner field $g_{p} = -dt^{2} + t^{2p_{1}}dx^{2} + t^{2p_{2}}dy^{2} + t^{2p_{3}}dz^{2}$, $t > 0$, with $p_{1} + p_{2} + p_{3} = 1$ (the Kasner plane of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.kasner-exit-needs-a-contracting-metric-stage-and-a-wall-matching} with three exponents; no field equation imposed, and under Einstein's equations the source is stiff, $P = \rho$). Put $S = \sum p_{i}^{2}$, $E_{1} = p_{1}^{2} - 2p_{1}p_{2} - p_{1} - 2p_{2}^{2} + 2p_{2}$, $E_{2} = 2p_{1}^{2} + 2p_{1}p_{2} - 2p_{1} - p_{2}^{2} + p_{2}$, and let $e_{0}, e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}$ be the orthonormal frame of $g_{p}$. The line element is written in the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ (dictionary C7); the eigenvalues $\lambda_{i}$ below are those of the Weyl part of the store's curvature operator $\mathcal{R}$ on the physical bivectors (in components the mixed $C_{0i}{}^{0i}$ of the round-sphere-positive tensor in that signature, which has the store's sign: both give $+2M/r^{3}$ on the radial boost plane of Schwarzschild and $\Lambda/3$ on de Sitter), and the scalar curvature $Rt^{2} = -\tfrac23$ has the same value in the store's sign in $(+,-,-,-)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The Weyl map; proved.)} The Weyl map on bivectors has the frame bivectors $e_{0}\wedge e_{i}$ and their duals $I_{4}\,e_{0}\wedge e_{i}$ as eigenvectors, with the same eigenvalue $\lambda_{i}$ on both ($\{i, j, k\} = \{1, 2, 3\}$; in components the mixed Weyl component $C_{0i}{}^{0i} = C_{jk}{}^{jk}$): $\lambda_{i} = (p_{i}^{2} - p_{i} + \tfrac{1 - S}{3})\,t^{-2}$, so $\lambda_{1} = E_{1}/(3t^{2})$, $\lambda_{2} = -E_{2}/(3t^{2})$, $\lambda_{1} + \lambda_{2} + \lambda_{3} = 0$. So the Weyl curvature vanishes exactly where $E_{1} = E_{2} = 0$, and elsewhere it is nonzero at every $t > 0$ and grows as $t^{-2}$ toward the wall.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The Weyl-flat points; proved.)} On the plane $E_{1} = E_{2} = 0$ holds exactly at the Milne points $(1, 0, 0)$, $(0, 1, 0)$, $(0, 0, 1)$, where $g_{p}$ is flat, and at the isotropic point $(\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$, where $Rt^{2} = -\tfrac23$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(No attached state at the wall; proved, a corollary.)} At every other point of the plane the Weyl curvature is nonzero on all of $t > 0$, so by Theorem \claimref{synthesis.attachment-transport-is-flat-only-where-weyl-vanishes} the tractor transport of the attachment supplies no state on any neighbourhood of the wall: on a four-dimensional Kasner approach as in Premise \claimref{synthesis.pre-descent-contracting-kasner-stage-premise} (P1), the state carried into the descended phase is not the attachment's, and must be supplied by the rule of Premise \claimref{synthesis.pre-descent-state-carried-into-descended-phase-premise} (P2).
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Not tame walls in cosmic time; proved.)} In the smooth structure of the cosmic coordinate $t$ neither Weyl-flat case is a tame corank-one wall (in the sense of the wall Fact \claimref{dark-energy.imported-walls-sphere-theorem}): at the isotropic point $g_{p} = t^{2/3}$ times a flat bracket whose cometric degenerates at order $\tfrac23$, and at a Milne point the metric itself degenerates at order two while the cometric has a pole. In its conformal time $\eta = \tfrac32 t^{2/3}$, and $t' = \eta^{2}/4$, the isotropic bracket is the radical-normal wall $-t'^{-1}dt'^{2} + \delta$, as for every decelerating power law (\claimref{synthesis.radical-normal-tame-wall-is-a-regular-initial-surface-whose-smoothness-selects-no-state}), (iv)).
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.kasner-field-is-weyl-flat-only.technical: If the descent ends a contracting four-dimensional Kasner approach, the state that reaches the descended phase is set on a field whose Weyl curvature this result computes exactly. Over the whole plane of Kasner exponents with sum one (under Einstein's equations, the stiff-source family) the Weyl curvature is the inverse square of the time times two quadratic forms in the exponents, and the two forms vanish together at only four points: the three flat Milne points and the isotropic point. Since the attachment's transport supplies a state only where the Weyl curvature vanishes, at every other Kasner point it supplies none near the wall, and the state must come from the matching rule of the second Kasner premise. In cosmic time the two Weyl-flat cases are not tame walls of the series' degenerate geometry, so in that coordinate the regular wall case and the conformally flat Kasner case do not meet; in conformal time the isotropic point is the regular wall. Transport-absent.
synthesis.kasner-field-is-weyl-flat-only.lay: One proposal for the very early universe is a stage that shrinks unevenly in different directions before the descent. The series' way of building a quantum state from its geometry works only where a certain part of the curvature, the part that distorts shapes, is absent. For such uneven stages in four dimensions, this result computes that part and finds that it is absent only in four special cases; in all the others the series' construction gives no state near the descent, so another rule must supply it. Measured in the usual cosmic time, even the four special cases do not have the regular form the series' wall theory uses.
flags: four-dimensional diagonal Kasner fields only; the stored setting also allows hidden directions (the five-dimensional end (0, 0, 0, 1) of (P2)), Bianchi I fields with rotating axes and the BKL sequence, none of which is covered
the not-tame clause holds in the smooth structure of cosmic time; in conformal time the isotropic point is the radical-normal wall

proofs.main:
The proof is in Gauge Theory Gravity on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}). By dictionary C7 the line element $g_{p}$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ is $-g$ for the derived metric $g = dt^{2} - \sum_{i}t^{2p_{i}}(dx^{i})^{2}$ of signature $(+,-,-,-)$, the derived metric of the synchronous gauge field
\[
\hb^{-1}(e_{t}) = e_{0}, \qquad \hb^{-1}(e_{i}) = t^{p_{i}}\,e_{i} \quad (i = 1, 2, 3),
\]
with $e_{0}, \dots, e_{3}$ the constant orthonormal physical frame and $B_{i} := e_{0}\wedge e_{i}$; so $\hb(e_{0}) = e_{t}$, $\hb(e_{i}) = t^{-p_{i}}e_{x^{i}}$.

\emph{(i)} \emph{The rotation-gauge field.} The torsion equation $D_{e_\mu}\hb^{-1}(e_\nu) = D_{e_\nu}\hb^{-1}(e_\mu)$ has the unique solution $\Omega(e_{t}) = 0$, $\Omega(e_{x^{i}}) = -p_{i}t^{p_{i}-1}B_{i}$, that is $\omega(e_{0}) = 0$ and $\omega(e_{i}) = \Omega(\hb(e_{i})) = -\tfrac{p_{i}}{t}B_{i}$ (dictionary C10): indeed $\partial_{t}(t^{p_{i}}e_{i}) = p_{i}t^{p_{i}-1}e_{i}$ equals $\Omega(e_{x^{i}})\cdot e_{0} = -p_{i}t^{p_{i}-1}B_{i}\cdot e_{0} = p_{i}t^{p_{i}-1}e_{i}$, and for $i \neq j$, $\Omega(e_{x^{i}})\cdot(t^{p_{j}}e_{j}) = 0$. \emph{The field strength.} With $B_{i}\times B_{j} = -e_{i}\wedge e_{j}$ for $i \neq j$,
\[
R(e_{t}\wedge e_{x^{i}}) = \partial_{t}\Omega(e_{x^{i}}) = -p_{i}(p_{i} - 1)t^{p_{i}-2}B_{i}, \qquad
R(e_{x^{i}}\wedge e_{x^{j}}) = \Omega(e_{x^{i}})\times\Omega(e_{x^{j}}) = -p_{i}p_{j}t^{p_{i}+p_{j}-2}\,e_{i}\wedge e_{j},
\]
so the store-sign curvature operator $\mathcal{R}(B) = -R(\hb(B))$ is diagonal on the frame planes,
\[
\mathcal{R}(B_{i}) = p_{i}(p_{i} - 1)\,t^{-2}B_{i}, \qquad \mathcal{R}(e_{i}\wedge e_{j}) = p_{i}p_{j}\,t^{-2}\,e_{i}\wedge e_{j}.
\]
\emph{Ricci and scalar.} $\mathcal{R}(b) = \partial_{a}\cdot\mathcal{R}(a \wedge b)$ with $e^{i}\cdot B_{i} = -e_{0}$, $e^{0}\cdot B_{j} = e_{j}$ and $e^{i}\cdot(e_{i}\wedge e_{j}) = e_{j}$ gives $\mathcal{R}(e_{0}) = \sum_{i}p_{i}(p_{i} - 1)\,t^{-2}e_{0} = (S - 1)\,t^{-2}e_{0}$ and $\mathcal{R}(e_{j}) = p_{j}\bigl(p_{j} - 1 + \sum_{i \neq j}p_{i}\bigr)t^{-2}e_{j} = 0$ by $\sum_{i}p_{i} = 1$; the scalar is $\mathcal{R} = (S - 1)\,t^{-2}$, and $\mathcal{G}(e_{0}) = \tfrac12(S - 1)t^{-2}e_{0}$, $\mathcal{G}(e_{j}) = -\tfrac12(S - 1)t^{-2}e_{j}$, so under the field equation $\mathcal{G}(a) = -8\pi T(a)$ the source has $T(e_0) = \rho\,e_0$, $T(e_j) = -P e_j$ with $P = \rho = (1 - S)/(16\pi t^{2})$, nonnegative exactly when $S \le 1$. \emph{The Weyl map.} $\mathcal{W}(a \wedge b) = \mathcal{R}(a \wedge b) - \tfrac12(\mathcal{R}(a)\wedge b + a \wedge \mathcal{R}(b)) + \tfrac16\mathcal{R}\,a \wedge b$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}(v)) gives
\[
\mathcal{W}(B_{i}) = \bigl(p_{i}^{2} - p_{i} - \tfrac12(S - 1) + \tfrac16(S - 1)\bigr)t^{-2}B_{i} = \lambda_{i}B_{i}, \qquad \lambda_{i} = \bigl(p_{i}^{2} - p_{i} + \tfrac{1 - S}{3}\bigr)t^{-2},
\]
and, for $\{i, j, k\} = \{1, 2, 3\}$, $\mathcal{W}(e_{j}\wedge e_{k}) = (p_{j}p_{k} + \tfrac{S - 1}{6})t^{-2}\,e_{j}\wedge e_{k}$, where $p_{j}p_{k} = \tfrac12\bigl((1 - p_{i})^{2} - (S - p_{i}^{2})\bigr)$ makes the coefficient $\lambda_{i}$ again. Since $e_{j}\wedge e_{k} = \pm I_{4}B_{i}$, the Weyl map has $B_{i}$ and $I_{4}B_{i}$ as eigenvectors with the same eigenvalue $\lambda_{i}$ (it is purely electric), as $\mathcal{W}(IB) = I\mathcal{W}(B)$ requires. With $p_{3} = 1 - p_{1} - p_{2}$, $1 - S = 2p_{1} + 2p_{2} - 2p_{1}^{2} - 2p_{2}^{2} - 2p_{1}p_{2}$, and $3t^{2}\lambda_{1} = p_{1}^{2} - 2p_{1}p_{2} - p_{1} - 2p_{2}^{2} + 2p_{2} = E_{1}$, $3t^{2}\lambda_{2} = -E_{2}$; $\sum_{i}\lambda_{i} = (S - 1 + 1 - S)t^{-2} = 0$. So $\mathcal{W} = 0$ exactly when every $\lambda_{i}$ vanishes, that is (by the trace) when $E_{1} = E_{2} = 0$, and otherwise a nonzero eigenvalue is a constant times $t^{-2}$, nonzero on all of $t > 0$. The values in $(-,+,+,+)$: by C11 the all-lower component of the round-sphere-positive Weyl tensor of $g$ is $C_{0i0i} = B_{i}\cdot\mathcal{W}(B_{i}) = \lambda_{i}$ ($B_{i}^{2} = 1$); for $g_{p} = -g$ the all-lower tensor changes sign, and raising the second pair in an orthonormal frame of $g_{p}$ multiplies by $(-1)(+1)$, so the mixed component $C_{0i}{}^{0i}$ of $g_{p}$ is $\lambda_{i}$ (the check's coordinate engine confirms it), and $\mathcal{R}t^{2} = S - 1$ is $-\tfrac23$ at $S = \tfrac13$. The check solves $\Omega$ from the torsion equation and computes the field strength, the Ricci map, the scalar and the Weyl map with the library's engine on exact jets at rational points of the plane, compares them with the closed forms above, and matches $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}$ with $E_{1}/3$, $-E_{2}/3$ (check\_gtg\_kasner\_field\_strength\_and\_weyl\_map).

\emph{(ii)} By (i), $\lambda_{1} = \lambda_{2} = \lambda_{3} = 0$ exactly when $p_{i}^{2} - p_{i}$ takes the same value for all $i$, and a value $c$ of $p^{2} - p$ is taken at the two roots $r$ and $1 - r$. So each $p_{i} \in \{r, 1 - r\}$ for one $r$. If $n$ of the exponents equal $r$ and $3 - n$ equal $1 - r$, the sum condition is $nr + (3 - n)(1 - r) = 1$, that is $(2n - 3)r = n - 2$: $n = 3$ gives $r = \tfrac13$, the isotropic point; $n = 2$ gives $r = 0$, the exponents $(0, 0, 1)$; $n = 1$ gives $r = 1$, again $(1, 0, 0)$ up to order; $n = 0$ is $n = 3$ with $r$ and $1 - r$ exchanged. Hence the Weyl-flat points are exactly the three permutations of $(0, 0, 1)$ and $(\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$; the check enumerates this. As an independent confirmation the check also eliminates $p_{2}$ from $E_{1} = E_{2} = 0$ over the rational functions of $p_{1}$: the Sylvester determinant is $-9p_{1}^{2}(p_{1} - 1)(3p_{1} - 1)$, and the fibres over $p_{1} = 0, 1, \tfrac13$ give exactly $(0, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$ and $(\tfrac13, \tfrac13)$ in $(p_{1}, p_{2})$. At the Milne points every $p_{i}(p_{i} - 1)$ and every $p_{i}p_{j}$ vanishes, so by (i) the field strength vanishes: the field is flat. At the isotropic point $\mathcal{R} = (S - 1)t^{-2} = -\tfrac23 t^{-2}$, the value stored for the isotropic disk point.

\emph{(iii)} Theorem \claimref{synthesis.attachment-transport-is-flat-only-where-weyl-vanishes} gives that the conformal spinors of the attachment can be parallel for the tractor gauge field only where the Weyl curvature vanishes, and that off Weyl-flat regions the transport supplies no state. A purely electric Weyl map with real eigenvalues is of Petrov type I or D, so the type N case of that theorem does not arise. By (i) and (ii), off the four points the Weyl curvature is nonzero at every $t > 0$, in particular on every neighbourhood of the wall. The rest is the reading of (P1) and (P2): (P1) supplies the contracting Kasner stage that Theorem \claimref{synthesis.kasner-exit-needs-a-contracting-metric-stage-and-a-wall-matching} requires, and (P2) a rule carrying its state across; the rule's form is not fixed there, and by this clause it cannot be the attachment's transport.

\emph{(iv)} At $p_{i} = \tfrac13$, $g_{p} = t^{2/3}(-t^{-2/3}dt^{2} + \delta)$, and the bracket is (up to the sign of C7) the derived metric of the field $\hb^{-1}(e_{t}) = t^{-1/3}e_{0}$, $\hb^{-1}(e_{x^{i}}) = e_{i}$, whose torsion equation is solved by $\Omega = 0$ (each $\hb^{-1}(e_\mu)$ depends only on the label $\mu$), so its field strength vanishes (the check also confirms the vanishing Riemann tensor of the bracket); its cometric entry $-t^{2/3}$ vanishes at order $\tfrac23$, not one, so in the smooth structure of $t$ condition (T3) of tameness fails (and the cometric is not smooth in $t$). With $\eta = \tfrac32 t^{2/3}$, $d\eta/dt = t^{-1/3}$ and the bracket is $-d\eta^{2} + \delta$; with $t' = \eta^{2}/4$, $dt'/d\eta = \eta/2$, so $-d\eta^{2} = -(4/\eta^{2})dt'^{2} = -t'^{-1}dt'^{2}$: the radical-normal tame wall in the coordinate $t'$. Tameness is therefore a property of the smooth structure; the general power-law statement, in cosmic and in conformal time, is clause (iv) of the result (\claimref{synthesis.radical-normal-tame-wall-is-a-regular-initial-surface-whose-smoothness-selects-no-state}). At the Milne point $(0, 0, 1)$ the field is flat by (i); its metric entry $t^{2}$ vanishes at order two, so the metric degenerates and the cometric entry $t^{-2}$ has a pole: the opposite of a tame wall, at which the cometric degenerates at order one and the metric has a simple pole (Fact \claimref{dark-energy.imported-walls-sphere-theorem}).

\emph{Reading (argued, not part of the statement).} Under (P1) and (P2), with four-dimensional Kasner exponents, the deposit chain's first step cannot start from the attachment's conformal vacuum at a generic Kasner point; the reference state must come with the (P2) rule. At the isotropic point a conformal vacuum exists for conformally covariant fields, and in conformal time its wall is the regular radical-normal wall; in cosmic time it is not tame. At the Milne points the field is flat and the restriction of the Minkowski vacuum to the Milne wedge is available, but those walls are null cones of flat space, not degenerate cometrics. So in the cosmic-time smooth structure the two routes to a state at the descent that the series has, the attachment where the Weyl curvature vanishes and the regular radical-normal wall, do not meet on the four-dimensional Kasner plane. Kasner approaches with hidden directions, such as the five-dimensional end of (P2), are not covered. Transport-absent.

\emph{In components (the source's route for (i)).} The source computes, for the diagonal metric, the Christoffel symbols, $R^{\rho}{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}$, the Ricci tensor and the Weyl components $C_{abab} = R_{abab} - \tfrac12(g_{aa}R_{bb} + g_{bb}R_{aa}) + \tfrac{R}{6}g_{aa}g_{bb}$, finding $R_{0i0i} = -p_{i}(p_{i} - 1)/t^{2}$, $R_{00} = (1 - S)/t^{2}$, $R = (S - 1)/t^{2}$ and $t^{2}C_{0i}{}^{0i} = p_{i}^{2} - p_{i} + \tfrac{1 - S}{3}$; the check's coordinate engine still confirms these on nine rational points of the plane.
