synthesis.kernel-bivector-is-the-unit-of.formal:
Let $N \ge 1$ and let $L_{N} = \Cl(N, N{+}2)$ be the tower level with orthogonal generators $e_{0}, e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}$ ($Q = +1, -1, -1, -1$) and the tower planes $(e_{j}', f_{j}')$, $Q(e_{j}') = 1$, $Q(f_{j}') = -1$, $j = 1, \dots, N - 1$ (floor $N - 1$ of the tower on $\Cl(1,3)$, Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}), read through the Witt decomposition of its vector space: the anisotropic kernel $\mathrm{span}\{e_{2}, e_{3}\}$, of signature $(0,2)$, orthogonal to $N$ hyperbolic (transport) planes, the radial plane $(e_{0}, e_{1})$ (mode $0$) and the tower planes (modes $1, \dots, N - 1$). $B_{N}$ is the subalgebra generated by the $2N$ plane generators. For a plane $(e, f)$, $v = \tfrac12(e + f) = a^{*}$, $w = \tfrac12(e - f) = a$, $n = vw$, $\omega = ef$; $\Gamma = \prod_{\text{planes}}\omega$; $J = e_{2}e_{3}$; $\sigma = e_{0}e_{1}$; $I_{4} = e_{0}e_{1}e_{2}e_{3}$; $I_{n}$ is the product of all $2N + 2$ generators in the order listed; $*$ is the frame adjoint of Theorem \claimref{tower.structure-tower-c-norms} on the real level (the antiautomorphism fixing the generators of square $+1$ and negating those of square $-1$).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(No unit in the hyperbolic tower.)} In $\Cl(N,N)$, generated by $N$ hyperbolic planes alone, the commutant of the even subalgebra is $\mathrm{span}\{1, \Gamma\}$, $\Gamma^{2} = +1$, and $(\alpha + \beta\Gamma)^{2} = \alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} + 2\alpha\beta\Gamma$: no element that commutes with every even element squares to $-1$. Inside the transport algebra, self-adjoint boson fields (even elements) have no unit that commutes with all bosonic elements.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The kernel bivector.)} In $L_{N}$, $J^{2} = -1$, $J^{*} = -J$, and $J$ commutes with every plane generator, hence with all of $B_{N}$ (every mode $v_{j}, w_{j}$ and every pair); $J = I_{4}\sigma$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The commutant of transport is a quaternion algebra.)} The commutant of $B_{N}$ in $L_{N}$ is $\mathrm{span}\{1, J, \Gamma e_{2}, \Gamma e_{3}\}$, with $(\Gamma e_{2})^{2} = (\Gamma e_{3})^{2} = -1$ and $(\Gamma e_{2})(\Gamma e_{3}) = J = -(\Gamma e_{3})(\Gamma e_{2})$: a quaternion algebra, the twisted copy of the ground $\Cl(0,2)$. Its even part is $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$, and $\pm J$ are its only even elements of square $-1$; they are also its only units fixed by the rotors $e^{\varphi J}$ of the kernel plane, which turn $(\Gamma e_{2}, \Gamma e_{3})$ through $2\varphi$. In the tower's limit only $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ commutes with every plane (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}(i) with ground signature $(0,2)$). The uniqueness needs the radial plane among the transport planes: if $(e_{0}, e_{1})$ is counted in the ground $\Cl(1,3)$ and only the tower planes as transport ($N \ge 2$), the even part of their commutant is $\Cl^{+}(1,3)$ (of dimension $8$), which contains $I_{4}$, $J$, $e_{1}e_{2}$ and $e_{1}e_{3}$, all of square $-1$; then $J$ and $I_{4} = J\sigma$ both commute with transport.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The level pseudoscalar.)} $I_{n} = J\Gamma$, $I_{n}^{2} = -1$, $I_{n}^{*} = -I_{n}$; $\Gamma^{*} = \Gamma = \prod_{j}(1 - 2n_{j})$, the fermion parity, which anticommutes with every $v_{j}, w_{j}$ and commutes with every product of two. Hence $I_{n}\tfrac12(1 \pm \Gamma) = \pm J\tfrac12(1 \pm \Gamma)$: $I_{n} = J$ on even and $-J$ on odd fermion number. $\operatorname{Ad}(I_{n})$ is the grade involution of $L_{N}$, which on $B_{N}$ is $\operatorname{Ad}(\Gamma)$. $I_{n}$ and $J$ are not identified.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Hermitian boson fields with unit $J$.)} For every $X \in B_{N}$, $\phi_{X} = X + X^{*}$ and $\pi_{X} = J(X^{*} - X)$ are self-adjoint and $[\phi_{X}, \pi_{X}] = 2J[X, X^{*}]$; for $X, Y \in B_{N}$ with $[X, Y] = 0$, $[\phi_{X}, \pi_{Y}] = J([X, Y^{*}] + [Y, X^{*}])$ and $[\phi_{X}, \phi_{Y}] = [\pi_{X}, \pi_{Y}] = [X, Y^{*}] - [Y, X^{*}]$.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Collective pairs.} For $N = 2M$ and $S = \sum_{k=0}^{M-1}v_{2k}w_{2k+1}$, $\phi = \phi_{S}$, $\pi = \pi_{S}$: $[\phi, \pi] = 2J\sum_{k}(n_{2k} - n_{2k+1})$ exactly. With $P_{\mathrm{pol}} = \prod_{k}n_{2k}(1 - n_{2k+1})$, $SP_{\mathrm{pol}} = 0$, $X_{j} = (S^{*})^{j}P_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is nonzero for $j \le M$ and zero for $j = M + 1$, and $[\phi, \pi]X_{j} = 2(M - 2j)JX_{j}$; so $\Phi = \phi/\sqrt{2M}$, $\Pi = \pi/\sqrt{2M}$ satisfy $[\Phi, \Pi]X_{j} = (1 - 2j/M)JX_{j}$: the Hermitian canonical relation $[\Phi, \Pi] = J$ holds exactly on the polarised element and, at fixed $j$, as $M \to \infty$.
\item \emph{Density modes.} On a window of the $N$ modes, $\rho_{q} = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1-q}v_{k}w_{k+q}$ ($1 \le q \le N - 1$) satisfy $[\rho_{q}, \rho_{q'}] = 0$ and $[\phi_{\rho_{q}}, \pi_{\rho_{q}}] = 2J(\sum_{k<q}n_{k} - \sum_{k \ge N-q}n_{k})$; for $2q \le N$ and $E_{q} = \prod_{k<q}n_{k}\prod_{k \ge N-q}(1 - n_{k})$ (the filled sea's edge-clean projector), $[\phi_{\rho_{q}}, \pi_{\rho_{q}}]\psi = 2qJ\psi$ whenever $E_{q}\psi = \psi$.
\item \emph{Lemma.} In any real $*$-algebra, let $u^{2} = -1$, $u^{*} = -u$, and let $u$ commute with a family $X_{q}$ with $[X_{q}, X_{q'}] = 0$ and $[X_{q}, X_{q'}^{*}] = c_{q}\delta_{qq'}$, $c_{q} > 0$ real. Then $\Phi_{q} = (X_{q} + X_{q}^{*})/\sqrt{2c_{q}}$ and $\Pi_{q} = u(X_{q}^{*} - X_{q})/\sqrt{2c_{q}}$ are self-adjoint and $[\Phi_{q}, \Pi_{q'}] = u\,\delta_{qq'}$, $[\Phi_{q}, \Phi_{q'}] = [\Pi_{q}, \Pi_{q'}] = 0$. The canonical relations of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(vi) on its domain $\mathcal{D}$ have this form with $X_{q} = \rho_{q}$, $c_{q} = q$, for any unit $u$ of that representation commuting with the band modes; such a $u$ is not exhibited here (the one-particle unit there is $I_{4}$ on $\mathfrak{h}$, not an element of the CAR algebra).
\end{itemize}
\item[(vi)] \emph{(The sign of $J$ and the phase circle.)} The map $\alpha$ with $e_{3} \mapsto -e_{3}$ and every other generator fixed extends to a $*$-automorphism of $L_{N}$; it fixes $B_{N}$ pointwise and $\sigma$, and sends $J \mapsto -J$, $I_{4} \mapsto -I_{4}$, $I_{n} \mapsto -I_{n}$, $(\phi_{X}, \pi_{X}) \mapsto (\phi_{X}, -\pi_{X})$. So nothing in the transport algebra fixes the sign of $J$; given $\sigma$, it is the orientation of $I_{4}$ ($J = I_{4}\sigma$). With $Q = \sum_{k}(n_{2k} - n_{2k+1})$ and $U_{\theta} = e^{\theta JQ/2} = \prod_{k}(1 - n_{2k} + n_{2k}e^{\theta J/2})(1 - n_{2k+1} + n_{2k+1}e^{-\theta J/2})$, the diagonal mode rotation with weights $s_{2k} = \tfrac12$, $s_{2k+1} = -\tfrac12$ of \claimref{synthesis.ladder-bosons-inherit-spin-statistics-from-the-single-modes}(i), which gives the product form, unitarity and the action on the modes, $U_{\theta}$ is unitary, $U_{\theta}SU_{\theta}^{*} = e^{\theta J}S$, and $(\phi, \pi) \mapsto (\phi\cos\theta - \pi\sin\theta, \phi\sin\theta + \pi\cos\theta)$, which keeps $[\phi, \pi]$. The phase $e^{\theta J} = \cos\theta + J\sin\theta$ has period $2\pi$; it is the rotor of the kernel plane, $\operatorname{Ad}(e^{\theta J})$ turns $e_{2}, e_{3}$ through $2\theta$ and fixes $B_{N}$ pointwise, and $e^{\pi J} = -1$ is the rotor of the turn by $2\pi$.
\end{enumerate}
Clauses (i) to (vi) are proved. \emph{Reading (argued).} The orientation of $I_{4}$ relative to time is the datum that Premise (N$_{+}$) assumes (\claimref{synthesis.n-plus-null-ground-state}); by (vi), with $\sigma$ fixed, it is the sign of $J$, which now orients both the fermion phase flow $v \mapsto e^{-Jt}v$ of \claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}(iv) and the boson relation $[\Phi, \Pi] = +J$ of (v): reversing it reverses both together.
synthesis.kernel-bivector-is-the-unit-of.technical: A boson field written as a self-adjoint pair needs a unit: something that squares to $-1$, is anti-self-adjoint, and commutes with the fields. The tower's hyperbolic planes alone do not supply one. In $\Cl(N,N)$ the elements commuting with every even element are $\alpha + \beta\Gamma$, with $\Gamma$ the product of the plane volume elements, and these square to $\alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} + 2\alpha\beta\Gamma$, never $-1$. A tower level over spacetime is $\Cl(N, N{+}2)$, whose vector space is $N$ hyperbolic planes, the radial plane among them, plus a two-dimensional kernel of square $-1$. The kernel bivector $J = e_{2}e_{3}$ squares to $-1$, is anti-self-adjoint, and commutes with every mode operator. The whole commutant of the transport algebra is a quaternion algebra $\mathrm{span}\{1, J, \Gamma e_{2}, \Gamma e_{3}\}$, and $\pm J$ is its only even unit, the one the kernel rotations fix, and the only one surviving in the tower's limit. The level pseudoscalar is $I_{n} = J\Gamma$, which equals $J$ on even and $-J$ on odd fermion number; the two are not identified. With $J$, any transport element $X$ gives the self-adjoint fields $\phi = X + X^{*}$ and $\pi = J(X^{*} - X)$, and $[\phi, \pi] = 2J[X, X^{*}]$. For the collective hopping pair $S$ of $M$ blocks this is $2J$ times the edge count $\sum(n_{2k} - n_{2k+1})$, so the normalised fields satisfy $[\Phi, \Pi] = (1 - 2j/M)J$ on the $j$-th rung of the polarised ladder; for density modes of a window it is $2qJ$ on the filled sea's edge-clean projector. A lemma gives the full Hermitian canonical relations for any family of commuting canonical pairs and any commuting unit. Uniqueness of $J$ depends on counting the radial plane as a transport plane: with the radial plane in the ground, the even commutant of the tower planes is the even spacetime algebra, where $I_{4}$ (the field theory's unit) and $J$ both serve. Finally, reflecting $e_{3}$ is an automorphism that fixes every transport element and reverses $J$ and $I_{4}$ together, so the sign of $J$ is not fixed by the fermions; given the radial plane's orientation it is the orientation of $I_{4}$, which we read (argued, not proved) as the datum Premise (N$_{+}$) assumes. The boson phase circle is $e^{\theta J}$, implemented inside the level by $e^{\theta JQ/2}$; it is the kernel plane's rotor, and its value $-1$ at $\theta = \pi$ is the rotor of a full turn.
synthesis.kernel-bivector-is-the-unit-of.lay: Quantum fields that describe bosons, the particles that can share a state, are usually written as pairs of real quantities whose commutator is the imaginary unit. The graph builds everything from fermions living in a tower of planes, so it has to find that unit inside its own algebra. The planes alone have none: nothing that commutes with all their pairs squares to minus one. The extra two directions of spacetime that are not part of any plane, the two directions along a horizon's sphere, supply one: the product of those two directions squares to minus one and commutes with every fermion operation. Counting the time-radial plane among the planes, it is the only such element of the right type (if that plane is left out, the field theory's own unit also works), it is what survives at the top of the tower, and with it the collective pairs of fermions give boson fields with the standard commutator, exactly in the states where the bosons were already known to appear. Its sign is a free choice that nothing among the fermions fixes, and it can be read, as an argument rather than a proof, as the same choice that the series' premise about horizons makes when it fixes the direction of time relative to the imaginary unit.

proofs.main:
\emph{Two facts used throughout.} (a) For a basis vector $e_{a}$ and a basis blade $e_{B}$ (index set $B$), $e_{a}e_{B} = (-1)^{|B| - [a \in B]}e_{B}e_{a}$: $e_{a}$ anticommutes with each factor of $e_{B}$ other than itself (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}) and commutes with itself. (b) Conjugation by a basis blade maps every basis blade to plus or minus itself: by the product formula of Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}, $e_{E}e_{B} = \pm e_{B}e_{E}$, both products being a sign times $(\prod_{E \cap B}Q)\,e_{E \triangle B}$. Hence if $x = \sum_{B}x_{B}e_{B}$ commutes with $e_{E}$, then $0 = e_{E}x - xe_{E} = \sum_{B}x_{B}(\epsilon_{B} - 1)e_{B}e_{E}$ with $\epsilon_{B} = \pm 1$, and since the $e_{B}e_{E}$ are, up to nonzero factors, distinct basis blades, $x_{B} = 0$ whenever $\epsilon_{B} = -1$. So the commutant of any set of basis blades is spanned by the basis blades that commute with all of them, and the commutant of a set of generators can be computed blade by blade. Every commutant below is the commutant of the algebra generated by a set of basis blades, so (b) applies to each.

\emph{(i).} In $\Cl(N,N)$, $n = 2N \ge 2$, the even subalgebra is spanned by even blades, products of the bivectors $e_{a}e_{b}$, so its commutant is the commutant of the bivectors. By (a), $e_{a}e_{b}e_{B} = (-1)^{2|B| - [a \in B] - [b \in B]}e_{B}e_{a}e_{b}$, so $e_{B}$ commutes with $e_{a}e_{b}$ exactly when $[a \in B] = [b \in B]$. Requiring this for every pair $a \ne b$ forces $B = \emptyset$ or $B = \{1, \dots, n\}$. In the order $e_{1}f_{1}e_{2}f_{2}\cdots$ the full blade is $\prod_{j}\omega_{j} = \Gamma$, which squares to $+1$ (Theorem \claimref{tower.volume-elements-planes}). So the commutant is $\mathrm{span}\{1, \Gamma\}$; it has no odd part. Its even part is the centre of $\Cl^{+}(N,N)$, which agrees with the parenthesis of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}(ii) at $r = 0$ ($\omega^{2} = (-1)^{r/2} = 1$). For real $\alpha, \beta$, $(\alpha + \beta\Gamma)^{2} = \alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} + 2\alpha\beta\Gamma$; equal to $-1$ would need $\alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} = -1$. The script checks (b) on all pairs of blades and computes the commutant of the bivectors for $N = 1, 2, 3$, and the square at four rational points.

\emph{(ii).} $J^{2} = e_{2}e_{3}e_{2}e_{3} = -e_{2}^{2}e_{3}^{2} = -1$. The $*$ of Theorem \claimref{tower.structure-tower-c-norms}, restricted to the real level, is the antiautomorphism with $x^{*} = x$ for generators of square $+1$ and $x^{*} = -x$ for those of square $-1$; on a blade it is reversion times $(-1)^{\#\{\text{factors of square } -1\}}$. So $J^{*} = e_{3}^{*}e_{2}^{*} = e_{3}e_{2} = -J$, $v^{*} = \tfrac12(e - f) = w$, and the ladder pairs satisfy the CAR (Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}; directly, $\{w_{j}, v_{k}\} = \tfrac14\{e_{j} - f_{j}, e_{k} + f_{k}\} = \tfrac12(Q(e_{j}) - Q(f_{j}))\delta_{jk} = \delta_{jk}$ and $\{v_{j}, v_{k}\} = \{w_{j}, w_{k}\} = 0$ since $v_{j}, w_{j}$ are null and orthogonal to the other planes). Every plane generator is orthogonal to $e_{2}$ and $e_{3}$, so anticommutes with each and commutes with $J$; $J$ therefore commutes with $B_{N}$. $I_{4}\sigma = e_{0}e_{1}e_{2}e_{3}e_{0}e_{1}$; moving $e_{0}e_{1}$ to the left past $e_{2}e_{3}$ costs four transpositions, so $I_{4}\sigma = \sigma\sigma J = \sigma^{2}J$, and $\sigma^{2} = e_{0}e_{1}e_{0}e_{1} = -e_{0}^{2}e_{1}^{2} = 1$: $J = I_{4}\sigma$, as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}(i). The script checks the CAR, $v^{*} = w$, the antiautomorphism property on all blade pairs for $N \le 2$, and the rest for $N = 1, 2, 3$.

\emph{(iii).} Let $P$ be the set of the $2N$ plane indices and $K = \{2, 3\}$. By (b) the commutant of $B_{N}$ (that of its generators) is spanned by the blades $e_{B}$ with, by (a), $|B| - [a \in B]$ even for every $a \in P$. If $B$ contained one plane index and missed another, $|B| - 1$ and $|B|$ would both be even; so $B \cap P = \emptyset$ or $B \supseteq P$. In the first case $B \subseteq K$ with $|B|$ even: $B = \emptyset$ or $K$, giving $1$ and $J$. In the second $|B|$ is odd, $|B| = 2N + |B \cap K|$, so $|B \cap K| = 1$: $B = P \cup \{2\}$ or $P \cup \{3\}$. Since $\Gamma = \pm e_{P}$, these blades are $\pm\Gamma e_{2}$ and $\pm\Gamma e_{3}$. So the commutant is $\mathrm{span}\{1, J, \Gamma e_{2}, \Gamma e_{3}\}$, of dimension $4$. By Theorem \claimref{tower.volume-elements-planes}, $\Gamma^{2} = 1$ and $\Gamma$ commutes with the non-plane generators $e_{2}$, $e_{3}$, so $(\Gamma e_{2})^{2} = \Gamma^{2}e_{2}^{2} = -1$, likewise $(\Gamma e_{3})^{2} = -1$, $(\Gamma e_{2})(\Gamma e_{3}) = e_{2}e_{3} = J$ and $(\Gamma e_{3})(\Gamma e_{2}) = e_{3}e_{2} = -J$: the quaternion relations. This is the twisted copy $A$ of Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies} for ground $\Cl(0,2)$ with the $N$ planes, generated by $e_{2}\Gamma$ and $e_{3}\Gamma$. A general element $q = a + bJ + c\,\Gamma e_{2} + d\,\Gamma e_{3}$ has $q^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2} - c^{2} - d^{2} + 2a(bJ + c\,\Gamma e_{2} + d\,\Gamma e_{3})$, the three units anticommuting pairwise, so $q^{2} = -1$ exactly when $a = 0$ and $b^{2} + c^{2} + d^{2} = 1$. $\Gamma e_{2}$ and $\Gamma e_{3}$ have odd grade $2N + 1$, so the even part is $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ and its units are $\pm J$. For the kernel rotor $R = e^{\varphi J} = \cos\varphi + J\sin\varphi$ (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential}), $J$ is fixed, while $\Gamma e_{2}$, $\Gamma e_{3}$ anticommute with $J$ ($Je_{2} = -e_{2}J$, $\Gamma$ commutes with $J$), so $R(\Gamma e_{2})R^{-1} = R^{2}\Gamma e_{2} = \cos 2\varphi\,\Gamma e_{2} + \sin 2\varphi\,J\Gamma e_{2}$ and $J\Gamma e_{2} = \Gamma e_{3}$: a turn through $2\varphi$ of the plane $(\Gamma e_{2}, \Gamma e_{3})$. A unit $bJ + c\,\Gamma e_{2} + d\,\Gamma e_{3}$ is fixed by every such $R$ exactly when $c = d = 0$. The limit: Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}(i), for ground signature $(p, q) = (0, 2)$ ($n = 2 \ge 1$), gives the commutant of all planes in the limit as $\Cl^{0}(0,2) = \mathrm{span}\{1, e_{2}e_{3}\} = \mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$. For $N = 1$ the commutant is the centraliser of $e_{0}, e_{1}$ in $\Cl(1,3)$ stored in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}(i). The contrast: with ground $\Cl(1,3)$ and transport the $N - 1 \ge 1$ tower planes, the same blade argument (now with $P$ the tower-plane indices and the four ground indices free) gives the blades $e_{B}$ with $B \cap P = \emptyset$, $|B|$ even, or $B \supseteq P$, $|B|$ odd: $2^{3} + 2^{3} = 16$ blades, the twisted copy of $\Cl(1,3)$ of Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}; its even part is $\Cl^{+}(1,3)$, spanned by $1$, the six bivectors $e_{\mu}e_{\nu}$ and $I_{4}$, of which $e_{1}e_{2}$, $e_{1}e_{3}$, $e_{2}e_{3}$ and $I_{4}$ square to $-1$. So $\pm J$ is not the only even unit there, and $I_{4} = J\sigma$ also commutes with every tower plane. The script computes the commutant blades for $N = 1, 2, 3$, the quaternion relations, the rotor action at $(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi) = (3/5, 4/5)$, the $N = 1$ centraliser, and the contrast at $N = 2$ (16 blades, 8 even, the four even blades of square $-1$).

\emph{(iv).} In the order $e_{0}e_{1}e_{2}e_{3}e_{1}'f_{1}'\cdots$, $I_{n} = \sigma J\prod_{j \ge 1}\omega_{j}$, and $\sigma$, $J$ commute (each of $e_{0}, e_{1}$ commutes with $J$), so $I_{n} = J\sigma\prod_{j \ge 1}\omega_{j} = J\Gamma$, $\sigma$ being the volume element of the radial plane. $J$ commutes with $\Gamma$ (by (ii)), so $I_{n}^{2} = J^{2}\Gamma^{2} = -1$. $\omega^{*} = (ef)^{*} = f^{*}e^{*} = -fe = ef = \omega$, and the $\omega_{j}$ commute pairwise (Theorem \claimref{tower.volume-elements-planes}), so $\Gamma^{*} = \Gamma$ and $I_{n}^{*} = \Gamma^{*}J^{*} = -\Gamma J = -I_{n}$. $n = vw = \tfrac14(e + f)(e - f) = \tfrac14(e^{2} - ef + fe - f^{2}) = \tfrac12(1 - \omega)$, so $\omega = 1 - 2n$ and $\Gamma = \prod_{j}(1 - 2n_{j})$, which is $+1$ on even and $-1$ on odd occupation: the fermion parity. By Theorem \claimref{tower.volume-elements-planes}, $\Gamma$ anticommutes with each plane generator, hence with $v_{j}, w_{j}$, and commutes with products of two. Then $I_{n}\tfrac12(1 \pm \Gamma) = J\tfrac12(\Gamma \pm \Gamma^{2}) = J\tfrac12(\Gamma \pm 1) = \pm J\tfrac12(1 \pm \Gamma)$. The dimension $2N + 2$ is even, so $I_{n}$ anticommutes with every vector (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.pseudoscalar-commutation}, $k = 1$), and $\operatorname{Ad}(I_{n})$ negates every generator: it is the grade involution. On $B_{N}$, $\operatorname{Ad}(I_{n}) = \operatorname{Ad}(J)\operatorname{Ad}(\Gamma) = \operatorname{Ad}(\Gamma)$, since $J$ commutes with $B_{N}$. For $N = 1$, $\Gamma = \sigma$ and $I_{n} = I_{4}$, and this is $I_{4}P_{\pm} = \pm JP_{\pm}$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}(iii) with $P_{\pm} = \tfrac12(1 \pm \sigma)$. The script checks all of this for $N = 1, 2, 3$.

\emph{(v).} $B_{N}$ is closed under $*$ (the adjoint of a plane generator is $\pm$ itself), and $J$ commutes with $B_{N}$. Then $\phi_{X}^{*} = X^{*} + X = \phi_{X}$ and $\pi_{X}^{*} = (X^{*} - X)^{*}J^{*} = (X - X^{*})(-J) = J(X^{*} - X) = \pi_{X}$. Since $J$ commutes with $X$ and $X^{*}$, $[\phi_{X}, \pi_{X}] = J[X + X^{*}, X^{*} - X] = J([X, X^{*}] - [X^{*}, X]) = 2J[X, X^{*}]$. For $[X, Y] = 0$ also $[X^{*}, Y^{*}] = -[X, Y]^{*} = 0$, so $[\phi_{X}, \pi_{Y}] = J([X, Y^{*}] - [X^{*}, Y]) = J([X, Y^{*}] + [Y, X^{*}])$; $[\phi_{X}, \phi_{Y}] = [X, Y^{*}] + [X^{*}, Y] = [X, Y^{*}] - [Y, X^{*}]$; and $[\pi_{X}, \pi_{Y}] = J^{2}[X^{*} - X, Y^{*} - Y] = [X^{*}, Y] + [X, Y^{*}]$, the same.

\emph{Collective pairs.} With $b_{k} = v_{2k}w_{2k+1}$, $[b_{k}, b_{k}^{*}] = n_{2k} - n_{2k+1}$ and even elements of distinct blocks commute (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(i), (iii)), so $[S, S^{*}] = \sum_{k}(n_{2k} - n_{2k+1}) =: Q$ and $[\phi, \pi] = 2JQ$. From the CAR, $[n_{j}, v_{j}] = v_{j}$, $[n_{j}, w_{j}] = -w_{j}$, and $n_{j}$ commutes with the modes of other planes (it is even and built from plane $j$); so $[Q, b_{k}] = 2b_{k}$ and $[Q, S^{*}] = -2S^{*}$. The $n_{j}$ are commuting idempotents ($n^{2} = v(wv)w = v(1 - vw)w = n$); $n_{2k}P_{\mathrm{pol}} = P_{\mathrm{pol}}$ and $n_{2k+1}P_{\mathrm{pol}} = 0$, so $QP_{\mathrm{pol}} = MP_{\mathrm{pol}}$ and, by $[Q, S^{*}] = -2S^{*}$, $QX_{j} = (M - 2j)X_{j}$, whence $[\phi, \pi]X_{j} = 2(M - 2j)JX_{j}$ ($J$ commutes with $Q$). $w_{2k+1}(1 - n_{2k+1}) = w_{2k+1}w_{2k+1}v_{2k+1} = 0$ gives $SP_{\mathrm{pol}} = 0$. The $b_{k}^{*}$ commute and $(b_{k}^{*})^{2} = 0$, so $(S^{*})^{j} = j!\sum_{|A| = j}\prod_{k \in A}b_{k}^{*}$, which vanishes for $j > M$. For $j \le M$: $P_{\mathrm{pol}} \neq 0$ (it is a product of $N$ commuting factors $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega_{j})$, with scalar part $2^{-N}$); $b_{k}b_{k}^{*} = v_{2k}w_{2k+1}v_{2k+1}w_{2k} = n_{2k}(1 - n_{2k+1})$ fixes $P_{\mathrm{pol}}$, so $\prod_{k \in A}b_{k}\prod_{k \in A}b_{k}^{*}P_{\mathrm{pol}} = P_{\mathrm{pol}}$ and each term $T_{A} = \prod_{k \in A}b_{k}^{*}P_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is nonzero; and $n_{2k}T_{A} = [k \notin A]\,T_{A}$, so terms with distinct $A$ lie in distinct joint eigenspaces of left multiplication by the commuting $n_{2k}$ and are linearly independent. Hence $X_{j} \neq 0$. This is the hopping ladder of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(ii) with the unit written in. Dividing by $2M$ gives $[\Phi, \Pi]X_{j} = (1 - 2j/M)JX_{j}$. The script checks the identities for $M = 1, 2$, the values $2(M - 2j)$ on $X_{j}$ for $j = 0, \dots, M$, $X_{M+1} = 0$, and the general identity on a generic element of $B_{2}$.

\emph{Density modes.} $[\rho_{q}, \rho_{q}^{*}] = \sum_{k<q}n_{k} - \sum_{k \ge N-q}n_{k}$ is the edge operator of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(v), so $[\phi_{\rho_{q}}, \pi_{\rho_{q}}] = 2J$ times it. For $2q \le N$ the two index sets are disjoint, $E_{q}$ commutes with every $n_{k}$, $n_{k}E_{q} = E_{q}$ for $k < q$ and $n_{k}E_{q} = 0$ for $k \ge N - q$, so the edge operator times $E_{q}$ is $qE_{q}$, and for $\psi = E_{q}\psi$ it gives $q\psi$. $[\rho_{q}, \rho_{q'}] = \sum_{k, l}[v_{k}w_{k+q}, v_{l}w_{l+q'}]$; by the CAR $[v_{k}w_{m}, v_{l}w_{p}] = \delta_{ml}v_{k}w_{p} - \delta_{pk}v_{l}w_{m}$, so the sum is $\sum_{k}v_{k}w_{k+q+q'} - \sum_{l}v_{l}w_{l+q'+q}$, both over the indices with $k + q + q' \le N - 1$ (the intermediate index then lies in the window automatically), and it vanishes. The script checks, on a window of four modes, the two commutators for $q = 1, 2$, their value $2qJ$ on $E_{q}$, $[\rho_{1}, \rho_{2}] = 0$ and the three mixed identities.

\emph{Lemma.} By the identities above with $u$ in place of $J$ (they used only $u^{2} = -1$, $u^{*} = -u$ and that $u$ commutes with $X$ and $Y$), $[\Phi_{q}, \Pi_{q'}] = u([X_{q}, X_{q'}^{*}] + [X_{q'}, X_{q}^{*}])/(2\sqrt{c_{q}c_{q'}}) = u(c_{q} + c_{q'})\delta_{qq'}/(2\sqrt{c_{q}c_{q'}}) = u\delta_{qq'}$, and $[\Phi_{q}, \Phi_{q'}] = [\Pi_{q}, \Pi_{q'}] = (c_{q} - c_{q'})\delta_{qq'}/(2\sqrt{c_{q}c_{q'}}) = 0$. On $\mathcal{D}$, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(vi) gives $[\rho_{q}, \rho_{q'}] = 0$ and $[\rho_{q}, \rho_{q'}^{*}] = q\delta_{qq'}$, which are the hypotheses with $c_{q} = q$.

\emph{(vi).} The map $e_{3} \mapsto -e_{3}$, others fixed, preserves $Q$; on blades put $\alpha(e_{B}) = (-1)^{[3 \in B]}e_{B}$. By the product formula of Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}, $e_{I}e_{J'} = \pm(\prod_{I \cap J'}Q)\,e_{I \triangle J'}$ with a sign depending only on the index sets, and $[3 \in I \triangle J'] \equiv [3 \in I] + [3 \in J'] \pmod 2$, so $\alpha(e_{I}e_{J'}) = \alpha(e_{I})\alpha(e_{J'})$: $\alpha$ is an automorphism. Both $\alpha$ and $*$ are diagonal on blades, so they commute and $\alpha$ is a $*$-automorphism. It fixes every plane generator, hence $B_{N}$ pointwise, and fixes $\sigma = e_{0}e_{1}$; $\alpha(J) = e_{2}(-e_{3}) = -J$, $\alpha(I_{4}) = -I_{4}$, $\alpha(I_{n}) = -I_{n}$, and $\alpha(\phi_{X}) = \phi_{X}$, $\alpha(\pi_{X}) = -J(X^{*} - X) = -\pi_{X}$. Any statement made with $B_{N}$, $*$ and the algebra structure is therefore true of $J$ exactly when it is true of $-J$. With $\sigma$ fixed, $J = I_{4}\sigma$ makes the sign of $J$ and the orientation of $I_{4}$ one datum.

The phase circle: $\tfrac12Q = \sum_{j}s_{j}n_{j}$ with $s_{2k} = \tfrac12$, $s_{2k+1} = -\tfrac12$, so $U_{\theta}$ is the diagonal mode rotation $U_{s}(\theta) = e^{\theta J\sum_{j}s_{j}n_{j}}$ of \claimref{synthesis.ladder-bosons-inherit-spin-statistics-from-the-single-modes}, whose clause (i) gives the product form $\prod_{j}(1 - n_{j} + n_{j}e^{\theta Js_{j}})$, unitarity and $U_{s}(\theta)v_{j}U_{s}(\theta)^{*} = e^{\theta Js_{j}}v_{j}$, $U_{s}(\theta)w_{j}U_{s}(\theta)^{*} = e^{-\theta Js_{j}}w_{j}$ (with $e^{\lambda J} = \cos\lambda + J\sin\lambda$, Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential}); that formula is cited, not re-derived here. Hence $U_{\theta}b_{k}U_{\theta}^{*} = e^{\theta J/2}v_{2k}\,e^{\theta J/2}w_{2k+1} = e^{\theta J}b_{k}$ ($J$ commutes with the modes), so $U_{\theta}SU_{\theta}^{*} = e^{\theta J}S$, and $U_{\theta}S^{*}U_{\theta}^{*} = (e^{\theta J}S)^{*} = S^{*}e^{-\theta J}$. Then $U_{\theta}\phi U_{\theta}^{*} = e^{\theta J}S + S^{*}e^{-\theta J} = \cos\theta\,\phi + \sin\theta\,J(S - S^{*}) = \phi\cos\theta - \pi\sin\theta$, and $U_{\theta}\pi U_{\theta}^{*} = J(S^{*}e^{-\theta J} - e^{\theta J}S) = \cos\theta\,\pi + \sin\theta\,(S^{*} + S) = \phi\sin\theta + \pi\cos\theta$; as conjugation, it keeps $[\phi, \pi]$. $e^{\theta J}$ commutes with $B_{N}$, so $\operatorname{Ad}(e^{\theta J})$ fixes it; on the kernel, $e_{2}$ anticommutes with $J$, so $e^{\theta J}e_{2}e^{-\theta J} = e^{2\theta J}e_{2} = \cos 2\theta\,e_{2} + \sin 2\theta\,e_{3}$ ($Je_{2} = e_{3}$), a turn through $2\theta$, and $e^{\pi J} = -1$ is the rotor of the turn through $2\pi$. The script checks $\alpha$ as a $*$-homomorphism on blades of grade at most $3$ and its values, and, at $M = 2$ and the rational point $(\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}, \sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}) = (5/13, 12/13)$, the unitarity of $U_{\theta}$, $U_{\theta}SU_{\theta}^{*} = e^{\theta J}S$, the turn of $(\phi, \pi)$, the invariance of $[\phi, \pi]$ and that $\operatorname{Ad}(e^{\theta J})$ fixes every plane generator. $\square$

\emph{Reading (argued).} Premise (N$_{+}$) assumes the orientation of $I_{4}$ relative to time (\claimref{synthesis.n-plus-null-ground-state}); with the radial plane's orientation $\sigma$ fixed, this is the sign of $J$ by (vi). The fermion phase flow on the atom, $v \mapsto e^{-Jt}v$ (\claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}(iv)), and the boson relation $[\Phi, \Pi] = +J$ of (v) are both written with it, and $\alpha$ reverses both. The identification is a reading of the premise's wording, not a theorem, and this result does not rest on the premise.

synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-.technical:
The store quantises the photon in Coulomb gauge on a positive polynomial representation, and its tower floors carry positive forms. Two standard tools of covariant quantum field theory need an indefinite metric instead: a self-adjoint nilpotent BRST charge, which vanishes on any positive space, and Pauli-Villars regulator fields, which enter loops with negative weights. This premise adopts one indefinite (Krein) inner product for both. On a polarisation quantum it is the Gupta-Bleuler form, the Minkowski metric of the polarisations, which is Lorentz invariant where the positive form singles out a frame; ghost pairs are tower modes with the floor's form twisted by the involution exchanging the pair; regulator fields of negative weight are negative-norm states of the same form. The physical space is the BRST cohomology at ghost number zero and is required to be positive: the unphysical polarisations and the ghosts appear only in zero-norm quartets (Kugo and Ojima), and regulators decouple at infinite mass. Strocchi's theorem says a local covariant vector potential obeying Maxwell's equations cannot live on a positive-metric space with nonzero field strength, so a covariant formulation needs some such form.

Results that rest on it say so: one-loop electrodynamics in the spacetime algebra in a covariant gauge with Pauli-Villars regulators, the one-loop running coefficients in the background Feynman gauge, the self-adjoint BRST charge with tower ghosts, and (from 2 November 2026) the two-loop vacuum polarisation, the free quartet positivity at every number of quanta, the charge renormalisation of electron-positron annihilation, the self-energy and vertex parts of the regulator-free one-loop extensions, the running of the rung-field quartics, the Krein quartet of induced gravity, the gauge parts of the slot-module coefficients and the interacting spin-statistics of causal perturbation theory. Note of 2 November 2026: the Pauli-Villars clause is not needed for the one-loop vacuum polarisation, which extends across the coincident point with no regulator (the clause is kept for the stored self-energy and vertex); the one-particle Gupta-Bleuler form is restated in the store as the trace form of Clifford conjugation, minus the metric, which restates and does not derive the premise; and given the polarisation and ghost clauses the free physical space is positive at every number of quanta. It is not derived from the series (the form is the same in any formalism), it supplies no native covariant regulator, and positivity of the physical space beyond the free charge is imported, not computed. It would be refuted by a negative-norm or stray null state in the physical space of the series' gauge fields (a failure of unitarity), by gauge-parameter or regulator dependence of physical amplitudes, or by a derivation that every state space of the series is positive.
synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-.lay: To describe light and the other force fields in a way that treats space and time alike, physicists use bookkeeping in which some unphysical states have negative or zero length, and remove them again before anything is measured. The same device is used to tame the infinities of quantum corrections, with auxiliary particles that count negatively. The series' quantum spaces all have positive lengths, so it cannot use this bookkeeping as it stands. This premise adopts it: the force fields of the series carry the standard indefinite measure built from the spacetime metric of their polarisations, and only states of positive length remain once the unphysical parts cancel in groups of four. Several results use it, among them the series' calculations of the first and second quantum corrections of electrodynamics, its calculation of how the force strengths change with energy, and its construction of the ghost bookkeeping. One of the two uses, the auxiliary negative particles, turns out not to be needed for the screening of charge by the vacuum, which can be computed without them. It is taken as given, not derived; it would be refuted if the physical states it leaves were found to include ones of negative length.

synthesis.ladder-bosons-inherit-spin-sta.formal:
Let $L_{N} = \Cl(N, N{+}2)$ be a tower level, written as the anisotropic kernel $\mathrm{span}\{g_{1}, g_{2}\}$ ($Q = -1, -1$) orthogonal to $N$ hyperbolic planes $(e_{j}, f_{j})$, $Q(e_{j}) = 1$, $Q(f_{j}) = -1$, with $v_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} + f_{j}) = a_{j}^{*}$, $w_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} - f_{j}) = a_{j}$ (the canonical anticommutation relations, Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}), $n_{j} = v_{j}w_{j}$, $\omega_{j} = e_{j}f_{j}$, $\Gamma = \prod_{j}\omega_{j}$, $J = g_{1}g_{2}$, and $*$ the adjoint (reversion composed with the sign flip of the generators of square $-1$). A \emph{spin assignment} is $s = (s_{1}, \dots, s_{N})$ with $s_{j} \in \tfrac12\mathbb{Z}$, the weights of a rotation of the one-particle space that is diagonal in the mode basis; it defines $L_{s} = \sum_{j}s_{j}n_{j}$ and
\[
U_{s}(\theta) = e^{\theta JL_{s}} = \prod_{j}\bigl(1 - n_{j} + n_{j}e^{\theta Js_{j}}\bigr), \qquad e^{\varphi J} = \cos\varphi + J\sin\varphi .
\]
An element $x$ has \emph{integer} (\emph{half-integer}) \emph{spin} if $U_{s}(2\pi)\,x\,U_{s}(2\pi)^{*} = x$ ($= -x$). Two elements obey Bose (Fermi) statistics if they commute (anticommute).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The turn by $2\pi$.)} $J^{2} = -1$, $J^{*} = -J$, and $J$ commutes with every plane generator. $U_{s}(\theta)$ is unitary, commutes with $J$, satisfies $U_{s}(\theta)U_{s}(\theta') = U_{s}(\theta + \theta')$, and $U_{s}(\theta)w_{j}U_{s}(\theta)^{*} = e^{-\theta Js_{j}}w_{j}$, $U_{s}(\theta)v_{j}U_{s}(\theta)^{*} = e^{\theta Js_{j}}v_{j}$. Since $n_{j} = \tfrac12(1 - \omega_{j})$,
\[
U_{s}(2\pi) = \prod_{j:\ s_{j} \in \mathbb{Z} + \frac12}\omega_{j} ,
\]
the product of the volume elements of the planes of half-integer weight.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Spin and statistics agree exactly when every mode is a spinor.)} $\operatorname{Ad}U_{s}(2\pi) = \operatorname{Ad}\Gamma$ on the algebra of the planes if and only if every $s_{j}$ is half-integer, and then $U_{s}(2\pi) = \Gamma$. In that case an element of definite spin has half-integer spin exactly when it is odd, two odd elements on disjoint sets of modes anticommute and every other pair on disjoint sets commutes; in particular every hopping element $v_{i}w_{j}$, pairing element $w_{i}w_{j}$, collective sum of them and density mode $\rho_{q} = \sum_{k}v_{k}w_{k+q}$ has integer spin and Bose statistics across blocks, exactly at every $N$, with no limit taken. \emph{(The bosons alone.)} $\operatorname{Ad}U_{s}(2\pi)$ fixes every even element (every product of two modes, hence every hopping, pairing, density and collective mode) if and only if the $2s_{j}$ all have the same parity: every $s_{j}$ half-integer, or every $s_{j}$ an integer.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Uniform integer and mixed assignments.)} If some $s_{j}$ is an integer, $w_{j}$ has integer spin and anticommutes with every other mode: a fermion of integer spin. If every $s_{j}$ is an integer, $U_{s}(2\pi) = 1$: the bosons obey the connection (integer spin, Bose statistics) while every single mode breaks it. \emph{Counter-model for a mixed assignment: a boson of half-integer spin.} Take $N_{b}$ blocks, the lower mode of each with weight $\tfrac12$ and the upper with weight $0$, and $b_{i} = v_{\mathrm{lower},i}w_{\mathrm{upper},i}$. Each $b_{i}$ has half-integer spin; the $b_{i}$ and $b_{i}^{*}$ of distinct blocks commute; and $B = N_{b}^{-1/2}\sum_{i}b_{i}$ is the hopping ladder of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(ii): on $(B^{*})^{k}P_{\mathrm{pol}}$, $[B, B^{*}] = 1 - 2k/N_{b}$, $k = 0, \dots, N_{b}$, so $B$ tends on states of bounded $k$ to a canonical boson mode of half-integer spin.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The level's own rotations give integer spin.)} If $R(\theta)$ is a one-parameter group of rotors of $L_{N}$ whose action $x \mapsto R(\theta)xR(\theta)^{\sim}$ on the vectors has period $2\pi$, then $R(2\pi) = \pm1$ (the kernel of the double cover, Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.spin-double-cover}), so $\operatorname{Ad}R(2\pi)$ is the identity on the whole level: every element has integer spin under rotations of the level's own vector space. Two instances: the kernel rotors $e^{\varphi J/2}$, with $e^{\pi J} = -1$, and $\operatorname{Ad}e^{\varphi J}$ fixes every element of the algebra of the planes, for every $\varphi$; The real rotation of two modes, $L = v_{0}w_{1} - v_{1}w_{0} = \tfrac12(e_{0}e_{1} - f_{0}f_{1})$, is a sum of two commuting bivectors of square $-1$; $[L, w_{0} \pm Jw_{1}] = \pm J(w_{0} \pm Jw_{1})$, so its weights are $\pm1$; $e^{\pi L} = \omega_{0}\omega_{1}$ negates both modes and $e^{2\pi L} = 1$. Half-integer weights need the unit $J$ at half angle, which is the datum $s$.
\end{enumerate}
Clauses (i) to (iv) are proved. \emph{Reading.} On the ladder, statistics is the grading of the algebra and holds exactly at every $N$; spin is the extra datum $s$. Spin and statistics agree on the whole algebra if and only if every mode is a spinor (ii). For the even elements, the bosons, every element has integer spin if and only if the $2s_{j}$ all have the same parity (all modes spinors, or all of integer weight); with a mixed assignment a hopping element between a spinor and an integer-weight mode is a commuting boson of half-integer spin (iii), and with all weights integer the bosons obey the connection while every single mode is a fermion of integer spin. So the collective modes cannot repair a mixed assignment, and they cannot detect a uniform integer one. The tower does not fix the datum: by (iv) the rotations of its own vector space give integer spin to everything, and half-integer weights need the kernel unit $J$ at half angle. For the attached free fields the spinor assignment of the CAR modes is supplied by locality with a positive norm (\claimref{synthesis.locality-of-the-attached-free-fields-fixes-their-statistics}), a continuum input.
synthesis.ladder-bosons-inherit-spin-sta.technical: On the tower, fermion modes anticommute and products of two modes on distinct blocks commute: this is the grading of the algebra and holds exactly for any number of modes. Spin is a separate datum: how a rotation acts on each mode. With the kernel bivector $J$ as the unit, a rotation diagonal in the mode basis with weights $s_{j}$ is implemented inside the level by $U(\theta) = e^{\theta J\sum s_{j}n_{j}} = \prod_{j}(1 - n_{j} + n_{j}e^{\theta Js_{j}})$, because each $n_{j}$ is an idempotent commuting with $J$ and the others. Since $n_{j} = \tfrac12(1 - \omega_{j})$ with $\omega_{j} = e_{j}f_{j}$, the turn by $2\pi$ is exactly the product of the plane volume elements of the modes of half-integer weight. It acts as the parity $\Gamma$ on all modes if and only if every weight is half-integer; then every odd element has half-integer spin and every even element, every boson built from pairs, has integer spin, at every size. On the bosons alone, the turn by $2\pi$ fixes every product of two modes exactly when the weights are all half-integer or all integer. If one mode has integer weight, that mode is a fermion of integer spin; if all weights are integer the bosons still obey the connection; if the assignment is mixed, pairing a spinor mode with a weight-zero mode in each block gives a hopping element of half-integer spin that commutes across blocks and whose normalised sum climbs the known Holstein-Primakoff ladder, a boson of half-integer spin in the limit. The level's own rotations give integer spin to everything: a rotor group whose action on vectors has period $2\pi$ ends at $\pm1$, the kernel of the double cover (instances: the kernel rotors, which fix every mode, and the real rotation of two modes, with weights $\pm1$). So the spinor assignment is an input, and the collective modes can neither repair a mixed assignment nor detect a uniform integer one. For the series' attached free fields it is supplied by locality with a positive norm, which is stored separately.
synthesis.ladder-bosons-inherit-spin-sta.lay: In the tower every particle is first a fermion, and bosons appear only as collective pairs. One would like the familiar rule that half-integer spin goes with fermions and whole-number spin with bosons to come out of this construction. The calculation shows exactly how much does. Whether two operators commute or anticommute is built into the algebra and holds exactly at every size. How an operator turns under a rotation is extra information: one has to say how each single mode turns. If every single mode turns like a spinor, picking up a minus sign after a full turn, then every pair, and so every collective boson, comes back to itself, and the rule holds exactly, without any limit. If some modes turn like spinors and others do not, the rule fails, and it fails for bosons too: a pair made of a spinor mode and a spinless mode builds a boson that picks up a minus sign after a full turn. If no mode turns like a spinor, the bosons still follow the rule but the single fermions break it. The tower itself does not decide which way the single modes turn; for the free fields the graph attaches, that input comes from the requirement that fields at separated points do not interfere, which the graph treats elsewhere.

proofs.main:
\emph{Preliminaries.} By Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors} the $v_{j}, w_{j}$ satisfy $\{v_{i}, w_{j}\} = \delta_{ij}$, $\{v_{i}, v_{j}\} = \{w_{i}, w_{j}\} = 0$, so $n_{j}^{2} = v_{j}(w_{j}v_{j})w_{j} = v_{j}(1 - v_{j}w_{j})w_{j} = n_{j}$, and the $n_{j}$ commute pairwise (each is even and built from one plane). Directly, $n_{j} = \tfrac14(e_{j} + f_{j})(e_{j} - f_{j}) = \tfrac14(e_{j}^{2} - e_{j}f_{j} + f_{j}e_{j} - f_{j}^{2}) = \tfrac12(1 - \omega_{j})$, since $f_{j}e_{j} = -e_{j}f_{j}$. By Theorem \claimref{tower.volume-elements-planes}, $\omega_{j}^{2} = 1$, $\omega_{j}$ anticommutes with $e_{j}, f_{j}$, commutes with the generators of the other planes and with $g_{1}, g_{2}$, and the $\omega_{j}$ commute pairwise. $J^{2} = g_{1}g_{2}g_{1}g_{2} = -g_{1}^{2}g_{2}^{2} = -1$; $J^{*} = (g_{2}g_{1})(-1)^{2} = g_{2}g_{1} = -J$; and $J$ commutes with every plane generator, which anticommutes with each of $g_{1}, g_{2}$. Hence $J$ commutes with every element of the algebra of the planes. The adjoint is an antiautomorphism with $v_{j}^{*} = w_{j}$, $n_{j}^{*} = n_{j}$.

\emph{(i).} The summands $\theta Js_{j}n_{j}$ commute pairwise, so $e^{\theta JL_{s}} = \prod_{j}e^{\theta Js_{j}n_{j}}$. Since $n_{j}$ is an idempotent commuting with $J$, $(\theta Js_{j}n_{j})^{k} = (\theta Js_{j})^{k}n_{j}$ for $k \ge 1$, so $e^{\theta Js_{j}n_{j}} = 1 - n_{j} + n_{j}e^{\theta Js_{j}}$, with $e^{\varphi J} = \cos\varphi + J\sin\varphi$ by Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential} ($J$ is a simple bivector of square $-1$). The group law follows from the exponential form, since all factors commute. Unitarity: $U_{s}(\theta)^{*} = \prod_{j}(1 - n_{j} + n_{j}e^{-\theta Js_{j}}) = U_{s}(-\theta)$ because $J^{*} = -J$ and $J$ commutes with $n_{j}$; so $U_{s}(\theta)^{*}U_{s}(\theta) = 1$. Commutation with $J$ is clear. For the action on modes, $[n_{j}, w_{j}] = v_{j}w_{j}w_{j} - w_{j}v_{j}w_{j} = -(1 - v_{j}w_{j})w_{j} = -w_{j}$ and $[n_{k}, w_{j}] = 0$ for $k \ne j$; so $[L_{s}, w_{j}] = -s_{j}w_{j}$, hence $L_{s}w_{j} = w_{j}(L_{s} - s_{j})$ and $U_{s}(\theta)w_{j} = w_{j}e^{\theta J(L_{s} - s_{j})} = e^{-\theta Js_{j}}w_{j}U_{s}(\theta)$; similarly $[L_{s}, v_{j}] = s_{j}v_{j}$ and $U_{s}(\theta)v_{j}U_{s}(\theta)^{*} = e^{\theta Js_{j}}v_{j}$. At $\theta = 2\pi$, $e^{2\pi Js_{j}} = \cos 2\pi s_{j} = (-1)^{2s_{j}}$, so the factor of plane $j$ is $1$ for integer $s_{j}$ and $1 - 2n_{j} = \omega_{j}$ for half-integer $s_{j}$. This gives the product formula. The script checks the product formula, the group law $U_{s}(\pi)^{2} = U_{s}(2\pi)$, unitarity, commutation with $J$ and the action on $v_{j}, w_{j}$ (with $e^{m\pi Js}$ in $\{\pm1, \pm J\}$) for $N = 1, 2, 3$ and all $5^{N}$ assignments with $s_{j} \in \{-\tfrac12, 0, \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32\}$.

\emph{(ii).} Let $S$ be the set of half-integer modes, so $U_{s}(2\pi) = \prod_{j \in S}\omega_{j}$. For a mode $j$, $\omega_{k}$ commutes with $v_{j}, w_{j}$ for $k \ne j$ and anticommutes for $k = j$. So $\operatorname{Ad}U_{s}(2\pi)$ negates $v_{j}, w_{j}$ for $j \in S$ and fixes them for $j \notin S$, while $\operatorname{Ad}\Gamma$ negates every mode. The two automorphisms agree on the generators $v_{j}, w_{j}$, hence on the algebra of the planes, exactly when $S$ is every mode; then $U_{s}(2\pi) = \prod_{j}\omega_{j} = \Gamma$. $\operatorname{Ad}\Gamma$ fixes products of an even number of modes and negates products of an odd number, so an element of definite spin has half-integer spin exactly when it is odd. Monomials in the modes of two disjoint sets of planes commute or anticommute according to the product of their parities, since modes of distinct planes anticommute; by linearity two odd elements on disjoint sets anticommute and every other pair commutes. Hopping elements $v_{i}w_{j}$, pairing elements $w_{i}w_{j}$, their sums and the density modes are even, so they have integer spin, and those on disjoint blocks commute, at every $N$. \emph{The bosons alone.} $\operatorname{Ad}U_{s}(2\pi)$ negates $v_{i}, w_{i}$ for $i \in S$ and fixes them otherwise, so it maps a product of two modes on planes $i, j$ to $(-1)^{[i \in S] + [j \in S]}$ times itself. All such products are fixed if and only if $[i \in S] = [j \in S]$ for every pair $i, j$, that is $S$ is empty or every mode; since the products of two modes span the even part, this is the condition for every even element to have integer spin. It is the statement that the commutant of the even part of $\Cl(N,N)$ is $\mathrm{span}\{1, \Gamma\}$ (clause (i) of \claimref{synthesis.kernel-bivector-is-the-unit-of-hermitian-boson-fields-on-the-tower}), seen on $U_{s}(2\pi) = \prod_{j \in S}\omega_{j}$, an element of the commutant of the even part exactly when it is $1$ or $\Gamma$. The script checks, for $N = 1, 2, 3$ and all $5^{N}$ assignments, that $\operatorname{Ad}U_{s}(2\pi)$ and $\operatorname{Ad}\Gamma$ agree on every mode exactly for the $3^{N}$ all-half-integer assignments ($39$ in all), that $U(2\pi) = \Gamma$ when every weight is $\tfrac12$, and then that all products of two modes are fixed and all modes negated; and that all products of two modes are fixed exactly for the $3^{N} + 2^{N}$ uniform assignments (all half-integer, or all integer: $5$, $13$, $35$ of $5$, $25$, $125$).

\emph{(iii).} If $s_{j}$ is an integer, $j \notin S$, so $\operatorname{Ad}U_{s}(2\pi)w_{j} = w_{j}$ by (ii), while $w_{j}$ anticommutes with every $v_{k}, w_{k}$, $k \ne j$, by the anticommutation relations. If every $s_{j}$ is an integer, $S$ is empty and $U_{s}(2\pi) = 1$ by (i), so every element is fixed: the even elements have integer spin and commute on disjoint blocks (ii), and every mode is a fermion of integer spin. The script checks this for $N = 1, 2, 3$ and every all-integer assignment. For the blocks, $\operatorname{Ad}U_{s}(2\pi)$ negates $v_{\mathrm{lower},i}$ and fixes $w_{\mathrm{upper},i}$, so it negates $b_{i}$. Elements of distinct blocks are even and supported on disjoint planes, so they commute by (ii). The relation $[B, B^{*}] = N_{b}^{-1}\sum_{i}(n_{\mathrm{lower},i} - n_{\mathrm{upper},i})$ and its value $1 - 2k/N_{b}$ on $(B^{*})^{k}P_{\mathrm{pol}}$, with $(B^{*})^{N_{b}+1}P_{\mathrm{pol}} = 0$, are Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(ii), which uses only the anticommutation relations and so holds whatever spin is assigned; $B$, a sum of elements of half-integer spin, has half-integer spin. On vectors $(B^{*})^{k}P_{\mathrm{pol}}$ of bounded $k$ the commutator tends to $1$. The script checks all of this for $N_{b} = 1, 2, 3$, with $P_{\mathrm{pol}} = \prod_{i}n_{\mathrm{lower},i}(1 - n_{\mathrm{upper},i})$ as the polarised vector of the left regular representation.

\emph{(iv).} Let $R(\theta)$ be a one-parameter group of rotors with $R(2\pi)xR(2\pi)^{\sim} = x$ for every vector $x$ of the level. Then $R(2\pi)$ lies in the kernel of the map from the spin group to the rotations, which is $\{\pm1\}$ by Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.spin-double-cover} (the level's form is nondegenerate), so $\operatorname{Ad}R(2\pi)$ is the identity on the whole level. For the kernel rotors, $e^{\pi J} = \cos\pi + J\sin\pi = -1$ by Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential}. By the preliminaries $J$ commutes with every plane generator, so $e^{\varphi J}$ commutes with the algebra of the planes and $\operatorname{Ad}e^{\varphi J}$ fixes it. For $L$: $v_{0}w_{1} = \tfrac14(e_{0}e_{1} - e_{0}f_{1} + f_{0}e_{1} - f_{0}f_{1})$ and $v_{1}w_{0} = \tfrac14(e_{1}e_{0} - e_{1}f_{0} + f_{1}e_{0} - f_{1}f_{0})$; using anticommutation of distinct generators the mixed terms cancel and $L = \tfrac12(e_{0}e_{1} - f_{0}f_{1})$. $B_{1} = e_{0}e_{1}$ and $B_{2} = f_{0}f_{1}$ commute (they share no generator and are even) and $B_{1}^{2} = -e_{0}^{2}e_{1}^{2} = -1$, $B_{2}^{2} = -f_{0}^{2}f_{1}^{2} = -1$. From the relations, $[L, w_{0}] = -w_{1}$ and $[L, w_{1}] = w_{0}$, so $[L, w_{0} \pm Jw_{1}] = -w_{1} \pm Jw_{0} = \pm J(w_{0} \pm Jw_{1})$: weights $\pm1$. By Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential}, $e^{\pi L} = e^{\pi B_{1}/2}e^{-\pi B_{2}/2} = B_{1}(-B_{2}) = -e_{0}e_{1}f_{0}f_{1} = e_{0}f_{0}e_{1}f_{1} = \omega_{0}\omega_{1}$, which negates $v_{0}, w_{0}, v_{1}, w_{1}$, and $e^{2\pi L} = (\omega_{0}\omega_{1})^{2} = 1$. The script checks each identity.

\emph{Reading.} By (ii), spin and statistics agree on the whole algebra if and only if every $s_{j}$ is half-integer. On the even part, $\operatorname{Ad}\prod_{j \in S}\omega_{j}$ fixes every product of two modes if and only if $S$ is empty or every mode (the commutant of the even part of $\Cl(N,N)$ is $\mathrm{span}\{1, \Gamma\}$), so the bosons have integer spin if and only if the assignment is uniform; (iii) is the mixed case and the uniform integer case. By (iv) rotations of the level's own vector space supply no half-integer weights; the assignment $s$ is extra data. That the attached free fields' CAR modes are spinors is the locality result cited in the statement, which is not used in the proof.

synthesis.ladder-states-are-locally-prod.formal:
Use the notation of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(ii): $N$ blocks of two tower planes, plane $j$ with $Q(e_{j}) = 1$, $Q(f_{j}) = -1$, $v_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} + f_{j}) = a_{j}^{*}$, $w_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} - f_{j}) = a_{j}$ (the anticommutation relations of Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}), $n_{j} = v_{j}w_{j}$; block $i$ has a lower mode $l_{i}$ and an upper mode $u_{i}$, hopping element $b_{i} = v_{l_{i}}w_{u_{i}}$, $K = \sum_{i}b_{i}$, $B = N^{-1/2}K$, and polarised element $P = \prod_{i}n_{l_{i}}(1 - n_{u_{i}})$. Vectors are elements $x$ of the algebra in its left regular representation, with $\langle x, y\rangle = \langle x^{*}y\rangle_{0}$ (scalar part); the basis blades are orthonormal for it. For $k = 0, \dots, N$ let $\psi_{k} = (K^{*})^{k}P$ and $\omega_{k}(X) = \langle\psi_{k}, X\psi_{k}\rangle/\langle\psi_{k}, \psi_{k}\rangle$; $\omega_{0}$ is the polarised product state, and $\omega_{k}(b_{i}) = 0$, so the fluctuation $F_{N}(b)$ of clause (vii) of the cited theorem, centred at $\omega_{k}$, is $B$. For integers write $(k)_{m} = k(k - 1)\cdots(k - m + 1)$ and $(x)^{(m)} = x(x + 1)\cdots(x + m - 1)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Exact moments.)} $KP = 0$, $K\psi_{k} = k(N - k + 1)\psi_{k-1}$ and $\langle\psi_{k}, \psi_{k}\rangle = k(N - k + 1)\langle\psi_{k-1}, \psi_{k-1}\rangle$, so $\psi_{k} \ne 0$ for $k \le N$. For all $m \ge 0$,
\[
\omega_{k}\bigl((B^{*})^{m}B^{m}\bigr) = \frac{(k)_{m}\,(N - k + 1)^{(m)}}{N^{m}},
\]
which is $0$ for $m > k$, and $\omega_{k}((B^{*})^{a}B^{c}) = 0$ for $a \ne c$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Local convergence to the polarised product state.)} For $m \le N$ and $P_{m} = \prod_{i<m}n_{l_{i}}(1 - n_{u_{i}})$, $\omega_{k}(P_{m}) = \binom{N - m}{k}\big/\binom{N}{k} \ge 1 - \varepsilon_{m}$ with $\varepsilon_{m} = km/(N - k + 1)$; $P_{m}$ is a minimal projection of the algebra of the first $m$ blocks, $P_{m}XP_{m} = \omega_{0}(X)P_{m}$ there, and for every $X$ in that algebra $|\omega_{k}(X) - \omega_{0}(X)| \le (2\sqrt{\varepsilon_{m}} + \varepsilon_{m})\|X\|$. So at fixed $k$ every finite marginal of $\omega_{k}$ tends in norm to that of the polarised product state as $N \to \infty$. The one-block occupation is $\omega_{k}(n_{u_{i}}) = k/N$, and for $i \ne j$, $\omega_{k}(b_{i}^{*}b_{j}) = k(N - k)/(N(N - 1))$ and $\omega_{k}(n_{u_{i}}n_{u_{j}}) = k(k - 1)/(N(N - 1))$: every pair of blocks is correlated at order $1/N$, every pair alike (the state is permutation symmetric), and $\sum_{j \ne i}\omega_{k}(b_{i}^{*}b_{j}) = k(N - k)/N \to k$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The fluctuation state is a number state.)} As $N \to \infty$ at fixed $k$, $\omega_{k}((B^{*})^{a}B^{c}) \to \delta_{ac}(k)_{a}$, the moments of the $k$-boson number state of a canonical mode (the canonical relation $[B, B^{*}] \to 1$ on these vectors is clause (ii) of the cited theorem). A quasi-free state of one canonical mode $a$ with $\langle a\rangle = \langle a^{2}\rangle = 0$ and $\langle a^{*}a\rangle = x$ has, by the pairing rule that defines it, $\langle(a^{*})^{m}a^{m}\rangle = m!\,x^{m}$. For $k \ge 1$ the limit is not of that form: at $m = 2$, $k(k - 1) \ne 2k^{2}$, and at $m = k + 1$ the limit is $0$ while $(k + 1)!\,k^{k+1} > 0$. For $k = 0$ (the product state) the limit is the vacuum, which is quasi-free.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The local state does not fix the fluctuation state.)} The states $\omega_{0}, \omega_{1}, \omega_{2}, \dots$ have the same local limit, the polarised product state, and pairwise different limits of their fluctuation states. Hence convergence of fluctuation states to a quasi-free state cannot be derived from the convergence of finite marginals alone; the known sufficient hypotheses (product structure, or a uniform clustering bound, at every $N$) are not implied by it. Their necessity is not claimed.
\end{enumerate}
Clauses (i) to (iv) are proved. \emph{Reading.} The quantum central limit theorem turns product states into quasi-free (Gaussian) boson states; the non-Gaussian boson states of a collective mode, its number states, are realised on the tower by the ladder vectors $(K^{*})^{k}P$, which are not product states though they look like the product state on every finite set of blocks. The correlation that carries the boson is spread over all pairs of blocks alike, at order $1/N$.
synthesis.ladder-states-are-locally-prod.technical: On $N$ blocks of two modes the polarised element has every lower mode filled and every upper mode empty; the collective hopping $K^{*}$ flips one block at a time, and $K$ unflips. The ladder vectors $\psi_{k} = (K^{*})^{k}P$ satisfy $K\psi_{k} = k(N - k + 1)\psi_{k-1}$, from the stored commutator $[K, K^{*}] = \sum_{i}(n_{l_{i}} - n_{u_{i}})$, which is $N - 2j$ on $\psi_{j}$. Hence the moments of the normalised mode $B = K/\sqrt{N}$ in the state of $\psi_{k}$ are $(k)_{m}(N - k + 1)\cdots(N - k + m)/N^{m}$ exactly, which tend to $k(k - 1)\cdots(k - m + 1)$: the moments of a state with exactly $k$ bosons. A Gaussian (quasi-free) state with the same mean occupation $k$ would have $m!\,k^{m}$, so at $m = 2$ it would give $2k^{2}$ instead of $k(k - 1)$. Yet each $\psi_{k}$ is, block by block, almost the polarised state: the chance that $m$ given blocks are all polarised is $\binom{N - m}{k}/\binom{N}{k}$, at least $1 - km/(N - k + 1)$, and since the polarised projector of $m$ blocks is minimal, every expectation on those blocks is within $2\sqrt{\varepsilon} + \varepsilon$ of the product value. The correlations are $k(N - k)/(N(N - 1))$ for every pair of blocks: tiny for each pair, but summing to about $k$. So the local state does not determine the limit of the fluctuation states, and the central limit theorem for states cannot replace its hypothesis at each size by local convergence in the limit.
synthesis.ladder-states-are-locally-prod.lay: When many small two-level units are put together, the collective wobble of the whole system usually behaves like a smooth bell-curve quantity, a Gaussian, and in the quantum case like a boson in a thermal or vacuum state. That is the quantum central limit theorem, and it needs the units to be independent. This entry shows that the independence cannot be replaced by something weaker that sounds almost the same. Take the state in which exactly k of N units have been flipped, spread evenly over all of them. Look at any fixed handful of units and, for large N, they are almost certainly unflipped, exactly as in the independent state where none is flipped. But the collective wobble is not Gaussian at all: it is a state holding exactly k bosons. The difference is carried by very weak correlations shared evenly by every pair of units. This is also where the tower keeps its states with a definite number of bosons.

proofs.main:
\emph{Preliminaries.} By Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}, $\{v_{i}, w_{j}\} = \delta_{ij}$ and modes of distinct planes anticommute, so each $n_{j}$ is an idempotent, the $n_{j}$ commute, and even elements supported on distinct blocks commute. The adjoint $*$ (reversion with a sign per generator of square $-1$) maps each basis blade $e_{S}$ to $\pm e_{S}$ with $e_{S}^{*}e_{S} = 1$ (each generator $g$ has $g^{*}g = Q(g)^{2} = 1$, and reversion reverses the order), so $\langle x, y\rangle = \langle x^{*}y\rangle_{0} = \sum_{S}x_{S}y_{S}$ is the Euclidean inner product of blade coefficients: positive definite, with $\langle x, Xy\rangle = \langle X^{*}x, y\rangle$ because $\langle a\rangle_{0} = \langle a^{*}\rangle_{0}$. Hence each $\omega_{k}$ is a state (a normalised vector state of the left regular representation) and self-adjoint idempotents act as orthogonal projections. The number $\mathcal{N}_{u} = \sum_{i}n_{u_{i}}$ is self-adjoint, $[\mathcal{N}_{u}, K^{*}] = K^{*}$ and $[\mathcal{N}_{u}, K] = -K$ (from $[n_{u}, v_{u}] = v_{u}$, $[n_{u}, w_{u}] = -w_{u}$), and $\mathcal{N}_{u}P = 0$, so $\mathcal{N}_{u}\psi_{k} = k\psi_{k}$; vectors with different eigenvalues are orthogonal. In particular $\omega_{k}(b_{i}) = 0$ and $\omega_{k}((B^{*})^{a}B^{c}) = 0$ for $a \ne c$, since $(B^{*})^{a}B^{c}\psi_{k}$ has eigenvalue $k + a - c$.

\emph{(i).} By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(ii), $[K, K^{*}] = \sum_{i}(n_{l_{i}} - n_{u_{i}})$, and on $\psi_{j}$ this equals $N - 2j$ (each block holds one particle on $\psi_{j}$: $n_{l_{i}} + n_{u_{i}}$ commutes with $K^{*}$ and is $1$ on $P$). $KP = 0$ because $w_{u_{i}}(1 - n_{u_{i}}) = w_{u_{i}}w_{u_{i}}v_{u_{i}} = 0$ and $w_{u_{i}}$ commutes past the factors of the other blocks up to sign. Then $K\psi_{k} = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(K^{*})^{j}[K, K^{*}](K^{*})^{k-1-j}P + (K^{*})^{k}KP = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(N - 2(k - 1 - j))\psi_{k-1} = (kN - k(k - 1))\psi_{k-1} = k(N - k + 1)\psi_{k-1}$. Also $\langle\psi_{k}, \psi_{k}\rangle = \langle K^{*}\psi_{k-1}, \psi_{k}\rangle = \langle\psi_{k-1}, K\psi_{k}\rangle = k(N - k + 1)\langle\psi_{k-1}, \psi_{k-1}\rangle$, positive for $1 \le k \le N$, and $\langle P, P\rangle > 0$. Iterating, $K^{m}\psi_{k} = c_{k,m}\psi_{k-m}$ with $c_{k,m} = \prod_{i=0}^{m-1}(k - i)(N - k + i + 1) = (k)_{m}(N - k + 1)^{(m)}$ (zero for $m > k$), and $\langle\psi_{k}, \psi_{k}\rangle = c_{k,m}\langle\psi_{k-m}, \psi_{k-m}\rangle$ for $m \le k$. So $\omega_{k}((B^{*})^{m}B^{m}) = N^{-m}\langle K^{m}\psi_{k}, K^{m}\psi_{k}\rangle/\langle\psi_{k}, \psi_{k}\rangle = N^{-m}c_{k,m}^{2}/c_{k,m} = N^{-m}c_{k,m}$ for $m \le k$, and $0$ for $m > k$. The script checks the ladder relations, the norms and these moments for $N = 1, 2, 3$, all $k \le N$ and $m \le N + 1$, and $\omega_{k}(B) = \omega_{k}(B^{2}) = 0$, after checking that the blades are orthonormal for $N = 1, 2$.

\emph{(ii).} Write $f_{i} = b_{i}^{*}$ (it flips block $i$). Since the $f_{i}$ commute and $f_{i}^{2} = 0$, $(K^{*})^{k} = k!\sum_{|A| = k}\prod_{i \in A}f_{i}$, so $\psi_{k} = k!\sum_{|A|=k}\phi_{A}$ with $\phi_{A} = \prod_{i\in A}f_{i}P$. The $\phi_{A}$ are pairwise orthogonal (they are eigenvectors of the $n_{u_{i}}$ with different eigenvalues) and have equal norms: $f_{i}^{*}f_{i} = b_{i}b_{i}^{*} = n_{l_{i}}(1 - n_{u_{i}})$ by the relations, which acts as $1$ on a vector in which block $i$ is polarised, so $\langle\phi_{A}, \phi_{A}\rangle = \langle P, P\rangle$ by induction on $|A|$. Hence $\omega_{k}$ is the uniform average over the $\binom{N}{k}$ sets $A$ in its diagonal part: $\omega_{k}(P_{m})$ is the fraction of $k$-sets avoiding the first $m$ blocks, $\binom{N - m}{k}/\binom{N}{k} = \prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(1 - m/(N - i))$; when $km/(N - k + 1) < 1$ each factor is at least $1 - m/(N - k + 1) \ge 0$ and $(1 - x)^{k} \ge 1 - kx$ gives $\omega_{k}(P_{m}) \ge 1 - \varepsilon_{m}$, and otherwise the bound is trivial. Likewise $\omega_{k}(n_{u_{i}}) = \binom{N-1}{k-1}/\binom{N}{k} = k/N$, $\omega_{k}(n_{u_{i}}n_{u_{j}}) = \binom{N-2}{k-2}/\binom{N}{k} = k(k - 1)/(N(N - 1))$, and $b_{i}^{*}b_{j}\phi_{A} = \phi_{A \setminus\{j\} \cup \{i\}}$ when $j \in A$, $i \notin A$ (and $0$ otherwise, the even factors commuting and $b_{j}f_{j}$ acting as $1$ on the polarised block), so $\omega_{k}(b_{i}^{*}b_{j}) = \binom{N-2}{k-1}/\binom{N}{k} = k(N - k)/(N(N - 1))$. \emph{Minimality.} For one plane, $n e n = n(v + w)n = 0$, $n f n = n(v - w)n = 0$ and $n(ef)n = n(1 - 2n)n = -n$ (as $ef = 1 - 2n$), and likewise with $1 - n$; a blade of the first $m$ blocks is, up to sign, a product of one factor per plane, and each idempotent factor of $P_{m}$ commutes with the factors of the other planes (it is even), so $P_{m}XP_{m} = \lambda(X)P_{m}$ for every $X$ there, with $\lambda(X) = \langle P_{m}X\rangle_{0}/\langle P_{m}\rangle_{0} = \omega_{0}(X)$. \emph{The bound.} With $\psi = \psi_{k}/\|\psi_{k}\|$ and $\varepsilon = 1 - \omega_{k}(P_{m}) \le \varepsilon_{m}$, $X - P_{m}XP_{m} = (1 - P_{m})X + P_{m}X(1 - P_{m})$, and by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality $|\langle\psi, (1 - P_{m})X\psi\rangle| \le \|(1 - P_{m})\psi\|\,\|X\psi\| \le \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\|X\|$, and the same for the second term; and $|\omega_{k}(P_{m}XP_{m}) - \omega_{0}(X)| = |\omega_{0}(X)|\varepsilon \le \varepsilon\|X\|$. The script checks the marginals, the off-diagonal moments $\omega_{k}((K^{*})^{a}K^{c}) = 0$ for $a \ne c \le 2$, and the pair values for $N = 1, 2, 3$, and minimality on all sixteen blades of one block.

\emph{(iii).} At fixed $k$, $\omega_{k}((B^{*})^{a}B^{c}) = \delta_{ac}(k)_{a}(N - k + 1)^{(a)}/N^{a} \to \delta_{ac}(k)_{a}$, since $(N - k + 1)^{(a)}/N^{a} \to 1$. In the $k$-boson number state $|k\rangle$ of a canonical mode, $a^{m}|k\rangle = \sqrt{(k)_{m}}\,|k - m\rangle$, so $\langle k|(a^{*})^{m}a^{m}|k\rangle = (k)_{m}$ and off-diagonal moments vanish: the limits are these. A quasi-free state of one mode with $\langle a\rangle = \langle a^{2}\rangle = 0$ assigns to $(a^{*})^{m}a^{m}$ the sum over pairings of each $a^{*}$ with an $a$ (pairings of two $a^{*}$ or two $a$ give $\langle a^{2}\rangle = 0$ or its adjoint), $m!$ pairings each contributing $x^{m}$. At $m = 2$, $k(k - 1) = 2k^{2}$ only for $k = 0$ or $k = -1$; at $m = k + 1$, $(k)_{k+1} = 0 < (k + 1)!\,k^{k+1}$. For $k = 0$ all moments with $a + c > 0$ vanish, which is the vacuum, quasi-free with $x = 0$. The script checks these integer facts for $k = 1, \dots, 40$.

\emph{(iv).} By (ii), for each fixed $k$ the marginals of $\omega_{k}$ on any fixed set of blocks tend in norm to those of $\omega_{0}$ (the bound is uniform over the $m$ blocks used, and any finite set of blocks can be moved to the first $m$ by the permutation symmetry of $\psi_{k}$). By (iii) the limits of $\omega_{k}((B^{*})^{k}B^{k})$ are $k!$, pairwise different. So no rule that assigns a limit fluctuation state to a local limit state can hold for these sequences, and the hypothesis at each $N$ of the known central limit theorems (product structure, under which $\omega_{0}$ gives the vacuum, or a uniform clustering bound) cannot be replaced by local convergence; its necessity is not claimed.
