synthesis.unit-i4-keeps-its-three-proper.formal:
Let $\Cl(1, D-1)$ have orthogonal generators $g_0, \ldots, g_{D-1}$ with $Q(g_0) = 1$ and $Q(g_a) = -1$ for $a \ge 1$, $I_D = g_0g_1\cdots g_{D-1}$ and $I_4 = g_0g_1g_2g_3$, and write $\hat{x}$ for the grade involution. For $D = 4$ the unit $I_4$ of Definition \claimref{obj.field-theory.single-algebra-field} has three properties: (a) $I_4^2 = -1$; (b) $I_4$ commutes with every bivector, so left multiplication by it commutes with every rotor; (c) $I_4$ anticommutes with every vector, so $I_4x = \hat{x}I_4$ for all $x$ and left and right multiplication by $I_4$ agree on even elements.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For $D \ge 3$ the elements of $\Cl(1, D-1)$ commuting with every bivector are exactly $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_D\}$.
\item[(ii)] In the signature $(1, D-1)$, $I_D^2 = (-1)^{D(D-1)/2 + D - 1}$, which is $-1$ exactly when $D \equiv 0$ or $3 \pmod 4$. (In the signature $(D-1, 1)$ it is $-1$ exactly when $D \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$.)
\item[(iii)] An element of $\Cl(1, D-1)$ with (a), (b) and (c) exists if and only if $D \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, and it is then $\pm I_D$; the same holds in $\Cl(D-1, 1)$. In the signature $(1, D-1)$, for $D = 5, 6$ no element has (a) and (b), and for $D = 7$ the only elements with (a) and (b), $\pm I_7$, commute with every vector. (In the signature $(D-1, 1)$, $\pm I_5$ have (a) and (b) and fail only (c).)
\item[(iv)] For $D > 4$, $I_4$ still has (a), anticommutes with $g_0, \ldots, g_3$, commutes with $g_4, \ldots, g_{D-1}$, and anticommutes with exactly the $4(D-4)$ mixed bivector blades $g_{\mu}g_{a}$ ($\mu \le 3 < a$), commuting with the others: left multiplication by $I_4$ does not commute with the rotors of the mixed planes.
\item[(v)] Right multiplication by $I_4$ squares to $-1$ and commutes with every left multiplication, rotors and vectors included. On an even blade, left and right multiplication by $I_4$ agree when the blade has an even number of indices in $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ and are opposite otherwise; for $D > 4$ they differ on $2^{D-2}$ of the $2^{D-1}$ even blades.
\item[(vi)] On the ground with one adjoined plane of Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-tower-limit}, $I_4$ commutes with the plane's null generators $v$, $w$ and anticommutes with every $g_{\mu}v$ and $g_{\mu}w$.
\end{enumerate}
Clauses (i) to (iii) are standard classification facts about the centre and the pseudoscalar of a Clifford algebra (\claimref{primer.sign}, \claimref{std-algebra.pseudoscalar-commutation}), read here as constraints on the unit. So no algebra $\Cl(1, D-1)$ with $4 < D < 8$ keeps all three properties of the unit, and a continuation through the integer-dimensional algebras must give up (b), as the four-dimensional $I_4$ of (iv) does, or (c), as the right unit of (v) does.
synthesis.unit-i4-keeps-its-three-proper.technical:
In the spacetime algebra the series' imaginary unit $I_4$ squares to $-1$, commutes with every bivector, so with the Lorentz rotors acting on the left, and anticommutes with every vector, so that left and right multiplication by it agree on even field values. Dimensional regularisation continues the Clifford algebra in the dimension; in the integer-dimensional algebras $\Cl(1, D-1)$ the elements commuting with all bivectors are $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_D\}$, and $I_D^2 = (-1)^{D(D-1)/2 + D - 1}$ is $-1$ only for $D \equiv 0, 3 \pmod 4$ (standard classification facts, read here as constraints on the unit). So the three properties hold together exactly when $D \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, with $\pm I_D$ the only such elements, in this signature and in the mostly-plus one; in the series' signature $(1, D-1)$, for $D = 5, 6$ no element even squares to $-1$ and commutes with the rotors, while in the signature $(D-1, 1)$ the five-dimensional $\pm I_5$ do and fail only the anticommutation with vectors.

The two available continuations each give up one property. The four-dimensional $I_4$ inside $\Cl(1, D-1)$ squares to $-1$, anticommutes with the four original generators and commutes with the extra ones, which is the $\gamma_5$ of the Breitenlohner-Maison and 't Hooft-Veltman scheme; it anticommutes with the $4(D-4)$ mixed bivectors, so it is not covariant under rotations in the mixed planes. Right multiplication by $I_4$ commutes with every left action, so it is covariant, but it no longer anticommutes with vectors: it disagrees with left multiplication exactly on the even blades with an odd number of four-dimensional indices, $2^{D-2}$ of the $2^{D-1}$ even blades for $D > 4$. The tower's adjoined plane generators commute with $I_4$, as the extra generators of that scheme do. These statements concern the integer-dimensional algebras; for the formal non-integer dimension of the scheme the same split is the known $\gamma_5$ obstruction.
synthesis.unit-i4-keeps-its-three-proper.lay: In this framework the imaginary number of quantum theory is the four-dimensional volume element of the spacetime algebra. The most common way of taming the infinities of quantum field theory pretends that spacetime has a slightly different number of dimensions. In the algebras of whole-number dimensions near four, this result shows that the volume element loses one of its three defining properties: it either stops respecting rotations that mix the old and new directions, or stops behaving oppositely to directions as it does in four dimensions. All three properties return only in dimensions four, eight, twelve and so on. The same split is the known difficulty with the chirality matrix in that method, here met by the imaginary unit itself.

proofs.main:
For a basis blade $e_A = g_{a_1}\cdots g_{a_k}$ ($a_1 < \cdots < a_k$) and a generator $g_b$, $g_be_A = (-1)^{k}e_Ag_b$ if $b \notin A$ and $g_be_A = (-1)^{k-1}e_Ag_b$ if $b \in A$, since $g_b$ anticommutes with every other generator and commutes with itself.

(i) For a bivector blade $g_bg_c$ ($b \ne c$) the two signs multiply: $g_bg_c$ commutes with $e_A$ when $b$, $c$ are both in $A$ or both outside it, and anticommutes when exactly one is in $A$. So conjugation by $g_bg_c$ sends each blade to $\pm$ itself, and an element commutes with $g_bg_c$ if and only if each of its blade components does. A blade $e_A$ with $A$ neither empty nor everything has some $b \in A$ and $c \notin A$ (for $D \ge 2$), and then $g_bg_c$ anticommutes with it. The blades $1$ and $I_D$ commute with every bivector blade, and the bivectors are spanned by the bivector blades. So the commutant is $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_D\}$. The check enumerates every blade for $D = 3, \ldots, 8$ (computed, complete for those $D$).

Clauses (i) to (iii) are standard facts of the classification of real Clifford algebras (the centre and the square of the pseudoscalar; stored as \claimref{primer.sign} and \claimref{std-algebra.pseudoscalar-commutation}; for example Lounesto, \emph{Clifford Algebras and Spinors}, or Porteous); they are proved here in the form used.

(ii) Reversing the product, $I_D\widetilde{I_D} = \prod_a Q(g_a) = (-1)^{D-1}$ and $\widetilde{I_D} = (-1)^{D(D-1)/2}I_D$, so $I_D^2 = (-1)^{D(D-1)/2 + D - 1}$. For $D = 4k, 4k+1, 4k+2, 4k+3$ the exponent's parity is odd, even, even, odd (from $2k(4k-1) + 4k - 1$, $2k(4k+1) + 4k$, $(2k+1)(4k+1) + 4k + 1$, $(4k+3)(2k+1) + 4k + 2$), so $I_D^2 = -1$ exactly for $D \equiv 0, 3 \pmod 4$. The check compares the product with the formula for $D = 2, \ldots, 12$. In the signature $(D-1, 1)$ the product of the squares is $-1$ for every $D$, so $I_D^2 = (-1)^{D(D-1)/2 + 1}$, which is $-1$ exactly for $D \equiv 0, 1 \pmod 4$; the check computes this for $D = 2, \ldots, 12$. The clauses for $D = 5, 6, 7$ therefore depend on the signature: in $\Cl(4, 1)$, $I_5^2 = -1$ and $\pm I_5$ have (a) and (b).

(iii) By (i) an element with (b) is $J = \alpha + \beta I_D$ with real $\alpha$, $\beta$. (c) forces $\alpha = 0$ (a scalar commutes with vectors) and needs $I_D$ to anticommute with every vector, which by the first paragraph ($k = D$, $b \in A$) holds exactly when $D$ is even. Then (a) is $\beta^2I_D^2 = -1$, which needs $I_D^2 = -1$ and $\beta = \pm 1$. By (ii), $D$ even with $I_D^2 = -1$ is $D \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, in either signature (for even $D$ the two formulas agree). For $D = 5, 6$, $I_D^2 = 1$ and $(\alpha + \beta I_D)^2 = \alpha^2 + \beta^2 + 2\alpha\beta I_D \ne -1$ for real $\alpha$, $\beta$, so no element has (a) and (b). For $D = 7$, $(\alpha + \beta I_7)^2 = -1$ forces $\alpha = 0$, $\beta = \pm 1$, and $I_7$, of odd grade in odd dimension, commutes with every generator.

(iv) Moving $g_a$ past the four factors of $I_4$ gives the sign $(-1)^{3}$ for $a \le 3$ (one factor is $g_a$ itself) and $(-1)^{4}$ for $a \ge 4$. A bivector blade $g_bg_c$ picks up the product of its two signs, $-1$ exactly when one index is at most $3$ and the other at least $4$: $4(D-4)$ blades. $I_4^2 = -1$ is (ii) at $D = 4$, unchanged by the extra generators. A rotor $\exp(\theta g_{\mu}g_a/2)$ in a mixed plane then satisfies $I_4\exp(\theta g_{\mu}g_a/2) = \exp(-\theta g_{\mu}g_a/2)I_4$; the check uses the rational rotor $\tfrac35 + \tfrac45 g_1g_4$.

(v) $(L_y \circ R_{I_4})(x) = y(xI_4) = (yx)I_4 = (R_{I_4} \circ L_y)(x)$ by associativity, and $R_{I_4}^2 = R_{I_4^2} = -1$. By (iv), $I_4e_A = (-1)^{k_4}e_AI_4$ with $k_4$ the number of indices of $A$ in $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$. An even blade has $k_4 + k_{\mathrm{extra}}$ even; those with $k_4$ odd number $\sum_{k_4\ \mathrm{odd}}\binom{4}{k_4}\cdot\sum_{m\ \mathrm{odd}}\binom{D-4}{m} = 8\cdot 2^{D-5} = 2^{D-2}$ for $D > 4$, and none for $D = 4$. The check enumerates every even blade for $D = 4, \ldots, 7$ and confirms the right unit commutes with a mixed rotor acting on the left while the left unit does not.

(vi) By Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-tower-limit} an adjoined plane gives null $v$, $w$ with $vw + wv = 1$ over the ground; modelled as $v = \tfrac12(g_4 + g_5)$, $w = \tfrac12(g_4 - g_5)$ with $Q(g_4) = 1$, $Q(g_5) = -1$, both orthogonal to the ground. By (iv) $I_4$ commutes with $g_4$ and $g_5$, hence with $v$ and $w$, and anticommutes with $g_{\mu}v$ and $g_{\mu}w$. This is the sense in which the definition's unit commutes with every mode.

The closing sentence follows from (iii) to (v); it concerns continuation through the integer-dimensional algebras $\Cl(1, D-1)$ only. \emph{Argued, not proved:} dimensional regularisation ('t Hooft and Veltman; Breitenlohner and Maison; Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-dimensional-regularisation-and-the-bmhv-gamma5}, whose split of $\gamma_5$ is $\{\gamma_5, \bar{\gamma}^{\mu}\} = 0$, $[\gamma_5, \hat{\gamma}^{\mu}] = 0$) is a formal continuation to non-integer $D$, where the same split is the known $\gamma_5$ obstruction; by (ii) the properties have period four in $D$, so none of the algebraic continuations interpolates all three. For vector-like couplings the right unit of (v) behaves as the standard scheme's external $i$, so one-loop quantum electrodynamics can be dimensionally regularised with no input beyond the standard scheme; the one-loop result \claimref{synthesis.one-loop-qed-in-the-spacetime-algebra}, regularised by Pauli-Villars, likewise needs the unit outside the Clifford product on massive lines, which is this right unit. For chiral couplings the series uses (c) to read one chirality as complex-linear and the other as conjugated (Proposition \claimref{field-theory.second-quantisation}); on the mixed blades of (v) that identification fails exactly as $\gamma_5$'s anticommutation fails in the scheme, so chiral loops inherit its finite symmetry-restoring counterterms. Regulators that stay in four dimensions (Pauli-Villars, the lattice, the Epstein-Glaser extension of distributions, and the tower's floors, a sharp mode cut-off that is not Lorentz covariant, \claimref{synthesis.floor-regulator-keeps-the-charge-and-the-central-term-below-the-cut-off}) need no continuation of the unit. Transport-absent.

synthesis.vacuum-polarisation-kernel-on-.formal:
Units $\hbar = c = 1$. Scope: one loop; the trace form of the Dirac Hadamard parametrix, not a state's current two-point function; a gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.hadamard-dirac-states-scale-to-the-flat-massless-vacuum-at-every-point-of-a-gravitational-field} with vanishing torsion; the normal coordinates of the point $x'$, with the vector index at $x$ compared by transport along the geodesic. In another smooth frame or chart the full curvature operator appears at degree four through the change of frame. Vanishing torsion is used in two ways. First, through the protraction identity $\partial_{a}\wedge\mathcal{R}(a\wedge b) = 0$ of the curvature operator $\mathcal{R}(B) = -R(\hb(B))$ of Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}, clause (c) ($R$ the covariant field strength of $\Omega$), and the symmetry of the Ricci map: both hold on a torsion-free field by Theorem \claimref{synthesis.protraction-identity-of-the-curvature-operator-from-vanishing-torsion}(iii) (the first Bianchi identity). Second, directly: the connection of the Dirac operator is then the spin connection of the derived metric (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-hadamard-parametrix-of-the-squared-dirac-operator-leads-with-van-vleck-root-times-spin-transport}(b)). The identity alone does not give vanishing torsion (the converse fails, by the same theorem), so the hypothesis on the field is vanishing torsion, not the identity. On a geodesically convex neighbourhood let $\sigma$ be the Synge function, $\Delta$ the Van Vleck determinant, $R(x, x')$ the transport rotor from $x'$ to $x$ ($R(x', x) = \rev{R}$; the rotor is written $R(x, x')$ or $R$ after a vector, the field strength never without its bivector argument), $U = \Delta^{1/2}R$, $s = D_{x}\sigma$ the physical tangent at $x$ of the geodesic from $x'$, so $Q(s) = 2\sigma$, and $s' = D_{x'}\sigma = -\rev{R}sR$. Let $G(x, x') = (D_{x} + m)\,(U/\sigma + V\log\sigma)$ be the parametrix of the cited theorem, clause (i), stripped of its normalising constant, its unit and its boundary prescription, and for a vector $a$ at $x$ and a vector $b$ at $x'$ let
\[
\Pi(a, b; x, x') = \langle a\,G(x, x')\,b\,G(x', x)\rangle_{0}, \qquad \hat b = R\,b\,\rev{R}, \qquad \Pi^{0} = -\frac{2\,(a\cdot s)(\hat b\cdot s) - (a\cdot\hat b)\,Q(s)}{\sigma^{4}} .
\]
Off the diagonal, with the Feynman prescription $\sigma + I_{4}0$ in both factors, this is the form of the time-ordered kernel, which is the one with an extension problem; with the two factors as boundary values from the same side it is the Wightman product, which is a distribution across the diagonal and needs no extension. On the flat field at $m = 0$, $\Pi = \Pi^{0}$ is, up to a constant factor and the Wick rotation used there, the kernel of clause (ii) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.one-loop-vacuum-polarisation-extends-without-a-regulator-and-ward-preserving-extensions-differ-only-by-the-renormalisation-constants}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The rotors cancel from the leading kernel; proved.)} The leading parts $-\Delta^{1/2}sR/\sigma^{2}$ of $G(x, x')$ and $-\Delta^{1/2}s'\rev{R}/\sigma^{2}$ of $G(x', x)$ give exactly $\Delta(x, x')\,\Pi^{0}$, for every field strength: $\langle a\,(sR)\,b\,(s'\rev{R})\rangle_{0} = -\langle a\,s\,\hat b\,s\rangle_{0}$, the flat trace of the stored result in the vector $s$ with the vector at $x'$ transported to $x$. No rotor remains, and $\Pi^{0}$ carries no field strength. The cross terms of the leading part with the mass term $mU/\sigma$ are scalar parts of odd elements and vanish identically. The mass-mass trace is $\langle a\,R\,b\,\rev{R}\rangle_{0} = a\cdot\hat b$; the sign of the term $m^{2}\Delta\,(a\cdot\hat b)/\sigma^{2}$ relative to the leading one is not fixed by the stripped trace form (it depends on the unit that has been dropped).
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The derivative of the transport rotor is Ricci; proved given the Taylor data of the cited theorem, clause (ii), which are labelled computed there; the protraction identity is Theorem \claimref{synthesis.protraction-identity-of-the-curvature-operator-from-vanishing-torsion}(iii).)} To first order in the separation $\xi$, in the store's convention for $\mathcal{R}$,
\[
a\cdot D_{x}R = +\tfrac14\,\mathcal{R}(a\wedge\xi)\,R, \qquad D_{x}R = \tfrac14\,\gamma^{\mu}\mathcal{R}(e_{\mu}\wedge\xi)\,R = +\tfrac14\,\mathcal{R}(\xi)\,R,
\]
$\mathcal{R}(\xi) = \partial_{a}\cdot\mathcal{R}(a\wedge\xi)$ the Ricci vector: the trivector part vanishes by the protraction identity, and a curvature operator of Weyl type contributes nothing. With $\Delta^{1/2} = 1 - \tfrac{1}{12}\,\xi\cdot\mathcal{R}(\xi)$ of the cited theorem, whose gradient is $-\tfrac16\mathcal{R}(\xi)$,
\[
D_{x}U = +\tfrac{1}{12}\,\mathcal{R}(\xi)\,R + O(\xi^{2}) .
\]
On the de Sitter operator $\mathcal{R}(B) = \tfrac{\Lambda}{3}B$ this is $\tfrac{\Lambda}{12}\,\xi R$. On a vacuum field ($\mathcal{R}(\xi) = 0$ for all $\xi$), $D_{x}U = O(\xi^{2})$ whatever the Weyl part.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Degrees; argued.)} Given the scaling-degree rules (SD1) to (SD4), which are clause (vi) of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extension-theorem-and-ward-preserving-time-ordered-products} (the higher-order Hadamard form is (SD4)), and, for the one coefficient at degree $4$ that it concerns and for nothing else, the coincidence value of $V$ from the first Hadamard transport equation, a hypothesis that is not stored: in the normal coordinates of $x'$ and the transported frame, $\Pi$ has scaling degree $6$ with leading part $\Pi^{0}$; nothing at degree $5$; at degree $4$ terms whose coefficients are $m^{2}$, the Ricci vector map (through $D_{x}U$ and through $(\Delta - 1)\Pi^{0}$) and the coincidence value of $V$ (a scalar, by the first transport equation and (ii)); and the Weyl part of the curvature operator only from degree $3$ down: at degree $3$ through derivatives of the curvature operator, and at degree $2$ through the Van Vleck determinant, $\Delta = 1 + \tfrac{1}{180}\operatorname{tr}K_{\xi}^{2} + O(\xi^{5})$ on a vacuum field, $K_{\xi}(a) = \mathcal{R}(a\wedge\xi)\cdot\xi$ the tidal map (cited), which is quadratic in the Weyl part and not zero.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The extension; argued, given (iii) and Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extension-theorem-and-ward-preserving-time-ordered-products}(ii).)} For each fixed $x'$ the time-ordered kernel, as a distribution in the relative normal coordinate off the origin, has degree of divergence $\omega = 6 - 4 = 2$, the flat value, whatever the Weyl part; the stored flat extension read in these coordinates extends $\Pi^{0}$ with the stored logarithmic coefficient; and two extensions of the same degree differ by the $15$ derivatives of $\delta$ of order at most $2$ per pair of indices. On the field these are $15$ coefficient functions of $x'$ per index pair, and nothing here constrains their dependence on $x'$: the joint extension across the diagonal of $M \times M$ is not treated. Even the Ward-preserving freedom on a fixed field is a function space, since $\partial_{\mu}(c(x)F^{\mu\nu})$ is conserved for every smooth $c$. The reduction of this freedom uses local covariance with scaling, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-local-covariance-with-scaling-of-time-ordered-products}(iii): for extensions that are local and covariant with almost homogeneous scaling, the coefficient of a derivative of $\delta$ of order $j$ is a polynomial with constant coefficients in the curvature operator, its covariant derivatives and the mass, of dimension $2 - j$, a finite list of constants in place of functions of $x'$. By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.curved-field-vacuum-polarisation-freedom-is-five-local-covariant-constants-of-which-one-is-transverse}(i) to (iii), given that Fact and the degree of divergence $2$ argued here, the finite list is five constants, and two extensions that are local and covariant with almost homogeneous scaling and both transverse differ by the single constant $Z_{3}$, which multiplies $D\cdot(D\wedge A)$. The existence of a transverse local covariant extension is not proved: the Ward identity on a gravitational field is not part of that Fact and is not derived in the store. Neither the degree of divergence nor this count uses the first Hadamard transport equation, which enters only one coefficient at degree $4$ in (iii). The clause stays argued as a whole: the degrees rest on (iii), the Fact is cited from memory and sourced for scalar fields, and the kernel is the trace form of the parametrix. This supports the first half of clause (v) of the cited vacuum-polarisation theorem; it does not prove it.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.vacuum-polarisation-kernel-on-.technical: The stored bulk Hadamard form writes the Dirac two-point function as a first-order operator applied to $U/\sigma + V\log\sigma$, with $U$ the Van Vleck root times the spinor transport rotor. In the vacuum-polarisation trace the leading term at $x$ carries the rotor and the leading term at $x'$ its reverse, and the tangent of the geodesic at $x'$ is the transported tangent at $x$ with the sign reversed; so the rotors cancel in pairs and the trace is the flat one in the vector $D\sigma$, with one vector index transported, times the Van Vleck determinant. This part is exact algebra. The curvature can then enter only through the Van Vleck determinant, the derivative of $U$ and the logarithmic coefficient. In the gauge $\Omega(a)(x_{0} + z) = -\tfrac12\mathcal{R}(z\wedge a)$, whose field strength is $-\mathcal{R}$ as the store's sign convention requires, the derivative of the transport rotor at first order is $+\tfrac14$ of the curvature operator on the plane of the direction and the separation; contracted with the frame vectors it gives the Ricci vector and a trivector that vanishes by the protraction identity, a stored theorem for torsion-free fields. With the gradient $-\tfrac16$ of the Van Vleck root the first-order part of $D_{x}U$ is $+\tfrac1{12}$ of the Ricci vector, checked against the de Sitter operator. The statements on scaling degrees and on the extension are argued: they rest on scaling-degree rules and a higher-order Hadamard form that the store holds as an imported Fact, one coefficient at degree four rests in addition on the first Hadamard transport equation, which the store does not hold, and they concern the time-ordered kernel for a fixed point $x'$ in its normal coordinates. In that reading the kernel has the flat degree six, no degree five, mass and Ricci coefficients at degree four, and the Weyl part from degree three down, at degree two through the Van Vleck determinant. The freedom of the extension at each point is the flat list of fifteen local terms per index pair, but with coefficients that are functions of the point; local covariance with scaling, an imported Fact, reduces them to a finite list of constants, five by a later stored result, and two transverse local covariant extensions then differ by the flat constant alone; that a transverse local covariant extension exists is not proved, since the Ward identity on the field is not derived.
synthesis.vacuum-polarisation-kernel-on-.lay: When a photon travels it can briefly turn into an electron and positron pair, and the mathematics of this effect, called vacuum polarisation, has an infinite part that must be fixed by a rule. In flat space the collection already contains a rule that needs no artificial cut-off. It had only argued that the same works where space is curved, and this result takes two exact steps towards that, without completing it. The setting is the standard leading approximation in curved space, for a gravitational field without the twisting of space that intrinsic spin would source. First, the most singular part of the expression is exactly the flat one written along the straight path between the two points, times one known smooth factor: all the rotation picked up along the path cancels. Second, the first correction to the next ingredient involves only the part of the curvature that is tied to matter, with a definite coefficient of one twelfth; the tidal part, which is all there is in empty space around a star or black hole, drops out at that order. From these it is argued, not proved, that the strength of the infinity is the same as in flat space and that the tidal curvature appears only in milder terms. The list of quantities left free by the rule is the same as in flat space at each point, but in curved space each of them may vary from point to point, and reducing them needs a further principle, which the collection holds as an imported fact. Given that principle, a later result of the collection shows that two rules which both conserve charge differ only by the single constant of flat space; whether a charge-conserving rule exists in curved space is not proved. The result does not show that charge conservation can be kept in curved space. The second step holds given the stored expansion data and one standard identity of curvature, which the collection now derives for gravity without twisting.

proofs.main:
\begin{proof}
Throughout, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.hadamard-dirac-states-scale-to-the-flat-massless-vacuum-at-every-point-of-a-gravitational-field} is cited as (H): its clause (i) gives the form $U/\sigma + V\log\sigma$ with $U = \Delta^{1/2}R$ and $D_{x}\sigma = \hb^{-1}(\dot\gamma(1))$, the physical tangent at $x$ of the geodesic $\gamma$ from $x'$ to $x$, and its clause (ii) the Taylor data (labelled computed there). The form of the parametrix is Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-hadamard-parametrix-of-the-squared-dirac-operator-leads-with-van-vleck-root-times-spin-transport}. The curvature operator is $\mathcal{R}(B) = -R(\hb(B))$, $R(a\wedge b) = a\cdot\nabla\Omega(b) - b\cdot\nabla\Omega(a) + \Omega(a)\times\Omega(b)$ the covariant field strength (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}(c)); (H)(ii) is written with $\mathcal{R}$.

\emph{(i).} $D_{x}(U/\sigma) = (D_{x}\sigma^{-1})U + \sigma^{-1}D_{x}U = -sU/\sigma^{2} + (D_{x}U)/\sigma$, so the leading part of $G(x, x')$ is $-\Delta^{1/2}sR/\sigma^{2}$. Exchanging the points reverses the geodesic: $\sigma$ and $\Delta$ are symmetric, the rotor becomes its reverse, and $D_{x'}\sigma$ is the physical tangent at $x'$ of the reversed geodesic. The physical tangent is transported by the rotor, $\hb^{-1}(\dot\gamma(1)) = R\,\hb^{-1}(\dot\gamma(0))\,\rev{R}$ (the geodesic equation and $\dot R = -\tfrac12\Omega(\dot\gamma)R$), so $s' = -\rev{R}sR$ and $Q(s') = Q(s) = 2\sigma$. Then
\[
\langle a\,(sR)\,b\,(s'\rev{R})\rangle_{0} = -\langle a\,s\,R\,b\,\rev{R}\,s\,R\,\rev{R}\rangle_{0} = -\langle a\,s\,\hat b\,s\rangle_{0} = -\bigl(2(a\cdot s)(\hat b\cdot s) - (a\cdot\hat b)Q(s)\bigr),
\]
by $R\rev{R} = 1$ and the trace $\langle a\,x\,b\,x\rangle_{0} = 2(a\cdot x)(b\cdot x) - (a\cdot b)Q(x)$ of clause (i) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.one-loop-vacuum-polarisation-extends-without-a-regulator-and-ward-preserving-extensions-differ-only-by-the-renormalisation-constants}. Multiplying by $\Delta^{1/2}\Delta^{1/2}/\sigma^{4}$ gives $\Delta\,\Pi^{0}$. In $\langle a\,(sR)\,b\,\rev{R}\rangle_{0}$ and $\langle a\,R\,b\,(s'\rev{R})\rangle_{0}$ the argument is an odd element, with no scalar part; and $\langle a\,R\,b\,\rev{R}\rangle_{0} = a\cdot\hat b$. The parametrix of (H) carries the field theory's unit on one of the two terms $D_{x}$ and $m$; stripping it leaves the parities and the traces unchanged but not the relative sign of the mass-mass and leading terms, which involves the square of the unit. The check verifies the identities with four exact rotors (Cayley transforms of rational bivectors, simple and not), six vectors $s$ and sixteen pairs $a$, $b$, as a control, and that the identity fails if the tangent at $x'$ is not transported.

\emph{(ii).} The statement $a\cdot D_{x}R = \tfrac14\mathcal{R}(a\wedge\xi)R + O(\xi^{2})$ is covariant under rotation gauge transformations, so it may be verified in one gauge. Take $x_{0}$ with $\hb(x_{0}) = 1$, first derivatives of $\hb$ zero at $x_{0}$, and
\[
\Omega(a)(x_{0} + z) = -\tfrac12\,\mathcal{R}(z\wedge a) + O(z^{2}) .
\]
Its field strength at $x_{0}$ is $a\cdot\nabla\Omega(b) - b\cdot\nabla\Omega(a) = -\tfrac12\mathcal{R}(a\wedge b) + \tfrac12\mathcal{R}(b\wedge a) = -\mathcal{R}(a\wedge b)$, which is the stored relation between the field strength and the curvature operator; any $\Omega$ vanishing at $x_{0}$ with this field strength differs from it at first order by the symmetric part of $a\cdot\nabla\Omega(b)$, which a rotation gauge transformation quadratic in $z$ removes. By (H)(ii), with $x = x_{0} + ly$, $x' = x_{0} + ly'$, $d = y - y'$, $\bar y = \tfrac12(y + y')$: the transport rotor is $1 - \tfrac{l^{2}}{2}(\bar y\cdot\nabla)\Omega(d) + O(l^{3}) = 1 + \tfrac{l^{2}}{4}\mathcal{R}(\bar y\wedge d) + O(l^{3})$. The scaled derivative $l\,a\cdot D = a\cdot\partial_{y} + \tfrac{l}{2}\Omega(a)(x_{0} + ly) + O(l^{2})$ applied to it gives, at order $l^{2}$,
\[
\tfrac14\bigl[\tfrac12\mathcal{R}(a\wedge d) + \mathcal{R}(\bar y\wedge a)\bigr] - \tfrac14\mathcal{R}(y\wedge a) = \tfrac14\bigl[\tfrac12\mathcal{R}(a\wedge d) - \tfrac12\mathcal{R}(d\wedge a)\bigr] = \tfrac14\mathcal{R}(a\wedge d),
\]
using $y - \bar y = \tfrac12 d$; with $\xi = ld$ this is the claim, and it does not depend on $\bar y$. Contracting, $D_{x}R = \tfrac14\gamma^{\mu}\mathcal{R}(e_{\mu}\wedge\xi)R$, and $\gamma^{\mu}\mathcal{R}(e_{\mu}\wedge\xi) = \partial_{a}\cdot\mathcal{R}(a\wedge\xi) + \partial_{a}\wedge\mathcal{R}(a\wedge\xi) = \mathcal{R}(\xi)$ by the protraction identity, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.protraction-identity-of-the-curvature-operator-from-vanishing-torsion}(iii), the field being torsion-free. A curvature operator of Weyl type is by definition one with $\partial_{a}\mathcal{R}(a\wedge\xi) = 0$ for every $\xi$. By (H)(ii), $\Delta = 1 + \tfrac16\Ric^{\circ}(\xi, \xi) + O(\xi^{3})$ with $\Ric^{\circ}(\xi, \xi) = -\xi\cdot\mathcal{R}(\xi)$, so $\Delta^{1/2} = 1 - \tfrac1{12}\xi\cdot\mathcal{R}(\xi)$ and its gradient is $-\tfrac16\mathcal{R}(\xi)$ (the Ricci map is symmetric, by the same clause). Hence $D_{x}U = (-\tfrac16 + \tfrac14)\mathcal{R}(\xi)R + O(\xi^{2}) = \tfrac1{12}\mathcal{R}(\xi)R + O(\xi^{2})$. For $\mathcal{R}(B) = \tfrac{\Lambda}{3}B$, $\mathcal{R}(\xi) = \Lambda\xi$ and $D_{x}U = \tfrac{\Lambda}{12}\xi R$. The corrections from $\hb - 1 = O(z^{2})$ and from the deviation of the geodesic from the straight line are of relative order $l^{2}$ and enter $D_{x}R$ at order $\xi^{2}$. The check verifies that the gauge has field strength $-\mathcal{R}$ and that the gauge of the opposite sign does not, the derivative formula for a general linear $\mathcal{R}$ at exact points (the symmetric difference of a quadratic polynomial is its derivative), the contraction on operators of type D ($B \mapsto c(B + 3\sigma_{r}B\sigma_{r})$ with $\sigma_{r}^{2} = 1$), on sums of rotated copies and on operators $a\wedge b \mapsto \tfrac12(P(a)\wedge b + a\wedge P(b))$ of Ricci type, that a map violating the protraction identity leaves a trivector, and the de Sitter value, against which the opposite relative sign gives $-\tfrac{5}{12}\Lambda\xi$.

\emph{(iii) (argued).} Write $G(x, x') = -\Delta^{1/2}sR/\sigma^{2} + (D_{x}U)/\sigma + mU/\sigma + Vs/\sigma + (D_{x}V + mV)\log\sigma$. With the rules (SD1) to (SD4) of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extension-theorem-and-ward-preserving-time-ordered-products}(vi), in the normal coordinates of $x'$: the first term has degree $3$; $mU/\sigma$ degree $2$; $(D_{x}U)/\sigma$ degree at most $1$ by (ii), with coefficient the Ricci vector map; $Vs/\sigma$ degree at most $1$, with coefficient the coincidence value of $V$; the logarithmic term degree at most $0$. In the product: degree $6$ is $\Pi^{0}$; degree $5$ could only come from the leading part times the mass term, which vanishes by (i); degree $4$ comes from mass times mass, from the leading part times $(D_{x}U)/\sigma$, from the leading part times $Vs/\sigma$, and from $(\Delta - 1)\Pi^{0}$ with $\Delta - 1 = \tfrac16\Ric^{\circ}(\xi, \xi) + O(\xi^{3})$; the coincidence value of $V$ is by the first transport equation a multiple of the squared Dirac operator applied to $U$ at coincidence, where the second derivative of the rotor enters through the contraction of (ii) and the zero-order term is a scalar by the Lichnerowicz form. The Weyl part is absent from all of these coefficients. It enters at degree $3$ through first derivatives of the curvature operator in $D_{x}U$ and $\Delta$, and at degree $2$ through the term $\tfrac1{180}\operatorname{tr}K_{\xi}^{2}$ of $\Delta$ (cited), for which the check verifies on the Weyl-type samples that the tidal map has zero trace and nonzero trace of its square. This clause is argued because the transport equation is not stored and the rules are imported from memory; the higher-order Hadamard form needed for the remainder is the rule (SD4), the stored parametrix theorem giving only class $C^{1}$.

\emph{(iv) (argued).} By (i), for fixed $x'$, in the normal coordinates $\xi'$ of $x'$ ($s' = D_{x'}\sigma$ is minus the position vector of $x$ in them) and with $a$ transported to $x'$, $\Pi^{0} = -(2(\hat a\cdot s')(b\cdot s') - (\hat a\cdot b)Q(s'))/\sigma^{4}$ is the flat massless kernel, homogeneous of degree $-6$ in $\xi'$. Given (iii), Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-epstein-glaser-extension-theorem-and-ward-preserving-time-ordered-products}(ii) applied to the time-ordered kernel in $\xi'$ gives $\omega = 6 - 4 = 2$ and that two extensions of degree $6$ differ by $\sum_{|\alpha| \le 2}c_{\alpha}\partial^{\alpha}\delta$; there are $1 + 4 + 10 = 15$ multi-indices. The coefficients $c_{\alpha}$ are chosen for each $x'$ separately; as functions of $x'$ they are unconstrained by this argument. For any smooth $c$, $\partial_{\mu}(c\,F^{\mu\nu})$ has zero divergence, so the transverse local terms on a fixed field include $c(x)$ times the flat transverse term for every $c$. The stored flat extension of clause (ii) of the cited vacuum-polarisation theorem, read in $\xi'$, extends $\Pi^{0}$ with the stored logarithmic coefficient. By Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-local-covariance-with-scaling-of-time-ordered-products}(iii), if the extension is taken local and covariant with almost homogeneous scaling, then in the difference of two such extensions $c_{\alpha}$ with $|\alpha| = j$ is a polynomial with constant coefficients in the curvature operator, its covariant derivatives and the mass, of dimension $2 - j$: a constant at $j = 2$, nothing at $j = 1$ beyond terms that are total derivatives of those, and at $j = 0$ a combination of $m^{2}$ and the curvature operator. This removes the dependence on $x'$ as a free function. Theorem \claimref{synthesis.curved-field-vacuum-polarisation-freedom-is-five-local-covariant-constants-of-which-one-is-transverse}, which depends on this one and is cited here for what follows from it, not as a premise, counts the list (five constants) and shows that two such extensions that are both transverse differ by $c\,D\cdot(D\wedge A)$, the single constant $Z_{3}$. The existence of a transverse local covariant extension needs the Ward identity on the field, which is not derived here and is not part of that Fact. The first Hadamard transport equation is used in (iii) for one coefficient at degree $4$ only, and not in this clause.
\end{proof}

synthesis.weak-factor-rotor-lattice-stro.formal:
Represent the $\su(2)$ factor of $\su(2) \oplus \su(3) \oplus \uu(1)$ (Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}) by the bivectors $B_1 = g_2g_3$, $B_2 = g_3g_1$, $B_3 = g_1g_2$ of $\Cl(3,0)$, and its group by the rotors $U = u_0 + u_1B_1 + u_2B_2 + u_3B_3$, $U\widetilde{U} = 1$, with the normalised Haar measure $dU$ of the unit three-sphere. On a square lattice give each oriented link a rotor ($\widetilde{U}$ for the reversed link), let $U_p$ be the ordered product round a plaquette $p$, and take the weight $\prod_p\exp(\beta\langle U_p\rangle_0)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] The $B_k$ close under the commutator with $[B_1, B_2] = -2B_3$ and cyclically, and $\langle B_jB_k\rangle_0 = -\delta_{jk}$: a compact $\su(2)$.
\item[(ii)] $\int u^{\alpha}\,dU = \prod_k(\alpha_k - 1)!!\,/\,\prod_{j=0}^{|\alpha|/2 - 1}(4 + 2j)$ when every $\alpha_k$ is even, and $0$ otherwise.
\item[(iii)] For all $X$, $Y$ in the even subalgebra, $\int\langle XU\rangle_0\,dU = 0$ and $\int\langle XU\rangle_0\langle\widetilde{U}Y\rangle_0\,dU = \tfrac14\langle XY\rangle_0$.
\item[(iv)] Under $U_{xy} \mapsto g_xU_{xy}\widetilde{g_y}$ with rotors $g$ at the sites, $\langle U_C\rangle_0$ is invariant for every closed path $C$, so expectations of gauge-invariant observables need no gauge fixing.
\item[(v)] For an $R \times T$ rectangle $C$ of area $A = RT$, the term of order $\beta^{A}$ in $\langle\langle U_C\rangle_0\rangle$ from the $A$ plaquettes of the rectangle is $\int\langle U_C\rangle_0\prod_{p \subset C}\langle U_p\rangle_0 = (\tfrac14)^{A}$, so its leading strong-coupling coefficient is $(\beta/4)^{A}$, an area law.
\item[(vi)] For compact $U(1)$, with links $a + bB_3$, the gluing coefficient is $\tfrac12$ and the corresponding coefficient is $(\beta/2)^{A}$: the same area law.
\item[(vii)] For a bivector $B$ of $\Cl(3,0)$, $B^2 = -\|B\|^2$ with $\|B\|^2 = \sum_k b_k^2$, so $1 - \langle\exp B\rangle_0 = \tfrac12\|B\|^2 - \tfrac1{24}\|B\|^4 + \cdots$, the cosine series.
\end{enumerate}
So at finite lattice spacing the weak factor is a quantised gauge field with no gauge fixing and no ghosts, as in Wilson's formulation for every compact group; its strong-coupling area law is shared with compact $U(1)$, so it is not evidence of confinement in the continuum, whose existence needs asymptotic freedom.
synthesis.weak-factor-rotor-lattice-stro.technical: Wilson's lattice formulation quantises any compact gauge group without gauge fixing (a standard result): link variables live in the group, the measure is Haar, and only gauge-invariant loops are observed. In geometric algebra the weak factor $\su(2)$ of the derived gauge algebra is the bivector algebra of $\Cl(3,0)$, its group the rotors, and the trace the scalar part. The Haar moments on the unit three-sphere are rational, and the averages that matter are reproduced exactly by the 24 Hurwitz units. Two rules carry the strong-coupling expansion: every gauge-variant link average vanishes, and integrating a link shared by two loops glues them with a factor $\tfrac14$, $\int\langle XU\rangle_0\langle\widetilde{U}Y\rangle_0\,dU = \tfrac14\langle XY\rangle_0$. With the weight $\exp(\beta\langle U_p\rangle_0)$ per plaquette, every rectangular Wilson loop of area $A$ then has leading coefficient $(\beta/4)^{A}$, an area law. Compact $U(1)$ gives $(\beta/2)^{A}$, so the area law at strong coupling is not specific to the non-abelian factor and says nothing about confinement in the continuum; four-dimensional compact $U(1)$ is known to deconfine at weak coupling. The plaquette action expands as the cosine series $\tfrac12\|B\|^2 - \tfrac1{24}\|B\|^4 + \cdots$ of the plaquette bivector.
synthesis.weak-factor-rotor-lattice-stro.lay: The weak force's symmetry, which the series derives, can be put on a spacetime lattice in the form introduced by Wilson, with each link carrying a rotation of the spacetime algebra. As in Wilson's construction for any such symmetry, this quantises the field directly, with no need to fix a gauge. When the coupling is strong, at leading order of the strong-coupling expansion the energy of a pair of test charges grows with their separation, the signature of confinement. The same happens for the electromagnetic symmetry on the lattice, so this alone does not show that the weak or strong force confines in the real, continuum world; that question needs the behaviour of the coupling at short distances.

proofs.main:
(i) $B_1B_2 = g_2g_3g_3g_1 = g_2g_1 = -B_3$ and $B_2B_1 = B_3$, so $[B_1, B_2] = -2B_3$, and cyclically; $B_k^2 = -1$ and $B_jB_k$ is a bivector for $j \ne k$, so $\langle B_jB_k\rangle_0 = -\delta_{jk}$. A three-dimensional real Lie algebra with these brackets and a negative-definite invariant form is the compact $\su(2)$, the first summand of Theorem \claimref{standard-model.gauge-algebra-minimal-massive-composite}; its simply connected group is the rotor group $\{U : U\widetilde{U} = 1\}$, the unit three-sphere in the coordinates $u_k$. The check verifies the four-component product used for rotors against the Clifford product on all basis pairs.

(ii) The moments of the normalised measure on the unit sphere $S^{n-1}$ are $\prod_k(\alpha_k - 1)!!/\prod_{j < |\alpha|/2}(n + 2j)$ for even $\alpha$ (the Gaussian integral factorised into radial and angular parts), and vanish otherwise by the reflections $u_k \mapsto -u_k$, which preserve the measure; here $n = 4$. \emph{Computed:} the 24 Hurwitz units ($\pm1$, $\pm B_k$, $\tfrac12(\pm1 \pm B_1 \pm B_2 \pm B_3)$) average every monomial of degree at most $5$ to these values, and the eight units $\pm1$, $\pm B_k$ every monomial of degree at most $3$ (not degree $4$: $\tfrac14$ against $\tfrac18$ for $u_0^4$). Every integrand below has degree at most $2$ in each link variable, so either finite group may replace $dU$ link by link.

(iii) $\langle XU\rangle_0$ is linear in $u$, so its average vanishes by (ii). The gluing integrand is bilinear in $u$, and by (ii) $\int u_ku_l\,dU = \tfrac14\delta_{kl}$, so $\int\langle XU\rangle_0\langle\widetilde{U}Y\rangle_0\,dU = \tfrac14\sum_k\langle Xe_k\rangle_0\langle\widetilde{e_k}Y\rangle_0$ over the basis $e_k = 1, B_1, B_2, B_3$; since $\langle\widetilde{e_k}e_l\rangle_0 = \delta_{kl}$, the sum is the expansion of $\langle XY\rangle_0$ in this orthonormal basis. Both sides are bilinear in $(X, Y)$, so the check on all sixteen basis pairs, by the moments and by the Hurwitz average, is complete.

(iv) Along a closed path the inner factors $\widetilde{g_y}g_y = 1$ cancel, leaving $g_xU_C\widetilde{g_x}$, whose scalar part is $\langle U_C\rangle_0$. The Haar measure is invariant under $U \mapsto gU\widetilde{h}$, so for gauge-invariant observables the expectation is unchanged by fixing any tree of links to $1$, and no gauge-fixing term or ghost is needed (the Faddeev-Popov determinant of a tree gauge is $1$); this is Wilson's standard observation for every compact lattice gauge theory, reproduced here for rotor links. The check uses rational rotors at every site of a $2 \times 2$ patch and confirms that an open line is not invariant.

(v) Fix the tree consisting of every horizontal link and the vertical links on the left edge to $1$. Then the plaquette in column $x$, row $y$ is $U_p = V_{x+1,y}\widetilde{V_{x,y}}$ with $V_{0,y} = 1$ and $V_{x,y}$ the vertical link at $x$, and the boundary product is $\langle U_C\rangle_0 = \langle V_{R,0}V_{R,1}\cdots V_{R,T-1}\rangle_0$. In each row the map $(V_{1,y}, \ldots, V_{R,y}) \mapsto (P_{0,y}, \ldots, P_{R-1,y})$, $P_{x,y} = V_{x+1,y}\widetilde{V_{x,y}}$, is a bijection preserving the product Haar measure (left invariance, one factor at a time), and $V_{R,y} = P_{R-1,y}\cdots P_{0,y}$. So the integral is $\int\langle\prod P\rangle_0\prod_{p}\langle P_p\rangle_0$ over $A$ independent Haar rotors, the ordered product running over every plaquette. Integrating one $P_p$ by (iii) with $Y = 1$ (using $\langle P_p\rangle_0 = \langle\widetilde{P_p}\rangle_0$) gives $\tfrac14$ and removes $P_p$ from the product; after $A$ steps the value is $(\tfrac14)^{A}\langle1\rangle_0 = (\tfrac14)^{A}$. In the expansion of the weight, the $A$ distinct plaquettes of the rectangle each taken once come with coefficient $\beta^{A}$, so the leading strong-coupling coefficient is $(\beta/4)^{A}$. \emph{Computed:} $\tfrac14$ for $1 \times 1$ with all four links averaged over the eight units and in the tree gauge over the Hurwitz units, $\tfrac1{16}$ for $2 \times 1$ (Hurwitz) and $\tfrac1{256}$ for $2 \times 2$ (eight units). \emph{Imported} (Wilson 1974; Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(i)): on the infinite lattice no term of lower order contributes, since a plaquette set not covering every link of the loop leaves a link whose average vanishes by (iii), and the normalisation is $1 + O(\beta^2)$; so the string tension at strong coupling is $-\ln(\beta/4) + O(\beta)$. The area law beyond leading order, for all small $\beta$, is the theorem of Osterwalder and Seiler (1978; Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(ii)).

(vi) For $U = a + bB_3$ with $a^2 + b^2 = 1$ and the uniform measure, $\int a^2 = \int b^2 = \tfrac12$ and $\int ab = 0$, so the gluing coefficient on $\mathrm{span}\{1, B_3\}$ is $\tfrac12$, and the argument of (v) gives $(\tfrac12)^{A}$; the four units $\pm1$, $\pm B_3$ reproduce these moments, and the check computes $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac14$ for the $1 \times 1$ and $2 \times 1$ loops.

(vii) $B^2 = -\|B\|^2$ is a scalar, so $\langle B^{2m}\rangle_0 = (-\|B\|^2)^{m}$ and the odd powers have no scalar part; the check compares the series term by term to sixth order on two rational bivectors.

\emph{Argued, not proved here:} reflection positivity of the Wilson weight (Osterwalder and Seiler; Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(ii)) gives a Hilbert space and a transfer matrix, so (iv) and (v) describe a quantised gauge field at finite spacing; reading $U_p = \exp(B_p)$ with $B_p$ of order the lattice spacing squared times the field strength, (vii) gives the Yang-Mills density with $\beta = 4/g^2$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(i)). By (vi) the area law at strong coupling does not distinguish the non-abelian factor (compact $U(1)$ in four dimensions is proved to deconfine at weak coupling, by Guth (1980) and by Fr\"ohlich and Spencer (1982); Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-wilson-lattice-gauge-theory-and-strong-coupling-confinement}(iv)), so confinement in the continuum is not decided; the continuum limit at $\beta \to \infty$ needs asymptotic freedom, the sign of the one-loop coefficient, which the result \claimref{synthesis.one-loop-running-coefficients-from-spacetime-algebra-spin-traces}, computes conditionally on the derived content and the doublet count. The same construction with the $\su(3)$ factor uses its own Haar moments ($\tfrac13$ in place of $\tfrac14$ for the normalised trace), not computed here. Transport-absent.

synthesis.wedge-reflections-compose-to-t.formal:
Units and signature of the store; $\Cl(1,3)$, $I_{4} = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$; $W = \{x : x^{1} > |x^{0}|\}$, its boost bivector $B = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}$, edge null directions $n_{\pm} = \pm\gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1}$ and dual plane $D = I_{4}B = \gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$; $\mathrm{Ad}(V)x = VxV^{-1}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The wedge reflection; proved.)} $B^{2} = 1$, $B\tilde B = -1$, and $\mathrm{Ad}(B)$ is the reflection $j_{W}$: $(x^{0}, x^{1}) \mapsto (-x^{0}, -x^{1})$, $x^{2}$, $x^{3}$ fixed. Since $I_{4}D = -B$, $\mathrm{Ad}(B) = \mathrm{Ad}(I_{4}) \circ \mathrm{Ad}(D)$: the PT inversion after the turn by $\pi$ in the dual plane, which is the half modular period on values by \claimref{synthesis.modular-period-on-values-is-the-dual-plane-turn}(ii). This is the geometric part of the Bisognano-Wichmann conjugation, CPT composed with the turn by $\pi$ about the boost axis (Fact \claimref{angle.imported-theorems-deliver-their-hypotheses}).
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Edge translations; geometric part proved, modular action imported.)} $j_{W}$ reverses $n_{\pm}$ and fixes $\gamma_{2}$, $\gamma_{3}$; the wedge's boosts map $W$ into itself and dilate $n_{\pm}$ by reciprocal factors ($(5 + 4B)/3$: $n_{+} \mapsto n_{+}/9$, $n_{-} \mapsto 9n_{-}$). Under the spectrum condition, Borchers' theorem (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-kuckert-modular-pct-spin-statistics-and-borchers-theorem}(ii)) gives that the modular group of every wedge algebra (with the vacuum cyclic and separating) acts on the translations as the wedge's boosts at rapidity $-2\pi t$ and its modular conjugation as $j_{W}$, for interacting nets as well.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Turned wedges; proved.)} Independently of signs: for $B_{\pi/2} = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{2}$, the reflection versor of the quarter-turned wedge, $(\pm B_{\pi/2}\cdot\pm B)^{2} = -1$, so the two reflections compose to a rotor representing the half turn whose square is the rotation by $2\pi$ in the spin group. For the wedge $W_{\theta}$ turned by $\theta$ in the plane $\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}$, $B_{\theta} = \gamma_{0}(\cos\theta\,\gamma_{1} + \sin\theta\,\gamma_{2})$ and $B_{\theta}B = \cos\theta + \sin\theta\,\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}$, the spin rotor of the turn by $2\theta$; $\theta \mapsto B_{\theta}B$ runs from $1$ to $-1$ on $[0, \pi]$, $W_{\pi} = W'$ and $B_{\pi} = -B$. As maps $\mathrm{Ad}(B_{\pi}) = \mathrm{Ad}(B)$; the sign $B_{\pi} = -B$ is the lift by continuity along $\theta$, and along that lift the product of the reflection versors of $W'$ and $W$ is the rotation by $2\pi$ of the spin group, $-1$ on spinor values and $(-1)^{2s}$ on spin-$s$ values.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The twist with the unit $I_{4}$; proved, the standard Klein-twist identity with $i$ written as $I_{4}$.)} For an even involution $k$ commuting with $I_{4}$, $V = (1 + I_{4}k)(1 + I_{4})^{-1}$ satisfies $VV^{*} = 1$, $Vk = kV$, $V^{2} = k$, and a conjugate-linear $J$ reversing $I_{4}$ and fixing $k$ has $JV^{*}J = V$, so $VJV^{*}J = k$.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Spin-statistics; imported, conditional.)} If the spectrum condition holds and the modular conjugation of the wedge algebra of the observables acts on the local algebras as $j_{W}$ (modular P1CT symmetry), with covering-group covariance, the spectrum condition, a unique vacuum, dimension at least $1 + 2$ and a compact group of internal symmetries, then for every covariant normal field the rotation by $2\pi$ equals the Bose-Fermi grading, $R(2\pi) = J_{W'}J_{W} = VJV^{*}J = k$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-kuckert-modular-pct-spin-statistics-and-borchers-theorem}(i), \cite{Kuckert1995}, Corollaries 3.2 and 3.5; there twisted duality is derived, from \cite{DoplicherRoberts1990}, not assumed); (iii) is the geometric step and (iv) the algebraic step in the spacetime algebra. Modular covariance (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-free-field-spin-statistics-and-guido-longo-theorem}(iii)) implies the premise.
\item[(vi)] \emph{(What remains; argued.)} The spectrum condition, a hypothesis of the theorem, gives by (ii) the action of the modular objects on translations; (N$_{+}$) is posed for quasi-free states of a CAR mode algebra (\claimref{synthesis.positive-null-energy-gives-r-premises}) and does not supply the spectrum condition of an interacting net. Nothing in the store gives the action of the modular conjugations on the local algebras, which is the remaining premise for interacting fields; (HS) and (HD) do not bear on it. Electric charge is not localisable in spacelike cones, so for the charged fields of QED the conclusion needs more than this premise.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.wedge-reflections-compose-to-t.technical:
The geometric side of the modular route to spin and statistics has a short form in the spacetime algebra. The reflection of a wedge, which reverses time and the wedge's spatial direction, is conjugation by the wedge's own boost bivector $B$; by the stored dual-plane result it is the PT inversion after the half modular period on values. The reflections of a wedge and of its quarter-turned copy compose, whatever signs the versors carry, to a rotor whose square is $-1$, the rotation by $2\pi$ in the spin group; along the turned wedges the product is $\cos\theta + \sin\theta\,\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}$, whose lift by continuity reaches $-1$ at the causal complement. With the unit $I_{4}$ the Klein twist $V = (1 + I_{4}k)/(1 + I_{4})$ squares to the grading $k$. These are the two steps of Kuckert's theorem (standard): if each wedge's modular conjugation acts on the local algebras as the wedge's reflection, a premise weaker than modular covariance, then the rotation by $2\pi$ is the grading for interacting fields.

The spectrum condition, a hypothesis of that theorem, gives through Borchers' theorem the action of the modular objects on translations; the reflection reverses the edge's null translations and the boosts dilate them. Nothing in the store gives their action on the local algebras, which is what remains; the null ground-state premise of the horizons is posed for free (quasi-free) states and does not supply the spectrum condition of an interacting net. It does not reach electric charge, which the Gauss law keeps out of spacelike cones.
synthesis.wedge-reflections-compose-to-t.lay: One way to explain why matter particles obey the exclusion rule and force particles do not uses a natural flow of the vacuum restricted to a wedge-shaped region of spacetime. In the series' algebra, the mirror image of such a wedge is a single algebraic element, the wedge's own boost plane, and mirroring twice in wedges turned by half a turn gives a full turn, which for a spin-one-half value is a sign change. If the vacuum's natural mirror operation matches the geometric mirror on every region, the spin rule follows for interacting particles. Positive energy gives that match for shifts along light rays, not for every region, and nothing in the series gives it for regions, so that match remains an assumption.

proofs.main:
\emph{Setting.} $\Cl(1,3)$ with $\gamma_{0}^{2} = 1$, $\gamma_{i}^{2} = -1$, $I_{4} = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$, $I_{4}^{2} = -1$, $\tilde I_{4} = I_{4}$. For a versor $V$ with $V\tilde V$ a nonzero scalar, $V^{-1} = \tilde V/(V\tilde V)$ and $\mathrm{Ad}(V)x = VxV^{-1}$ preserves $Q$. The wedge is $W = \{x^{1} > |x^{0}|\}$, $B = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}$, $D = I_{4}B$.

\emph{(i).} $B^{2} = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1} = -\gamma_{0}^{2}\gamma_{1}^{2} = 1$ and $\tilde B = -B$, so $B\tilde B = -1$ and $B^{-1} = B$: $B$ is a versor of the full spin group outside the identity component. $B$ anticommutes with $\gamma_{0}$ and $\gamma_{1}$ and commutes with $\gamma_{2}$, $\gamma_{3}$, so $\mathrm{Ad}(B)$ negates $x^{0}$, $x^{1}$ and fixes $x^{2}$, $x^{3}$: it is $j_{W}$, and it maps $W$ to $\{x^{1} < -|x^{0}|\}$, the causal complement $W'$. Next $D = I_{4}\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1} = \gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$ (moving $\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}$ through), $D^{2} = -1$, so $\mathrm{Ad}(D)$ is the turn by $\pi$ in the plane $\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}$, and $\mathrm{Ad}(I_{4})x = -x$ for every vector since $I_{4}$ anticommutes with vectors. As $I_{4}D = I_{4}^{2}B = -B$, $\mathrm{Ad}(B) = \mathrm{Ad}(I_{4}D) = \mathrm{Ad}(I_{4}) \circ \mathrm{Ad}(D)$. That the turn by $\pi$ in the dual plane is the boost continued over half a modular period, differing from it by $x \mapsto -x$ on vectors, is \claimref{synthesis.modular-period-on-values-is-the-dual-plane-turn}(ii), cited, not re-proved. The Bisognano-Wichmann conjugation of a Wightman field is CPT composed with the turn by $\pi$ about the boost axis, acting on spacetime as $j_{W}$ (Fact \claimref{angle.imported-theorems-deliver-their-hypotheses}); (i) gives its geometric part as PT after the dual-plane turn. The script checks every identity and the action on three vectors.

\emph{(ii).} The geometric part is proved here and the modular action is imported. $Bn_{\pm} = \mp n_{\pm}$ with $n_{\pm} = \pm\gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1}$, so $\mathrm{Ad}(B)n_{\pm} = -n_{\pm}$; $\gamma_{2}$, $\gamma_{3}$ are fixed. For the boost rotor $R = \cosh(\eta/2) + B\sinh(\eta/2)$, $R n_{\pm}\tilde R = R^{2}n_{\pm} = e^{\mp\eta}n_{\pm}$, checked exactly at $R = (5 + 4B)/3$ ($R\tilde R = 1$, $e^{\eta} = 9$), and $R$ maps a point of $W$ into $W$. The translations by $a n_{+}$ and $a n_{-}$, $a \ge 0$, map $W$ into itself ($x^{1} + a > |x^{0} \pm a|$ when $x^{1} > |x^{0}|$). Under the spectrum condition (the generators of the future null translations are positive) and if the vacuum is cyclic and separating for the wedge algebra $M$, Borchers' theorem \cite{Borchers1992} (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-kuckert-modular-pct-spin-statistics-and-borchers-theorem}(ii); its modular-group form also in Fact \claimref{angle.imported-theorems-deliver-their-hypotheses}) gives $\Delta^{I_{4}t}U(a)\Delta^{-I_{4}t} = U(e^{-2\pi t}a)$ and $JU(a)J = U(-a)$ (the Hilbert space's scalars read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$, the unit of (iv), as the Fact now states it) on each half-sided translation group; the transverse translations map $M$ onto itself and fix the vacuum, so they commute with $\Delta$ and $J$. Hence the modular objects act on all translations as the boost at rapidity $-2\pi t$ and as $j_{W}$, which is the geometric action of (i) and (ii); nothing in the argument uses free fields. The spectrum condition of the interacting net is a hypothesis here (Kuckert's Assumption I); the store's (N$_{+}$) is posed for quasi-free states of a CAR mode algebra on horizon generators (\claimref{synthesis.positive-null-energy-gives-r-premises}) and does not supply it. The conjugation half of Borchers' theorem is cited from memory.

\emph{(iii).} Let $R_{\theta} = a + b\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}$ with $a^{2} + b^{2} = n$; $R_{\theta}\tilde R_{\theta} = n$ and $\mathrm{Ad}(R_{\theta})$ turns $\gamma_{1}$ toward $\gamma_{2}$ by $\theta$ with $\cos\theta = (a^{2} - b^{2})/n$, $\sin\theta = 2ab/n$. Since $\gamma_{0}$ commutes with $\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}$, $B_{\theta} = R_{\theta}B\tilde R_{\theta}/n = \gamma_{0}(\cos\theta\,\gamma_{1} + \sin\theta\,\gamma_{2})$, the boost bivector of $W_{\theta} = \mathrm{Ad}(R_{\theta})W$, and $B_{\theta}B = -\gamma_{0}^{2}(\cos\theta\,\gamma_{1} + \sin\theta\,\gamma_{2})\gamma_{1} = \cos\theta + \sin\theta\,\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2} = R_{\theta}^{2}/n$, the spin rotor whose $\mathrm{Ad}$ is the turn by $2\theta$ (checked at five Pythagorean half-angles with the double-angle action on $\gamma_{1}$). At $\theta = \pi$, $R_{\pi} = \gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}$, $B_{\pi} = -B$, $W_{\pi} = W'$ and $B_{\pi}B = -1$; at $\theta = 0$ the product is $1$. The path $\theta \mapsto \cos\theta + \sin\theta\,\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}$, $\theta \in [0, \pi]$, is the lift starting at $1$ of the loop of turns by $2\theta$, a closed loop of rotations, and it ends at $-1$: the rotation by $2\pi$ of the spin group, $-1$ on spinor values and $(-1)^{2s}$ on spin-$s$ values. As maps $\mathrm{Ad}(B_{\pi}) = \mathrm{Ad}(-B) = \mathrm{Ad}(B)$, so the sign at $\theta = \pi$ is fixed only by the continuity of the lift. A form that does not depend on any choice of sign: $B_{\pi/2} = \gamma_{0}\gamma_{2}$ and $(\epsilon_{1}B_{\pi/2}\,\epsilon_{2}B)^{2} = (\gamma_{0}\gamma_{2}\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1})^{2} = (\gamma_{2}\gamma_{1})^{2} = -1$ for $\epsilon_{1}, \epsilon_{2} = \pm 1$, so the reflections of $W$ and of its quarter-turned copy compose to a rotor of the half turn whose square is the rotation by $2\pi$ in the spin group (checked for all four sign choices, with $\mathrm{Ad}$ of the product negating $\gamma_{1}$). In Kuckert's theorem the sign that matters is carried at the field level by the twist (iv). In Kuckert's notation $R(\varphi) = J_{\varphi/2}J_{W}$ \cite{Kuckert1995} (Corollary 3.2; Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-kuckert-modular-pct-spin-statistics-and-borchers-theorem}(i)), the product of the conjugations of the turned wedge and of $W$; (iii) is its geometric content: the product of the reflections is the lift of the rotation by $\varphi$, continuous in $\varphi$ and $-1$ at $\varphi = 2\pi$.

\emph{(iv).} This is the standard Klein-twist identity of the field net with $i$ written as $I_{4}$; the script represents the grading by even involutions of $\Cl(1,3)$ commuting with $I_{4}$ and the conjugate-linear $J$ by the reversal of $I_{4}$. $I_{4}$ is central in the even subalgebra, so a real span of $1$, $I_{4}$, $k$, $I_{4}k$ is commutative. With $k^{2} = 1$: $(1 + I_{4}k)^{2} = 1 + 2I_{4}k + I_{4}^{2}k^{2} = 2I_{4}k$ and $(1 + I_{4})^{2} = 2I_{4}$, so $V^{2} = k$; $(1 + I_{4})^{-1} = (1 - I_{4})/2$. The adjoint reverses the unit and fixes $k$: $V^{*} = (1 - I_{4}k)(1 - I_{4})^{-1}$, and $VV^{*} = (1 - I_{4}^{2}k^{2})/(1 - I_{4}^{2}) = 1$. A conjugate-linear $J$ reverses $I_{4}$ again and fixes $k$, so $JV^{*}J = V$ and $VJV^{*}J = V^{2} = k$. The script checks these for three even involutions $k$ commuting with $I_{4}$ and that $V \ne k$. This is the step $R(2\pi) = J_{\pi}J_{\mathcal{F}} = VJ_{\mathcal{F}}V^{*}J_{\mathcal{F}} = V^{2} = k$ of \cite{Kuckert1995} (Corollary 3.5), where $J_{\pi} = VJ_{\mathcal{F}}V^{*}$ comes from twisted duality, which Kuckert derives (from \cite{DoplicherRoberts1990}) rather than assumes, and $VJ_{\mathcal{F}} = J_{\mathcal{F}}V^{*}$; with the field theory's unit $I_{4}$ in place of $i$.

\emph{(v).} Imported: under Kuckert's Assumptions I to III (covering-group covariance with the spectrum condition, a unique cyclic vacuum, irreducibility, separability; modular P1CT symmetry $J_{W}\mathcal{A}(O)J_{W} = \mathcal{A}(j_{W}O)$ for double cones; a compact group of internal symmetries) in dimension $1 + s$, $s \ge 2$, every covariant normal field has $R(2\pi) = k$ \cite{Kuckert1995}; the paper notes that the modular groups need not act geometrically, so the premise is weaker than modular covariance, which implies it (Bisognano and Wichmann for Wightman fields \cite{BW1976}; Guido and Longo, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-free-field-spin-statistics-and-guido-longo-theorem}(iii)). For the series' free fields the same sign is already fixed by locality with positive norm (\claimref{synthesis.locality-of-the-attached-free-fields-fixes-their-statistics}); the theorem matters for interacting fields.

\emph{(vi).} Argued. The premise has a translation part and an algebra part. The translation part follows by (ii) from the spectrum condition, which is a hypothesis of the theorem and is not supplied by the store for an interacting net: (N$_{+}$) concerns quasi-free states of a CAR mode algebra, and the positive conformal energy result concerns the representation on a given state's GNS space. The algebra part, $J_{W}\mathcal{A}(O)J_{W} = \mathcal{A}(j_{W}O)$ for all double cones, is not implied: Borchers' relations constrain $J_{W}$ only through its commutation with the translations, and the KMS property at period $2\pi$ for the boosts, which (N$_{+}$) gives for quasi-free states, identifies the modular group on the wedge algebra but says nothing about where $J_{W}$ sends the algebras of regions inside $W$ (and \claimref{synthesis.modular-period-on-values-is-the-dual-plane-turn} shows that KMS at $2\pi$ does not fix statistics). Neither (HS), a statement about two-point functions on generators, nor (HD), about the state's occupation profile, bears on it. The field net of the theorem carries charges localisable in double cones or spacelike cones; the electric charge, constrained by the Gauss law, is not localisable there, so the electron's spin-statistics connection beyond perturbation theory needs more than this premise. Transport-absent: the theorem is standard; the reading of the reflection as the PT inversion after the half modular period and the twist with the unit $I_{4}$ re-express it, as the stored modular-period result classifies its own $I_{4}$ reading.

synthesis.window-energy-of-one-generatio.formal:
On a window of $L$ levels $k = 0, \dots, L - 1$ with $n$ channels, let the modes $c_{x,k}$ be tower modes (Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-tower-limit}), $j^{xy}_{m} = \sum_{k}c^{*}_{x,k}c_{y,k+m}$ the pair currents (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.null-plane-photon-data-and-the-pair-currents-of-the-generators}(iv)), $N_{m} = \sum_{x}j^{xx}_{m}$ and $H = \sum_{x,k}(k + \tfrac12)n_{x,k}$. For a tensor $C_{xy,zu}$ with entries in $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ ($J$ the kernel unit of the tower level) and $C_{xy,zu} = C_{zu,xy}$ put
\[
\Phi(C) = \sum_{x,y,z,u}C_{xy,zu}\Bigl(2\sum_{q \ge 1}j^{xy}_{-q}j^{zu}_{q} + j^{xy}_{0}j^{zu}_{0}\Bigr), \quad (K_{C})_{xu} = \sum_{y}C_{xy,yu}, \quad A_{C}(a, b, c, d) = C_{ac,bd} - C_{ad,bc},
\]
and $Q(A) = \sum A(x_{\alpha}, x_{\beta}, x_{\gamma}, x_{\delta})\,c^{*}_{\alpha}c^{*}_{\beta}c_{\gamma}c_{\delta}$, summed over the quadruples of modes $\alpha = (x_{\alpha}, k_{\alpha})$, \dots\ of the window with $k_{\alpha} + k_{\beta} = k_{\gamma} + k_{\delta}$. For a family of matrices $M_{A}$ with trace-dual family $M^{A}$, $C = \sum_{A}M^{A}\otimes M_{A}$ gives $\Phi(C) = 2\sum_{q \ge 1}J(M^{A})_{-q}J(M_{A})_{q} + J(M^{A})_{0}J(M_{A})_{0}$, $J(M)_{m} = \sum M_{xy}j^{xy}_{m}$, and the Sugawara energy of the family is $H_{\mathfrak{f}} = \Phi(C)/(2 + \lambda_{\mathfrak{f}})$ with $\sum_{A}[M^{A}, [M_{A}, X]] = \lambda_{\mathfrak{f}}X$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Window quadratic forms.)} On every window, exactly in the algebra,
\[
\Phi(C) = \sum_{x,u}(K_{C})_{xu}\sum_{l}(2l + 1)\,c^{*}_{x,l}c_{u,l} - \tfrac12 Q(A_{C}) .
\]
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The level-one $\uu(n)$ form.)} For $C = \sum_{x,y}E_{xy}\otimes E_{yx} + 1\otimes 1$, $K_{C} = (n + 1)1$ and $A_{C} = 0$, so on every window
\[
(n + 1)H = \sum_{q \ge 1}\Bigl(\sum_{x,y}j^{yx}_{-q}j^{xy}_{q} + N_{-q}N_{q}\Bigr) + \tfrac12\Bigl(\sum_{x,y}j^{xy}_{0}j^{yx}_{0} + N_{0}^{2}\Bigr),
\]
with no edge correction; for $n = 1$ this is Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exact-window-sugawara-identity-and-luttinger-normal-modes-of-tower-density-waves}(i), and in general $H = H_{\su(n)} + H_{N}$ ($\lambda_{\su(n)} = 2n$, $H_{N} = \Phi(\tfrac1n 1\otimes 1)/2$).
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The $\so(10)$ form for one generation.)} Take for the $n = 16$ channels of a light ray of one generation the even-degree states of the slot module $\Lambda^{\bullet}\C^{5}$ (Theorems \claimref{synthesis.slot-module-light-ray-arrays-are-weyl-components}(ii), \claimref{synthesis.cpt-closure-forces-slot-module-and-chirality}) and for the family the $45$ bilinears $a^{*}_{a}a_{b} - \tfrac12\delta_{ab}$, $a^{*}_{a}a^{*}_{b}$, $a_{a}a_{b}$ of the five modes, which preserve this half (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.spin10-clause-content-is-the-neutral-singlet-choice}). Then $K_{C} = \tfrac{45}{16}1$, $A_{C} = -\tfrac{3}{16}(\delta_{ac}\delta_{bd} - \delta_{ad}\delta_{bc})$ and $\lambda_{\so(10)} = 4$ ($\so(10)$ at level $4$: $\lambda = 2h/k$ with $h = 8$; $c = 15$), so on every window and every vector
\[
H = H_{\so(10)} + H_{N}, \qquad H_{\so(10)} = \tfrac16\Phi(C_{\so(10)}), \quad H_{N} = \tfrac{1}{32}\Phi(1\otimes 1);
\]
equivalently $H_{\su(16)} = H_{\so(10)}$. The two sides have central values $2\cdot 45/6 = 15 = 2\cdot 255/34$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(What it needs.)} The number-conserving part $\uu(5)$ alone does not give this (its $A_{C}$ is not a multiple of $\delta_{ac}\delta_{bd} - \delta_{ad}\delta_{bc}$): the pair bilinears are needed. For any subfamily $\mathfrak{f}_{1}, \dots, \mathfrak{f}_{r}$ of commuting, trace-orthogonal subalgebras of this $\so(10)$, among them the gauge algebra $\su(3) \oplus \su(2) \oplus \uu(1)$ acting through $\sum X_{ab}a^{*}_{a}a_{b}$, $H - H_{N} - \sum_{i}H_{\mathfrak{f}_{i}} = H_{\so(10)} - \sum_{i}H_{\mathfrak{f}_{i}}$ exactly: the part of the channels' energy not carried by the gauge factors and the number current is a function of the $\so(10)$ currents alone, on every window.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Reading.} The energy of one generation's sixteen channels along a light ray is, on every finite window and with no edge term, the Sugawara energy of the $\so(10)$ of the five internal modes plus that of the fermion number: the $\so(10)$ currents carry all of the energy that the full set of $\uu(16)$ pair currents carries apart from the number current, a finite exact form of a conformal embedding.
synthesis.window-energy-of-one-generatio.technical: For any symmetric tensor $C$ of pair-current coefficients, the window operator $\Phi(C) = \sum C(2\sum_{q\ge1}j_{-q}j_{q} + j_{0}j_{0})$ equals a one-body term with weights $2l + 1$ and coefficient matrix $K_{C} = \sum_{y}C_{xy,yu}$, minus half a level-conserving quartic whose coefficients are the antisymmetrised tensor $A_{C}(a,b,c,d) = C_{ac,bd} - C_{ad,bc}$; this holds exactly on every finite window, by the antisymmetrisation argument of the stored one-channel identity. For the $\uu(n)$ Casimir plus the number term, $A = 0$ and $K = (n + 1)1$: the energy with half-integer weights is the level-one $\uu(n)$ Sugawara form on every window. For one generation's sixteen channels and the $\so(10)$ of all bilinears of the five internal modes, $K = \tfrac{45}{16}$ and $A_{\so(10)} = -3A_{N}$, so the $\so(10)$ Sugawara energy (coefficient $\tfrac16$, adjoint Casimir $4$) plus the number term equals the channels' energy exactly: the $\su(16)$ Sugawara energy equals the $\so(10)$ one on every window. The number-conserving $\uu(5)$ alone fails. Hence the remainder of the energy after the gauge factors and the number current is built from the $\so(10)$ currents alone.
synthesis.window-energy-of-one-generatio.lay: On a light ray at a horizon, one generation of matter supplies sixteen fermion channels. Their energy along the ray can be written as a sum of squares of currents built from pairs of fermions. The result is that, on any finite stretch of the ray and exactly, a much smaller set of currents suffices: those of the forty-five-dimensional symmetry of the five internal modes that build a generation, together with the total fermion number. This symmetry contains the Standard Model forces; here it is a symmetry of the currents along the light ray, not a unified gauge symmetry. Whatever energy the forces do not account for is still expressed through it.

proofs.main:
\emph{Conventions.} The modes of distinct channels and levels are distinct tower planes, $\{c_{\alpha}, c^{*}_{\beta}\} = \delta_{\alpha\beta}$, all other anticommutators zero (Fact \claimref{field-theory.imported-tower-limit}); the check realises them by Jordan-Wigner signs and verifies the Clifford relations of the planes $e = c^{*} + c$, $f = c^{*} - c$. $J$ commutes with every mode. The pair currents are those of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.null-plane-photon-data-and-the-pair-currents-of-the-generators}(iv), $j^{xy}_{-q} = \sum_{k}c^{*}_{x,k+q}c_{y,k}$ for $q \ge 1$.

\emph{(i)} For $q \ge 0$, moving $c_{y,k}$ past $c^{*}_{z,k'}$,
\[
j^{xy}_{-q}j^{zu}_{q} = \delta_{yz}\sum_{k}c^{*}_{x,k+q}c_{u,k+q} - \sum_{k,k'}c^{*}_{x,k+q}c^{*}_{z,k'}c_{y,k}c_{u,k'+q},
\]
sums over the levels in the window. With the weights $2$ for $q \ge 1$ and $1$ for $q = 0$, the first terms give $\sum_{x,u}(K_{C})_{xu}\sum_{l}(2l + 1)c^{*}_{x,l}c_{u,l}$, since a level $l$ is reached from $q = 1, \dots, l$ with weight $2$ and from $q = 0$ with weight $1$. Label a quartic term $c^{*}_{\alpha}c^{*}_{\beta}c_{\gamma}c_{\delta}$ by four modes: here $\alpha = (x, k + q)$, $\beta = (z, k')$, $\gamma = (y, k)$, $\delta = (u, k' + q)$, with coefficient $W(\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta) = C_{x_{\alpha}x_{\gamma}, x_{\beta}x_{\delta}}$, and each quadruple with $k_{\alpha} + k_{\beta} = k_{\gamma} + k_{\delta}$ and $k_{\alpha} \ge k_{\gamma}$ arises exactly once ($q = k_{\alpha} - k_{\gamma}$). So the quartic part of $\Phi(C)$ is $-(2X + D)$, $X$ the sum of $W\,c^{*}_{\alpha}c^{*}_{\beta}c_{\gamma}c_{\delta}$ over $k_{\alpha} > k_{\gamma}$ and $D$ over $k_{\alpha} = k_{\gamma}$. The relabelling $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta) \mapsto (\beta, \alpha, \delta, \gamma)$ maps the quadruples with $k_{\alpha} < k_{\gamma}$ (then $k_{\beta} > k_{\delta}$) onto those with $k_{\alpha} > k_{\gamma}$, leaves the product unchanged (two transpositions), and leaves $W$ unchanged because $C_{x_{\beta}x_{\delta}, x_{\alpha}x_{\gamma}} = C_{x_{\alpha}x_{\gamma}, x_{\beta}x_{\delta}}$. Hence $2X + D = S$, the sum of $W\,c^{*}_{\alpha}c^{*}_{\beta}c_{\gamma}c_{\delta}$ over all level-conserving quadruples. Exchanging the names $\gamma$ and $\delta$ preserves that index set and reverses $c_{\gamma}c_{\delta}$, so $S = \tfrac12\sum(W(\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta) - W(\alpha, \beta, \delta, \gamma))c^{*}_{\alpha}c^{*}_{\beta}c_{\gamma}c_{\delta} = \tfrac12 Q(A_{C})$, which gives (i); this is the antisymmetrisation argument of the proof of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.exact-window-sugawara-identity-and-luttinger-normal-modes-of-tower-density-waves}(i), with the channel tensor carried along. The check verifies (i) on every basis state for three generic symmetric tensors with $A_{C} \ne 0$ ($(n, L) = (2, 3), (2, 2), (3, 2)$). For $C = \sum_{A}M^{A}\otimes M_{A}$ the tensor is symmetric because the Casimir element is ($\sum_{A}M^{A}\otimes M_{A} = \sum_{A}M_{A}\otimes M^{A}$, the trace-dual of the trace-dual being the original basis), and $\Phi(C)$ is the stated bilinear in the currents by linearity.

\emph{(ii)} $C_{xy,zu} = \delta_{yz}\delta_{xu} + \delta_{xy}\delta_{zu}$ is symmetric, $(K_{C})_{xu} = \sum_{y}(\delta_{yy}\delta_{xu} + \delta_{xy}\delta_{yu}) = (n + 1)\delta_{xu}$, and $A_{C}(a, b, c, d) = \delta_{cb}\delta_{ad} + \delta_{ac}\delta_{bd} - \delta_{db}\delta_{ac} - \delta_{ad}\delta_{bc} = 0$. So $\Phi(C) = 2(n + 1)H$, and since $\Phi(C)$ is $2\sum_{q\ge1}(\sum_{x,y}j^{yx}_{-q}j^{xy}_{q} + N_{-q}N_{q}) + \sum_{x,y}j^{xy}_{0}j^{yx}_{0} + N_{0}^{2}$ (relabel $x \leftrightarrow y$ in the first term) the display follows. For $n = 1$ both bilinears are the stored $\rho_{q}^{*}\rho_{q}$ and $N_{0}^{2} = \hat N^{2}$, so $4H = 4T + 2\hat N^{2}$, that is $\sum_{j}(j + \tfrac12)n_{j} = T + \tfrac12\hat N^{2}$, the stored identity $T = \sum_{j}j\,n_{j} - \tfrac12\hat N(\hat N - 1)$. Since $\sum_{x,y}E_{xy}\otimes E_{yx} + 1\otimes 1 = C_{\su(n)} + \tfrac{n + 1}{n}1\otimes 1$ ($C_{\su(n)}$ the Casimir tensor of the trace-orthogonal complement of $1$) and $\sum_{x,y}[E_{yx}, [E_{xy}, X]] = 2nX - 2\operatorname{tr}(X)1$ gives $\lambda_{\su(n)} = 2n$, $H = \Phi(C_{\su(n)})/(2n + 2) + \Phi(1\otimes 1)/(2n) = H_{\su(n)} + H_{N}$ with $H_{N} = \tfrac12\Phi(\tfrac1n 1\otimes 1)$. The check verifies (ii) on every basis state for $(n, L) = (1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 3)$ and on three states of sixteen channels, and that the coefficient $n$ in place of $n + 1$ fails.

\emph{(iii)} The sixteen channels of a light ray and generation are the Weyl components valued in the particle half (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.slot-module-light-ray-arrays-are-weyl-components}(ii)). The pair bilinears change the mode number by $\pm 2$ and preserve the even half (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.spin10-clause-content-is-the-neutral-singlet-choice}); the diagonal generators $a^{*}_{a}a_{a} - \tfrac12$ have trace $8 - 8 = 0$ there, the others are off-diagonal. With the trace-dual basis computed exactly, the check finds: $\sum_{A}M^{A}M_{A} = \tfrac{45}{16}1$ (the trace of the left side is $\dim = 45$, and it is scalar), $A_{C} = -\tfrac{3}{16}\Delta$ with $\Delta(a,b,c,d) = \delta_{ac}\delta_{bd} - \delta_{ad}\delta_{bc}$ on all $16^{4}$ index quadruples, and $\lambda_{\so(10)} = 4$. (The reason $A_{C}$ is a multiple of $\Delta$: $A_{C}$ is the matrix of the operator $\sum_{A}M^{A}\otimes M_{A}$ on $16\otimes 16$ restricted to the antisymmetric part $\Lambda^{2}$, where it equals $\tfrac12$ of the Casimir of $\Lambda^{2}$ minus those of the two factors, and $\Lambda^{2}$ of the half-spinor of $\so(10)$ is irreducible, of dimension $120$; this is argued, the multiple is computed.) For $1\otimes 1/16$, $K = \tfrac1{16}1$ and $A = \tfrac{1}{16}\Delta$. By (i),
\[
H_{\so(10)} = \tfrac16\Bigl(\tfrac{45}{8}H + \tfrac{3}{32}Q(\Delta)\Bigr) = \tfrac{15}{16}H + \tfrac{1}{64}Q(\Delta), \qquad H_{N} = \tfrac12\Bigl(\tfrac18 H - \tfrac{1}{32}Q(\Delta)\Bigr) = \tfrac{1}{16}H - \tfrac{1}{64}Q(\Delta),
\]
using $\sum_{l}(2l + 1)n_{x,l} = 2\sum_{l}(l + \tfrac12)n_{x,l}$, and the sum is $H$. By (ii) with $n = 16$, $H - H_{N} = H_{\su(16)}$. The central values $2\dim/(2 + \lambda)$ are $90/6 = 15$ and $510/34 = 15$. The check also verifies $H = H_{\so(10)} + H_{N}$ directly, by applying the current bilinears, on three arbitrary states of a two-level window and on the sea, a state of charge $+1$, one of charge $-1$ and a particle-hole state of a six-level window.

\emph{(iv)} For the $25$ number-conserving generators alone the check finds that $A_{C}$ has entries off the support of $\Delta$, so it is not a multiple of $\Delta$ and (i) does not reduce their Sugawara energy to a multiple of $H$ plus a multiple of $Q(\Delta)$. For $X$ traceless in $\gl(5)$, $\sum X_{ab}a^{*}_{a}a_{b} = \sum X_{ab}(a^{*}_{a}a_{b} - \tfrac12\delta_{ab})$ lies in the span of the $45$ generators, so the gauge algebra of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.cpt-closure-forces-slot-module-and-chirality} lies in this $\so(10)$; the displayed equality is (iii) with $\sum_{i}H_{\mathfrak{f}_{i}}$ subtracted from both sides.
